# Installation

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/getting-started.md

Hinoki is pre-alpha and installs from a source checkout. You need:

- Python 3.12 or newer
- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) 0.9 or newer
- a stable Rust toolchain from [rustup](https://rustup.rs/)

## Install from source

```sh
git clone https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki
cd hinoki
uv sync --locked
uv run hinoki version
```

`uv sync --locked` builds the Rust extension and installs the development tools.
The last command confirms the installation:

```text
hinoki 0.0.1
```

!!! warning "Not on PyPI yet"
    Hinoki's package name is `hinoki-api` and it is not published yet. The
    [`hinoki` name on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/hinoki/) belongs to an
    unrelated legacy package: do not install it. A project created with
    `hinoki new` points `uv` at this checkout in `pyproject.toml`
    (`[tool.uv.sources]`), so `uv sync` never fetches either package by name.

Next: the [Quick start](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md) creates and serves a project.

# Quick start

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md

Create a project, run its tests and serve it. Everything runs locally; the
database is a SQLite file.

## Create a project

From the Hinoki checkout:

```sh
uv run hinoki new
```

`hinoki new` asks only what it needs. Give these answers and keep the other
defaults:

| Prompt | Default | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project name | | `notes` |
| Parent directory | `.` | `..` (beside the checkout) |
| Database | `none` | `sqlite` |
| Server | `kiso` | `kiso` |
| Agent instructions and MCP config? | yes | yes |
| Agent skills? | no | no |
| Initialize a git repository? | yes | yes |
| Install dependencies (uv sync)? | yes | yes |
| Create an app now? | yes | yes |
| App name | `core` | `entries` |

It writes the project and the `entries` app, runs `git init` and `uv sync`, and
prints the next commands. The files that matter:

```text
notes/
├── hinoki.toml        manifest: application, routes and the entries app
├── notes/
│   ├── main.py        the application
│   ├── api.py         GET /health
│   ├── routes.py      routes = [health]
│   ├── settings.py    typed settings, NOTES_* variables
│   ├── rules.py       architecture rules
│   └── apps/
│       └── entries/   starter app registered in hinoki.toml
│           ├── api.py
│           ├── routes.py
│           ├── models.py
│           └── migrations/
├── tests/             pytest suite
└── AGENTS.md          agent instructions
```

The generated project serves `/health`. The `entries` app starts with an empty
route list and space for its models and migrations. Choosing no at **Create an
app now?** creates just the project. [Add another app](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md#add-another-app) shows
how to add one later.

!!! tip "Scripts and CI"
    `uv run hinoki new notes --dir .. --no-input --database sqlite --git --install --app entries`
    gives the same answers without prompts. Plain `--no-input` uses the defaults
    instead: no database, no `git init`, no `uv sync` and no app. All options are
    in [`hinoki new`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md).

## Check and test it

```sh
cd ../notes
uv run hinoki check
uv run pytest
```

`hinoki check` runs the project's rules (the eight listed in `notes/rules.py`)
and prints one line for each; a violation names the file, the line and a fix.
The test calls `/health` in process and needs no database. Run both again after
every change, as `AGENTS.md` tells an agent to.

## Serve it

```sh
uv run hinoki dev
```

`hinoki dev` serves on `http://127.0.0.1:8000` and reloads when a file changes. In another terminal:

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/health
```

```text
{"status":"ok"}
```

At startup `hinoki dev` logs a warning that `allowed_hosts is '*'`: the
application answers to any `Host` header. It is harmless on your machine. To
name the hosts you serve, and silence it, add
`NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=127.0.0.1,localhost` to `.env`; see
[`allowed_hosts`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md#allowed_hosts).

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs` for the generated OpenAPI UI, or run
`uv run hinoki routes` to inspect the route map that `Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, ...)`
loaded automatically from `notes/routes.py` (`[project] routes` in `hinoki.toml`):

```sh
uv run hinoki routes
```

```text
GET     /health  public                   notes.api.health
```

## What the manifest does

`hinoki.toml` registers the application, the project's route map (`[project] routes`),
the rules it runs and each app's persistence and dependencies. `notes/main.py`
loads `[project] routes` automatically, while `notes/routes.py` decides which
apps are mounted over HTTP:

```toml
[project]
application = "notes.main:app"
routes = "notes.routes:routes"
rules = ["notes.rules:project_rules"]
```

`notes/main.py` declares the application:

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki

from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

app = Hinoki(
    settings=ProjectSettings,  # NOTES_* variables and .env
    title="Notes",
    openapi_url="/openapi.json",
    docs_url="/docs",
)  # routes, rules and middleware come from hinoki.toml
```

`Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, ...)` reads `hinoki.toml` automatically,
loading `notes/routes.py` (`[project] routes`) and `rules`, so `main.py` stays
short. Commands read the same manifest, so inside the project they need no
module paths.

## Where the database is configured

Answering `sqlite` added one field to `notes/settings.py`:

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env"):
    database: settings.DatabaseSettings
```

With no value set, it is the SQLite file `.hinoki/local.sqlite3`. Each field
of `DatabaseSettings` is a `NOTES_DATABASE__<FIELD>` variable (two underscores
between the group and the field), read from the environment or from `.env` in
the project directory. `uv run hinoki settings` lists every variable and where
its value came from. To use another file:

```sh
# .env
NOTES_DATABASE__URL=sqlite://./.hinoki/notes.sqlite3
```

[Configure a database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md) covers PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, and
connection fields instead of a URL. The project has no models yet; add them in
the app, as [the next section](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md#your-first-app) and the
[tutorial](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/index.md) show.

## Your first app

Models live in apps, not in the project package. `hinoki new` created `entries`
when you answered the last question:

```text
notes/apps/entries/
├── api.py         starter for the app’s endpoints
├── routes.py      empty app route list
├── models.py      starter for the app’s models
└── migrations/    migration package
```

It is registered in `hinoki.toml`:

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "entries"
models = "notes.apps.entries.models"
migrations = "notes.apps.entries.migrations"
requires = []
```

After adding an endpoint or a group to the app's own route list, mount that list
in the project's route map:

```python
# notes/routes.py
from hinoki import Includable, Mount

from notes.api import health
from notes.apps.entries.routes import routes as entries_routes

routes: list[Includable] = [health, Mount("/entries", entries_routes)]
```

Endpoints inside the app declare paths relative to the `/entries` prefix.

App names are lower-case letters and digits with single underscores between words
(for example `api_v1`), starting with a letter. Define the
app's models in `notes/apps/entries/models.py`, then
`uv run hinoki migrations plan entries`; [9. Projects and apps](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/8-projects.md)
walks through it.

### Add another app

If you answered no, or want a second app, create it from the project:

```sh
uv run hinoki app create billing
```

## Next

- [Tutorial](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/index.md): build an API layer by layer.
- [9. Projects and apps](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/8-projects.md): add an app with its own
  models and migrations to this project.
- [Notes example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/tree/main/examples/notes):
  a separate, complete project with a model, schemas and generated CRUD routes.

# Overview

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/index.md

Follow the Tracker, an API where members keep their own tasks, one layer per
chapter. Each chapter walks through files of the checked-in example in
[`examples/tracker`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/tree/main/examples/tracker)
and runs its commands, so every step runs as shown. Chapter 9 then adds an app
to your own project.

| Chapter | It covers | You learn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1. Models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/1-models.md) | tables, a foreign key, an index, a default order | models and migrations |
| [2. Schemas](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/2-schemas.md) | what clients send and receive | strict validation, derived schemas |
| [3. Endpoints](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/4-endpoints.md) | the HTTP layer and explicit app mounts | access, generated CRUD with filters, transactions, declared errors |
| [4. Implement a business rule](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/3-operations.md) | `complete_task(...)` and `delete_task(...)` | why domain rules live in `operations.py` with ownership in SQL |
| [5. Events between apps](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/events.md) | `Created[Task]`, `Updated[Task]` and `activity` | decoupled `in_transaction` handlers and `hinoki events` |
| [6. Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/5-rules.md) | checks that keep the layers apart | `hinoki check` |
| [7. Run and test it](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/6-run.md) | the manifest, settings, a server, tests | `hinoki dev`, the test client |
| [8. Validate input](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/7-validation.md) | normalizers and checks | field and cross-field errors |
| [9. Projects and apps](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/8-projects.md) | an app in your own project | `hinoki app create`, planned migrations |

Chapters 1–7 cover the Tracker. Chapter 8 uses standalone examples, and
chapter 9 continues the project from the [Quick start](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md).

## The Tracker's shape

The Tracker is one project with three apps that depend on each other on
purpose. Each app is a package with its own models, endpoints and migrations:

```text
tracker/
├── main.py, settings.py   the application and its typed settings
├── routes.py              the project route map (GET /health and explicit app mounts)
├── middleware.py          a project-wide middleware
├── rules.py               architecture rules
└── apps/
    ├── members/           Member, the bearer token and the access policy
    ├── tasks/             Task: models, schemas, filters, operations, api
    └── activity/          Activity, written by listening to task events
```

`hinoki.toml` registers the application, its route map, middleware, rules and
apps, while `tracker/routes.py` decides where each exposed app is mounted:

```toml
# examples/tracker/hinoki.toml
[project]
application = "tracker.main:app"
routes = "tracker.routes:routes"
middleware = ["tracker.middleware:middleware"]
rules = ["tracker.rules:policy", "tracker.rules:layers"]

[[apps]]
name = "members"
models = "tracker.apps.members.models"
migrations = "tracker.apps.members.migrations"
requires = []

[[apps]]
name = "tasks"
models = "tracker.apps.tasks.models"
migrations = "tracker.apps.tasks.migrations"
requires = ["members"]

[[apps]]
name = "activity"
models = "tracker.apps.activity.models"
migrations = "tracker.apps.activity.migrations"
events = "tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers"
requires = ["tasks", "members"]
```

Inside the `tasks` app, the layers point one way:

```text
api.py          HTTP: shapes, status codes, access, transactions
   ↓
operations.py   business rules: plain async functions, no HTTP types
   ↓
models.py       tables and relations
```

`activity` reacts to what `tasks` announces, and `tasks` never imports it
([chapter 3](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/3-operations.md) and [chapter 5](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/5-rules.md)).

## Before you start

[Install Hinoki](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/getting-started.md). Chapters 1–6 run in the Tracker's own
directory of the checkout, which is a complete project with its own
`hinoki.toml`:

```sh
cd examples/tracker
```

Commands there take no target: `uv run hinoki check`, `uv run hinoki dev` and
`uv run hinoki migrations apply` read the manifest, as they do in your own
project. They create `examples/tracker/.hinoki/local.sqlite3`, which the
repository ignores.

# 1. Models

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/1-models.md

A model declares a table. A relation is loaded only when you ask for it, never
as a side effect of reading an attribute.

The Tracker keeps one model per app, each in the app's `models.py`. The members
app owns the table of people:

```python
# tracker/apps/members/models.py
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from hinoki import db
from hinoki.orm import Model, field, pk


@db.table("tracker_members")
class Member(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    name: str = field(max_length=80)
    token_hash: str = field(unique=True)  # SHA-256 hex digest, never the token
```

The tasks app belongs to a member through a foreign key:

```python
# tracker/apps/tasks/models.py
from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from hinoki import db
from hinoki.orm import Model, OnDelete, field, foreign_key, pk
from hinoki.utils import utc_now
from tracker.apps.members.models import Member


@db.indexed("owner_id", "created_at")
@db.ordered_by("-created_at", "-id")
@db.table("tracker_tasks")
class Task(Model, label="Task", plural="Tasks"):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    owner_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Member, on_delete=OnDelete.RESTRICT, related_name="tasks"
    )
    title: str = field(max_length=120)
    priority: int = 3
    done: bool = False
    created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now)
    completed_at: datetime | None = None
```

- `pk(...)` declares the primary key; `field(...)` adds column options such as
  `max_length` and `unique`.
- `@db.indexed("owner_id", "created_at")` adds a composite index.
  `@db.ordered_by(...)` sets the order of every query that does not call
  `order_by`.
- `foreign_key(Member, ...)` stores the owner's id. `task.owner` is fetched only
  when a query asks for it. Because `tasks` imports `Member`, its entry in
  `hinoki.toml` says `requires = ["members"]`.
- `@db.table(...)` pins the table name, because a Tracker rule requires it
  ([chapter 5](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/5-rules.md)). Without it, Hinoki derives `<app>_<models>`, as
  [chapter 8](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/8-projects.md) shows.

The third app, `activity`, has an `Activity` model of the same kind: a line per
task change. [Chapter 3](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/3-operations.md) shows how it gets written.

## Apply the migrations

A migration is a SQL file generated from the models and checked in beside them.
Each app has its own `migrations/` directory. Tasks ships one:

```sql
-- tracker/apps/tasks/migrations/0001-create-table-tracker-tasks.sql
-- hinoki migration 0001-create-table-tracker-tasks
-- generated from the models; review it.

-- create table tracker_tasks
CREATE TABLE "tracker_tasks" (
    "id" UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    "owner_id" UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES "tracker_members" ("id") ON DELETE RESTRICT,
    "title" varchar(120) NOT NULL,
    "priority" integer NOT NULL,
    "done" boolean NOT NULL,
    "created_at" timestamptz NOT NULL,
    "completed_at" timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX "ix_tracker_tasks_owner_id_created_at_e46b5006" ON "tracker_tasks" ("owner_id", "created_at");
```

From `examples/tracker`, list and apply them:

```sh
uv run hinoki migrations status
uv run hinoki migrations apply
```

```text
database: sqlite:///…/examples/tracker/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default)
members          pending  0001-create-table-tracker-members
tasks            pending  0001-create-table-tracker-tasks
activity         pending  0001-create-table-tracker-activity
database: sqlite:///…/examples/tracker/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default)
members: 0001-create-table-tracker-members
tasks: 0001-create-table-tracker-tasks
activity: 0001-create-table-tracker-activity
```

Each command first names the database it uses. With no database configured,
that is `.hinoki/local.sqlite3` beside `hinoki.toml`. `apply` runs the apps in
`requires` order, so `tracker_members` exists before the table that references
it. Migrations run only when you call `apply`; an application never migrates at
startup.

When a model changes, `uv run hinoki migrations plan tasks` writes the next
migration of that app. Review its SQL, then apply it.

## Recap

- A model is a typed class; decorators state table facts such as indexes and order.
- Each app owns its models and migrations; `requires` orders them.
- Migrations are reviewed files, applied by an explicit command.
- Relations are never loaded implicitly.

Next: [2. Schemas](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/2-schemas.md).

# 2. Schemas

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/2-schemas.md

A model describes a table; a `Schema` describes what crosses the API. A column
reaches a client only when a schema names it.

```python
# tracker/apps/tasks/schemas.py
from typing import Annotated

from hinoki import Field, Schema, derive

from .models import Task


class TaskIn(Schema):
    """What a client may set. The owner is the caller, never a field."""

    title: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=120)]
    priority: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=5)] = 3


@derive(Task, exclude=("owner_id",))
class TaskOut(Schema):
    """Every column of a task except its owner (derived from the model)."""
```

- `TaskIn` is strict: no coercion, no unknown keys, and every problem is reported
  with its path. Validation runs in Rust before your code does. `priority` is
  optional and, when sent, must be from 1 to 5.
- `TaskOut` takes its fields from `Task`, with the model's types and limits.
  `exclude=("owner_id",)` keeps the owner out. Relations are never derived;
  you name them on purpose.
- The owner is not a field of `TaskIn`, so a client cannot choose it. Server
  values passed to `Task.acreate(data, owner_id=...)` always win, and a schema
  never carries the primary key.
- Every response is a `Schema`, never a model, a dict or a dataclass. The
  `members` app does the same with `MemberOut`, which names `id` and `name`
  and so never sends the token digest.

Schemas also support aliases, computed fields and tagged unions; see
[discriminated unions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-collections.md#discriminated-unions).

## Recap

- Input schemas list what a client may send, nothing more.
- Output schemas can be derived from a model, minus what must stay private.
- Ownership comes from the caller, never from the request body.

Next: [3. Endpoints](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/4-endpoints.md).

# 3. Endpoints

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/4-endpoints.md

The HTTP layer maps requests to operations and results to responses. It holds
no business rule and no SQL.

First, who may call. A bearer token resolves to a `Member` through its SHA-256 digest (the table never holds the token), and the policy
names the permission that every task action requires. The policy lives in the
members app, so every app reuses it:

```python
# tracker/apps/members/security.py
"""Authentication: an opaque bearer token resolved to a ``Member``."""

import hashlib

from hinoki import Access, BearerAuth, Caller, Permission

from .models import Member


def hash_token(token: str) -> str:
    """The SHA-256 hex digest stored instead of the token (high-entropy, so no KDF)."""
    return hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()


class MemberPermission(Permission):
    USE = "tracker:use"


class MemberTokens(BearerAuth[Member]):
    async def resolve_token(self, token: str) -> Caller[Member] | None:
        member = await Member.aget_or_none(token_hash=hash_token(token))
        if member is None:
            return None
        return Caller(
            id=str(member.id), user=member, permissions={MemberPermission.USE}
        )


member_only = Access(auth=MemberTokens(), permissions=[MemberPermission.USE])
```

Next, what a client may ask of the task list. A `FilterSet` declares each query
parameter once; only what it declares is accepted:

```python
# tracker/apps/tasks/filters.py
from datetime import datetime

from hinoki.filters import Eq, FilterSet, In, Range, Search


class TaskFilters(FilterSet):
    done: Eq[bool]
    priority: In[int]
    created_at: Range[datetime]
    completed_at: Eq[datetime | None]
    search = Search("title")
    ordering = ("created_at", "priority", "title")
```

Then the actions. List, retrieve, create and delete are generated from the
model by `@crud`; the one action it cannot know, `complete`, is handwritten in
the same class:

```python
# tracker/apps/tasks/api.py
"""HTTP layer of the tasks app: generated CRUD plus one handwritten action."""

from uuid import UUID

from hinoki import API, Caller, Includable, crud, errors, http
from hinoki.orm import QuerySet
from tracker.apps.members.models import Member
from tracker.apps.members.security import member_only

from . import operations
from .errors import TaskAlreadyDone
from .filters import TaskFilters
from .models import Task
from .schemas import TaskIn, TaskOut


@crud(
    Task,
    path="",
    read=TaskOut,
    create=TaskIn,
    delete=True,
    access=member_only,
    owner="owner_id",
    filters=TaskFilters,
)
class Tasks(API):
    """The caller's own tasks: list (filtered), retrieve, create and delete."""

    def get_queryset(self, caller: Caller[Member]) -> QuerySet[Task]:
        return operations.mine(caller.user.id)

    async def remove(
        self, item: Task, _scoped: QuerySet[Task], caller: Caller[Member]
    ) -> bool:
        await operations.delete_task(caller.user.id, item.id)
        return True

    @http.post(
        "/{item_id}/complete",
        access=member_only,
        atomic=True,
        errors=(errors.NotFound, TaskAlreadyDone),
    )
    async def complete(self, item_id: UUID, caller: Caller[Member]) -> TaskOut:
        """Mark an own open task done."""
        return TaskOut.from_model(
            await operations.complete_task(caller.user.id, item_id)
        )


routes: list[Includable] = [Tasks]
```

The hooks `get_queryset` and `remove` take a typed `caller: Caller[Member]`.
That is valid because every generated action that calls them has the
`member_only` policy, so the caller is never `None`; Hinoki checks this when
the class is declared and raises `RegistrationError` otherwise. For a resource
that mixes public and protected actions, annotate `Caller[Member] | None`. See
[hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#hooks-in-the-class-form) in the CRUD guide.

The project's `tracker/routes.py` defines the public `GET /health` check and
mounts each exposed app explicitly with `Mount(...)`:

```python
# tracker/routes.py
from hinoki import Includable, Mount, Schema, http

from .apps.activity.api import routes as activity_routes
from .apps.members.api import routes as members_routes
from .apps.tasks.api import routes as tasks_routes


class Health(Schema):
    status: str


@http.get("/health")
async def health() -> Health:
    return Health(status="ok")


routes: list[Includable] = [
    health,
    Mount("/members", members_routes),
    Mount("/tasks", tasks_routes),
    Mount("/activity", activity_routes),
]
```

- **`@crud(...)`** generates the list, retrieve, create and delete actions with
  the policy, the schemas and the filters you name. `owner="owner_id"` sets
  the owner of a created task to the caller, and `read=TaskOut` is the only
  shape that leaves the server. Writes of generated actions are transactional
  by default.
- **`get_queryset`** scopes every generated action to the caller, so another
  member's task is a 404. **`remove`** replaces the generated delete body with
  the operation, which keeps completed tasks.
- **`access=`** names a reusable policy. Actions are public unless they name
  one, so protect on purpose; a rule in the next chapter enforces it.
- **`atomic=True`** runs the handwritten write in a transaction. It commits
  after the response is encoded and rolls back before an error becomes HTTP.
- **`errors=(...)`** declares what an action may raise. The OpenAPI document,
  the MCP tool description and the strict test client all read it.
- **`caller: Caller[Member]`** is the authenticated caller, typed:
  `caller.user` is your `Member`.
- **`TaskOut.from_model(...)`** converts a row into the response. A handler
  never returns a model.

The list accepts exactly the filters of `TaskFilters`, next to the pagination
parameters:

```text
GET /tasks?done=false&priority=1,2&created_at.from=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z&search=docs&ordering=-created_at
```

A name, an operator or an ordering key that `TaskFilters` does not declare is a
`422` that lists every problem. See [filter, order and search the
list](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#filter-order-and-search-the-list).

The two smaller apps follow the same shape. `members` has one handwritten
action, `GET /members/me`, and `activity` has a read-only generated list scoped
to the caller:

```python
# tracker/apps/activity/api.py
"""HTTP layer of the activity app, mounted at ``/activity`` by hinoki.toml."""

from hinoki import API, Caller, Includable, crud
from hinoki.orm import QuerySet
from tracker.apps.members.models import Member
from tracker.apps.members.security import member_only

from .models import Activity
from .schemas import ActivityOut


@crud(Activity, path="", read=ActivityOut, access=member_only)
class Feed(API):
    """The caller's activity, newest first. Read only."""

    def get_queryset(self, caller: Caller[Member]) -> QuerySet[Activity]:
        return Activity.filter(member_id=caller.user.id)


routes: list[Includable] = [Feed]
```

Declare `request: Request` as the first parameter only when you need headers,
cookies or the raw body. File uploads are covered in
[upload files](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#upload-files).

## Register the routes

Nothing in `main.py` lists these routes. `hinoki.toml` points each app at its
`routes` list and gives it the prefix (`/tasks`, `/members`, `/activity`, by
default `/<app name>`), which is why `path=""` above repeats nothing
([chapter 6](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/6-run.md)).

## Recap

- `@crud` generates the standard actions from the model, the policy, the
  schemas and a `FilterSet`; a handwritten action sits beside them.
- Handlers call operations and convert rows with `from_model`.
- Every error an action raises is declared.

Next: [4. Implement a business rule](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/3-operations.md). In the guides: [function-based APIs](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/function-endpoints.md) and [class-based APIs](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/class-endpoints.md).

# 4. Implement a business rule

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/3-operations.md

Generated CRUD ([chapter 3](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/4-endpoints.md)) already handles listing, retrieving,
creating and deleting rows. When an action encodes a domain rule — such as
marking an open task done or refusing to delete a completed one — put that rule
in `operations.py` instead of writing SQL or state checks directly inside the
HTTP handler:

- **Reuse across entry points**: plain `async def` functions take `owner_id` and
  plain values, never a `Request`, so an endpoint, a management command, a test
  or an admin hook can call the same rule.
- **Layer isolation**: `api.py` stays responsible only for HTTP shapes, status
  codes, `Access` policies and `atomic=True` transaction boundaries, while
  [chapter 6](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/5-rules.md) enforces that `operations.py` never imports HTTP types.
- **Single-statement ownership**: writes include the owner in the `WHERE` clause
  so there is no race between reading a row, checking ownership and updating it.

It starts with one scoped query that every action reuses:

```python
# tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py
from uuid import UUID

from hinoki import events
from hinoki.events import Updated
from hinoki.orm import QuerySet
from hinoki.utils import utc_now

from .errors import DoneTasksAreKept, TaskAlreadyDone
from .models import Task


def mine(owner_id: UUID) -> QuerySet[Task]:
    return Task.filter(owner_id=owner_id)
```

Writes put the owner in the statement itself:

```python
# tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py (continued)
async def complete_task(owner_id: UUID, task_id: UUID) -> Task:
    """Mark an own open task done in one statement."""
    changed = await Task.aupdate_where(
        {"id": task_id, "owner_id": owner_id, "done": False},
        {"done": True, "completed_at": utc_now()},
    )
    if changed:
        # aupdate_where emits no model event, so announce the change ourselves.
        await events.emit(Updated(Task, changed[0], ("done", "completed_at")))
        return changed[0]
    await mine(owner_id).filter(id=task_id).aget()  # missing or not yours: 404
    raise TaskAlreadyDone()


async def delete_task(owner_id: UUID, task_id: UUID) -> None:
    """Delete an own open task; completed ones are kept."""
    removed = await Task.adelete(id=task_id, owner_id=owner_id, done=False)
    if removed:
        return
    await mine(owner_id).filter(id=task_id).aget()  # missing or not yours: 404
    raise DoneTasksAreKept()
```

There is no gap between reading a row, checking its owner and writing it.
Another member's task looks exactly like a missing one (404), so nothing leaks.

Business failures are named after the rule they report. Each carries its HTTP
status (409 for `Conflict`) and a stable code:

```python
# tracker/apps/tasks/errors.py
from hinoki import errors


class TaskAlreadyDone(errors.Conflict):
    code = "task_already_done"
    message = "The task is already done."


class DoneTasksAreKept(errors.Conflict):
    code = "done_tasks_are_kept"
    message = "Completed tasks are kept as a record and cannot be deleted."
```

## Recap

- Business rules such as `complete_task(...)` belong in `operations.py`,
  separate from HTTP handlers in `api.py`.
- Ownership is part of the `WHERE` clause, not a separate check.
- Errors are classes with a status and a stable code.

Next: [5. Events between apps](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/events.md).

# 5. Events between apps

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/events.md

Creating a task and completing one both leave a line in the member's activity
feed, but `tasks` does not know the feed exists. It announces: generated create
emits `Created[Task]`, and `complete_task` ([chapter 4](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/3-operations.md)) emits
`Updated[Task]` itself because `aupdate_where` emits no model event. The
`activity` app listens:

```python
# tracker/apps/activity/events.py
from hinoki import events
from tracker.apps.tasks.models import Task

from .models import Activity

handlers = events.Handlers("activity")


async def record(task: Task, kind: str) -> None:
    await Activity.acreate(member_id=task.owner_id, task_id=task.id, kind=kind)


@handlers.in_transaction(events.Created[Task])
async def task_created(event: events.Created[Task]) -> None:
    await record(event.instance, "created")


@handlers.in_transaction(events.Updated[Task])
async def task_updated(event: events.Updated[Task]) -> None:
    await record(event.instance, "updated")
```

`in_transaction` runs the handler inside the transaction of the change, so the
task and its activity line commit together or not at all. The handlers are
registered by the `events` entry of the `activity` app in `hinoki.toml`
([chapter 7](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/6-run.md)), and one command lists them:

```sh
uv run hinoki events
```

```text
Created[Task]  in_transaction  activity     async  tracker.apps.activity.events.task_created
Updated[Task]  in_transaction  activity     async  tracker.apps.activity.events.task_updated

limits: events.handler_timeout=5.0, events.max_handlers=16, events.max_depth=4
declared in hinoki.toml: activity -> tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers
```

The dependency points from `activity` to `tasks` only, which is also why
`activity` lists `requires = ["tasks", "members"]`. [Chapter 6](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/5-rules.md)
makes the other direction a failing check. See [events](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md) for
`after_commit` handlers and the limits.

## Recap

- An app announces what happened; another app listens without an import in the
  other direction.
- `in_transaction` keeps the main write and its audit trail atomic.
- `hinoki events` inspects the handlers declared in `hinoki.toml`.

Next: [6. Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/5-rules.md).

# 6. Rules

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/5-rules.md

Rules turn the project's promises into checks. A failure names the rule, the
file and the line.

The Tracker keeps its promises in `tracker/rules.py`, as two `RuleSet` values:
`policy` says what an action, a schema and a model must declare, and `layers`
says which module may import which.

```python
# tracker/rules.py
from hinoki import Actions, Imports, Models, Schemas, Transactions
from hinoki.rules import RuleSet

PKG = "tracker"
TASKS = f"{PKG}.apps.tasks"

policy = RuleSet(
    Actions.require_access(match=f"{PKG}.*", except_=[f"{PKG}.routes.health"]),
    Actions.require_permissions(match=f"{PKG}.*", except_=[f"{PKG}.routes.health"]),
    Actions.forbid_model_responses(match=f"{PKG}.*"),
    Actions.require_return_type(match=f"{PKG}.*"),
    Actions.require_pagination(match=f"{PKG}.*"),
    Transactions.require_atomic(),
    Schemas.forbid_exposure("token_hash"),
    Schemas.require_string_limits(),
    Models.require_explicit_table(match=f"{PKG}.*"),
    Models.require_foreign_key_index(match=f"{PKG}.*"),
)

layers = RuleSet(
    # api -> operations -> models, and tasks never imports its listener.
    Imports.forbid(source=f"{TASKS}.models", target=f"{TASKS}.operations"),
    Imports.forbid(source=f"{TASKS}.models", target=f"{TASKS}.api"),
    Imports.forbid(source=f"{TASKS}.operations", target=f"{TASKS}.api"),
    Imports.forbid(source=f"{TASKS}", target=f"{PKG}.apps.activity"),
)
```

`hinoki.toml` lists both under `rules` in `[project]`, and the application
merges them in that order, so a worker refuses to start while one is violated.
`main.py` passes no `rules=` argument ([chapter 6](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/6-run.md)).

## Run the check

From `examples/tracker`:

```sh
uv run hinoki check
```

```text
14 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived
```

The check reads the rules from the manifest, imports the models of every app
and scans the `tracker` package for the import rules.

## Break a rule

Take `complete` out of its transaction by changing `atomic=True` to
`atomic=False` in its decorator in `tracker/apps/tasks/api.py`, then run the
check again:

```text
tracker/apps/tasks/api.py:39: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /tasks/{item_id}/complete (Tasks.complete) does not declare atomic=True
  fix: add atomic=True to the action (or declare it on a RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) group)
14 rule(s): 1 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived
```

The command exits with status 1. Put `atomic=True` back to restore the check.

The import rules fail the same way. Add `from tracker.apps.activity import models`
as the last line of `tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py` and the check reports it:

```text
tracker/apps/tasks/operations.py:46: HNK-IMP-001 [violated] tracker.apps.tasks.operations imports tracker.apps.activity, which is forbidden for tracker.apps.tasks
  fix: move the code to an allowed layer, or depend on it through the layer in between
```

(the check also lists the same line for `tracker.apps.activity.models`, which
brings the total to `2 violated`). Remove the import to restore it.

## Waivers

An accepted exception is a **waiver** in `hinoki-rules.toml`, with a reason, an
owner and a bounded target. `hinoki check` and application startup apply the
same waivers. The project owner writes waivers; tools and agents read them but
never edit them to make a check pass. The Tracker needs none; the
[Blog example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/hinoki-rules.toml)
carries one.

## Recap

- Rules are Python values in the project, checked by `hinoki check` and at startup.
- Each failure has a stable id, a location and a fix.
- Exceptions are explicit, owned waivers.

Next: [7. Run and test it](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/6-run.md).

# 7. Run and test it

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/6-run.md

## Settings

Settings are a typed class. Tracker declares a database; with no value set it
is local SQLite. Each field of `DatabaseSettings` is a `TRACKER_DATABASE__<FIELD>`
variable, two underscores between the group and the field, so
`TRACKER_DATABASE__URL` selects another database ([Configure a
database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md)):

```python
# tracker/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class TrackerSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="TRACKER_"):
    database: settings.DatabaseSettings
```

`main.py` declares the application at module level. It names no route, event
handler, middleware or rule, because `Hinoki()` reads them from `hinoki.toml`:

```python
# tracker/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki

from .commands import Seed
from .settings import TrackerSettings


def create_app(settings: TrackerSettings | None = None) -> Hinoki:
    """Routes, events, middleware and rules come from the manifest."""
    return Hinoki(
        settings=settings or TrackerSettings,
        title="Tracker",
        openapi_url="/openapi.json",
        docs_url="/docs",
        commands=[Seed],
    )


app = create_app()
```

What the manifest ([the index](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/index.md#the-trackers-shape)) supplies:

| `hinoki.toml` | What `Hinoki()` loads |
| --- | --- |
| `[project] routes` | `tracker/routes.py`: `GET /health` and explicit `Mount(...)` entries for `members`, `tasks` and `activity` |
| `[[apps]] events` | the handlers of `activity` |
| `[project] middleware` | `ApiVersion`, which adds `x-tracker-version` to every answer of a matched route |
| `[project] rules` | `policy` and `layers`, checked at startup and by `hinoki check` |

`Hinoki()` fills each of `include=`, `events=`, `middleware=` and `rules=` from
the manifest when you leave it out, and only in the module that
`[project] application` names (`tracker.main`). An argument you pass yourself,
even an empty one, replaces the manifest's list for that argument; do that only
when you want an explicit application, such as a test that serves one app.
`create_app` takes the settings so a test can point it at its own database.

`Hinoki(settings=TrackerSettings)` reads the `TRACKER_*` variables at import;
nothing connects until a worker starts.

## Serve it

From `examples/tracker`:

=== "SQLite (default)"

    ```sh
    uv run hinoki migrations apply
    uv run hinoki manage seed
    uv run hinoki dev
    ```

=== "PostgreSQL"

    ```sh
    export TRACKER_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://user:password@127.0.0.1:5432/tracker
    uv run hinoki migrations apply
    uv run hinoki manage seed
    uv run hinoki dev
    ```

The migration commands, `manage` and the server all read the `database` setting
of the application that `hinoki.toml` names, so `TRACKER_DATABASE__URL` alone
configures all of them ([which database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md#which-database)).
`hinoki dev` serves on `http://127.0.0.1:8000` and reloads on change; open
`/docs`. `hinoki serve` runs without reload and takes host, port and workers
from the `server` settings ([serving](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md)).

## Try it

Every task route needs a member's token, and the Tracker has no sign-up route.
`hinoki manage seed` is a management command of the example
(`tracker/commands.py`) that creates the member `Ada Demo` and prints a random token once; the table stores only its SHA-256 digest, so the token cannot be shown again. Export it:

```text
member 'Ada Demo' created; token '<random token>' (shown once)
```

```sh
export TOKEN='<the printed token>'
```

With the server running, call the API from a second terminal:

```sh
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Write docs","priority":2}'
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks?done=false&priority=1,2&search=docs&ordering=-created_at' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/activity -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

The first call answers `201` with the new task, the second a page with it that
matches the filters, and the third the `created` line that the `activity` app
wrote. Without the header every one of them answers `401`.

```text
{"id":"…","title":"Write docs","priority":2,"done":false,"created_at":"…","completed_at":null}
```

Completing the task answers `200`; completing it again is a `409`
`task_already_done`, and deleting a completed task a `409`
`done_tasks_are_kept`:

```sh
curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/tasks/<id>/complete -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

## Test it

The tests of the Tracker need no environment variable: the fixture in
`tracker_tests/conftest.py` migrates each app, in the order of its `requires`,
into a SQLite file in a temporary directory, creates the members Ann and Ben and
builds the application with `create_app(settings)` around that file:

```python
# tracker_tests/conftest.py (excerpt)
@pytest.fixture
async def world(tmp_path: Path) -> AsyncIterator[World]:
    url = f"sqlite://{tmp_path / 'tracker.sqlite3'}"
    database = await Database.connect(url, max_size=1)
    for name in ORDER:
        await migrator.apply(database, APPS / name / "migrations", namespace=name)
    with use_database(database):
        ann = await Member.acreate(name="Ann", token_hash=hash_token("ann-token"))
        ben = await Member.acreate(name="Ben", token_hash=hash_token("ben-token"))
    database.close()
    settings = TrackerSettings.load(overrides={"database": {"url": url}})
    async with ASGIClient(create_app(settings)) as client:
        yield World(client, ann, ben)
```

Operations need no HTTP, so test them directly. Then drive the whole stack with
the in-process client:

```python
# tracker_tests/trackerapitest.py (excerpt)
async def test_completing_twice_is_a_conflict_and_done_tasks_are_kept(
    world: World,
) -> None:
    task = await create(world, "Ship")
    path = f"/tasks/{task['id']}"
    ann = "ann-token"

    done = await world.client.post(f"{path}/complete", token=ann)
    again = await world.client.post(f"{path}/complete", token=ann)
    removed = await world.client.delete(path, token=ann)

    assert (done.status, done.body["done"]) == (200, True)
    assert (again.status, again.body["error"]) == (409, "task_already_done")
    assert (removed.status, removed.body["error"]) == (409, "done_tasks_are_kept")
```

Run all of them from the repository root:

```sh
uv run --locked pytest examples/tracker/tracker_tests
```

`ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True)` fails a test when an action answers an
error it did not declare. For tests without `async`, use `SyncClient`. See
[testing](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md) for disposable databases of other backends.

## Recap

- Settings are typed and read from prefixed environment variables.
- `hinoki.toml` wires routes, events, middleware and rules; `main.py` only
  configures the application.
- `hinoki dev` serves with reload; migrations stay a separate step.
- Test operations directly and the stack with `ASGIClient`.

Next: [8. Validate input](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/7-validation.md).

# 8. Validate input

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/7-validation.md

A `Schema` validates in three steps, all before your code runs: built-in
constraints reject invalid input, normalizers make valid strings canonical, and
checks reject values that are valid but not acceptable.

## Normalize and check fields

```python
# registration.py
from typing import Annotated

from hinoki import (
    Field,
    Invalid,
    Schema,
    errors,
    field_check,
    field_normalize,
    object_check,
)


class Registration(Schema):
    username: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=3, max_length=32, pattern=r"[a-z0-9_]+")]
    email: Annotated[str, Field(format="email")]
    password: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=12)]
    confirmation: str

    @field_normalize("email")
    def lowercase_email(self, value: str) -> str:
        return value.lower()

    @field_check("password")
    def reject_common_password(self, value: str) -> None:
        if value.lower() in {"password12345", "qwerty123456"}:
            raise Invalid("common_password", "choose a less common password")

    @object_check
    def passwords_match(self) -> None:
        if self.password != self.confirmation:
            raise Invalid(
                "password_mismatch", "passwords do not match", path="confirmation"
            )
```

```python
# registration.py (continued)
user = Registration.validate(
    {
        "username": "mari_23",
        "email": "Mari@Example.test",
        "password": "correct-horse-battery",
        "confirmation": "correct-horse-battery",
    }
)
assert user.email == "mari@example.test"

try:
    Registration.validate(
        {
            "username": "mari_23",
            "email": "mari@example.test",
            "password": "password12345",
            "confirmation": "different-password",
        }
    )
except errors.ValidationError as error:
    for detail in error.details:
        print(detail.path, detail.code, detail.message)
```

```text
password common_password choose a less common password
confirmation password_mismatch passwords do not match
```

- **Constraints** come first: `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern`, and
  `format=` (`email`, `url`, `slug`, `hex_color`); numbers take `gt`, `ge`,
  `lt` and `le`, and `one_of` fixes the allowed values. A failed constraint
  stops validation of that field.
- **`@field_normalize`** receives a valid string and returns a `str`; the result
  is checked against the same constraints. It also runs for `Schema(...)` and
  `from_model(...)`.
- **`@field_check`** sees the final value of one field, **`@object_check`** the
  whole schema. Both raise `Invalid(code, message)` and return `None`.

Normalizers and checks are synchronous and do no I/O. A rule that needs the
database, such as "this email is not registered yet", belongs in an operation,
where it can be race-safe.

## Ignore unknown fields

Unknown fields are rejected by default. For an external payload that adds
metadata you do not use, discard unknown keys on that `Schema`:

```python
# webhooks.py
from hinoki import Schema, SchemaConfig, SchemaExtra


class Webhook(Schema, config=SchemaConfig(extra=SchemaExtra.IGNORE)):
    event_id: str
    revision: int


event = Webhook.validate(
    {"event_id": "evt-1", "revision": 2, "provider_data": {"trace": "abc"}}
)
assert event.dump() == {"event_id": "evt-1", "revision": 2}
```

Declared fields stay strict, and ignored keys are never stored or dumped.
Constructor keywords and `from_model(..., **extra)` stay strict too, and each
nested `Schema` applies its own policy.

## Validate model writes

Data can also reach a table without an HTTP `Schema`: from a management command
or the admin. Put the same constraints on the model:

```python
# catalog/models.py
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from hinoki import Field, db
from hinoki.orm import Model, field, pk


def trimmed(value: str) -> None:
    if value != value.strip():
        raise ValueError("surrounding whitespace is not allowed")


@db.table("catalog_products")
class Product(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    sku: str = field(
        max_length=32, constraints=Field(min_length=3, pattern=r"[A-Z0-9-]+")
    )
    name: str = field(max_length=120, validators=(trimmed,))
    price: float = field(constraints=Field(gt=0))
```

The checks run before `acreate`, `asave` and queryset `aupdate`, and their
synchronous forms. An invalid write raises `ModelValidationError` (import it
from `hinoki.errors`) with structured `details` and sends no SQL. Rows that are
read are not revalidated.
See [field constraints and validators](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md#model-field-constraints-and-validators).

## Recap

- Constraints, then normalizers, then checks; all before the handler.
- Unknown keys are an error unless a `Schema` opts out.
- Model constraints guard writes that bypass HTTP.

Next: [9. Projects and apps](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/8-projects.md).

# 9. Projects and apps

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/8-projects.md

An app is a package with its own models, migrations and routes, registered in
`hinoki.toml`. This chapter adds a `billing` app to the `notes` project from the
[Quick start](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md).

## Create the app

From the project root:

```sh
uv run hinoki app create
```

| Prompt | Default | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App name | | `billing` |
| Depends on | | (none) |

The command writes the package and registers it:

```text
notes/apps/billing/
├── api.py         endpoints of the app
├── routes.py      the app’s route list, initially empty
├── models.py      tables of the app
└── migrations/    migration history
```

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "billing"
models = "notes.apps.billing.models"
migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations"
requires = []
```

Hinoki reads apps only from `hinoki.toml`; it never scans installed packages.
If billing later references a model of another app, list that app in
`requires`: migrations then run in dependency order.

## Add a model

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py
"""Models owned by this app."""

from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from hinoki import db
from hinoki.orm import Model, field, pk
from hinoki.utils import utc_now


@db.ordered_by("-created_at")
class Invoice(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    reference: str = field(max_length=40, unique=True)
    paid: bool = False
    created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now, index=True)
```

The table name is derived: `billing_invoices`, the app followed by the plural
model name. `@db.table("billing_invoices")` pins it, so renaming the class
keeps the physical name; the model rules below ask for it.

## Plan and apply the migration

```sh
uv run hinoki migrations plan billing
uv run hinoki migrations apply
```

```text
database: sqlite:///…/notes/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default)
create table billing_invoices
wrote notes/apps/billing/migrations/0001-create-table-billing-invoices.sql
database: sqlite:///…/notes/.hinoki/local.sqlite3 (from local SQLite default)
entries: nothing to apply
billing: 0001-create-table-billing-invoices
```

`plan` compares the models with the recorded migration state and writes the
next migration; the number and the slug come from the change. Review the
`.sql` file before you apply it. With more than one app, `plan` needs the app
name; `apply` runs every app in dependency order.

!!! note "Where the data goes"
    `apply` uses the application's `database` setting, so the variable that
    configures the server, such as `NOTES_DATABASE__URL`, also configures the
    migrations; `plan`, `status` and `apply` print the database they chose. With no
    database configured, `apply` creates `.hinoki/local.sqlite3` beside
    `hinoki.toml`. `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL` overrides the setting for one run.
    If the application cannot be loaded, the commands stop (exit 2) instead of guessing.
    Migrations never run when the application starts.

## Check the project

```sh
uv run hinoki check
uv run pytest
```

```text
8 rule(s): 0 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived
```

`notes/rules.py` keeps two model rules commented out:
`Models.require_explicit_table` and `Models.require_foreign_key_index`.
`hinoki check` imports the models of every `[[apps]]` entry, so a project with
no model at all would report them as `unverifiable`, which fails the check.
Now that billing has `Invoice`, turn them on (and import `Models`):

```python
# notes/rules.py (excerpt)
from hinoki import Actions, Models, Schemas, Transactions

project_rules = RuleSet(
    # …the rules the scaffold wrote…
    Models.require_explicit_table(match="notes.*"),
    Models.require_foreign_key_index(match="notes.*"),
)
```

The check then reports the derived table name:

```text
notes/apps/billing/models.py:11: HNK-DB-001 [violated] Invoice uses the derived table name 'billing_invoices'
  fix: name the table with @db.table(...) or table=... on the model
10 rule(s): 1 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived
```

Add `@db.table("billing_invoices")` above the class (the first line of its
decorators) and the check passes. Pinning the derived name changes no table:
`migrations plan billing` then reports `no changes`.

Endpoints for billing go in `notes/apps/billing/api.py`, and
`notes/apps/billing/routes.py` exports them. You decide where they are served by
mounting them in `notes/routes.py` with `Mount("/billing", billing_routes)`, so
paths inside the app never repeat the prefix, and `notes/main.py` loads
`notes/routes.py` from `hinoki.toml` automatically:

```python
# notes/main.py (as hinoki new wrote it)
from hinoki import Hinoki

from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

app = Hinoki(
    settings=ProjectSettings,  # NOTES_* variables and .env
    title="Notes",
    openapi_url="/openapi.json",
    docs_url="/docs",
)  # routes, rules and middleware come from hinoki.toml
```

Passing `include=` explicitly overrides `[project] routes` when you need it (for
example in tests or conditional mounts). The same manifest can also list
project-wide `middleware`, an `events` module per app and more than one rule
set (`rules`), as the Tracker's `hinoki.toml` does.

The project's rules (listed in `hinoki.toml`) require every action to name an
`Access` policy with permissions; build one as in [chapter 3](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/4-endpoints.md).

## Recap

- `hinoki app create` writes an app and registers it in `hinoki.toml`.
- Table names, migration numbers and slugs are derived; you review the SQL.
- The project's `routes.py` mounts each exposed app explicitly; code inside the app never repeats the prefix.

# Overview

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/guides.md

One page per task. Start with data and endpoints, then add access, rules and runtime concerns as you need them. New to Hinoki? Take the [tutorial](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/tutorial/index.md) or the [quick start](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md) first, or read the [examples](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/tree/main/examples) in order: Notes (easy), Tracker (medium) and Blog (complete), plus the focused Mailroom (outbound email).

## Data

- [Configure a database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md): choose the backend, set the URL or connection fields, keep credentials secret.
- [Define models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md): columns, primary keys, column types, table names and write-time validators.
- [Model options](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-options.md): indexes, composite uniqueness, default order, update timestamps and names, as decorators.
- [Relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md): foreign keys, one-to-one, many-to-many association models and explicit loading.
- [Query and write rows](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md): filters, pagination, reusable queries, creates, updates and bulk writes.
- [Lifecycle hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-hooks.md): react to a model's own writes and inspect its changed columns.
- [Events](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md): typed events with explicit handlers that run inside the transaction or after the commit.
- [Migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md): plan, review, apply and check migrations for every app.
- [Schemas](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schemas.md): declare the data that crosses the API boundary and convert it to and from rows.
- [Scalar field types](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-types.md): enums, literals, dates, decimals, bytes, addresses, secrets and paths.
- [Collections and unions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-collections.md): sets, tuples, dictionaries, unions, discriminated unions, TypedDicts and dataclasses.
- [Validate input](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-validation.md): constraints, normalization, field and object checks, and input reshaping.
- [Schemas from models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-schemas.md): derive a `Schema` from a `Model` and convert rows with `from_model`.
- [Time and utilities](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/utilities.md): UTC time, the application timezone, test clocks and update timestamps.

## Endpoints

- [Function-based APIs](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/function-endpoints.md): the default pattern: plain functions grouped by a `RouteGroup` that states access, transactions and errors once.
- [Class-based APIs](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/class-endpoints.md): `API` classes for `@crud` resources with hooks, inheritance and resources you ship to others.
- [Register routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/routes.md): how `routes.py` and `hinoki.toml` build the route map, with `Mount`, `include=` in tests and `hinoki routes`.
- [Requests and responses](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md): what an action receives (path, query, body, forms, XML, files) and how its result is checked.
- [Store uploaded files](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/storage.md): bounded memory or local-disk storage with opaque keys and streamed downloads.
- [Generate CRUD routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md): list, retrieve and write actions from a model, with access and ownership rules.
- [Errors](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/errors.md): malformed requests, authentication failures and declared application errors.
- [Stream a response](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md): `Stream`, `EventStream` and `File` answers sent while they are produced, on Kiso and Granian.
- [WebSockets](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/websockets.md): `@http.websocket` actions with `Access`, typed JSON messages, limits and back-pressure, on Kiso and Granian.
- [Compress responses](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/compression.md): optional brotli and gzip compression of bodies, on Kiso only.
- [Export Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md): request counters and histograms on a dedicated listener, on Kiso only.
- [Middleware](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md): typed `Middleware` around an action or the whole app, identical on Kiso and Granian.
- [Pagination](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md): page-number pagination with `PageNumberPagination` and keyset cursors with `CursorPagination`.
- [Filter, order and search a CRUD list](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#filter-order-and-search-the-list): `FilterSet` with `Eq`, `In`, `Range`, `Search` and an ordering allow-list.
- [Parsers and renderers](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/codecs.md): other body formats in and out.
- [OpenAPI document](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md): the OpenAPI 3.2 document (3.1 on request) generated from routes, signatures and `Schema` declarations.

## Security and checks

- [Authentication and access](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md): providers resolve a `Caller`; `Access` policies check permissions.
- [Application sessions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sessions.md): server-side state, cookie lifecycle, CSRF checks, session authentication and explicit stores.
- [Hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md): restrict the host names an app answers to, which browser origins may read it, browser security headers, HTTPS redirects and trusted proxies.
- [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md): typed promises about your application, checked with a stable ID, a location and an explanation.

## Runtime

- [Application modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md): resources that live as long as a worker, such as a database pool.
- [Cache values](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cache.md): bounded Rust memory cache or a shared database backend with explicit TTL and failure behavior.
- [Transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md): `atomic=True` on actions, `db.atomic` in application code.
- [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md): typed, immutable settings from the environment, dotenv and TOML, with redacted secrets.
- [Serve an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md): `hinoki dev` while you work, `hinoki serve` in production, on Kiso (the default) or Granian.
- [Kiso server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md): what Hinoki's Rust server runs natively, its limits, workers and signals, reload and reverse-proxy behaviour.
- [Test an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md): test through the whole stack with `ASGIClient`, against a disposable database, from the test `hinoki new` generates.
- [Command line](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md): every `hinoki` command, the short forms inside a project and the explicit forms outside one.
- [Create a project](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md): the interactive `hinoki new` flow, its options and what the generated project contains.
- [Inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md): check rules, list routes, export the OpenAPI document, show settings and diagnose the environment.
- [Interactive shell](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/shell.md): an async-capable prompt with the app's settings and models.
- [Typing](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/typing.md): what a type checker catches in handlers, decorators and `Schema` construction.

## Integrations

- [Add an admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md): staff pages for your models, with a sign-in page, users and per-model permissions.
- [Customize the admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin-customize.md): columns, hooks, bulk actions, templates and themes.
- [Send email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md): SMTP, console and memory backends from a per-worker mailer, sent after a commit; no queue.
- [Email templates](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md): typed TOML templates rendered in Rust, checked at startup and previewed from the CLI.
- [Expose actions over MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/app-mcp.md): selected actions as tools for a remote MCP client.
- [Development MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md): a server that describes your app to a coding agent; it can run requests against the app only when you enable `--scenarios`.
- [Build with a coding agent](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ai-workflow.md): a project, rules and tools ready for an agent, the llms.txt files and Markdown mirrors of these docs, and where its authority ends.

## Operating

- [Best practices](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/best-practices.md): project structure, `Schema` contracts, `Access` policies, queries, Rust fast paths, testing and production operations.
- [Sync and async code](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md): the event loop, the bounded sync pool and which style each surface accepts.
- [Benchmarks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/benchmarks.md): retained measurements with their environment, method and limits.
- [Changelog](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/changelog.md): every user-facing change, explorable by version and type.
- [Native CRUD orientation run](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rust-crud-orientation.md): a workload-specific measurement of generated CRUD.

- [Concepts](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/concepts.md): how models, `Schema` classes, actions, workers and rules fit together.
- [Request lifecycle](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/request-lifecycle.md): the order of routing, access, binding, handler, commit and response.
- [Structure an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md): layers, where each concern lives, and why.

# Configure a database

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md

Hinoki's ORM runs on SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB. The database URL
selects the backend; models and queries stay the same wherever the backends'
SQL features overlap. With nothing configured, the database is local SQLite at
`.hinoki/local.sqlite3`.

## Set up a database in four steps

1. **Declare it.** `hinoki new notes --database postgresql` does this for you;
   otherwise add the field to your settings class. Name a TOML file only if
   you will use one (step 2): the file named by `toml=` must exist.

    ```python
    # notes/settings.py
    class ProjectSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env"):
        database: settings.DatabaseSettings
    ```

2. **Populate it.** With nothing set, `DatabaseSettings` points at a local
   SQLite file, `.hinoki/local.sqlite3`. To use another database, pick one
   source:

    | Source | Use it for | Example |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Nothing | local development on SQLite | – |
    | `.env` | one URL on your machine (`hinoki new --database postgresql` writes a `.env.example` to copy; keep `.env` out of git) | `NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@localhost:5432/notes` |
    | Environment | containers and CI | `export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE=/run/secrets/database-url` |
    | `settings.toml` | non-secret fields (`engine`, `host`, `name`, `user`), with the password from the environment; add `toml="settings.toml"` to the class | [connection fields](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md#connection-fields) |

    The prefix (`NOTES_`) comes from the settings class, and `__` separates the
    group from the field. Until you set one of them, a project created with
    `--database postgresql` still uses the local SQLite file, and so do its
    migrations.

3. **Check it.** `hinoki settings`, run from the project root, shows each
   value with its source; the URL and the password are redacted:

    ```console
    $ hinoki settings | grep DATABASE__URL
    NOTES_DATABASE__URL                      .env         ***
    ```

    `hinoki migrations status` names the database it will use, and fails with
    a clear error if the server does not answer:

    ```console
    $ hinoki migrations status
    database: postgresql://***@127.0.0.1:5432/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database)
    ```

    `status` connects and records its migration ledger, so on SQLite it
    creates the database file.

4. **Create the tables.** Hinoki never creates tables or runs migrations at
   startup (it only creates the local SQLite file): run
   `hinoki migrations apply` once you have models ([migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md)).

The rest of this page lists every field, the URL forms and each backend.

## Configure the application

Declare a `database` field on the project settings. `hinoki new` adds it when
you choose a database.

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(
    settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env", toml="settings.toml"
):
    database: settings.DatabaseSettings
```

Each worker opens one bounded pool during startup and closes it during
shutdown. The [Notes example's settings](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/notes/notes/settings.py)
are exactly this field with nothing else. Importing models or routes never opens a connection, and no
`modules=` entry is needed. The file named by `toml=` must exist, even if it
is empty: otherwise the settings fail to load with
`settings.toml: TOML file cannot be read or parsed`.

Configure a server database with **connection fields** or with **one URL**.
Setting both is an error when settings load.

## Connection fields

Put non-secret fields in the TOML file named by `toml=`. Keep the settings in
their own file: `hinoki.toml` is the project manifest, and its tables are not
settings.

=== "PostgreSQL"

    ```toml
    # settings.toml
    [database]
    engine = "postgresql"
    name = "notes"
    user = "notes"
    host = "db.example.test"
    port = 5432
    options = ["sslmode=verify-full", "sslrootcert=/run/secrets/db-ca.pem"]
    max_size = 10            # per worker
    ```

=== "MySQL"

    ```toml
    # settings.toml
    [database]
    engine = "mysql"
    name = "notes"
    user = "notes"
    host = "db.example.test"
    ```

=== "MariaDB"

    ```toml
    # settings.toml
    [database]
    engine = "mariadb"
    name = "notes"
    user = "notes"
    host = "db.example.test"
    ```

=== "SQLite"

    ```toml
    # settings.toml
    [database]
    engine = "sqlite"
    name = ".hinoki/local.sqlite3"
    ```

The password is a secret setting. It never comes from TOML:

```sh
export NOTES_DATABASE__PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/db-password
```

| Field | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `engine` | `sqlite`, `postgresql`, `mysql` or `mariadb` (`settings.DatabaseEngine`) | – |
| `name` | database name, or the file path for SQLite | – |
| `user`, `password` | credentials; `password` is secret (`*_PASSWORD` or `*_PASSWORD_FILE`) | – |
| `host`, `port` | server address; for PostgreSQL `host` may be a Unix-socket directory such as `/var/run/postgresql` | `localhost`, backend port |
| `options` | `key=value` URL query pairs, such as `sslmode` | `()` |
| `max_size` | connections per worker | `10` |

Hinoki builds `DatabaseSettings.url` from these fields and percent-encodes the
user, password and name. SQLite takes only `name`. `options` cannot carry
credentials or override `user`, `host`, `port` or the name. In an environment
variable, `options` uses the settings sequence syntax (commas between pairs);
a value that itself contains a comma belongs in the TOML array.

## One URL

```sh
export NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE=/run/secrets/database-url
```

| Backend | URL |
| --- | --- |
| SQLite | `sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3` |
| PostgreSQL | `postgresql://notes:password@db.example.test/notes?sslmode=verify-full` |
| MySQL | `mysql://notes:password@db.example.test/notes` |
| MariaDB | `mariadb://notes:password@db.example.test/notes` |

Percent-encode reserved characters in the user name and password of a
hand-written URL. Prefer `NOTES_DATABASE__URL_FILE` or a secret manager over a
URL in shell history or a process argument. Hinoki redacts the URL in settings
output and connection errors.

!!! warning "Credentials"
    `settings.Secret` values, `url` and `password` included, are never read from
    TOML. SQLite has no database credentials: protect the file and its backups
    with operating-system permissions.

## Backends

| Backend | Security defaults | Limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQLite | no network, no TLS | one writer at a time; bounded connections and a busy timeout of at least five seconds, extended when `Database.connect(wait=...)` is larger; a relative path resolves from the server's working directory (start it from the project root; migrations anchor it beside `hinoki.toml`) |
| PostgreSQL | `sslmode=prefer`; use `verify-full` for remote servers; `sslrootcert` adds a PEM CA to the system roots. `require`, `verify-ca` and `verify-full` all verify the certificate | native UUID, timestamp, JSON and byte types |
| MySQL | TLS required, certificate and host verified against the system trust store; `require_ssl=false` only for an isolated disposable local server | InnoDB, native JSON; no `RETURNING` |
| MariaDB | TLS required by default | separate backend, tested on MariaDB 11.4 with its own conformance job. `JSON` is a text alias: typed `dict`/`list` fields decode by declaration; low-level `Database.fetch()` returns JSON values as bytes |

SQL Server and Oracle are not supported. Any other scheme, such as `oracle://`
or `mssql://`, fails when the pool is created with
`DatabaseError: unsupported database URL scheme`; the message does not repeat
the URL. A supported scheme written without its slashes, such as
`sqlite:./app.db`, fails with `invalid database URL: the scheme needs ://`.

### PostgreSQL TLS

PostgreSQL URLs accept `sslmode=disable`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca` or
`verify-full`, and `sslrootcert=/path/to/ca.pem`. `prefer` tries TLS first and
falls back to plaintext only if the server declines TLS; a certificate or
handshake error fails closed. All TLS connections verify the server
certificate chain and hostname: `require`, `verify-ca` and `verify-full` all
require TLS, and Hinoki's `verify-ca` also verifies the hostname. Trust uses
Mozilla WebPKI roots plus any PEM certificates in `sslrootcert` (at most
1 MiB), so `sslmode=require` needs a trusted certificate too. `sslmode=allow`
is unsupported. A URL to a remote host without `sslmode` logs a warning at
connect: `prefer` lets a network attacker strip TLS, so use `verify-full`.
Mount the CA file where each worker can read it.

Hinoki does not create the PostgreSQL role or database: create them once with
your usual tools before the first `hinoki migrations apply`.

### SQLite storage

SQLite uses bundled SQLite 3.35 or newer. UUID and timestamp columns use text
storage; JSON uses JSON text. `contains` matching is ASCII case-insensitive.
In-memory databases are not supported, because each pooled connection would
have an independent database. SQLite allows one writer at a time. Its internal
lock wait is the larger of five seconds and the pool's configured `wait`; the
pool acquisition wait itself remains bounded by `wait`:

```python
from hinoki.db import Database

database = await Database.connect("sqlite://./app.sqlite3", wait=10)
```

This gives SQLite writes up to ten seconds to acquire the writer lock. The
default `wait=5` keeps the existing five-second limit.

## Use the database from a script

A script, a one-off task or a test fixture opens its own pool with
`Database.connect` and makes it current with `use_database`, so model queries
find it. Run it from the project root so a relative SQLite path and `.env`
match the server's:

```python
# scripts/unpaid.py
import asyncio

from hinoki.db import Database
from hinoki.orm import use_database

from notes.apps.billing.models import Invoice
from notes.settings import ProjectSettings


async def main() -> None:
    settings = ProjectSettings.load()
    database = await Database.connect(
        settings.database.url.reveal(), max_size=settings.database.max_size
    )
    try:
        with use_database(database):
            print(await Invoice.filter(paid=False).acount())
    finally:
        database.close()


asyncio.run(main())
```

`Database.close()` is a plain call, not awaited. The script does not create
tables: run `hinoki migrations apply` against the same database first.

## Replace the database module

A `DatabaseModule` in `modules=`, or installed with `app.install(...)`, replaces
the one Hinoki builds from the settings, for example to use a URL chosen at
runtime:

```python
# notes/main.py (excerpt)
from hinoki.db import DatabaseModule

app.install(DatabaseModule(url, max_size=4))
```

The migration commands use this module's URL too, and print
`(from application: DatabaseModule)`. A database module of your own whose URL
Hinoki cannot read stops them; pass `--database` or `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL`.

## Migrations use the application's database

`hinoki migrations` reads the database of the project's application (its
`DatabaseModule`, or its `database` setting),
so the variables above configure both the server and the migration commands.
`--database` or `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL` override it for one run; with none of
them set, the local SQLite default is anchored beside `hinoki.toml`:

```sh
export NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes
hinoki migrations status   # database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ...)
hinoki migrations apply
```

Hinoki never runs migrations at startup. An application that declares no
`database` setting and installs no `DatabaseModule` has no database at run
time, although its migrations still fall back to the local SQLite file:
declare the field before you add models. See [which database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md#which-database)
for the full order, and [migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md) for planning, review and
per-backend behaviour.

## See also

- [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md): source precedence, secrets and validation
- [Application modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md): resource ownership and the `Database` instance
- [Database API reference](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/reference/database.md): raw SQL, placeholders and backend limits

# Define models

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md

A `Model` maps a Python class to one table. Annotated fields are the columns;
indexes, ordering and other options are [decorators](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-options.md). A model
never opens a connection on import and never loads a relation implicitly.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py
from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from hinoki import db
from hinoki.orm import Model, OnDelete, field, foreign_key, pk
from hinoki.utils import utc_now


class Customer(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    name: str = field(max_length=120)
    email: str = field(max_length=254, unique=True)


@db.indexed("customer_id", "created_at")
@db.ordered_by("-created_at", "-id")
class Invoice(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Customer, on_delete=OnDelete.RESTRICT, related_name="invoices"
    )
    reference: str = field(max_length=40, unique=True)
    paid: bool = False
    created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now)
```

The tables are `billing_customers` and `billing_invoices`. Changing a model
never changes the database: create the tables with
`hinoki migrations plan billing` and `hinoki migrations apply`
([migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md)).

## Declare columns

| Declaration | Column |
| --- | --- |
| `name: str` | required, not null |
| `note: str \| None = None` | nullable, optional in the constructor |
| `paid: bool = False` | default value |
| `id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)` | the primary key |
| `email: str = field(max_length=254, unique=True)` | bounded text, unique |
| `created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now, index=True)` | factory default, single-column index |
| `customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(Customer, on_delete=...)` | a reference ([relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md)) |

`field()` takes `unique`, `index`, `max_length`, `default`, `default_factory`,
`constraints` and `validators`. The annotation gives the type and nullability.

* **One primary key.** `pk()` declares it; pass `default` or
  `default_factory` when the constructor may omit it. A nullable key
  (`int | None`) raises `RegistrationError` when the class is defined.
