* **Keyword-only constructor.** `Invoice(reference="INV-1", customer_id=c.id)`.
* **Indexes.** `field(index=True)` indexes one column; it cannot be combined
  with `unique=True` or `pk()`, which are already indexed. A `foreign_key` has
  no `index=` option: index it with `@db.indexed(...)`, or a composite index
  that starts with it, as `Invoice` does ([model options](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-options.md)).
* **Composite uniqueness** is `@db.unique("a", "b")`; there is no nested
  `class Meta`.

## Column types

| Python type | Stored as | Read back as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool` | the backend's text, integer, float and boolean types | the same type |
| `UUID`, `datetime` | native on PostgreSQL; text on SQLite | `UUID`, `datetime` |
| `dict[...]`, `list[...]` | JSON (JSON text on SQLite, text alias on MariaDB) | decoded by the annotation |
| `bytes` | `BYTEA` on PostgreSQL, blob on SQLite | `bytes` |
| `date`, `time` | ISO text (`time` with microseconds, no timezone) | `date`, `time` |
| `timedelta` | whole microseconds, `bigint` | `timedelta` |
| `Enum` subclass | its value: `bigint` when every value is an integer, else text | the member |
| `IPv4Address`, `IPv6Address`, `IPv4Network`, `IPv6Network` | text | the `ipaddress` object; writes accept only that class |
| `Decimal` | exact, per backend (below) | `Decimal` |

A stored value that does not read back as its annotation raises `FieldError`.
`date` and `timedelta` compare and order by value. A column type without a
SQL type (a set, tuple, `Literal`, `Path`, `Secret`, `Any`, `object`, or a
union of several types such as `int | str`) raises `RegistrationError` when the
class is defined. `Annotated[str, Field(max_length=32)]` sizes the column like
`field(max_length=32)`. SQLite's `contains` folds ASCII case only.

### `Decimal` columns

| Backend | Column | Filters and ordering |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL | `numeric` | `=`, `ne`, `in`, `isnull`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `order_by` |
| MySQL, MariaDB | `decimal(65,30)` | the same; read back with scale 30 (`Decimal("1.5")` returns as `Decimal("1.500…0")`, equal in value) |
| SQLite | `text` (its exact spelling) | `=`, `ne`, `in`, `isnull` only; `12.3` and `12.30` differ; range filters and `order_by` raise `FieldError` |

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
from decimal import Decimal


class Price(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    amount: Decimal
```

```python
# inside an async operation
# every backend
cheap = await Price.filter(amount=Decimal("9.99"))
# not SQLite
ordered = await Price.filter(amount__gte=Decimal("5")).order_by("amount")
```

* A filter value is a `Decimal`, an `int` or a numeric string; a `float`, a
  `bool`, `NaN`, an infinity or `contains` raises `FieldError`.
* `decimal(65,30)` bounds MySQL and MariaDB to 35 digits before the point;
  PostgreSQL `numeric` is unbounded.
* A table that already stores a `Decimal` as text on PostgreSQL or MySQL needs a
  reviewed migration that changes the column type.
* A generated CRUD list whose `@db.ordered_by` names a `Decimal` column takes the
  Python path on SQLite, where that ordering is refused.

## Table and display names

Hinoki derives the table name `<app>_<models>` and display names from the class.

| Model | Module | Table | Labels |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Invoice` | `notes.apps.billing.models` | `billing_invoices` | Invoice / Invoices |
| `LineItem` | `notes.apps.billing.models` | `billing_line_items` | Line item / Line items |
| `Note` | `notes.models` or `notes.models.note` | `notes_notes` | Note / Notes |
| `APIKey` | `notes.models` | `notes_api_keys` | API key / API keys |

The app is the package that holds the `models` module; a module without a
`models` segment uses its own last name. The plural is a small English rule:
consonant + `y` → `ies`; `s`, `x`, `z`, `ch`, `sh` → `es`; otherwise `s`. It
does not know irregular nouns (`Person` → `persons`).

| Override | Form |
| --- | --- |
| app part of the name | `class Invoice(Model, app="accounts")` |
| whole table name (never prefixed) | `@db.table("invoices")` |
| display names | `class Person(Model, label="Person", plural="People")` |

Pin the table name with `@db.table(...)` when a model already has migration
history and you rename the class or move its module: a changed derived name is
planned as a drop and a create, which the destructive-migration guard stops; it
is never a rename. The optional `HNK-DB-001` rule
(`Models.require_explicit_table`) requires every matching model to pin it.

Names must be portable ASCII of at most 63 characters. A derived name that is
rejected (`sqlite_…`, `hinoki_migrations`, non-ASCII such as `class Café`) does
not stop the class from being defined: `@db.table("cafes")` can still name it.
Without one, the error is raised when the model is first used (query, write,
migration plan, project or admin registration, or a foreign key to it).

## Model field constraints and validators

`field()` can also check values before every ORM write. Use
`constraints=Field(...)` for built-in checks and `validators=(...)` for
synchronous application rules:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
from hinoki import Field


def no_padding(value: str) -> None:
    if value != value.strip():
        raise ValueError("surrounding whitespace is not allowed")


class Product(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    sku: str = field(
        max_length=32, constraints=Field(min_length=3, pattern=r"[A-Z0-9-]+")
    )
    weight_kg: float = field(constraints=Field(gt=0))
    name: str = field(max_length=120, validators=(no_padding,))
```

* **When.** Immediately before inserts and ORM updates, filtered bulk updates
  included; never on construction, assignment or reads. Invalid declarations
  fail when the class is created.
* **Checks.** String and list lengths, patterns, membership, numeric bounds
  on `int`, `float` and `Decimal` (a `NaN` or infinite `Decimal` is refused),
  and `multiple_of` on `int` and `Decimal`. `strip`, `lower` and `upper`
  normalize a `str` before the other checks, and the normalized text is what
  is written (an instance being saved gets it too). A JSON column
  (`dict[...]`, `list[dict[...]]`) takes no built-in checks; validators still
  run on it.
* **Failure.** `ModelValidationError`, before any SQL, with `details` holding
  each field's `path`, `code` and `message`. In a request it becomes the
  standard 422 response; the admin shows the messages.
* **Validators** are synchronous, raise `ValueError` to refuse, perform no I/O
  and do not change the value. Rules about other rows, permissions or current
  state belong in an operation.

These checks protect CLI, admin and direct ORM writes; a `Schema` still
validates HTTP input first ([validate input](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-validation.md)). Database
constraints remain authoritative.

## Share fields: abstract models and mixins

An abstract model has no table: it is not migrated, cannot be queried and only
exists to be subclassed.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
class Keyed(Model, abstract=True):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)


@db.timestamps()
@db.ordered_by("-updated_at")
class Tracked(Model, abstract=True):
    created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now)
    updated_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now, index=True)


class Article(Keyed, Tracked):
    title: str = field(max_length=120)
```

`Article` has `created_at`, `updated_at`, `id` and `title`, is ordered by
`-updated_at`, indexes `updated_at` and refreshes it on every update.
`Tracked.all()` raises `ModelError`.

* `abstract=True` is not inherited; an abstract model needs no primary key, a
  table model needs exactly one, its own or inherited.
* **Options** from abstract bases are inherited: all `@db.unique` and
  `@db.indexed`, the order and timestamp column of the first base that sets
  one, a soft-delete option, and status tracks. A decorator on the subclass
  *replaces* that kind of option. A
  `field(index=True)` index belongs to its column and is dropped when a subclass
  redeclares the column without it. Constraint names are not inherited: an
  abstract model cannot use `@db.unique(..., name=...)`.
* **Plain mixins** (non-model classes) contribute annotated fields and methods;
  `ClassVar` annotations are not fields. Type checkers do not see mixin fields
  as constructor arguments: prefer an abstract model.
* **Conflicting types.** Two bases giving one field different types are refused
  unless the class redeclares the field.
* **Subclassing a table model** copies its columns into a separate, unrelated
  table; no join, no shared rows, no inherited options.
* **Column order** follows dataclass rules: model bases (last listed first),
  then mixins, then the class's own fields.

A foreign key in an abstract model needs a per-subclass reverse name; see
[relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md#foreign-keys-in-abstract-models-and-mixins).

## Lifecycle utilities

`UUIDModel`, `TimestampedModel` and `SoftDeleteModel` are composable abstract
bases. Their columns remain ordinary typed fields and are included in
`table_state()` and migration plans. `UUIDModel` supplies a UUIDv4 primary key
(`id: UUID = uuid_pk()`); `TimestampedModel` supplies `created_at` and
`updated_at`; `SoftDeleteModel` supplies an indexed nullable `deleted_at`
column.

For configurable UUID primary keys, use `uuid_pk()`: it defaults to UUIDv4,
accepts `version=7` (time-ordered RFC 9562 UUIDv7 generated in Rust, also
available as `hinoki.orm.uuid7` / `hinoki.utils.uuid7`), or any custom
`default_factory`. For opaque URL-safe identifiers or share codes, use
`urlsafe_token(nbytes=32, unique=True)` — values are generated by Rust's CSPRNG
(`hinoki.core.make_token`) and validated against `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`. For
authentication secrets (password reset tokens, API keys, sessions), store a
hash instead of a raw token column.

```python
from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID

from hinoki import db
from hinoki.orm import (
    Model,
    SoftDeleteModel,
    TimestampedModel,
    UUIDModel,
    field,
    urlsafe_token,
    uuid_pk,
)
from hinoki.utils import utc_now


class Document(UUIDModel, TimestampedModel, SoftDeleteModel):
    title: str
    share_token: str = urlsafe_token()


@db.track_status("status", changed_at="status_changed_at")
class Order(Model):
    id: UUID = uuid_pk(version=7)
    status: str = "draft"
    status_changed_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now)
```

`@db.soft_delete(column="archived_at", clock=...)` and
`@db.track_status(field="state", changed_at="state_changed_at", clock=...)`
can use custom declared columns. Decorators validate columns and types when the
model is registered; tracked status decorators can be stacked. The supplied
clock is used for managed timestamps, otherwise the model's
`@db.timestamps(clock=...)` clock is used.

On a soft-delete model, `all()`, `filter()` and model lookups see live rows
only. `with_deleted()` includes every row and `only_deleted()` selects deleted
rows. Instance `asoft_delete()` / `soft_delete()` and `arestore()` / `restore()`
run normal save hooks. `is_deleted` reports the instance state. These methods
are idempotent; unsaved instances are refused. `previous(name)` returns the
stored value (or `UNSET` on a new instance), and `changed_fields` lists fields
that differ from the last snapshot.

Status tracking updates its timestamp only when an instance save actually
changes the tracked value; an explicit timestamp value is preserved. A bulk
`QuerySet.aupdate()` is a single SQL statement and cannot compare old values, so
it updates the timestamp whenever the tracked field is included in `values`,
even when the supplied status equals the current value.

Soft deletion is an `UPDATE`; database `ON DELETE CASCADE` and `RESTRICT`
actions apply only to physical `ahard_delete()` calls. Ordinary `unique=True`
and `@db.unique(...)` constraints continue to include soft-deleted rows. A
partial unique index for live rows needs a custom SQL migration.

## Relate models through a link table

`many_to_many(...)` is a class attribute, not a column: the model keeps its own columns and Hinoki generates (or adopts) a bridge model that holds the links.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
class Label(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    name: str = field(max_length=40)


class Memo(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    labels: ClassVar[ManyToMany[Label]] = many_to_many(Label, related_name="memos")
```

`Memo.__bridges__` lists the generated bridge model, `MemoLabels` on the table `<memo table>_labels`; `@db.table` on `Memo` names the bridge after the new table (set it before the first migration: later table changes are not planned as renames, see [migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md#bridge-tables-of-many-to-many-relations)). Declaration, link writes, scopes and limits are in [relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md#many-to-many).

## See also

- [Model options](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-options.md)
- [Query and write rows](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md)
- [Relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md)
- [Migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md)

# Model options

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-options.md

Options that describe a model beyond its columns are decorators, read top to
bottom like action decorators. There is no nested `class Meta`; only names stay
class keywords.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py
from datetime import datetime
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from hinoki import db
from hinoki.orm import Model, OnDelete, field, foreign_key, pk
from hinoki.utils import utc_now

# Customer is the model declared earlier in this file (see Models).


@db.unique("customer_id", "reference")
@db.indexed("customer_id", "created_at")
@db.ordered_by("-created_at", "-id")
@db.timestamps()
class Quote(Model, label="Quote", plural="Quotes"):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Customer, on_delete=OnDelete.RESTRICT, related_name="quotes"
    )
    reference: str = field(max_length=40)
    created_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now)
    updated_at: datetime = field(default_factory=utc_now)
```

| Option | Form | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| single-column index | `field(index=True)` | `CREATE INDEX` on one column |
| composite or foreign-key index | `@db.indexed("a", "b")` | `CREATE INDEX` on the columns, in order |
| composite uniqueness | `@db.unique("a", "b", name=None)` | `UNIQUE (a, b)`, named with `name=`; one column uses `field(unique=True)` |
| default order | `@db.ordered_by("-created_at", "id")` | order of queries without `order_by`; `-` is descending |
| update timestamp | `@db.timestamps()` | refreshes `updated_at` on every ORM update |
| soft delete | `@db.soft_delete("deleted_at")` | marks a nullable datetime column; `delete()` sets it and queries skip those rows ([soft delete](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md#lifecycle-utilities)) |
| status change time | `@db.track_status("status", changed_at="status_changed_at")` | records when the status column changes; decorators stack ([lifecycle utilities](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md#lifecycle-utilities)) |
| table name | `@db.table("quotes")` (optional) | replaces the derived `<app>_<models>` name |
| app part of the name | `app="sales"` (class keyword, optional) | replaces `<app>`; ignored with an explicit table |
| display names | `label=`, `plural=` (class keywords, optional) | replace the derived singular and plural |

Every option decorator is reached through `from hinoki import db`. The same
objects are also importable from `hinoki.orm`, which keeps older imports such
as `from hinoki.orm import unique, timestamps` working.

## Composite uniqueness

`@db.unique("a", "b")` adds `UNIQUE (a, b)` to the table; it needs two or more
distinct columns. A single column uses `field(unique=True)`.

```python
@db.unique("customer_id", "reference", name="uq_quotes_customer_reference")
class Quote(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(Customer, on_delete=OnDelete.RESTRICT)
    reference: str = field(max_length=40)
```

* Without `name=` the backend names the constraint. With it, the migration
  renders `CONSTRAINT "uq_quotes_customer_reference" UNIQUE (...)` on
  PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB, so the constraint keeps a stable,
  chosen name in the database.
* A name is a letter or underscore followed by up to 62 letters, digits or
  underscores, compared without case (as MySQL and MariaDB do). Planning
  refuses a name already used by another constraint, a table, or an index or
  foreign key that Hinoki names, among the planned models and, in a project
  with `hinoki.toml`, in every app.
* Only a table model can name a constraint: on an abstract model `name=`
  raises `RegistrationError`, because every table inheriting it would repeat
  the name. Unnamed constraints are inherited as usual.
* Changing the constraints or their names on an existing table is not planned
  on PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB (write that migration by hand). SQLite
  rebuilds the table; a rename alone is not destructive, while changed columns
  are reported as destructive because existing rows may violate them.

## Indexes

Use `field(index=True)` for one ordinary column and `@db.indexed(...)` for a
composite index. A `foreign_key` has no `index=` option: index it with
`@db.indexed("customer_id")`, or with a composite index that starts with it.
The optional `HNK-DB-002` rule (`Models.require_foreign_key_index`) checks this.

* `index=` takes `True` or `False`; a primary key or unique column is already
  indexed and refuses `index=True`.
* `field(index=True)` and `@db.indexed("column")` on the same column produce
  one index.
* Names are `ix_<table>_<columns>_<digest>`, cut to the backend limit (63 bytes
  on PostgreSQL, 64 on MySQL and MariaDB); the digest keeps
  `indexed("a_b")` and `indexed("a", "b")` apart.
* Adding or removing an index is a non-destructive migration.

## Default order

`@db.ordered_by(...)` orders every query that has no `order_by`, lists and
pages included. An explicit `order_by` replaces it; counts and bulk updates
ignore it. End with a unique column (`"-id"`) so pages are stable.

## Update timestamps

`@db.timestamps()` sets a declared, non-nullable `updated_at: datetime` on every
ORM update statement, including `asave` and `abulk_update`.
`@db.timestamps("modified_at", clock=my_clock)` names another column or injects
a clock. The parentheses are required: a bare `@db.timestamps` raises
`RegistrationError`. See [utilities](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/utilities.md#model-update-timestamps).

## Names

Leave the table name derived for new models. Pin it with `@db.table(...)` when
the model has migration history and its class or module may change: a changed
derived name is planned as a guarded drop and create, never a rename. Naming
the table twice with different names (`@db.table` twice, or with `table=`) is
an error naming both. Use `label=`/`plural=` for irregular or localized nouns.
See [table and display names](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md#table-and-display-names).

## Rules for all options

* Column names are checked when the decorator runs; a typo fails at import with
  the model and the unknown names.
* Apply options before the model is used: the migration planner, the query
  layer and the admin read them from the class.
* Options of [abstract bases](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md#share-fields-abstract-models-and-mixins)
  are inherited; a decorator on the subclass replaces that kind of option. A
  table model does not pass its options to a subclass.

!!! note "Not yet"
    Partial and expression indexes are not available.

## See also

- [Define models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md)
- [Migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md)

# Relations

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md

A relation is an ordinary foreign-key column. Related rows load only when a
query asks for them: attribute access never performs I/O.

## Declare a foreign key

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py
from typing import ClassVar
from uuid import UUID, uuid4

from hinoki import db
from hinoki.orm import Model, OnDelete, Related, field, foreign_key, pk


class Customer(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    name: str = field(max_length=120)
    invoices: ClassVar["Related[list[Invoice]]"]


@db.indexed("customer_id")
class Invoice(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Customer, on_delete=OnDelete.RESTRICT, related_name="invoices"
    )
    reference: str = field(max_length=40, unique=True)
    customer: ClassVar[Related[Customer]]
```

`customer_id` is stored on `billing_invoices`. `invoice.customer` is the
forward relation (named after the column without `_id`); `customer.invoices` is
the reverse relation, created only when `related_name` is set. The
`ClassVar[Related[...]]` lines are for type checkers. The column type must match
the referenced primary key.

`on_delete` is required and takes an `OnDelete` member:

| `on_delete` | When the referenced row is deleted |
| --- | --- |
| `OnDelete.RESTRICT` | the delete is refused while references exist |
| `OnDelete.CASCADE` | referencing rows are deleted too |
| `OnDelete.SET_NULL` | the column becomes `NULL`; the field must be `\| None` |
| `OnDelete.NO_ACTION` | like `RESTRICT`, checked at the end of the statement |

A refused delete raises `hinoki.db.DatabaseError` (`database request failed`),
not `UniqueViolation`, so it is not translated to `409`: check for references
first, or register an error handler for it.

Text such as `on_delete="cascade"`, and `SET_NULL` on a non-nullable field, are
refused with `RegistrationError` at import:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
@db.indexed("invoice_id")
class Payment(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    invoice_id: UUID | None = foreign_key(
        Invoice, on_delete=OnDelete.SET_NULL, default=None
    )
```

The rule becomes the migration's `REFERENCES … ON DELETE` clause and the
database enforces it.

## Load related rows

```python
# inside an async operation
invoices = await Invoice.all().select_related("customer")
names = [invoice.customer.name for invoice in invoices]

customers = await Customer.all().prefetch_related("invoices")
counts = {c.id: len(c.invoices) for c in customers}
```

| Method | Use for | SQL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `select_related("customer")` | a forward foreign key (one row) | one `LEFT JOIN` in the same statement |
| `prefetch_related("invoices")` | a reverse or collection relation | separate, bounded queries per owner chunk |

Reading a relation that was not loaded raises `RelationNotLoaded`. `acount()`
and `apaginate()` drop a `select_related` join from their `COUNT` (a to-one
join cannot change the count) but keep a join a filter needs, such as
`customer__name=...`.

## One-to-one

A one-to-one relation is a foreign key with `unique=True`:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
class BillingProfile(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Customer, on_delete=OnDelete.CASCADE, unique=True, related_name="profile"
    )
    vat_number: str = field(max_length=20)
    customer: ClassVar[Related[Customer]]
```

Add `profile: ClassVar["Related[BillingProfile | None]"]` to `Customer` for
type checkers. `profile.customer` has one required target; `customer.profile` is
`BillingProfile | None`. Load them with `select_related("customer")` and
`prefetch_related("profile")`. If the database has drifted and holds several
rows for one customer, `prefetch_related` raises `MultipleObjectsReturned`.

The migration creates the foreign key and the unique constraint together. It
fails on existing duplicates; clean them up first. Turning an existing foreign
key into `unique=True` rebuilds the table on SQLite and needs a hand-written
migration on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB.

## Many-to-many

Declare the relation on a model; Hinoki generates and migrates the bridge table
(`<owner table>_<name>`, one column per side, a composite unique constraint).

```python
class Tag(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    name: str = field(max_length=40, unique=True)


class Post(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    title: str = field(max_length=80)
    tags: ClassVar[ManyToMany[Tag]] = many_to_many(
        Tag, related_name="posts", ids_name="tag_ids"
    )
```

```python
# inside an async operation
await post.tags.aadd(red, blue)  # idempotent
await post.tags.aset([red], within=Tag.filter(owner=user))
tags = await post.tags.alist()
posts = await Post.filter(tags__name="red").prefetch_related("tags")
print(posts[0].tags.loaded, posts[0].tag_ids)  # only after prefetch_related
```

`aadd`, `aremove` and `aset` take model instances or keys, run in one
transaction that locks the owner row, and refuse more than `max_items` links
(`LinkLimitExceeded`). With `within=` a key outside that query is treated as
missing (`UnknownLinkTarget`, a `422`), and `aset` replaces only the links
inside the scope. `ids_name` (default `<name>_ids`) names the ids field that
[generated CRUD](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#many-to-many-fields) and `derive` use (`derive` takes it only when `only=` names it). `within` is keyword-only on every read and write of the relation, and `prefetch_related(tags=queryset)` loads only targets in that queryset.
The `max_items` limit applies from both ends. A write through the reverse
relation (`tag.posts`) locks the declaring rows it touches that the caller may
see (the `within=` scope applies, so a row outside it is neither locked nor
revealed), in key order, and
refuses (`LinkLimitExceeded`) a write that would leave one of them past its own
`max_items`, so the limit cannot be raced past from either side; the reverse
relation itself holds the library-wide cap. Both ends lock in one order, the
declaring rows first and then the owner row, so two writers on opposite ends
never wait for each other. A refused write (`LinkLimitExceeded`,
`UnknownLinkTarget`) undoes its own statements in a savepoint, so a handler
that catches the error and commits leaves no link behind. Reading links stored
beyond `max_items` (the data broke its bound) raises `StoredLinksOverLimit`, a
server fault (`500`), not a validation error. Every write also locks the owner row
and re-checks it against the owner scope of generated CRUD and the admin inside
that lock, so a row that left the caller's scope reads as missing. The targets a
write resolves are held (`FOR KEY SHARE` on PostgreSQL, `LOCK IN SHARE MODE` on
MySQL and MariaDB) until the commit, so a target deleted at the same moment
either makes the write fail with `UnknownLinkTarget` or removes the new link
with it; on MySQL and MariaDB the reads that decide a write use locking reads,
because a transaction there reads one snapshot. SQLite has a single writer.
For each chunk of owners, the many-to-many prefetch runs one bounded query
from the target table with an inner join to the bridge. It returns one target
row per link, so a target shared by owners is repeated in the result. Each
statement sees its chunk under the database's transaction isolation; different
chunks can observe different states. Rust builds and groups eligible model
rows, and Python orchestrates the queries, shares instances across chunks and
stores the loaded relations. Custom row builders use the Python fallback.

`prefetch_related` orders targets by the target's default ordering (else its
key), with the primary key as the final tie-breaker. NULL sorts before values
in ascending order and after values in descending order, including on
PostgreSQL. A scoped query may supply an ordering when the model has a default
ordering.
When the target model is soft-deleting, a deleted target is not linked: reads,
filters and prefetches skip it, adding it raises `UnknownLinkTarget`, it does
not count towards `max_items`, and `aset`/`aremove` leave its link alone unless
`within=Tag.with_deleted()` reaches it. A restored target is linked again.
`bridge="PostTag"` adopts a model you wrote instead of generating one (a bridge
that is never defined raises `RegistrationError` at startup, in `hinoki check`
and when planning migrations), and an
association model with extra columns stays available as in earlier releases
(declare two foreign keys and a composite unique constraint).

### An association model with its own columns

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
class Tag(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    name: str = field(max_length=40, unique=True)
    invoice_links: ClassVar["Related[list[InvoiceTag]]"]


@db.unique("invoice_id", "tag_id")
@db.indexed("tag_id")
class InvoiceTag(Model):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
    invoice_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Invoice, on_delete=OnDelete.CASCADE, related_name="tag_links"
    )
    tag_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Tag, on_delete=OnDelete.CASCADE, related_name="invoice_links"
    )
```

The composite unique constraint stops duplicate pairs and indexes `invoice_id`;
`@db.indexed("tag_id")` indexes the other side. Link and read:

```python
# inside an async operation
tag = await Tag.acreate(name="priority")
await InvoiceTag.acreate(invoice_id=invoice.id, tag_id=tag.id)

links = await InvoiceTag.filter(invoice_id=invoice.id).select_related("tag")
tag_names = [link.tag.name for link in links]
```

`invoice.tag_links` holds `InvoiceTag` rows (load it with
`prefetch_related("tag_links")`), not `Tag` objects. The association model can
carry its own columns, such as when the tag was added.

## Foreign keys in abstract models and mixins

A foreign key in an [abstract model or mixin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md#share-fields-abstract-models-and-mixins)
is registered once per table model that inherits it. Give the reverse relation
a per-model name with the `{model}` placeholder (the class name in lower case):

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
class CustomerOwned(Model, abstract=True):
    customer_id: UUID = foreign_key(
        Customer, on_delete=OnDelete.CASCADE, related_name="{model}_set"
    )


class CreditNote(CustomerOwned):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)


class Estimate(CustomerOwned):
    id: UUID = pk(default_factory=uuid4)
```

`Customer` gets `creditnote_set` and `estimate_set`. A fixed `related_name`
makes the second inheriting model fail with an error naming both. Without
`related_name` there is no reverse relation. A foreign key cannot reference an
abstract model. `{model}` is the only placeholder.

## See also

- [Query and write rows](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md)
- [Migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md): foreign-key changes and backend notes

# Query and write rows

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md

Queries are explicit: nothing runs until you evaluate a query, values are bound
parameters, and relations load only when you ask. Examples use the Billing
models from [Define models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md).

## Query rows

=== "Async"

    ```python
    # inside an async operation or handler
    invoice = await Invoice.aget(id=invoice_id)
    maybe = await Invoice.aget_or_none(reference="INV-7")
    unpaid = await Invoice.filter(customer_id=customer.id, paid=False).order_by("reference")
    first = await Invoice.filter(paid=False).afirst()
    count = await Invoice.filter(paid=False).acount()
    page = await Invoice.all().apaginate(PageParams(page=1, page_size=20))
    projected = await Invoice.filter(paid=False).order_by("reference").aproject(InvoiceOut)
    one_projected = await Invoice.aget_as(InvoiceOut, id=invoice_id)
    maybe_projected = await Invoice.aget_or_none_as(InvoiceOut, reference="INV-7")
    ```

=== "Sync"

    ```python
    # inside a sync handler (runs in the bounded worker pool)
    invoice = Invoice.get(id=invoice_id)
    maybe = Invoice.get_or_none(reference="INV-7")
    unpaid = (
        Invoice.filter(customer_id=customer.id, paid=False).order_by("reference").list()
    )
    first = Invoice.filter(paid=False).first()
    count = Invoice.filter(paid=False).count()
    page = Invoice.all().paginate(PageParams(page=1, page_size=20))
    projected = Invoice.filter(paid=False).order_by("reference").project(InvoiceOut)
    one_projected = Invoice.get_as(InvoiceOut, id=invoice_id)
    maybe_projected = Invoice.get_or_none_as(InvoiceOut, reference="INV-7")
    ```

`PageParams` comes from `hinoki.pagination`. `aget` and `aget_as` raise
`Invoice.NotFound` (a 404 in a request) or `MultipleObjectsReturned`. Building a
query (`filter`, `order_by`, `limit`, `offset`, `select_related`,
`prefetch_related`) issues no SQL; awaiting it or calling an evaluation method
does. `aproject` / `project`, `apaginate_as` / `paginate_as`, `aget_as` /
`get_as`, and `aget_or_none_as` / `get_or_none_as` encode eligible scalar,
`select_related`, and 1-level `prefetch_related` (reverse foreign keys and
many-to-many) schemas directly from Rust rows, materializing Python `Schema`
instances lazily from the owned rows if inspected and falling back transparently
when hooks, computed fields, validators, or scoped prefetches are present. A projected item passes `isinstance`, `dataclasses.is_dataclass`, `dataclasses.asdict`, `dataclasses.replace` and `copy.replace` as the `Schema` itself. `dataclasses.fields(type(item))` sees no fields (the class of a projected item is not the `Schema`); use `dataclasses.fields(item)`.

## Query methods

Every read and write entry point has an async form (`a*`) for `async def`
handlers and a matching sync form for `def` handlers.

### Starting a query on `Model`

| Method | Returns | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Model.all()` | `QuerySet[M]` | All rows (live rows only on `@db.soft_delete()` models). |
| `Model.filter(**conditions)` | `QuerySet[M]` | Shortcut for `Model.all().filter(**conditions)`. |
| `Model.with_deleted()` | `QuerySet[M]` | Includes soft-deleted rows on `@db.soft_delete()` models. |
| `Model.only_deleted()` | `QuerySet[M]` | Only soft-deleted rows on `@db.soft_delete()` models. |
| `Model.aget(**conditions)` / `Model.get(...)` | `M` | Fetch exactly one row; raises `Model.NotFound` or `MultipleObjectsReturned`. |
| `Model.aget_or_none(**conditions)` / `Model.get_or_none(...)` | `M \| None` | Fetch one row or `None`; still raises `MultipleObjectsReturned` if more than one matches. |

### Chainable `QuerySet` methods

These methods return a new `QuerySet` without touching the database.

| Method | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `.filter(**conditions)` | Add one or more `AND` conditions (`field=value` or `field__op=value`). |
| `.order_by(*names)` | Sort ascending (`"issued_at"`) or descending (`"-issued_at"`). Overrides `@db.ordered_by`. |
| `.limit(count)` | Cap the number of returned rows. |
| `.offset(count)` | Skip the first `count` rows. |
| `.select_related(*names)` | Load forward foreign-key relations in the same query (`JOIN`). See [Relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md). |
| `.prefetch_related(*names, **scoped)` | Load forward, reverse, or many-to-many relations in bounded follow-up queries. Many-to-many links accept scoped querysets (`prefetch_related(tags=Tag.filter(...))`). |

### Evaluating a `QuerySet` (reads)

| Async | Sync | Returns | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `await qs` | `qs.list()` | `list[M]` | Fetch all matching model instances. |
| `await qs.afirst()` | `qs.first()` | `M \| None` | First matching row, or `None`. |
| `await qs.aget()` | `qs.get()` | `M` | Exactly one matching row; raises `Model.NotFound` or `MultipleObjectsReturned`. |
| `await qs.acount()` | `qs.count()` | `int` | Count matching rows (ignores `order_by`). |
| `await qs.aexists()` | `qs.exists()` | `bool` | `True` if at least one row matches. |
| `await qs.aproject(Schema)` | `qs.project(Schema)` | `list[S]` | Project matching rows to a `Schema` via the lazy Rust row path when eligible. |
| `await qs.apaginate(params=None, *, concurrent=False)` | `qs.paginate(...)` | `Page[M]` | Offset page plus `total`. `concurrent=True` runs rows and count concurrently outside a transaction. |
| `await qs.apaginate_as(Schema, params=None, *, concurrent=False)` | `qs.paginate_as(...)` | `Page[S]` | Offset page projected to `Schema` via the lazy Rust row path. |
| `await qs.apaginate_cursor(params)` | `qs.paginate_cursor(params)` | `CursorPage[M]` | Keyset page using a signed cursor, with no `COUNT` query. |

* `apaginate` runs the count and the page as two statements; concurrent writes
  can make `total` and `items` disagree slightly. `apaginate_cursor` runs one
  statement and no count; see [cursor pagination](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md#cursor-keyset-pagination).
* `@db.ordered_by` applies only when a query has no `order_by`. Counts and bulk
  updates ignore it.

### Write and soft-delete methods

| Async | Sync | Target | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Model.acreate(data=None, /, *, returning=True, **values)` | `Model.create(...)` | `Model` | Insert one row from a `Schema` and/or server keywords. |
| `row.asave()` | `row.save()` | instance | Persist changed columns on an existing instance. |
| `row.aupdate_from(data=None, /, **values)` | `row.update_from(...)` | instance | Apply a `Schema` / keywords and save changed columns. |
| `Model.aupdate(*, returning=True, **values)` | `Model.update(...)` | `Model` | Update one row by primary key; raises `NotFound` if missing (`returning=True`). |
| `Model.aupdate_where(conditions, values, *, returning=True)` | `Model.update_where(...)` | `Model` | Conditional `UPDATE` matching `conditions` (supports `field__op`). |
| `qs.aupdate(values, *, returning=True)` | `qs.update(...)` | `QuerySet` | Update all matching rows (refuses `limit`/`offset`). |
| `Model.adelete(**conditions)` / `qs.adelete()` | `delete(...)` | `Model` / `QuerySet` | Delete matching rows (sets delete timestamp on `@db.soft_delete()` models). |
| `row.asoft_delete()` | `row.soft_delete()` | instance | Soft-delete one `@db.soft_delete()` instance. |
| `row.arestore()` / `qs.arestore()` | `restore()` | instance / `QuerySet` | Clear the soft-delete timestamp (`Model.only_deleted().filter(...).arestore()`). |
| `row.ahard_delete()` / `qs.ahard_delete()` | `hard_delete()` | instance / `QuerySet` | Physical SQL `DELETE` on a `@db.soft_delete()` model. |
| `Model.abulk_create(items, *, returning=True)` | `Model.bulk_create(...)` | `Model` | Insert many `Schema` objects or dicts in one transaction/savepoint. |
| `Model.abulk_update(instances)` | `Model.bulk_update(...)` | `Model` | Save changed instances in one transaction/savepoint. |
| `Model.abulk_delete(items)` | `Model.bulk_delete(...)` | `Model` | Delete instances or primary keys in chunks of up to 10 000. |

## Filter operators

`filter(field=value)` and `filter(field__op=value)` accept model field names and
a fixed set of lookup operators compiled in Rust. Every condition in a
`filter(...)` call (or chained `.filter(...).filter(...)`) is combined with
`AND`, values are bound parameters, and SQL identifiers come from model
metadata.

| Lookup | Example | Compiled SQL | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| *(exact)* | `paid=False` | `paid = $1` | Passing `None` (`voided_at=None`) compiles to `IS NULL`. |
| `ne` | `status__ne="draft"` | `status <> $1` | Passing `None` compiles to `IS NOT NULL`. For non-`None` values, `NULL` rows do not match. |
| `gt` | `total__gt=100` | `total > $1` | Rejects `None` (`FieldError`). |
| `gte` | `total__gte=100` | `total >= $1` | Rejects `None` (`FieldError`). |
| `lt` | `total__lt=500` | `total < $1` | Rejects `None` (`FieldError`). |
| `lte` | `total__lte=500` | `total <= $1` | Rejects `None` (`FieldError`). |
| `in` | `status__in=["open", "overdue"]` | `status IN ($1, $2)` | Takes a sequence/set; rejects `str` and `bytes` (`FieldError`) so strings are never split by character. |
| `isnull` | `voided_at__isnull=True` | `voided_at IS NULL` | `False` compiles to `IS NOT NULL`. |
| `contains` | `reference__contains="inv-"` | case-insensitive `LIKE` | Escapes `%`, `_` and `\` literally. Rejected on `Decimal` columns (`FieldError`). |

* `field__ne=value` compiles to `<>`: rows where the column is `NULL` are not
  returned. Add an `isnull` filter when they matter.
* `contains` matches text case-insensitively and treats `%`, `_` and `\`
  literally. SQLite folds ASCII case only; MySQL and MariaDB assume the
  `NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES` mode is off (the default).
* Passing `None` with any operator other than exact equality or `ne` raises
  `FieldError`.

### Filtering across relations

* **Forward foreign keys**: traverse a foreign-key relation with `__` and any
  operator above:

  ```python
  invoices = await Invoice.filter(customer__name__contains="acme", paid=False)
  ```

  Hinoki adds the required `JOIN` automatically and matches only live rows when
  the target model uses `@db.soft_delete()`.
* **Many-to-many links**: filter on a target field (`tags__slug="rust"`) or
  test whether any live link exists (`tags__isnull=True` / `False`):

  ```python
  rust_posts = await Post.filter(tags__slug="rust")
  untagged = await Post.filter(tags__isnull=True)
  ```

  Many-to-many filters compile to a subquery against the bridge table and ignore
  soft-deleted targets. `<link>__isnull` cannot be combined with other
  conditions on the same link.
* **Reverse foreign keys**: filtering from the parent across a reverse relation
  raises `FieldError`; query the child model directly instead.

### Client query filters (`FilterSet`)

For generated CRUD list endpoints, declare accepted HTTP query parameters with
`FilterSet` from `hinoki.filters` instead of passing raw query parameters to
`filter()`. Only declared fields and shapes are accepted; validation and query
compilation run in Rust.

| Declaration | Query string | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `paid: Eq[bool]` | `?paid=false` | Exact match (`=`). |
| `status: In[Literal["open", "paid"]]` | `?status=open,paid` | Membership (`IN`, up to 50 comma-separated values). |
| `issued: Range[date]` | `?issued.from=2026-01-01&issued.to=2026-01-31` | Inclusive bounds (`>=` / `<=`); either end is optional (`Bounds[T]`). |
| `search = Search("reference", "notes")` | `?search=inv` | Case-insensitive `contains` matching any listed text column. |
| `ordering = ("issued", "reference")` | `?ordering=-issued` | Allowed sort columns; prefix `-` for descending. |

Supported scalar types for `Eq`, `In`, and `Range` are `bool`, `int`, `float`,
`str`, `Literal["..."]`, `UUID`, `date`, `datetime`, and `Decimal` (optionally
nullable with `| None`). See [Generate CRUD routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md) for full `FilterSet`
usage.

## Reusable queries

A reusable query is a typed class method returning a `QuerySet`. There is no
hidden manager: `Model.all()` means every live row on a soft-delete model and
every row on an ordinary model.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
from typing import Self

from hinoki.orm import QuerySet


class Invoice(Model):
    ...  # fields as in Define models
    voided_at: datetime | None = None

    @classmethod
    def open(cls) -> QuerySet[Self]:
        return cls.filter(voided_at=None, paid=False)
```

Pass it where the framework asks for a base query, so every operation sees the
same rows:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/api.py
from typing import Any

from hinoki import API, Caller, crud
from hinoki.admin import ModelAdmin
from hinoki.filters import Eq, FilterSet
from hinoki.orm import QuerySet

from notes.security import billing_staff

from .models import Invoice
from .schemas import InvoiceOut


class InvoiceFilters(FilterSet):
    paid: Eq[bool]


@crud(
    Invoice,
    path="/invoices",
    read=InvoiceOut,
    access=billing_staff,
    filters=InvoiceFilters,
)
class Invoices(API):
    def get_queryset(self, principal: Caller[Any] | None) -> QuerySet[Invoice]:
        return Invoice.open()


class InvoiceAdmin(ModelAdmin[Invoice]):
    def queryset(self, principal: Caller[Any]) -> QuerySet[Invoice]:
        return Invoice.open()
```

| Rule | Where |
| --- | --- |
| row order | `@db.ordered_by(...)` ([model options](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-options.md)) |
| an app-wide policy, such as hiding voided rows | a named class method, used in `get_queryset()` and `ModelAdmin.queryset()` |
| rows that depend on the caller | `get_queryset(principal)` or `ModelAdmin.queryset(principal)` |

!!! warning "Not a security boundary"
    `Model.all()` and raw SQL skip a reusable query. Keep ownership and
    permissions in `access=`, `owner=` and `ModelAdmin.can()`.

## Create and update

```python
# inside an async operation
invoice = await Invoice.acreate(InvoiceIn(reference="INV-8"), customer_id=customer.id)
invoice.paid = True
await invoice.asave()  # updates the changed columns
await invoice.aupdate_from(InvoicePatch(paid=False))
changed = await Invoice.aupdate_where({"id": invoice.id, "paid": False}, {"paid": True})
```

* Keywords set by the server win over values from a `Schema`; a `Schema` never
  carries the primary key.
* `asave()` writes changed columns and refuses a primary-key change.
* `aupdate_where(conditions, values)` puts ownership and state checks in the
  SQL condition: use it for conditional writes instead of read-then-write.
* `QuerySet.aupdate(values)` and `adelete()` act on every matching row, ignore
  ordering and refuse a query with `limit` or `offset`; select the keys first
  and filter on `id__in=[...]`.

On a model decorated with `@db.soft_delete()`, `adelete()` / `delete()` sets the
delete timestamp with a scoped `UPDATE`; use `arestore()` / `restore()` to clear
it, and `ahard_delete()` / `hard_delete()` for a physical `DELETE`. Model
queries are live-only by default; `Model.with_deleted()` and
`Model.only_deleted()` are explicit class-level scopes. Relations use the live
scope too: reverse relations, many-to-many links, and forward
`select_related`/`prefetch_related`, where a referenced soft-deleted row reads
as `None`. A filter across a relation (`parent__name=...`) joins live rows
only.

For `@db.track_status()`, instance saves bump `changed_at` only when the value
actually changes. Bulk `QuerySet.aupdate()` cannot compare stored values and
bumps the timestamp whenever the tracked field appears in `values`, including
when it equals the stored value.

## Writing many rows at once

`abulk_create`, `abulk_update` and `abulk_delete` (sync `bulk_*`) each run in
one transaction, or a savepoint inside an open one:

```python
# inside an async operation
rows = await Invoice.abulk_create(
    [
        {"reference": "A-1", "customer_id": customer.id},
        {"reference": "A-2", "customer_id": customer.id},
    ]
)
rows[0].paid = True
await Invoice.abulk_update(rows)  # saves changed rows only
deleted = await Invoice.abulk_delete([rows[0], rows[1].id])  # instances or keys
```

* `abulk_create` takes `Schema` objects or dicts, each carrying every required
  value, and returns the rows in order; defaults, factories, validation and
  hooks apply as for `acreate`. It takes no server keywords: put them in each
  item.
* `abulk_update` refuses an unsaved instance and returns every instance it
  was given, unchanged ones included; `abulk_delete` returns how many
  rows existed, deletes in chunks of at most 10 000 keys and runs no hooks.
* One statement per row (per chunk for deletes): these give atomicity, not a
  batching speed-up.

## Writes that do not read the row back

By default a write returns the stored row (`RETURNING` on PostgreSQL and SQLite,
a follow-up `SELECT` in the same transaction on MySQL and MariaDB).
`returning=False` skips that:

```python
# inside an async operation
draft = await Invoice.acreate(reference="D-1", customer_id=customer.id, returning=False)
count = await Invoice.aupdate(id=draft.id, paid=True, returning=False)
count = await Invoice.filter(customer_id=customer.id).aupdate(
    {"paid": False}, returning=False
)
```

| Method | Default | `returning=False` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `acreate`, `insert` | the stored row | the same instance, holding the sent values |
| `aupdate` | the stored row; `NotFound` when nothing matches | `int` row count; `0`, no `NotFound` |
| `aupdate_where`, `QuerySet.aupdate` | `list` of stored rows | `int` row count |

Nothing is re-read: database-side changes (timestamp precision, numeric scale,
JSON normalization, triggers) are not reflected; read with `aget` when you need
them. `@db.timestamps()` and validation still run. PostgreSQL and SQLite count
matched rows; MySQL and MariaDB count rows whose values changed. A model cannot
declare a field named `returning`.

## See also

- [Relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md): `select_related` and `prefetch_related`
- [Generate CRUD routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md): `FilterSet` client query parameters
- [Model options](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-options.md): `@db.soft_delete()`, `@db.ordered_by()`, `@db.timestamps()`
- [Lifecycle hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-hooks.md)
- [Transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md)
- [Typing](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/typing.md): what type checkers see for keyword-based methods

# Lifecycle hooks

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-hooks.md

A model can react to its own writes with `before_save`, `before_create`,
`after_create` and `after_save`. Each is an ordinary method, `def` or
`async def`, taking only `self`. A model without hooks pays nothing.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/models.py (continued)
import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class Invoice(Model):
    ...  # fields as in Define models

    def before_save(self) -> None:
        if self.was_changed("reference"):
            self.reference = self.reference.strip().upper()

    async def after_create(self) -> None:
        self.after_commit(lambda: log.info("invoice %s created", self.id))
```

## Order

| Write | Hooks |
| --- | --- |
| insert (`acreate`, `insert`, `asave` of a new instance) | `before_save`, `before_create`, write, `after_create`, `after_save` |
| update (`asave` of a loaded instance, `aupdate_from`) | `before_save`, write, `after_save` |

`before_*` hooks may change the values about to be written. `after_*` hooks see
the stored row (generated keys, database defaults, `@db.timestamps()`). An update
with no changed column after `before_save` writes nothing and skips
`after_save`. To extend an inherited hook, call `super()`.

## Instance state

| Member | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `is_new` | `True` until the row is written or loaded; still `True` inside the hooks of an insert |
| `is_dirty` | `True` for a new instance or when a column differs from the stored row |
| `changes` | `{column: Change(old, new)}`; a new instance lists every column with `old=UNSET` |
| `was_changed("reference")` | whether one column differs; an unknown name raises `FieldError` |

Stored values are refreshed after the `after_*` hooks, so `changes` still shows
this write's changes while they run.

## Transactions and `after_commit`

With any hook defined, the write runs in a transaction (a savepoint inside an
open one): an exception in a hook rolls the write back and reaches the caller.
A hook that opens its own `db.atomic()` fails with `DatabaseError` (`nested
atomic scopes (savepoints) must be opened by the task that owns the
transaction`) when a sync write runs inside a sync handler's
`with db.atomic():`; from async code it nests as a savepoint.
`after_*` hooks run before the commit. Work that must happen only after it goes
through `self.after_commit(callback)`, a sync or async callable without
arguments. Callbacks run in order after the outermost commit; a rollback drops
them; an exception in one is logged and does not undo the commit. See
[transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md#after-commit-callbacks).

## Limits

* Hooks belong to instances: `QuerySet.aupdate`, `adelete`, `Model.aupdate`,
  `aupdate_where` and raw SQL do not run them.
* Events complete hooks for code that is not the model: `Created`, `Updated`
  and `Deleted` [model events](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md#model-events) fire from the same
  writes (and from `adelete`), with handlers registered per application
  instead of overridden on the class. `after_commit` on a model and
  `db.after_commit` keep working unchanged.
* Sync hooks run inline on the event loop: keep them short and use
  `async def` for I/O.
* `is_new`, `is_dirty`, `changes`, `was_changed`, `after_commit` and the four
  hook names are reserved field names.
* From a helper task of a transaction (the sync model methods of a sync
  handler), a hooked write joins that transaction; an error still rolls the
  whole transaction back.
* A hook assigned to the class after creation is used from the next write.
* Generated CRUD and the admin's create and edit forms save through the same
  methods, so hooks run there too; deletes run none
  ([CRUD](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#model-hooks-and-kiso)).

## See also

- [Query and write rows](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md)
- [Transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md)

# Events

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md

An event is a class; a handler is a function registered for that class. Events let one part of an application announce that something happened without importing the parts that react. Nothing registers by import: the application lists its handler collections, and the order they run in is the order of that list.

Events are typed (mypy checks the payload), they have no string names, and the moment a handler runs is part of how you register it. Events are not a message queue: delivery stays inside one worker process, with no retry and no at-least-once guarantee.

## A minimal example

```python
from hinoki import Hinoki, Schema, events, http


class NoteSaved(Schema):
    text: str


class Saved(Schema):
    status: str


handlers = events.Handlers("notes")


@handlers.after_commit(NoteSaved)
async def tell_search(event: NoteSaved) -> None:
    print("index", event.text)


@http.post("/notes", access=None)
async def save() -> Saved:
    await events.emit(NoteSaved(text="hello"))
    return Saved(status="saved")


app = Hinoki(events=[handlers], include=[save])
```

`events=` and `include=` are passed by hand here because the example is one file. A project lists the collection in `hinoki.toml` instead ([below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md#declaring-handlers-in-hinokitoml)). The [Tracker example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/tracker/tracker/apps/activity/events.py) keeps its handlers in `tracker/apps/activity/events.py`, and the [Blog example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/apps/blog/events.py) also emits its own event from an action.

Your own events can be a `Schema` (as above: frozen, keyword-only and validated when built) or a frozen `dataclass`; registration accepts any class. A `Schema` costs a validation per event, and it cannot hold a model class or instance, so the built-in model events below (`subject: type[M]`, `instance: M`) are dataclasses and an event that carries a row should carry its identifier instead.

`events.emit` uses the bus of the current worker. Outside a request, a startup hook or a management command it raises `EventError` unless you wrap the code in `events.use(app.events)`.

## Two moments, named in the registration

| Decorator | Runs | May fail the write | Function kind |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@handlers.in_transaction(E)` | Inside the writer's transaction, when the event is emitted | Yes: an exception rolls the transaction back | `async def` only |
| `@handlers.after_commit(E)` | After the outermost transaction commits | No | `def` or `async def` |

- An `in_transaction` handler must be quick and may only use the active transaction's connection. It is `async def` only because its timeout can be enforced on awaiting code only, and a synchronous call on another thread cannot join a transaction another task opened. Emitting such an event with no transaction active raises `EventError`.
- An `after_commit` handler is queued on the transaction and dropped if the transaction (or its savepoint) rolls back. Outside a transaction it runs at once. Its failure is logged, counted and never propagated: the write has already committed. A plain `def` runs on the bounded sync executor.
- A handler that writes to the database from `after_commit` must open its own transaction.

## Typing and subjects

A handler's first parameter is annotated with the event class, and the registration is checked against it when the collection is built: a missing or mismatched annotation raises `EventRegistrationError` at startup, not at the first emit. An event with a `subject` attribute (a model class, for example) can be registered as `Event[Note]` to receive only that subject, or bare `Event` to receive every subject (annotate it `Event[Any]`).

## Order and limits

Handlers run in the order of the `events=` collections, then in registration order inside each collection. The limits are the `events` settings:

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `events.handler_timeout` | `5.0` | Seconds each handler may run; `EventTimeout` when exceeded. |
| `events.max_handlers` | `16` | Handlers per (event, phase); registering more raises `EventRegistrationError`. |
| `events.max_depth` | `4` | How deep handlers may emit events from handlers; more raises `EventError`, which stops cycles. |

An `in_transaction` failure or timeout propagates to the writer, which rolls back before any HTTP error is translated. An `after_commit` failure is isolated: the remaining handlers still run.

## Declaring handlers in `hinoki.toml`

```toml
[[apps]]
name = "activity"
models = "tracker.apps.activity.models"
migrations = "tracker.apps.activity.migrations"
routes = "tracker.apps.activity.api:routes"
events = "tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers"
requires = ["tasks", "members"]
```

```python
from hinoki import Hinoki

app = Hinoki()  # reads routes, events, middleware and rules from hinoki.toml
```

Events stay per app because a handler belongs to the models and behaviour of one app and runs in dependency order, whereas [middleware](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md#declaring-middleware-in-hinokitoml) and [rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-rules-run) are project-wide lists. When the manifest's `project.application` names the module that builds the app, `Hinoki()` loads `events=` if you did not pass it (independently of `include=`, `middleware=` and `rules=`); an explicit argument (even `()`) wins and skips that key. `manifest_events()` does the same load explicitly, for combining lists or building an app elsewhere. It imports each app's `Handlers` in dependency order (`requires`) and fails with a message naming the app when the target does not import or is not a `Handlers`. Hinoki does not generate the module: you create it yourself (for example `tracker/apps/activity/events.py` with `handlers = events.Handlers("activity")`, as in the Tracker example) and name it in the key, so there is no template to copy and a mistyped target is reported when the application is built. `hinoki app add notes --models ... --events pkg.events:handlers` registers an existing one; `hinoki app list` shows it.

## Testing

```python
with app.events.capture() as seen:
    ...  # code under test emits events
assert seen == [NoteSaved(text="hello")]

with app.events.muted():
    ...  # events emitted here run no handler
```

`capture()` records every event emitted in the block and still runs the handlers; `muted()` runs no handler (`capture()` still records what is emitted). `app.events.stats()` returns the counters of `(event, phase, outcome)`, which are low-cardinality by construction. `app.events.registrations` lists what is registered.

## Seeing what is registered

`hinoki events` lists every handler of the application without starting a server, opening a database or writing anything. It builds the application the way `hinoki routes` does and takes the same optional target (default: the project's `application`).

From `examples/tracker`:

```sh
uv run hinoki events
```

```text
Created[Task]  in_transaction  activity     async  tracker.apps.activity.events.task_created
Updated[Task]  in_transaction  activity     async  tracker.apps.activity.events.task_updated

limits: events.handler_timeout=5.0, events.max_handlers=16, events.max_depth=4
declared in hinoki.toml: activity -> tracker.apps.activity.events:handlers
```

Each row is the event (`Event` or `Event[Model]`), the phase, the name of the `Handlers` collection (`-` when it has none), `async` or `sync`, and the handler as `module.qualname`, in execution order. The last line shows the `events` limits in force. In a project, a line `declared in hinoki.toml: APP -> module:attribute` follows for each app that sets `events` in `hinoki.toml`. An application with no handlers prints `no event handlers registered` and exits `0`. `--format json` prints an object with `handlers` (`event`, `phase`, `handler`, `collection`, `async`), `limits` (`handler_timeout`, `max_handlers`, `max_depth`) and `apps` (`app`, `events`). A target that cannot be loaded prints `error: cannot load TARGET: ...` and exits `2`. The listing shows what is registered, not whether a handler will run: that depends on the code that emits.

## Authentication and rate-limit events

These events describe a request the application refused. They are plain frozen dataclasses (`Schema` cannot hold arbitrary types, and an event emitted on every refused request should cost nothing to build).

| Event | Payload | Emitted when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AuthRejected` | `reason`, `route`, `method` | A route's `Access` policy refused the request: `reason` is `"missing"` (no credentials, `401`), `"invalid"` (credentials the provider rejected, `401`) or `"forbidden"` (a caller without a required permission, `403`). Also for a WebSocket handshake (`method` is `WEBSOCKET`). |
| `RateLimited` | `policy`, `route`, `method`, `retry_after` | A route's `rate_limit` policy refused with `TooManyRequests` (`429`), including `RateLimit` and the admin's shared sign-in limit. A storage failure is not a refusal and emits no event. `policy` is the class name of the policy; `retry_after` is the whole seconds sent in `Retry-After`. |

```python
from hinoki import events
from hinoki.events import AuthRejected, RateLimited

security = events.Handlers("security")


@security.after_commit(AuthRejected)
async def count_rejection(event: AuthRejected) -> None:
    rejections.labels(event.reason, event.route).inc()


@security.after_commit(RateLimited)
def log_limit(event: RateLimited) -> None:
    log.warning(
        "rate limited %s %s (%ss)", event.method, event.route, event.retry_after
    )
```

- **No secrets, no high-cardinality values.** `route` is the path template (`/notes/{note_id}`), never the requested path or query string. The payloads carry no credential, token, user name, caller id, address or header, so a handler can count or log them without handling personal data. Add nothing of that kind if you define similar events.
- **They cannot change the answer.** The `401`, `403` or `429` is decided before the event is emitted. Only `after_commit` handlers are accepted: there is no transaction, so `@handlers.in_transaction(AuthRejected)` raises `EventRegistrationError` when it is registered (an event class opts out of transactions with the class attribute `has_transaction: ClassVar[bool] = False`). A failing handler is logged and counted and never reaches the response, and the whole delivery of one event, handlers included, takes at most `events.handler_timeout` seconds before the answer is sent. A slow handler still delays the refusal up to that limit, so keep handlers short and hand heavy work to a queue.
- **Zero cost without a listener.** The runtime builds the payload only when a handler is registered for the event (one context-variable read and one dictionary lookup).
- **Native lane.** Kiso authenticates generated CRUD and handler routes protected by an unmodified `ClaimsJWTAuth` in Rust and answers `401` and `403` there. When a handler is registered for `AuthRejected`, those routes are authenticated by Python so the event can fire (`hinoki routes --lanes` reports `auth_event_handlers` for generated CRUD). Without such a handler nothing changes. A route with an `access` policy or a `rate_limit` also stays off the native handler lane while a handler is registered for `AuthRejected` or `RateLimited`, because the event is delivered from an asyncio task; `hinoki routes` shows the reason.
- **What is not an event.** A `401`, `403` or `429` raised by your own handler code or by ownership checks inside generated CRUD is not an access-policy decision and emits nothing. There is no `AuthSucceeded`: it would fire on every authenticated request, and Rust authenticates the fast path, so it would turn that path off for everyone who listens.
- **Startup and shutdown.** Worker lifecycle, migration and configuration-reload events are not provided: use the `on_startup` and `on_shutdown` hooks of the application.

## Model events

`Created`, `Updated` and `Deleted` (`from hinoki.events import Created, Updated, Deleted`) are emitted by the model write path itself. Each carries `subject`, the model class, so `@handlers.after_commit(Created[Note])` receives only notes and a bare `Created` receives every model (annotate it `Created[Any]`).

| Event | Payload | Emitted by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Created[M]` | `subject`, `instance` (the stored instance) | `acreate`, `asave` of a new instance, `abulk_create` (one per row), generated CRUD create, admin create |
| `Updated[M]` | `subject`, `instance`, `changed` (the changed column names, read before the write) | `asave`, `aupdate_from`, `aupdate_within`, `abulk_update` (one per row that changed), generated CRUD update, admin edit. Nothing is emitted when no column changed. |
| `Deleted[M]` | `subject`, `count` (rows one DELETE statement removed) | `Model.adelete`, `QuerySet.adelete`, `abulk_delete` (one per chunk of keys), generated CRUD delete, admin delete. No key or row is loaded, so there is no instance; nothing is emitted when no row was deleted. |

```python
from hinoki import Hinoki, db, events
from hinoki.events import Created, Updated
from hinoki.orm import Model, pk


@db.table("notes")
class Note(Model):
    id: int = pk()
    title: str


@db.table("audit_lines")
class Audit(Model):
    id: int = pk()
    note_id: int


handlers = events.Handlers("notes")


@handlers.in_transaction(Created[Note])
async def audit(event: Created[Note]) -> None:
    # Runs in the insert's transaction: raising here rolls the note back.
    await Audit.acreate(id=event.instance.id, note_id=event.instance.id)


@handlers.after_commit(Updated[Note])
async def reindex(event: Updated[Note]) -> None:
    if "title" in event.changed:
        print("reindex", event.instance.id)


app = Hinoki(events=[handlers])
```

Any code the application runs (a request, a startup hook, a command) that calls `await Note.acreate(...)` or `await note.asave()` now emits; in a script or test wrap it in `with events.use(app.events):` and a database.

How it runs:

- A write emits only when the application's bus has a handler for that event and model. With none, the write takes the path it always took: one context-variable read and one dictionary lookup, with no extra await or allocation.
- With an `in_transaction` handler the write runs in a transaction (a savepoint inside an open one), so an exception or timeout in the handler rolls the row back and reaches the caller. With only `after_commit` handlers no transaction is added: the handler is queued on the open transaction and dropped on rollback, or runs at once when none is open. `Updated` and `Created` are emitted after the instance holds the stored row and after the [lifecycle hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-hooks.md), so the instance is what a hook left.
- A handler that writes another model with handlers emits again, bounded by `events.max_depth`.
- Not emitted: `QuerySet.aupdate`, `Model.aupdate`, `aupdate_where` (one UPDATE by filter, no instances), raw SQL and migrations. Use `asave` or `abulk_update` on loaded instances when a handler must see the change.
- Events never reveal rows a caller cannot see: they come from the same write that applied ownership and tenant scoping. Generated CRUD update saves the instance with the scoped UPDATE (a row that left the scope is refused before any event), and the `Updated` instance is the row the caller was allowed to write.
- Native lane: Kiso runs generated create, update and delete in Rust without the model, so a model with a handler for `Created`, `Updated` or `Deleted` (any phase, bare or for that model) loses native eligibility for the matching action only (`create`, `update`, `delete`); it runs on the Python lane, where the event fires. `hinoki routes` and the plan diagnostics report the reason `model_event_handlers`. A hand-written `async def` handler that awaits `acreate`, `abulk_create`, `abulk_update`, `adelete` or `abulk_delete` on such a model stays off the native handler lane for the same reason. Models without handlers are unchanged.

## Metrics

With [`metrics.listen`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md) set on Kiso, every handler run is counted and timed on the metrics listener. The label set is fixed at startup from the registered handlers: `event` is the event class (`Created[Note]` for a handler registered for one model), `phase` is `in_transaction` or `after_commit`, and `outcome` is `ok`, `error` or `timeout`. No payload, handler name or request value becomes a label, so the series count never exceeds the number of registered (event, phase) pairs.

```text
hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="ok",worker="0"} 3
hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="error",worker="0"} 3
hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="timeout",worker="0"} 3
hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_count{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",worker="0"} 9
```

With metrics off, or under another server, `EventBus.stats()` still counts runs per worker and nothing else is recorded: a handler run pays one `None` check. See [export Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md#event-handlers).

## What events do not do

- To send an email from a handler, use `mail.send` in an `after_commit` handler: it runs once the data is durable. See [send email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md).
- No delivery between services or processes, no queue, no retry, no at-least-once guarantee. For work that must survive a crash, use a job queue.
- Worker lifecycle, migration and reload events are not part of this release; use `on_startup` and `on_shutdown` for startup and shutdown.
- Events never carry rows a caller cannot see: emit them from code that already applied ownership and tenant policy, and put identifiers rather than whole rows in the payload.

See also [Lifecycle hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-hooks.md), [Transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md) and [Application modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md).

# Migrations

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md

Hinoki compares each app's models with the migration state recorded in its
migration package and writes SQL files you review and commit. Nothing changes a
database until you run `apply`; an application never migrates at startup.

```sh
hinoki migrations plan billing
hinoki migrations apply
```

Commands run from the project, where `hinoki.toml` registers each app's models
and migrations (`hinoki new`, `hinoki app create`). Prefix them with `uv run`
or activate `.venv`.

## Plan a migration

```sh
hinoki migrations plan                  # a project with one app
hinoki migrations plan billing          # one app of several
hinoki migrations plan billing --name add-invoice-index
```

`plan` writes two files into the app's migration package:
`0001-create-table-billing-invoices.sql` and its `.state.json`. The number is
automatic; the slug comes from the first change (`create table
billing_invoices`) unless `--name` replaces it.

In a project with several apps, `plan` needs the app name; `--check` and
`--dry-run` without one cover every app.

!!! warning "Plan for the backend you deploy"
    The SQL uses the dialect of the [selected database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md#which-database):
    usually the application's own `database` setting. Point it at the
    production backend (a disposable database of the same kind) before
    planning. The state file is backend-neutral.

## Review before applying

Read both files. Changes that can lose data are **destructive** and are not
written unless you pass `--allow-destructive`:

* dropping a table or column, changing a type or constraint, adding a
  non-null column;
* a changed derived table name (renaming the class or moving its module), which
  is planned as a drop and a create. Pin the name with `@db.table(...)`
  ([table names](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md#table-and-display-names)).

```sh
hinoki migrations plan billing --dry-run
hinoki migrations plan billing --allow-destructive
```

`--dry-run` prints the plan, destructive operations included, and writes
nothing. Changing a constraint on an existing column may need a hand-written
migration.

## Apply and inspect

```sh
hinoki migrations status
hinoki migrations sql 0001-create-table-billing-invoices
hinoki migrations apply
hinoki migrations apply billing
```

| Command | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `status [APP]` | lists applied and pending migrations (nothing when there are none); writes nothing (connecting still creates a missing SQLite file): a database without the ledger has none applied, and `apply` creates it |
| `sql NAME` | prints one migration's SQL; add `--app APP` only when the name is ambiguous |
| `apply [APP]` | applies pending migrations of every app, or of `APP` and its prerequisites, in dependency order |

### Which database

`plan`, `status` and `apply` use the first of:

1. `--database URL`;
2. the `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL` environment variable;
3. the project's application (`project.application` in `hinoki.toml`): a
   `DatabaseModule` it passes in `modules=` or installs with `app.install(...)`,
   otherwise its `database` setting, read from its settings sources as the
   server reads them, for example `NOTES_DATABASE__URL` or `.env`;
4. local SQLite, `sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3`.

The application is imported from the project root to read its settings, so
`.env` and other relative settings files are the ones beside `hinoki.toml`,
even from a subdirectory. Anything it prints while importing goes to standard
error. No connection opens until the command needs one, and nothing is
started. The command never falls back to another database: it stops with exit
`2` when

- the application cannot be imported (the message names the missing module or
  attribute) or its settings cannot be loaded;
- it installs a database module of its own whose URL Hinoki cannot read;
- the application's database is in-memory SQLite (`sqlite://:memory:`), where
  nothing it migrates would survive. A `--database sqlite://:memory:` URL is
  refused with exit `1` instead, because SQLite needs a file URL there.

Fix the application, or choose the database with `--database` or
`HINOKI_DATABASE_URL`, which skip step 3 and never import the application. An
application without a database still migrates the local SQLite default, but
the server has none to use: declare `database: settings.DatabaseSettings`
([configure a database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md#set-up-a-database-in-four-steps)).
Outside a project (`--models`/`--dir`), step 3 is skipped.

`plan`, `status` and `apply` print the chosen database and its source on
standard error. Everything before the host (user and password) and the URL
options are masked, and a URL that does not parse is not echoed:

```text
$ NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://notes:secret@db.internal/notes hinoki migrations status
database: postgresql://***@db.internal/notes (from settings: ProjectSettings.database)
```

A relative SQLite path from the settings or the default is anchored beside
`hinoki.toml`, so migrations run from a subdirectory use the same file; a
relative SQLite URL given with `--database` or `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL` stays
relative to the current directory. The server and `hinoki settings` do not
anchor: they resolve the path, and read `.env`, from the directory they start
in, so start them from the project root. A connection failure prints
`error: database: …` and exits `1`. A
`--database` URL is visible in the process list and shell history: do not put
a password in it.

An older scaffold's root app keeps unprefixed ledger keys; apps from `hinoki app create` use namespaced keys, so
`accounts/0001-initial.sql` and `billing/0001-initial.sql` are distinct records.

Run `apply` once per deployment, from one process, never from every worker's
startup ([settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#8-database-connection-ownership)). Concurrent
runs are serialized: each file runs in one transaction under a PostgreSQL
advisory lock, a MySQL/MariaDB migration lock or SQLite `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, and
reads the ledger inside it. On SQLite a second runner waits at most the busy
timeout (5 seconds), then fails as locked.

## Check migration drift

```sh
hinoki migrations plan --check
```

Exits `1` when any app has model changes without a migration file, destructive
ones included, `0` otherwise, and `2` when the database whose dialect it plans
for cannot be resolved ([which database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md#which-database)). It covers every
app in dependency order (`plan billing --check`: that app and its
prerequisites), writes nothing and opens no connection. It imports every
registered model and migration module and, unless `--database` or
`HINOKI_DATABASE_URL` names the database, the project's application to read
its database, so those imports must be safe in CI:

```sh
HINOKI_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://ci@localhost/notes hinoki migrations plan --check
```

`status` compares files with a live database instead.

## Apps and dependencies

An app that references another app's models declares it in `requires`:

```toml
# hinoki.toml
[[apps]]
name = "billing"
models = "notes.apps.billing.models"
migrations = "notes.apps.billing.migrations"
requires = ["accounts"]
```

`hinoki app create billing` asks for `requires`; `hinoki app add NAME --models
MODULE` registers an existing package. Hinoki ships two such apps whose tables
are optional: `admin` (`hinoki.admin.users.models`, see the [admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md#create-the-admins-tables))
and `ratelimit` (`hinoki.ratelimit_store.models`, the `hinoki_rate_limits` table of
[`RateLimit`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#rate-limit-an-action)). Neither is applied unless you
register it. Each app's tables belong only to its
