handler, which is also where tenant or ownership checks belong; WebSocket
actions are not part of generated CRUD.

```python
# chat/security.py
from hinoki import Access, BearerAuth, Caller


class Tokens(BearerAuth[str]):
    async def resolve_token(
        self, token: str
    ) -> Caller[str] | None: ...  # look the token up; return None when it is unknown


READ = Access(Tokens(), permissions=["chat:read"])
```

```python
# chat/inbox.py
from hinoki import Caller, http

from chat.security import READ


@http.websocket("/inbox", access=READ)
async def inbox(who: Caller[str], socket: http.WebSocket) -> None:
    await socket.send_text(f"hello {who.id}")
```

## Origin

A request without an `Origin` header (not a browser) is accepted. A request
with one must match the host the request was sent to, an origin listed in
`origins=` on the route (`origins=["https://app.example"]`, or `"*"`), or an
origin the application's CORS policy lists by name. A CORS wildcard
(`cors` origins `*`) is not honoured here: a browser sends cookies on a
WebSocket handshake and does not hide the answer from other sites, so an open
policy would let any site use a cookie-authenticated action. Anything else is
refused with `403` before the upgrade. On Granian the check covers the same
sources, through the same Rust predicate. The same-host match requires the
scheme the connection has: `https://` where the connection is `https` (direct
TLS, a trusted proxy reporting `https`, or `wss` on Granian) and `http://`
otherwise, never both. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS without reporting the
scheme, list the page's origin in `origins=` or the CORS origins. The host is
compared exactly, in lower case, port included: no default port or trailing dot
is folded in. Granian handshakes also go through
`allowed_hosts` and trusted-proxy handling, and the route is matched on the raw
path, as for HTTP requests. The same-host match trusts the `Host` header, so an app with
WebSocket routes and `allowed_hosts` left at `*` refuses to start unless `debug` is on, which is for local development only; with `debug` on the app then accepts loopback `Host` names only (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `[::1]`), any other `Host` receives `400`, and a handshake to it is refused. Name the served hosts with `allowed_hosts` to serve other names.

## Subprotocols

`subprotocols=` names the subprotocols an action speaks, each an HTTP token
(letters, digits and ``!#$%&'*+-.^_`|~``, so `chat.v1` but not `chat/v1`). The server picks the
first one the client offered and returns it in the `101` answer
(`socket.subprotocol`). A client that offers none of them is refused with `400`.
A mapping gives each subprotocol its own `Access`, which runs after the
action's:

```python
# chat/feed.py
from hinoki import http

from chat.security import READ


@http.websocket("/feed", subprotocols={"public.v1": None, "staff.v1": READ})
async def feed(socket: http.WebSocket) -> None:
    await socket.send_text(socket.subprotocol or "")
```

## Messages

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `await socket.receive_text()` | the next text message; a binary one closes with `1003` |
| `await socket.receive_bytes()` | the next binary message; a text one closes with `1003` |
| `await socket.receive_json(schema=None)` | text parsed as JSON, then validated against the `Schema` given or the route's `message` |
| `await socket.send_text(text)`, `send_bytes(data)` | queue a message, waiting while the outgoing queue is full |
| `await socket.send_json(value)` | a JSON text message; with `reply=` on the route, a `dict` is validated against it and an instance of a subclass of it is sent with the fields of `reply` only |
| `await socket.close(code=1000, reason="")` | close after the queued messages |
| `async for message in socket` | each message, until the connection ends; with `message=` on the route, each is a validated `Schema` instance |

Reading or sending on a closed connection raises `http.WebSocketClosed` (with `code` and
`reason`); a handler may let it propagate, since it is not an error. Text that
is not JSON closes with `1007`, JSON that fails validation with `1008`.

```python
from hinoki import Schema, http

from chat.security import READ


class Move(Schema):
    x: int
    y: int


class Position(Schema):
    x: int
    y: int
    by: str


@http.websocket("/board", access=READ, message=Move, reply=Position)
async def board(socket: http.WebSocket) -> None:
    async for move in socket:
        await socket.send_json({"x": move.x + 1, "y": move.y, "by": "server"})
```

## Limits and back-pressure

Settings under `execution` (see [settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md)); each is enforced by
Kiso:

| Setting | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_websockets` | `1000` | open connections per worker; more are refused with `503` before the upgrade |
| `ws_max_message_bytes` | `1048576` | a message (reassembled from its frames) over this closes with `1009`; `max_message_bytes=` on the route overrides it |
| `ws_queue` | `64` | messages queued in each direction; a slow handler stops being read from, so TCP back-pressure reaches the client, and `send_*` waits while the client is slow |
| `ws_ping_interval` | `20.0` | seconds between pings; `None` turns them off |
| `ws_pong_timeout` | `20.0` | a peer that does not answer a ping within this is dropped (reported to the handler as `1006`) |
| `ws_close_timeout` | `5.0` | how long the close handshake may take before the connection is dropped |

`idle_timeout=` on the route (seconds without a data message from the client,
closing with `1001`) is off by default, since a server-push connection can be
silent from the client on purpose. Frames that are malformed, unmasked from a
client, reserved or oversized control frames, invalid UTF-8 in text, and bad
close codes end the connection with `1002` or `1007` as RFC 6455 requires. A
fragmented message may span at most 4,096 frames, its first one included; a
fragment past that ends the connection with `1002`, whatever the message size. A
write that makes no progress for `execution.request_timeout` seconds drops the
connection.

## Shutdown and reload

When the server stops, Kiso closes every open connection with `1001` and the
handler's `receive` and `send` calls end (`async for` stops, the explicit calls
raise `http.WebSocketClosed`). Connections are part of the graceful drain, so they
get the shutdown timeout to finish and are aborted after it. A `SIGHUP`
reload replaces a worker through the same graceful stop, so its connections
get `1001` and a client is expected to reconnect, which reaches the new worker.

## OpenAPI

OpenAPI 3.1 and 3.2 have no WebSocket operation, so the document describes the actions
under the vendor extension `x-hinoki-websockets`, keyed by path: the handler
docstring, the `message` and `reply` schema components, the subprotocols, the
origins and the handshake's security requirement. They are not listed under
`paths`.

## Not provided

WebSocket over HTTP/2, `permessage-deflate`, `@http.websocket` on a
`RouteGroup`, and a native (GIL-free) handler lane for WebSockets.

# Compress responses

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/compression.md

[Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md), Hinoki's Rust server, can compress the bodies it sends with brotli or gzip. It is off by default and it is **Kiso only**: Granian and any other ASGI server never compress what Hinoki gives them, and `hinoki serve --server granian` refuses `compression.enabled` instead of ignoring it.

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki, Schema, http
from hinoki.settings import AppSettings, CompressionSettings

app = Hinoki(
    settings=AppSettings(
        allowed_hosts=("localhost", "127.0.0.1"),
        compression=CompressionSettings(enabled=True),
    )
)


class Note(Schema):
    id: int
    title: str


class NoteList(Schema):
    items: list[Note]


NOTES = NoteList(
    items=[Note(id=number, title=f"note {number}") for number in range(1, 301)]
)


@http.get("/notes", access=None)
async def notes() -> NoteList:
    return NOTES


app.include(notes)
```

`hinoki serve main:app` and `curl` show what the client asked for (headers other than the ones below are left out):

```text
$ curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "accept-encoding: br" http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: application/json
content-length: 591
vary: accept-encoding
content-encoding: br
```

For `gzip` the same request answers `content-encoding: gzip` with `content-length: 1438`, and a request without `accept-encoding` gets the 8795 bytes unchanged. `curl --compressed` decodes the answer. These figures were produced by running this example; they describe this body, not a general ratio.

## What is compressed

Kiso decides once per answer, after the application has decided it, so a plain action, `Stream`, `EventStream` and `File` are treated by the same rules and HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 behave alike.

An answer is compressed when all of these hold:

* The request sends an `accept-encoding` that allows `br` or `gzip` (quality values and `*` are honoured, `q=0` refuses a coding, and a malformed entry is ignored). With several acceptable codings the order of `compression.encodings` breaks ties. A request with no `accept-encoding` gets the body unchanged.
* The status can carry a body: `1xx`, `204`, `206`, `304` and an answer with `content-range` are left alone.
* The answer has no `content-encoding` already and its `cache-control` does not contain `no-transform`: that directive is the way for an action to opt out.
* Its `content-type` matches `compression.types`. The default is `text/*`, `application/json`, `*/*+json`, `application/xml`, `*/*+xml`, `application/javascript`, `application/x-ndjson` and `image/svg+xml`. A response without a `content-type` is not compressed.
* A body known to be smaller than `compression.min_size` (1024 bytes) is left alone. A streamed body whose size is not known is compressed.
* `text/event-stream` only with `compression.event_streams = True`, and a `File` only while `compression.files` is `True` (the default).

When Kiso considers an answer, it adds `Vary: accept-encoding`, even if the client asked for no coding, so a cache keeps the variants apart. A strong `etag` is weakened (`W/"..."`) on a compressed answer.

## How the body is sent

* A body of at most 64 KiB held in memory is compressed at once, and its `content-length` becomes the compressed size. If the result would not be smaller, the original goes out.
* A larger body, a `Stream`, an `EventStream` and a `File` are compressed as they are read, 64 KiB at a time. They have no `content-length`: HTTP/1.1 uses `transfer-encoding: chunked` and HTTP/2 uses data frames. A `File` is still read by the server, so its bytes do not enter Python.
* When the producer of a stream pauses, Kiso flushes what it has compressed so far, so a client receives each piece when the producer yields it and not at the end. An event stream's keep-alive comments are flushed too.
* A stream that fails after the head is cut, as without compression: the compressed body is never ended as if it were complete.
* `HEAD` receives the head its `GET` would get when the `GET` is compressed, with `content-encoding` and `vary` and without `content-length`. It takes no compression slot, so it does not depend on the load, and it is not a promise: the `GET` can still go out as it is when a body of at most 64 KiB does not get smaller or when every slot is taken, and then the `HEAD` named an encoding (and a weak `etag`) that the `GET` did not use.

## Limits

Compression runs on Kiso's runtime threads, without spawning blocking tasks, one piece of at most 64 KiB per step, and an encoder gives the thread back after four steps. Two settings bound the work:

* `compression.max_concurrent` (64) is the number of compressions in progress in one worker. An answer that arrives when all are taken is sent uncompressed at once; it never waits. The count of answers sent that way is kept by the server (`Compression::busy` in the Rust crate); no setting or log line reports it yet.
* `gzip_level` (1 to 9, default 5) and `brotli_quality` (0 to 9, default 4) trade CPU for size. Brotli qualities 10 and 11 are refused because one 64 KiB piece would hold a runtime thread for tens of milliseconds. The brotli window is fixed at 2^18 bytes.

Each compression in progress holds an encoder, which is why `max_concurrent` exists and is 64. The repository has no measurement of the memory of one encoder or of the CPU time per piece, so none is claimed here. `benchmarks/compressionbench.py` measures what a client sees over loopback, with compression off, with gzip and with brotli, and prints the body bytes and the median time per request over alternating rounds:

```sh
uv run --locked python benchmarks/compressionbench.py --rounds 5 --requests 300
```

One run on a development machine (Apple M4 Pro, Python 3.13, debug-profile extension as built by `uv sync`, one synthetic JSON body of 12,980 bytes and a stream of sixteen distinct pieces of about 70 KB, five rounds of 300 sequential requests on one connection) gave these bodies and times:

| Scenario | Identity | gzip | brotli |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `small`, bytes | 12,980 | 1,911 | 733 |
| `small`, median per request | 0.145 ms | 0.175 ms | 0.194 ms |
| `stream`, bytes (with chunk framing) | 1,161,929 | 150,933 | 40,374 |
| `stream`, median per request | 0.426 ms | 4.36 ms | 3.33 ms |

The coefficient of variation across rounds was 0.3% to 3.2%. These are loopback numbers for one machine and one body, with the client sharing the host; they say what this body costs here, not a rate, and your content and hardware will differ.

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `compression.enabled` | `false` | Turns compression on (Kiso only) |
| `compression.encodings` | `("br", "gzip")` | Codings offered, in order of preference; each at most once |
| `compression.min_size` | `1024` | Bodies known to be smaller are left alone; `0` to 16 MiB |
| `compression.types` | see above | `type/subtype`, `type/*` or `*/*+suffix` |
| `compression.event_streams` | `false` | Also compress `text/event-stream` |
| `compression.files` | `true` | Also compress a `File` |
| `compression.gzip_level` | `5` | `1` to `9` |
| `compression.brotli_quality` | `4` | `0` to `9` |
| `compression.max_concurrent` | `64` | `1` to `65536` compressions at once per worker |

A value outside its range stops the application at startup with the usual settings error. A plain WSGI callable (`--interface wsgi` without `WSGIAdapter`) has no settings of its own, so its `compression` group comes from the environment (`COMPRESSION__ENABLED=true`), and Granian refuses it the same way. The settings are declared and validated in Python; the negotiation, the rules above and the encoding run in Rust.

## What stays in Python

Only the declaration and validation of `CompressionSettings`, the refusal under Granian, and passing the values to the server at start-up. No Python object is held by the compression path, and no compression runs on the asyncio loop.

## Not provided

* Compression on Granian or another ASGI server, in `ASGIClient` and in the test client: tests see the body the action produced.
* Other codings (`deflate`, `zstd`), and precompressed files kept next to a `File`.
* A per-route option other than `cache-control: no-transform`.
* Compression of request bodies.
* A compression ratio, throughput or latency figure beyond the benchmark above.
* A test of a WSGI callable hosted on Kiso with compression on: the same policy is passed to that server, but it has not been exercised.

# Export Prometheus metrics

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md

[Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md), Hinoki's Rust server, can count the requests it answers and serve the counts in the Prometheus text exposition format. It is off by default and it is **Kiso only**: `hinoki serve --server granian` refuses `metrics.listen` instead of ignoring it. The counters live in Rust and cost a few atomic additions per request; the exposition is served by a dedicated listener, never by the application's own port.

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki, Schema, http
from hinoki.settings import AppSettings, MetricsSettings


class Note(Schema):
    id: int


@http.get("/notes/{note_id}")
async def note(note_id: int) -> Note:
    return Note(id=note_id)


app = Hinoki(
    settings=AppSettings(
        allowed_hosts=("localhost", "127.0.0.1"),
        metrics=MetricsSettings(listen="127.0.0.1:9100"),
    ),
    include=[note],
)
```

Run `hinoki serve notes.main:app --server kiso --port 8765`, request `/notes/1`, `/notes/2` and `/nope`, then scrape `http://127.0.0.1:9100/metrics`. The lines for those requests (comments and the other families left out) are:

```text
hinoki_http_requests_total{route="/notes/{note_id}",method="GET",status="2xx",worker="0"} 2
hinoki_http_requests_total{route="",method="GET",status="4xx",worker="0"} 1
hinoki_http_requests_in_flight{worker="0"} 0
hinoki_http_response_bytes_total{route="/notes/{note_id}",worker="0"} 16
hinoki_http_response_bytes_total{route="",worker="0"} 69
```

The application's own port answers `/metrics` like any other unknown path (`404`).

## What is exported

Every sample carries a `worker` label: the number of the process that counted it.

| Metric | Type | Labels | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `hinoki_http_requests_total` | counter | `route`, `method`, `status` | Requests answered. `status` is the class: `1xx` to `5xx` |
| `hinoki_http_request_duration_seconds` | histogram | `route`, `method` | Time from the request head to the answer's head |
| `hinoki_http_requests_in_flight` | gauge | none | Requests the backend has not answered yet |
| `hinoki_http_response_bytes_total` | counter | `route` | Body bytes handed to the connection, after compression |
| `hinoki_http_errors_total` | counter | `route`, `kind` | `invalid_response`: the backend's answer could not be sent as given and became a `500`. `stream_aborted`: a stream failed after its head |
| `hinoki_events_total` | counter | `event`, `phase`, `outcome` | [Event handler](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md#metrics) runs. `outcome` is `ok`, `error` or `timeout` |
| `hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds` | histogram | `event`, `phase` | Time a handler ran, whatever its outcome |
| `hinoki_email_messages_total` | counter | `backend`, `outcome` | [Email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md) sends. `outcome` is `sent` or the error kind (`invalid_address`, `invalid_header`, `invalid_message`, `limit_exceeded`, `closed`, `busy`, `connect`, `timeout`, `tls`, `auth`, `rejected`, `temporary`, `protocol`, `template`). `template` counts a `Template.message` that could not be rendered while a mailer is current (`Template.render` alone counts nothing, it is not a send); startup and compile failures are not sends and are not counted |
| `hinoki_email_send_duration_seconds` | histogram | `backend` | Time of a `send`, whatever its outcome |
| `hinoki_email_retries_total` | counter | `backend` | Delivery attempts made again after a transient failure |
| `hinoki_rate_limit_decisions_total` | counter | `decision` | [Rate limit](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#rate-limit-an-action) decisions. `decision` is `allowed`, `refused`, `unavailable` (storage could not answer, or the key, tenant or clock function failed) or `failed_open` (storage could not answer and the route admitted the request). A route's own policy is counted too, as `allowed`, `refused` or `unavailable`; a key, route or address is never a label |
| `hinoki_build_info` | gauge | `version`, `server` | Always `1` |
| `hinoki_worker_start_time_seconds` | gauge | none | Start of the worker, in Unix seconds |
| `hinoki_metrics_snapshot_errors_total` | counter | none | Snapshots of other workers that were unreadable, too large or not valid UTF-8 |

* `route` is the route's pattern (`/notes/{note_id}`), never the path of the request, so the number of series is bounded by the number of routes. An answer no route produced (an unknown path, a refused host, the documentation pages) has `route=""`.
* `method` is `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`, `QUERY` or `OTHER`.
* The duration is measured when the answer's head is ready, as the access log does. The time a stream takes to send its body is not in it, and a request is *in flight* only until the backend has answered, not until a stream ends.
* Bytes are counted as the pieces are handed to the connection: a stream's pieces one by one, a `File` as it is read, a compressed body at its compressed size. A `HEAD` counts none. The exposition itself is never compressed and never counted.

The duration buckets are `0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10` seconds. Set `metrics.buckets` to change them.

## Event handlers

The two event families exist only when the application registers [event handlers](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md). Their series are created at startup, one per registered (event, phase) pair (`Created[Note]`, `after_commit`), in a fixed table in Rust; Python records each run with one call that adds to a counter and a histogram bucket, so nothing grows with traffic and no label comes from a payload. The histogram uses the same buckets as the request duration. A series with no run yet is not printed. Handler runs of events emitted inside a request, a startup hook or a command are all counted by the worker that ran them, under the same `worker` label; the table is built from the handlers of the Hinoki application served by the ASGI path of Kiso; Kiso's WSGI mode records none.

Example from a real run (three emits of an event with an `ok`, a failing and a timed-out handler, `events.handler_timeout=0.05`):

```text
hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="ok",worker="0"} 3
hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="error",worker="0"} 3
hinoki_events_total{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",outcome="timeout",worker="0"} 3
hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_bucket{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",le="0.05",worker="0"} 6
hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_bucket{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",le="0.1",worker="0"} 9
hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_sum{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",worker="0"} 0.153349
hinoki_event_handler_duration_seconds_count{event="NoteSaved",phase="after_commit",worker="0"} 9
```

Measured cost of recording on one Apple-silicon laptop (an `after_commit` handler that returns at once, 200,000 emits per sample, 15 interleaved samples per variant, medians over three runs): about 3.3 µs per emit with metrics off and 3.4 to 3.5 µs with them on, that is roughly 50 to 110 ns (about 2 %) more; the extension was a debug build. A handler that does real work makes the share smaller.

## Email

The three email families exist only when the application has an [email module](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md) (an `email: settings.EmailSettings` field). The `backend` label is `smtp`, `console` or `memory` and every `outcome` series is created at startup, so no recipient, subject, host or error text becomes a label; a series with no send yet is not printed, except the retries counter. The send duration uses the same buckets as the request duration. Example from a real run of one send with the `memory` backend:

```text
hinoki_email_messages_total{backend="memory",outcome="sent",worker="0"} 1
hinoki_email_send_duration_seconds_count{backend="memory",worker="0"} 1
hinoki_email_retries_total{backend="memory",worker="0"} 0
```

Without metrics, or under Granian, `Mailer.stats()` still counts sent and failed messages, retries and connections per worker.

## Settings

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `listen` | unset | `host:port` of the metrics listener (an IPv6 host in brackets). Unset keeps metrics off |
| `path` | `/metrics` | The only path the listener serves |
| `allow` | empty | Addresses or CIDRs of the peers that may scrape (the TCP peer, not `X-Forwarded-For`); empty allows every peer |
| `token` | unset | A `Secret` bearer token a scrape must send as `Authorization: Bearer ...` |
| `buckets` | see above | 1 to 32 positive, finite, strictly increasing upper bounds in seconds |
| `snapshot_interval` | `1.0` | `0.1` to `60` seconds; how often each worker writes its snapshot when there are several |

A `listen` address off the loopback needs `allow` or `token`, so the metrics are never open to everyone by accident. The listener answers `GET` and `HEAD` only (`405` otherwise), `404` for another path, `403` for a peer outside `allow` and `401` with `www-authenticate: Bearer` for a missing or wrong token (compared in constant time). It takes at most 64 connections, waits 5 seconds for a request head and reads at most 8 KiB of headers. [`Access`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md) policies do not apply to it: it does not pass through application code.

## Several workers

`hinoki serve --workers N` opens the metrics listener once, like the main one, and every worker accepts scrapes on it. Counters are not added up: each worker writes a snapshot of its own numbers to a private directory (created by the supervisor, readable only by its user, removed when it exits) every `snapshot_interval`, and the worker that receives a scrape answers with its live numbers and the fresh snapshots of the others. Each process keeps its own series, told apart by `worker`, so Prometheus can `sum without (worker)` them and handles a restarted worker's counter reset as usual. A peer's numbers are at most one interval old (and a snapshot older than five intervals, from a worker that is gone, is ignored); the answering worker's own are live. A snapshot that is unreadable, too large or not valid UTF-8 is skipped and counted in `hinoki_metrics_snapshot_errors_total`.

With one worker nothing is written to disk when `server.sighup` is `"stop"`: the worker binds `listen` itself and answers from memory. Otherwise (the default) the supervisor owns the listener and the directory even for one worker, because a [reload on `SIGHUP`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#reload-on-sighup) runs the old and the new worker side by side. A replacement worker takes the next free `worker` number (a reload of `worker="0"` continues as `worker="1"`), starts its counters at zero, and the snapshot of the worker it replaces is removed when that one has stopped. Under `hinoki dev` the supervisor owns the listener, so it stays open while the worker reloads, and the counters restart with the worker.

## What it does not cover

A worker's snapshot is limited to 4 MiB, which is roughly 2000 active route and method pairs with the default buckets and roughly 800 with 32 buckets (approximate figures). A worker whose snapshot would be larger keeps its previous file, logs the problem once to stderr, and its series leave the other workers' scrapes once that file is older than five intervals; its own scrape still shows live numbers.

Pool and executor gauges, process metrics (`process_*`) and tracing are not exported. Metrics are not available under Granian or another ASGI server; wrap the ASGI application there as described in [serving](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#metrics-and-tracing).

# Send email

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md

Hinoki sends outbound email over SMTP from a per-worker `Mailer`. The message is rendered, the SMTP conversation, TLS, the connection pool, timeouts and retries all run in Rust (`crates/mail`); the Python side is the `Message` you build, the settings and the module that owns the mailer. The call crosses the Python/Rust boundary once per message, with Python objects for the message and its result.

What it is **not**: there is no queue, no delivery guarantee and no HTTP provider (the SMTP and the two local backends below are all there is). `send` returns when the server accepted the message, or raises. The [admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md) sends no email in 0.1.0.

## Set it up

Declare an `email: settings.EmailSettings` field. Hinoki installs `EmailModule` for you, like the database module, and opens one `Mailer` in every worker's lifespan.

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_"):
    email: settings.EmailSettings
```

`backend` is required and has no default, so nothing is sent by accident. In development use `console` (the message is printed) and in tests `memory`:

```sh
NOTES_EMAIL__BACKEND=console
NOTES_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER=noreply@example.com
```

For production SMTP:

```sh
NOTES_EMAIL__BACKEND=smtp
NOTES_EMAIL__HOST=smtp.example.com
NOTES_EMAIL__USERNAME=mailer
NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/smtp-password
NOTES_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER=noreply@example.com
```

Importing Hinoki or the application opens no connection: the mailer is created when the worker starts and closed (`aclose`) when it stops. Each worker has its own pool; nothing is shared between workers or event loops.

## Send a message

```python
# notes/routes.py
from hinoki import http, mail


@http.post("/welcome")
async def welcome() -> dict[str, str]:
    sent = await mail.send(
        mail.Message(
            to=("ada@example.com",),
            subject="Welcome",
            text="Your account is ready.",
            html="<p>Your account is ready.</p>",
        )
    )
    return {"message_id": sent.message_id}
```

`mail.send` uses the mailer of the running worker. It returns a `SentMail` (`message_id`, the envelope `recipients`, `attempts`) and raises `EmailError` on failure.

A `Message` is frozen and keyword-only. `to`, `cc`, `bcc` and `reply_to` are tuples; passing one string where a tuple is expected is a `TypeError`. At least one of `text` or `html` is required (both make a `multipart/alternative`), and at least one recipient in `to`, `cc` or `bcc`. `sender` defaults to `default_sender`; with neither set, `send` raises `invalid_message` for `sender`.

- An address given as `str` is a bare `user@example.com`. To add a display name use `mail.Address("ada@example.com", "Ada Lovelace")`; `"Ada <ada@example.com>"` as a `str` is refused.
- `bcc` recipients are in the SMTP envelope and never in a header.
- `headers=(("X-Campaign", "welcome"),)` adds headers. Names and values are checked: a line break or any other control character (below U+0020 except a tab, or U+007F) in a header value, the subject or a display name is `invalid_header`, and the headers Hinoki writes itself (`From`, `To`, `Date`, `Message-ID`, `Subject`, ...) cannot be set. Text that contains `=?` is always written as encoded words so a reader cannot mistake it for one.
- The sizes are measured before anything is copied or encoded: text, HTML and attachments over `max_message_bytes` are `limit_exceeded` for `text`, `html` or `attachments`.
- A message refused in Python (no sender, a malformed header or attachment) counts as a failed send in `mailer.stats()` and in the metrics, like any other refusal. On a closed mailer every send is `closed`.
- `attachments=(mail.Attachment("report.pdf", data, "application/pdf"),)`. A non-ASCII file name is sent with an RFC 2231 `filename*` parameter.
- Header-injection attempts (a `\r` or `\n` in the subject, a display name or an address) are refused as `invalid_header` or `invalid_address` before anything is sent.

SMTPUTF8 (a non-ASCII address), XOAUTH2, DKIM signing, inline images, DSN requests and PIPELINING are not supported.

## Send after a commit

Send once the data is durable, never from inside a transaction that can still roll back. Register the send with `after_commit`: it runs after the outermost commit and is dropped on rollback.

```python
# notes/apps/accounts/operations.py
from hinoki import db, mail
from hinoki.orm import current_database


async def invite(address: str) -> None:
    async with db.atomic():
        await Invite.acreate(InviteIn(email=address))
        current_database().after_commit(
            lambda: mail.send(
                mail.Message(to=(address,), subject="You are invited", text="Join us.")
            )
        )
```

A send that fails after the commit is logged and does not undo the commit; the callback is not retried. See [after-commit callbacks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md#after-commit-callbacks).

### When the message must not be lost

Hinoki keeps no queue and cannot promise delivery: a crash after the commit and before the send loses the message. When that matters, write the message into your own table in the same transaction (an outbox) and send it from a [management command](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md) that marks each row sent. That table, its retry policy and its cleanup are yours.

## Send from a synchronous handler

A sync handler runs on a thread. Run the send on the worker's loop with `run_sync`:

```python
from hinoki import http, mail
from hinoki.blocking import run_sync


@http.post("/notify")
def notify() -> dict[str, str]:
    sent = run_sync(
        mail.send(mail.Message(to=("ada@example.com",), subject="Hi", text="Hello"))
    )
    return {"message_id": sent.message_id}
```

The mailer is also available in `on_startup` hooks, [management commands](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md) that require `EmailModule`, and `hinoki shell`.

## Backends

| `backend` | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `smtp` | Delivers to `host:port` over a pooled, bounded set of connections |
| `console` | Writes the rendered message to standard output, followed by a line of 72 dashes. Nothing leaves the process |
| `memory` | Renders the message and keeps it in `mailer.outbox` (a bounded deque, `memory_capacity` messages); nothing leaves the process |

`console` and `memory` validate and render exactly as `smtp` does, so a message that is refused in one is refused in all, and `SentMail.raw` holds the bytes that would be sent.

## SMTP, TLS and authentication

| `security` | Default port | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `starttls` (default) | 587 | Plain connect, then upgrade. The upgrade is required: a server that does not offer `STARTTLS` is a `tls` error |
| `tls` | 465 | TLS from the first byte |
| `none` | 25 | No encryption. On a host off the loopback it needs `allow_insecure = true` |

- The server certificate and host name are always verified, against the public roots bundled with Hinoki plus the certificates of `tls_ca_file` (a PEM file) when set: the file adds trust, it does not replace the bundled roots, and the operating system's store is not read. There is no setting that turns verification off. An IPv6 `host` may be written `::1` or `[::1]`.
- `username` and `password` are set together. `password` is a [`Secret`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md): it is read from the environment or `PASSWORD_FILE`, never appears in a `repr`, a log line or an exception, and is revealed only to hand it to the SMTP login. Authentication tries `PLAIN`, then `LOGIN`, and a password is never sent in clear text to a non-loopback peer unless `allow_insecure` is set.
- `check_on_startup = true` connects and authenticates while the worker starts and aborts the start on failure; `await mailer.check()` does the same on demand without sending a message. Both are off by default.

## Settings

All fields are in the `email` group. Durations are seconds, more than 0 and at most 3600 (one hour).

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `backend` | required | `smtp`, `console` or `memory` |
| `default_sender` | unset | The `From` address when a message has none |
| `host`, `port`, `security` | `localhost`, by `security`, `starttls` | The server |
| `username`, `password` | unset | Both or neither |
| `allow_insecure` | `false` | Permit `security=none` off the loopback, and plain `AUTH` there |
| `tls_ca_file` | unset (bundled public roots only) | PEM file of certificates trusted in addition to the bundled roots |
| `helo_name` | the local address as a literal (`[192.0.2.1]`) | Name sent in `EHLO`: a domain name, `localhost` or an address literal (`[192.0.2.1]`, `[IPv6:::1]`) |
| `message_id_domain` | domain of `default_sender` (an internationalized domain in its punycode form), else `helo_name`, else `localhost` | Right-hand side of the `Message-ID`; same forms as `helo_name` |
| `connect_timeout`, `command_timeout`, `data_timeout` | `10`, `30`, `120` | Per connect, per command and per message body |
| `timeout` | `60` | The whole `send`, including the wait for a connection and the retries; at least `connect_timeout` |
| `max_connections` | `4` | Connections per worker |
| `pool_wait` | `5` | How long a send waits for a free connection before a `busy` error |
| `idle_timeout` | `60` | Idle connections older than this are closed |
| `max_messages_per_connection` | `100` | A connection is replaced after this many messages |
| `retries`, `backoff_base`, `backoff_max` | `2`, `0.5`, `5` | See [retries](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md#errors-and-retries) |
| `max_recipients`, `max_message_bytes`, `max_attachments` | `100`, 10 MiB, `20` | Limits checked before connecting |
| `memory_capacity` | `1000` | Size of the `memory` outbox |
| `check_on_startup` | `false` | See above |

A value out of range, a duration over one hour, an empty `username`, `username` without `password`, a `host` longer than 253 characters or with a control character, a `default_sender`, `helo_name` or `message_id_domain` that is not valid, or `security=none` to a remote host without `allow_insecure` is refused when the settings load, with the variable named and the value never shown. `tls_ca_file` is read when the worker starts, not when the settings load.

## Errors and retries

Every failure is an `EmailError` with a `kind` (`EmailErrorKind`):

| `kind` | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `invalid_address`, `invalid_header`, `invalid_message` | The message is refused before any connection. `field` names the part (`to`, `subject`, `attachments`, ...) and `index` the entry |
| `limit_exceeded` | `max_recipients`, `max_message_bytes` or `max_attachments` |
| `closed` | The mailer was closed (the worker is stopping) |
| `busy` | No connection became free within `pool_wait` |
| `connect`, `timeout`, `tls`, `auth` | The connection, a timeout, the TLS handshake or the login failed |
| `rejected` | The server refused with a permanent `5xx` reply; `code` and `enhanced_status` hold it |
| `temporary` | A `4xx` reply that survived the retries |
| `protocol` | The server broke the SMTP protocol |

The exception text is a fixed sentence plus the field and reply code. It never contains a recipient, a subject, a body, a password or the server's reply text, so it is safe to log.

Connection failures (`connect`), timeouts, `4xx` replies and protocol errors are retried up to `retries` times, all inside `timeout`. The wait before a retry doubles from `backoff_base` up to `backoff_max` and is then scaled by a random factor between one half and one. `attempts` counts the tries. A permanent `5xx` reply, a TLS or authentication failure, a validation error, a full pool and a closed mailer are never retried.

`possibly_sent` is `True` when the connection failed or stalled after the end of the message data was written: the server may have accepted the message. Nothing is retried then, because a retry could send a duplicate; decide in your code whether to send again.

## Test with the memory backend

```python
# tests/test_invite.py
from hinoki import Hinoki, mail, settings
from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient


class TestSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_"):
    email: settings.EmailSettings


async def test_welcome_mail() -> None:
    app = Hinoki(
        settings=TestSettings(
            email=settings.EmailSettings(
                backend=settings.EmailBackend.MEMORY,
                default_sender="noreply@example.com",
            )
        ),
        include=[welcome],
    )
    async with ASGIClient(app) as client:
        await client.post("/welcome")
        [sent] = next(
            m for m in app.modules if isinstance(m, mail.EmailModule)
        ).mailer.outbox
        assert sent.message is not None and sent.message.subject == "Welcome"
        assert b"Your account is ready." in (sent.raw or b"")
```

`outbox` holds `SentMail` entries with `message` and `raw`; `clear_outbox()` empties it. Each started application, and each worker, has its own outbox. For SMTP behaviour, point `host` at a fake server on `127.0.0.1`; never send real mail from a test.

## Templates

Instead of building `subject`, `text` and `html` by hand, declare a `mail.Template` (a TOML file or strings) with a typed context, list it in `Hinoki(email_templates=[...])` and send `template.message(context, to=(...))`. Rendering and escaping are Rust, the template is checked against its context `Schema` when a worker starts, and `hinoki mail preview` shows the result. See [email templates](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md).

## Metrics

With `metrics.listen` on [Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md) and an email module installed, three families are exported. The series are fixed at startup, so no address, subject or error text becomes a label. See [export Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md#email).

`Mailer.stats()` is always available, under Granian too: it returns the counts of sent and failed messages, retries, and open and idle connections of that worker.

## What email does not do

- No queue, no scheduled sends and no guaranteed delivery; see [when the message must not be lost](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md#when-the-message-must-not-be-lost).
- No template language beyond the small fixed one of [email templates](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md); you can also build `text` and `html` yourself.
- No HTTP email providers (only SMTP, console and memory).
- No bounce or delivery tracking, no DKIM signing, no SMTPUTF8, no XOAUTH2.
- The admin sends no email in 0.1.0.
- No sharing of a mailer between workers, processes or event loops.

# Email templates

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md

A template turns a typed context into the subject, the plain text and the HTML of a message. The language is small and fixed, the template is parsed, checked against the context `Schema` and rendered in Rust (`crates/mail`), and the result is an ordinary `mail.Message` for [`mail.send`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md). The call from Python to the renderer is one synchronous native call per message, with Python objects for the context and the three rendered strings.

The code on this page is the code of [`examples/mailroom`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/tree/main/examples/mailroom); a test (`tests/mailtemplatesdoctest.py`) proves that every quoted block is a piece of that example and that every printed output is what the command prints now. Use only synthetic addresses such as `example.com`; nothing here sends real mail.

## A template file

A template file is TOML with a `subject`, a `template` (the HTML) and, optionally, a `text` and a `description`. The context it reads is a `Schema`:

```python
# mailroom/messages.py
class Account(Schema):
    name: Annotated[str, Field(max_length=80, examples=("Ada",))]
    trial_days: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0, examples=(14,))]


class Step(Schema):
    title: Annotated[str, Field(max_length=80, examples=("Create a project",))]
    url: Annotated[str, Field(format="url", examples=("https://example.com/start",))]


class Welcome(Schema):
    user: Account
    steps: Annotated[list[Step], Field(max_length=10)]
```

```toml
# mailroom/templates/welcome.toml
description = "Sent once, after sign-up"
subject = "Welcome to Mailroom, {{ user.name }}"
template = '''
<html><body>
<h1>Welcome, {{ user.name }}</h1>
{% if user.trial_days %}
<p>Your trial lasts {{ user.trial_days }} days.</p>
{% else %}
<p>Your plan is active.</p>
{% endif %}
<ol>
{% for step in steps %}
<li><a href="{{ step.url }}">{{ step.title }}</a></li>
{% endfor %}
</ol>
</body></html>
'''
```

`mail.Template.file(path, context=Welcome)` names the file and its context. Nothing is read when the module is imported; the name defaults to the file's stem (`welcome`):

```python
# mailroom/messages.py
WELCOME = mail.Template.file(HERE / "welcome.toml", context=Welcome)
RESET_PASSWORD = mail.Template.file(HERE / "reset_password.toml", context=ResetPassword)

templates: list[mail.TemplateBase] = [WELCOME, RESET_PASSWORD]
```

A template built in code takes the same parts: `mail.Template(name="x", subject=..., html=..., text=..., context=Ctx)`, or `mail.Template.from_toml(source, name="x", context=Ctx)` for TOML text. Those compile when they are built, with no I/O.

## Register and send

List the templates when you create the application. Nothing registers by import:

```python
# mailroom/main.py
def build_app(settings: MailroomSettings) -> Hinoki:
    """The application; the routes need the API key and the public base URL."""
    return Hinoki(
        settings=settings,
        title="Mailroom",
        include=build_routes(settings),
        email_templates=templates,
    )
```

The auto-installed `EmailModule` receives the list. If you declare the module yourself, pass `EmailModule(settings, templates=[...])`. Every worker reads and checks the files in its lifespan, and the worker does not start when one fails. At most 256 templates are registered, with distinct names.

A route builds the context, renders it with `Template.message(context, to=...)` and sends the message:

```python
# mailroom/routes.py
    @group.post("/signup", status=202)
    async def sign_up(data: SignUp) -> Sent:
        """Send the welcome message of a new account."""
        welcome = Welcome(
            user=Account(name=data.name, trial_days=data.trial_days),
            steps=[Step(title="Create a project", url=START)],
        )
        sent = await mail.send(WELCOME.message(welcome, to=(data.email,)))
        return Sent(message_id=sent.message_id)
```

`message` takes the other `Message` options (`cc`, `bcc`, `reply_to`, `headers`, `attachments`, `sender`) as keywords. A test sends through the `memory` backend, which keeps the message in the mailer's outbox:

```python
# mailroom_tests/mailroomsendtest.py
def messages() -> list[mail.Message]:
    module = next(m for m in app.modules if isinstance(m, mail.EmailModule))
    return [sent.message for sent in module.mailer.outbox if sent.message]


async def test_sign_up_sends_the_welcome_message(client: ASGIClient) -> None:
    response = await client.post(
        "/signup", json={"email": "ada@example.com", "name": "Ada <1>"}, headers=KEY
    )

    assert response.status == 202
    (message,) = messages()
    assert message.to == ("ada@example.com",)
    assert message.subject == "Welcome to Mailroom, Ada <1>"
    assert message.text is not None
    assert "Your trial lasts 14 days." in message.text
    assert message.html is not None
    assert "<h1>Welcome, Ada &lt;1&gt;</h1>" in message.html
```

To see a message printed while developing, run `MAILROOM_API_KEY=dev-key MAILROOM_EMAIL__BACKEND=console MAILROOM_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER=noreply@example.com uv run hinoki dev` from `examples/mailroom` and `POST` to `/signup` with the header `x-api-key: dev-key`. The console output is not reproduced here because its `Date` and `Message-ID` headers change on every run.

## The language

A template is text with three constructs:

| Construct | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `{{ path }}` | Insert a value. `path` is one to eight identifiers joined by dots (`user.name`) |
| `{% if path %}` … `{% else %}` … `{% endif %}` | Render a branch by truthiness; `else` is optional |
| `{% for name in path %}` … `{% endfor %}` | Render the body once per item of a list; `name` exists only inside the body |

An identifier is ASCII letters, digits and `_`, not starting with a digit, up to 64 bytes. `if`, `else`, `endif`, `for`, `in` and `endfor` are reserved as loop variables. A loop variable may not have the name of a field of the context or of an enclosing loop (`shadowed_name`). There are no filters, expressions, comparisons, `not`, `elif`, comments, includes, macros or inheritance: anything else inside `{{ }}` or `{% %}` is a syntax error. A literal `{{` or `{%` cannot appear in the text; a lone `{`, `}` or `%` is text, so CSS works.

**Standalone lines.** A `{% … %}` tag that is the only non-blank content of its line removes that line (its leading and trailing spaces and tabs, and one line ending). `{{ }}` lines are never removed. This is why the preview below has no blank lines where the `if` and `for` tags are.

**Values.** The context is read as these values:

| Python / `Schema` field | In the template |
| --- | --- |
| `str`, `Email`, `Url`, `StrEnum` | Text as is |
| `int`, `float` | Decimal digits (an `int` of any size); a float with no fractional part gets `.0` (`1.0`), never an exponent |
| `bool` | `true` or `false` |
| `None` | Nothing (empty text); a path through a `None` object is also empty |
| `Decimal`, `date`, `datetime`, `UUID` | The text `dump()` gives |
| nested `Schema` | An object: use `user.name` |
| `list[...]` | Something `for` iterates; `for` over `None` renders nothing |
| `Secret`, `bytes`, `Any`, `tuple`, a mapping field | Refused when the template is checked |

An object or a list cannot be inserted with `{{ }}` (`not_text`); a `for` over a value that is not a list is `not_a_list`; a path through a non-object is `not_an_object`.

**Truthiness.** `None`, `false`, `0`, `0.0`, empty text, an empty list and an empty object are false; everything else is true.

**Escaping.** In `html` every inserted value is escaped (`&` `<` `>` `"` `'` become `&amp;`, `&lt;`, `&gt;`, `&quot;`, `&#x27;`); the literal text of the template is not touched. `subject` and `text` insert values as they are. A value inserted into the subject that has a line break, a NUL or another control character other than a tab (including `U+0085`, `U+2028` and `U+2029`) is refused (`header_injection`), so a value cannot add a header. A NUL in a value inserted into `text` or `html` is refused (`control_character`).

Escaping is enough in text and inside a quoted attribute, so the template is also checked for where each `{{ }}` sits in the HTML. A `{{ }}` inside `<script>` or `<style>`, in an unquoted attribute value, in a tag or attribute name, or in an event handler attribute (`onclick`, ...) is refused when the template is compiled (`unsafe_context`). A value inside a quoted `href`, `src`, `action`, `formaction`, `background` or `poster` is checked when the template is rendered: with a scheme it must be `http`, `https`, `mailto` or `tel`, otherwise the render fails (`unsafe_url`); an address without a scheme is relative and passes. The check also covers the dict shortcut. A `Schema` context is not allowed `Unset` fields (`str | Unset`), a `dump()` override, or a computed field that returns a secret: the first two are `unsupported_field` when the template is built, the last is `secret_value` when it is rendered.

**Limits.** These are fixed in `crates/mail/src/template/limits.rs`; they are not settings:

| What | Limit | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject source | 1 KiB | `too_large` |
| Text or HTML source, each | 256 KiB | `too_large` |
| TOML file | 512 KiB | `too_large` |
| Nodes in a template | 10 000 | `too_many_nodes` |
| Nesting of `if` and `for` | 16 | `too_deep` |
| Path segments, identifier | 8, 64 bytes | `invalid_path` |
| Rendered subject | 998 bytes | `output_too_large` |
| Rendered text or HTML, each | 1 MiB | `output_too_large` |
| Loop iterations in one render | 10 000 | `too_many_iterations` |
| Context depth, nodes, bytes | 16, 100 000, 4 MiB | `context_too_large` |
| Name | `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,63}` | `invalid_name` |
| Problems reported at once | 20 | |

The send path still applies `max_message_bytes` to the whole message.

## Text from HTML

When a template has no `text`, the plain text is derived from the rendered HTML by a single scanner in Rust, not by an HTML parser. Comments and the content of `head`, `style`, `script`, `title` and `template` are dropped; `br` is a line break; paragraphs, headings, lists, tables, blocks and `hr` make paragraph breaks; a list item starts with `- `; runs of white space collapse (except in `pre`); the entities `&amp; &lt; &gt; &quot; &apos; &#39; &nbsp;` and numeric ones are decoded; every other tag is removed. A link whose `href` starts with `http://`, `https://` or `mailto:` becomes `label (URL)`, or only the label when the label is the URL.

The `reset_password` template has no `text`. Printed from the sample context in `examples/mailroom` (`--part text` prints only that part):

```sh
uv run hinoki mail preview reset_password --context mailroom/samples/reset_password.json --part text
```

<!-- output: reset-text -->
```text
Hello Ada,

Someone asked to reset your password from Lisbon.

Choose a new password (https://example.com/reset?token=sample)

You are signed in on:

- Laptop
- Phone <work>

If it was not you, ignore this message.
```

The text part holds the value `Phone <work>` as it is; the HTML part holds `Phone &lt;work&gt;`. Write a `text` in the file when the derived text is not what you want.

## Checked at startup

A template is checked against its context `Schema` before any message is rendered: every variable must exist in the `Schema`, every `Schema` field must be used by some part, and a variable must have the right shape (a loop over a list, a path through an object, text where text is inserted). Change `{{ user.name }}` in the `<h1>` of `welcome.toml` to `{{ user.nickname }}` and the worker does not start; the error names the template, the variable and the position in the template, never a value:

<!-- output: unknown-variable -->
```text
template 'welcome': unknown variable 'user.nickname' in html at line 2, column 17
```

Removing the `<ol>` list from the HTML leaves the `steps` fields unused, which is also an error:

<!-- output: unused-field -->
```text
template 'welcome': unused field 'steps[].title' (and 1 more problem)
```

`hinoki mail check [TARGET]` runs the same check without starting anything. It reads every registered template, prints one line for each, and exits `1` when one is refused (`2` when the application cannot be loaded or has no email module). With the first change above:

<!-- output: mail-check -->
```text
template 'welcome': unknown variable 'user.nickname' in html at line 2, column 17
ok  reset_password  (mailroom/templates/reset_password.toml)
```

The rule `HNK-MAIL-001` (`from hinoki.rules import EmailTemplatesMatch`) makes the same check part of `hinoki check`. It is opt-in: put `EmailTemplatesMatch()` in your `RuleSet`. It reads the template files, so it declares the effect `files` and needs `--allow-effects`:

```sh
uv run hinoki check --rules myproject.rules:rules --allow-effects
```

## Preview

`hinoki mail preview NAME [TARGET]` renders a registered template from the command line, with no server and no sending. Without `--context` it builds a sample from the `examples=` of the context fields (a field that is not required and has no example is left out). Run it from `examples/mailroom` with the `memory` backend and a sender set:

```sh
export MAILROOM_API_KEY=dev-key
export MAILROOM_EMAIL__BACKEND=memory
export MAILROOM_EMAIL__DEFAULT_SENDER=noreply@example.com
uv run hinoki mail check
```

<!-- output: mail-check-ok -->
```text
ok  welcome  (mailroom/templates/welcome.toml)
ok  reset_password  (mailroom/templates/reset_password.toml)
```

```sh
uv run hinoki mail preview welcome
```

<!-- output: welcome-preview -->
```text
Subject: Welcome to Mailroom, Ada
----- text -----
Welcome, Ada

Your trial lasts 14 days.

- Create a project (https://example.com/start)
----- html -----
<html><body>
<h1>Welcome, Ada</h1>
<p>Your trial lasts 14 days.</p>
<ol>
<li><a href="https://example.com/start">Create a project</a></li>
</ol>
</body></html>
```

`--context FILE` (or `-` for standard input, at most 1 MiB) reads a JSON object that is validated as the context `Schema`; `--part subject|text|html` prints one part; `--format json` prints the three parts as JSON. The preview opens no mailer and sends nothing.

## Templates from strings

Some templates live in a database table, not in a file. `examples/mailroom/mailroom/notices.py` builds one from strings, without a `Schema`:

```python
# mailroom/notices.py
def notice_template(slug: str) -> mail.Template[mail.Context]:
    """The template of a stored notice; ``KeyError`` when there is none."""
    subject, html = NOTICES[slug]
    return mail.Template(name=f"notice-{slug}", subject=subject, html=html)
```

The context is a plain `dict` (`mail.Context`). Only the syntax is checked when the template is built; there is no `Schema` to check the variables against, so a missing key is found when the template is rendered, for the message being sent. A `Secret` in the `dict` is refused (`secret_value`). The error names the variable of the template:

<!-- output: missing-variable -->
```text
template 'notice-maintenance': missing variable 'from' in html at line 1, column 47
```

The `/notices/{slug}` route turns that error into `400 invalid_notice`, so the caller learns that the notice could not be rendered without seeing a value.

## Errors

Every failure is a `mail.TemplateError`, a subclass of `EmailError` with `kind` `template`. It carries `reason`, `template` (the name), `field` (the part), `line`, `column`, `variable` and `problems` (a tuple of `TemplateProblem`, at most 20; `truncated` says there were more). Its text never holds a recipient, a subject, a rendered text or a value of the context. A secret never reaches the engine: a `Secret` field in a `Schema` context is `secret_field`, and one in a `dict` is `secret_value`.

| Reason | When |
| --- | --- |
| `syntax`, `unclosed_tag`, `unexpected_tag`, `unclosed_block`, `invalid_path`, `shadowed_name`, `control_character`, `too_large`, `too_many_nodes`, `too_deep`, `invalid_name`, `unsafe_context` | The template does not compile |
| `unknown_variable`, `unused_field`, `not_text`, `not_a_list`, `not_an_object`, `secret_field`, `unsupported_field` | The template does not match its context `Schema` |
| `missing_variable`, `header_injection`, `output_too_large`, `too_many_iterations`, `context_too_large`, `unsupported_value`, `secret_value`, `unsafe_url` | A render fails |
| `unreadable`, `invalid_file` | The file cannot be read or is not a valid template TOML |

With metrics on [Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md), a `Template.message` that cannot be rendered while a mailer is current is counted in `hinoki_email_messages_total{outcome="template"}` (`Template.render` alone is not a send and counts nothing). Compile and startup failures are not sends and are not counted. See [export Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md#email).

## What templates do not do

- No filters, expressions, includes, macros or inheritance, and no comments.
- No translation: a template is one language; choose the template or write one per language.
- No inline images or attachment templates; `attachments` are the `Message` option.
- No registration in `hinoki.toml`: templates are listed in `Hinoki(email_templates=[...])` or `EmailModule(templates=[...])`.
- The limits above are fixed and are not settings.
- Rendering does not send: delivery, retries and the lack of a queue are those of [`mail.send`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md).

# Middleware

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md

A middleware runs around an action. It is Hinoki's own typed interface, so it
behaves the same on Kiso and on Granian: you do not wrap the ASGI application,
and an application served by Kiso can use it.

```python
# notes/middleware.py
from hinoki.http import Middleware, MiddlewareRequest, Next, Response


class Tenant(Middleware):
    async def __call__(self, request: MiddlewareRequest, call_next: Next) -> Response:
        if "x-tenant" not in request.headers:
            return Response(400, "missing x-tenant", content_type="text/plain")
        response = await call_next()
        return response.with_header("x-served-by", "tenant")
```

Declare it on an action, or for the whole application. `middleware=` on
`Hinoki(...)` is the explicit form; a project lists it in `hinoki.toml`
instead ([below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md#declaring-middleware-in-hinokitoml)):

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki, Schema, http

from .middleware import Tenant


class Pong(Schema):
    ok: bool


@http.get("/ping")
async def ping() -> Pong:
    return Pong(ok=True)


app = Hinoki(include=[ping], middleware=[Tenant()])
```

`RouteGroup` actions take the same option. The application's middleware runs
first, then the action's, in the order listed; each one returns what the next
one returned unless it answers itself.

## Declaring middleware in `hinoki.toml`

The `[project]` table can list middleware for the whole application. Hinoki does not generate the module: you create it
yourself, and you edit the list by hand (there is no command for it). The
Tracker example does this with one middleware that adds a version header
([`middleware.py`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/tracker/tracker/middleware.py),
listed on line 4 of its
[`hinoki.toml`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/tracker/hinoki.toml)).

```python
# shop/middleware.py
tenant = Tenant()
timing = [Timing(), Audit()]  # a list or tuple is flattened
```

```toml
[project]
application = "shop.main:app"
middleware = ["shop.middleware:tenant", "shop.middleware:timing"]
```

```python
from hinoki import Hinoki

app = Hinoki()  # reads routes, events, middleware and rules from hinoki.toml
```

Each entry is `module:attribute` and resolves to one object with an
`async def __call__` or a list or tuple of them. The listed order is the
execution order: the first one listed runs outermost. There is no dependency
ordering. When the manifest's `project.application` names the module that
builds the app, `Hinoki()` loads the list if you did not pass `middleware=`; an
explicit `middleware=` (even `()`) wins and skips the manifest.
`manifest_middleware()` is the explicit form, to combine lists. The result is
the application's own middleware: it runs before an action's and obeys
[the order below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md#order-and-what-stays-outside). `project.middleware` that is
not a list of `module:attribute` strings is rejected when the manifest loads,
and a target that does not import or does not hold middleware raises a
`ProjectError` naming the entry.

## What a middleware sees

`MiddlewareRequest` is the head of the request: `method`, `path`, the matched
route template in `route` (for example `/items/{item_id}`, safe to use as a
metrics label), lower-case `headers`, the raw `query` string, `client`,
`scheme` and `request_id`. It has no body and cannot change the request:
`headers` is a read-only mapping, so authentication and the action see the
headers the client sent.

```python
class Forge(Middleware):
    async def __call__(self, request: MiddlewareRequest, call_next: Next) -> Response:
        request.headers["authorization"] = "Bearer x"  # TypeError: a 500
        return await call_next()
```

A middleware that needs to pass data on should answer itself or add response
headers instead.

The `Response` a middleware returns is checked like one a handler returns,
also when it is built with `Response.raw(status, body, headers)` from encoded
parts: a framing or server header (`content-length`, `transfer-encoding`,
`connection`, `x-request-id`), an invalid name or a line break in a value is a
`ValueError`, so the request answers `500` instead of a corrupt response.

`call_next()` returns a `Response` with the action's answer. An error the action
raised is already an HTTP answer, and an `atomic=True` transaction is already
rolled back, so a middleware that reads the database after `call_next()` sees
the state after the rollback. Call `call_next()` at most once (a second call is
a `500`). A middleware that raises is translated like an action error; one that
returns anything but a `Response` is a `500`.

For an action that returns `Stream`, `EventStream` or `File`, `call_next()` returns that object with an empty `body`: a middleware never sees the pieces, and `with_header` keeps the class and the source. A middleware that answers with another `Response` instead of the stream does not serve it, and Hinoki closes its source. See [stream a response](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md#middleware).

Security, CORS and request-id headers are added after the middleware returns.

## Order and what stays outside

1. Hinoki answers what needs no action first: the ready check, request size
   limits, host, CORS preflight and HTTPS redirect policies, the startup probe
   and the documentation pages.
2. The route is chosen. An unknown path (`404`) or method (`405`) never reaches
   a middleware.
3. The application's middleware, then the action's.
4. Authentication, rate limit, negotiation, body binding, the transaction and
   the handler.

`execution.request_timeout` applies to the whole of it: when it expires the
`504` is produced outside the middleware, which only sees the cancellation.

## Cost

An action with middleware is served by Python for the whole request, so it
leaves [the native lane](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#what-is-native-and-what-still-runs-in-python):
`hinoki routes --lanes` shows `lane_reason` `middleware`. A deprecated action
([deprecate an action](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md#deprecate-an-action)) leaves the lane the same
way, with `lane_reason` `deprecated`. Actions without
middleware keep their lane. A middleware that only needs to observe requests can
use the [access log](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#the-native-handler-lane) instead, which does not
change the lane.

## Errors and edge cases

- A middleware must have `async def __call__`; any other object is a `TypeError`
  when the application or the action is declared.
- Keep a middleware free of request state kept in globals: use the
  `MiddlewareRequest` it receives.

## See also

- [Request lifecycle](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/request-lifecycle.md)
- [Serve an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md)
- [Transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md)

# Pagination

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md

An action opts into page-number pagination with `pagination=PageNumberPagination()`, or into [cursor pagination](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md#cursor-keyset-pagination) with `pagination=CursorPagination()`. A size you leave out comes from the application's `pagination` settings group; without settings the defaults are `page_size=20` and `max_page_size=100`. The framework parses and validates `page` and `page_size`, injects a `PageParams` value, and documents both query parameters in OpenAPI.

The Billing app lists invoices a page at a time. The handler asks the model for one page, and `Page.map()` turns its rows into `Schema` instances:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/api.py
from hinoki import RouteGroup
from hinoki.pagination import Page, PageNumberPagination, PageParams

from notes.security import billing_staff

from .models import Invoice
from .schemas import InvoiceOut

invoices = RouteGroup("/invoices", access=billing_staff, atomic=True)


@invoices.get("/", pagination=PageNumberPagination())
async def list_invoices(page: PageParams) -> Page[InvoiceOut]:
    return (await Invoice.all().apaginate(page)).map(InvoiceOut.from_model)
```

Pages are one-based. `page_size` defaults to the strategy's configured size and cannot exceed its maximum. Invalid values produce a validation response before the handler runs; `page` is limited to 1 000 000 000, and longer or larger values answer `422` with the code `le`.

`Page` contains `items`, `page`, `page_size`, `total` and the computed `pages`. Empty result sets have zero pages; a page beyond the end has an empty `items` list. `Page.map()` converts each item while preserving the counts and requested page.

## Defaults for the whole application

`settings.AppSettings` has a `pagination` group, set in code, in the environment or in TOML. With the project's settings class:

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_"):
    pass
```

```sh
export NOTES_PAGINATION__PAGE_SIZE=25
export NOTES_PAGINATION__MAX_PAGE_SIZE=200
```

The application in `notes/main.py` reads them through `Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, ...)`.

Precedence, from strongest to weakest: a size set on the action's `PageNumberPagination(...)`, the application's `pagination` settings, then 20 and 100. Each size is resolved separately, so `PageNumberPagination(page_size=10)` keeps its 10 and takes its maximum from the settings. The result must satisfy `1 <= page_size <= max_page_size`: invalid settings fail when they load, and an action whose own size does not fit the resolved other one (for example `PageNumberPagination(max_page_size=10)` under a settings `page_size` of 25) fails when it is included, naming the action. The generated OpenAPI parameters show the resolved values.

Use the queryset's `apaginate`/`paginate` methods for database rows. They append the primary key as the last sort key (after any `order_by`), so rows with equal sort values keep one position across pages. `Page.of(rows, params)` slices an in-memory sequence and counts that sequence; it is not a substitute for database pagination on large tables.

### Concurrent count and rows

Pass `concurrent=True` to run the `COUNT(*)` and page-row queries together on PostgreSQL or MySQL pools with `max_size >= 2`:

```python
@invoices.get("/fast", pagination=PageNumberPagination(), atomic=False)
async def list_invoices_fast(page: PageParams) -> Page[InvoiceOut]:
    return (await Invoice.all().apaginate(page, concurrent=True)).map(
        InvoiceOut.from_model
    )
```

Because the two queries check out separate pool connections, they may observe slightly different snapshots under concurrent writes (the same trade-off as any non-transactional read). Inside an active transaction (`atomic=True` or `async with db.atomic():`), on SQLite, or when the pool has `max_size < 2`, `apaginate(..., concurrent=True)` automatically runs the count and row queries sequentially on one connection so transactions preserve read-your-writes and single-connection pools never deadlock.

### Direct schema projection

Use `apaginate_as` (or `paginate_as` in sync handlers) to project rows directly to a `Schema` in Rust without constructing intermediate Python `Model` or `Schema` objects on the response path:

```python
@invoices.get("/projected", pagination=PageNumberPagination())
async def list_invoices_projected(page: PageParams) -> Page[InvoiceOut]:
    return await Invoice.all().apaginate_as(InvoiceOut, page, concurrent=True)
```

The returned `Page[InvoiceOut]` carries the pre-encoded JSON bytes and owned rows. Returning it from a handler emits the exact same JSON as `(await Invoice.all().apaginate(page)).map(InvoiceOut.from_model)` and passes `validate_response=True` checks. Accessing `.items`, calling `.map()`, or inspecting elements materializes the `InvoiceOut` instances from the owned rows without issuing a second database query. Scalar fields, `select_related`, and 1-level `prefetch_related` (reverse foreign keys and many-to-many) are encoded directly in Rust; schemas with computed fields, hooks, validators, custom `dump()`, or scoped prefetches fall back to normal Python hydration transparently.

## Cursor (keyset) pagination

`pagination=CursorPagination(...)` pages by position instead of by offset. A response carries `next` and `previous` cursors that clients should treat as opaque; the database starts each page at the cursor's row through the sort index, so a page costs the same at any depth, and no `COUNT` runs. Use it for long, growing lists or feeds; keep page numbers when users jump to page *n* or need a total.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/api.py
from hinoki.pagination import CursorPage, CursorPagination, CursorParams


@invoices.get("/feed", pagination=CursorPagination(page_size=20))
async def feed(page: CursorParams) -> CursorPage[InvoiceOut]:
    return (await Invoice.all().apaginate_cursor(page)).map(InvoiceOut.from_model)
```

```sh
export NOTES_PAGINATION__CURSOR_SECRET="$(openssl rand -hex 32)"
```

`GET /invoices/feed?limit=20` answers `{"items": [...], "next": "<cursor>", "previous": null, "page_size": 20}`. Pass `next` as `cursor` to read forward and `previous` to read back. `next` is `null` on the last page; `previous` is `null` on the first. Generated lists switch with `crud(..., pagination=CursorPagination())` and return the same envelope.

* **Ordering.** The page follows the query's `order_by` (or the model's `ordered_by`), with the primary key appended as the final tie-break, so rows with equal sort values are never skipped or repeated. Sort columns must be non-null `int`, `str`, `uuid`, `datetime` or `float` columns; anything else raises a `FieldError`, and a `crud(...)` whose model ordering is invalid fails at registration with a `RegistrationError` naming the model and column (an ordering added by a custom `get_queryset` is checked on each request). A `str` sort value is bounded: at most 1024 bytes per value, and a whole cursor at most 4096 characters, the same limit for issuing and reading. A page whose boundary row exceeds it, and whose link is needed, answers `422` with the field `cursor` and the code `unencodable` (it never answers `500`); order by a shorter column when values can be long. The queryset's own `limit` and `offset` are ignored.
* **Filters and scope.** The cursor holds a position. `get_queryset`, ownership and tenant policies are applied to every page exactly as for the first one, so a cursor cannot reach rows its holder could not list. On a generated list with [client filters](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#filter-order-and-search-the-list), the cursor is also bound to the filters and the `ordering` that the client sent: a cursor used with different ones answers `422` with the code `invalid`. A list without client filters keeps its cursors valid as before. The `ordering` columns of the `FilterSet` must be non-null `int`, `str`, `uuid`, `datetime` or `float` columns, checked when the routes are declared.
* **Signing.** Cursors are signed with HMAC-SHA256 in Rust and bound to the table and the ordering they were issued for, so they are tamper-proof. They are not encrypted: a cursor is base64 and readable, and it contains the sort-key values of the boundary row. Do not order a cursor list by a column whose value must stay private, even when the read `Schema` hides it. The secret comes from `CursorPagination(secret=...)` or `pagination.cursor_secret` and must have at least 32 bytes; without one, including the action fails with a `RegistrationError`. Changing the secret invalidates outstanding cursors.
* **Expiry.** `cursor_ttl_seconds` (setting) or `CursorPagination(ttl=...)` makes a cursor expire; the default never does.
* **Errors.** A tampered, malformed, foreign or differently ordered cursor answers `422` with the field `cursor` and the code `invalid`; an expired one answers `422` with `expired`; an unencodable boundary value answers `422` with `unencodable`. `limit` follows the same bounds as `page_size`.
* **Rust path.** The keyset `WHERE`, the signature, the direction handling and, for a generated plain list, the JSON page are produced in Rust.
* **Indexes.** Index the sort columns in the sort order (for example `(rank DESC, id)`) to get the constant-time pages; without one the database sorts the table for every page.
* **Admin.** The admin lists keep page-number pagination.

The `pagination` settings group also takes `cursor_secret` and `cursor_ttl_seconds`; sizes resolve as described above, and `page_size`/`max_page_size` apply to `limit`. The measurements are in `benchmarks/README.md` (`cursorbench.py`).

# Parsers and renderers

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/codecs.md

A **parser** turns a request body into Python data; a **renderer** turns a handler's result into response bytes. Built-ins use Rust for selected parsing and JSON encoding work; Python still selects codecs, calls customization hooks and assembles framework objects.

| Built in | Rust work | Python work and options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `JSONParser` | Strict JSON decoding (no NaN, no lone surrogates, depth limit) | `prepare(data)` hook and `media_type` |
| `Form[Schema]` marker | A `Schema` read from form text, converted per field | Rust conversion, then strict `Schema` validation |
| `XMLParser` | `application/xml` into a tree (children → `dict`, repeated name → `list`, text → `str`, empty → `None`), parsed with the GIL released; no DTDs, custom entities, characters XML 1.0 forbids or encodings other than UTF-8; depth and element caps | Rust; `max_depth` (default 32, at most `MAX_XML_DEPTH` = 1000, larger raises `ValueError`), `max_elements` (default 10,000); attributes are not read |
| `XML[Schema]` marker | A `Schema` read from an XML body, converted per field | Rust conversion, then strict `Schema` validation |
| `Query[Schema]` marker | A `Schema` read from the query string, converted per field | Rust conversion, then strict `Schema` validation |
| `FormParser` | `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` parsing with a field cap | Builds the Python mappings; `max_fields` |
| `MultiPartParser` | `multipart/form-data` parsing and byte/part limits | Builds `UploadedFile` and form objects; `max_parts`, `max_part_bytes` (each part, including text fields) |
| `TextParser` | — | Decodes UTF-8 in Python; `media_type` |
| `BytesParser` | — | Hands `request.data` the raw `bytes` of an `application/octet-stream` body |
| `JSONRenderer` | Encodes `dict`, `list`, `Schema`, UUID, datetime and `dump()` objects | `prepare(value, request)` and `default` callbacks run in Python; `indent`, `sort_keys`, `media_type` |
| `HTMLRenderer`, `TextRenderer` | — | Type-check and UTF-8 encode strings in Python; `media_type` |
| `XMLRenderer` | Encodes what `JSONRenderer` encodes (`dict`, `list`, `Schema`, UUID, datetime, `dump()` objects) as UTF-8 XML, with the GIL held; ASCII element names, U+FFFD for characters XML 1.0 forbids, depth limit 200 | `root`, `item` |

Content negotiation (`Accept`, quality values, wildcards) also runs in Rust; with nothing acceptable the answer is 406 before the handler runs.

## Upload files

An action that binds an `UploadedFile` and has no parsers of its own gets `MultiPartParser()` with its default limits (100 parts, 1 MiB per part), unless the application's `parsers=` already include a `MultiPartParser`, which is then used. Other actions accept multipart only when it is listed. The parser handles bounded multipart bytes in Rust, then Python creates `UploadedFile` objects. For typed handler binding, annotate a parameter as `UploadedFile`, `UploadedFile | None = None`, or `list[UploadedFile]`; the parameter name selects the multipart field. A single value rejects duplicates, while a list preserves repeated values. The same objects are visible through `request.FILES`; text fields are available in `request.POST`.
