See [endpoint upload declarations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#upload-files) for a complete example and status-code behavior.

The complete request body and every part are buffered in memory. The default body cap is 1 MiB; increasing it also increases potential memory use across concurrent requests. This parser does not stream or spool files. Keep both the runtime body cap and `max_part_bytes` bounded, and treat filenames and media types as untrusted client input.

`JSONParser`, `JSONRenderer`, `HTMLRenderer`, `XMLParser`, `XMLRenderer`, `FormParser`, `MultiPartParser` and `BytesParser` are importable from `hinoki`; `TextParser` and `TextRenderer` come from `hinoki.parsers` and `hinoki.renderers`.

## Choose them

Per action, or for the whole application (an action's own choice wins):

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki, JSONRenderer
from hinoki.renderers import TextRenderer

from notes.rules import project_rules
from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

app = Hinoki(
    settings=ProjectSettings,
    rules=project_rules,
    renderers=[JSONRenderer(sort_keys=True), TextRenderer()],
)
```

```python
# notes/apps/billing/api.py (continued)
from hinoki import JSONParser, JSONRenderer, Request
from hinoki.parsers import TextParser


@invoices.get("/report", renderers=[JSONRenderer(indent=2)])
async def report() -> InvoiceReport: ...


@invoices.post("/hook", parsers=[JSONParser(), TextParser()], atomic=True)
async def hook(request: Request) -> HookReceipt: ...  # request.data is a dict or a str
```

## Answer XML

`XMLRenderer` renders the handler's result as `application/xml; charset=utf-8` with an XML declaration. It is written by the Rust encoder, which accepts what the JSON encoder accepts: `dict`, `list`, `tuple`, `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `None`, `Schema` instances, UUIDs, datetimes and `dump()` objects, at any depth. `date`, `time`, `timedelta`, `Decimal`, `bytes`, sets and frozensets, IP addresses and networks, `PurePath`, `Secret` (written masked) and enum members are written in their wire form at any depth, as in `JSONRenderer`: a `Decimal` as its text, `bytes` as base64, a set as a sorted list, an enum member as its value. A `JSONRenderer`'s own options (`default`, `prepare`, `sort_keys`) do not apply to it:

```python
from hinoki import JSONRenderer, XMLRenderer


@http.get("/report", renderers=[JSONRenderer(), XMLRenderer(root="report")])
async def report() -> dict[str, object]:
    return {"id": 1, "tags": ["a", "b"], "note": None}
```

`Accept: application/xml` answers `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?><report><id>1</id><tags><item>a</item><item>b</item></tags><note/></report>`; without it the first renderer (JSON) answers. A mapping becomes child elements named by its keys, a list becomes repeated `item` elements (`item=` renames them), `None` an empty element and booleans `true`/`false`. Keys are spelled as the JSON encoder spells them: a string as is, an integer in decimal, `None` as `null` and booleans as `true`/`false`; any other key (a float, a UUID, a tuple) raises an error (`500`), as it does for JSON. A key that is not a valid XML name (a space, a leading digit, a name starting with `xml`, so also an integer key) is written as `<item key="...">`, escaped, instead of failing the request. Tab and line breaks are written as character references so a parser keeps them, and characters XML 1.0 cannot carry are replaced by U+FFFD. Non-finite floats, which JSON refuses, are written `NaN`, `INF` and `-INF`; finite floats are spelled as the JSON encoder spells them (`1e-7`, `1e+16`). Element names are ASCII (`[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*`, not starting with `xml` in any case, no colon), so `root=` and `item=` that do not match raise `ValueError` when the renderer is created. Nesting deeper than 200 levels (the JSON encoder's limit; the reading limit is separate: `XMLParser(max_depth=)`, default 32, at most 1000), an integer of more than 4300 digits or a value it cannot write raises an error (`500`) whose message names the type or the limit. The encoder holds the GIL, as the JSON encoder does, because it reads Python objects as it writes; it never reads the request, so an action that lists the renderer stays on the native handler lane.

### What a round trip keeps

`XMLParser` is not the inverse of `XMLRenderer`. Reading back what was written, with `XMLParser` or `XML[Schema]`:

| Written | Read back |
| --- | --- |
| `None`, `""`, `{}` and `[]` (all an empty element) | `None` |
| `1`, `1.5`, `true` | the strings `"1"`, `"1.5"` and `"true"` (use `XML[Schema]` to convert per field) |
| a list of one item | `{"item": "1"}` (a mapping with the item name as its key) |
| a list of two or more items | `{"item": ["1", "2"]}` |
| a key written as `<item key="...">` | the key `item` |
| the root element's name | lost |
| a character XML 1.0 cannot carry | U+FFFD |

Attributes and namespace prefixes are ignored on reading, and mixed text and elements are refused. A document of more than 32 levels needs `XMLParser(max_depth=...)`. Use XML for interchange, not to store Python values.

## Configure the Rust JSON encoder

```python
JSONRenderer(indent=2, sort_keys=True)  # pretty, stable output
JSONRenderer(default=str)  # values outside a Schema the hook sees first
```

`default` is a Python callback for a value the encoder does not know and must return something that is JSON (returning the same object is an error). It does not override what the encoder always handles (UUID, datetime, `Schema`, anything with `dump()`). Without `default`, `date`, `time`, `timedelta`, `Decimal`, `bytes`, sets, IP addresses, paths, `Secret` and enum members are written in their wire form anywhere, including at the top level; with `default`, such a value outside a `Schema` instance is passed to the hook first, and inside a `Schema` the wire form always applies. A `Secret` is the exception: it is always written as `"**********"` and never passed to `default`. With `sort_keys=True` object keys are ordered by their encoded text (quotes and escapes included), which is deterministic but not always `json.dumps` order for unusual keys, and integer keys sort as text. The public renderer accepts `indent` from 0 to 16, or `None` for compact output.

## Inherit and override

```python
# notes/apps/billing/codecs.py
from hinoki import JSONParser, JSONRenderer


class Envelope(JSONRenderer):
    media_type = "application/vnd.myapp+json"

    def prepare(self, value, request):  # reshape, then Rust encodes
        return {"data": value, "request_id": request.request_id}


class SnakeCase(JSONParser):
    def prepare(self, data):  # Rust decodes, then reshape
        return rename_keys(data) if isinstance(data, dict) else data
```

For a different format write a `Renderer` (`media_type`, `render(value, request) -> bytes`) or a `Parser` (`media_type`, `parse(raw, content_type) -> Parsed`); set `consumes_objects = True` on a renderer that can take `Schema` instances directly. Every instance in a position that declares a `Schema` ([subclass instances](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-schemas.md#subclass-instances))—whether a subclass or an exact instance of the declared class—reaches a custom object-consuming renderer (such as one with `consumes_objects = True`, or a `JSONRenderer` subclass overriding `prepare`) as a `hinoki.core.Narrowed` view, never the raw instance: `isinstance(value, Declared)` holds, the declared fields and `@computed_field` values read as attributes, and `dump()` (with the keywords of `Schema.dump`: `include`, `exclude`, `exclude_unset`, `by_alias`) gives the declared fields only; any fields a subclass added are not readable through it, and a field or computed value that holds a `Schema` (or subclass) reads as a `Narrowed` of the class its own type declares, at every depth. `Narrowed(value, declared)` raises `TypeError` unless `declared` is a `Schema` class that `value` is an instance of. A subclass returned for a top-level declared class that overrides `dump()` reaches the renderer as the dict returned by the declared class's `dump()` restricted to the declared fields (an exact instance of that class arrives as a `Narrowed` whose `dump()` runs the same declared `dump()`). The built-in `JSONRenderer`, `XMLRenderer` and `Schema.dump()` narrow fields directly without wrapping exact instances in `Narrowed`. Media types must be distinct within one list; a failing `parse` raises `InvalidBody(code, message)` (a 400 with that stable code).

# OpenAPI document

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md

`Hinoki.openapi()` builds an OpenAPI 3.2 document from the routes registered with the app (3.1 on request, see [the document version](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md#the-document-version)). Paths, parameters, request bodies, response schemas, declared errors and supported authentication schemes come from the action declarations and type annotations.

Generate the document from the application without starting a server:

```sh
hinoki openapi --output openapi.json
hinoki openapi --check openapi.json
hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json
```

`--output` writes stable, sorted JSON. `--check` compares parsed JSON with a committed file, so whitespace-only changes do not report drift. `--breaking-against` compares with an earlier document (the released one) and prints one `breaking: …` line per change that would break an existing client. The three options are exclusive. The command opens no database and works even when `openapi_url` is disabled. See [inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#openapi) for output and exit status.

## Serve the document and viewers

All three URLs are disabled by default. Set `openapi_url` to serve JSON; add `docs_url` for the bundled Swagger UI or `redoc_url` for ReDoc. A project created with `hinoki new` already sets the first two:

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki

from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

app = Hinoki(
    settings=ProjectSettings,
    openapi_url="/openapi.json",
    docs_url="/docs",
    redoc_url="/redoc",
)
```

The corresponding `docs.openapi_url`, `docs.docs_url` and `docs.redoc_url` settings provide the same defaults. A viewer requires `openapi_url`. `llms_url` does not: see [describe the API for agents](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md#llms). `Hinoki(...)` arguments override settings; passing `None` disables a page. The packaged viewers (Swagger UI 5.35.1 and ReDoc 3.2.0, which read OpenAPI 3.2 and list `QUERY` operations) work without a CDN; ReDoc 3 is loaded as a JavaScript module with its usage reporting turned off.

The generated OpenAPI document, Swagger UI, ReDoc and their assets answer `HEAD` with the same status and representation headers as `GET`, without a response body. Each request still has its own request ID in the configured response header (`x-request-id` by default).

## Describe the API for agents (`llms.txt`) {#llms}

The same document can be rendered as an [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org/) Markdown text for a coding agent or an LLM client: the title and version, then the operations grouped by their first tag, each with its method, path, operation ID, summary and a few facts (`deprecated`, the security scheme names, the request and success response components). Untagged operations are listed under `Operations`.

```sh
hinoki llms
hinoki llms --output llms.txt
hinoki llms --check llms.txt
```

The command opens no database and works when `openapi_url` is disabled. `--check` exits `1` when the committed file differs from the generated text. See [inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#llms) for output and exit status.

Serving it is opt-in. Set `llms_url`, or `docs.llms_url`, and the text is answered at that path; the default `None` serves nothing:

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki

app = Hinoki(llms_url="/llms.txt")
```

The `Hinoki(...)` argument overrides the setting and `None` disables the page. Unlike the viewers it does not need `openapi_url`: the text is rendered from `Hinoki.openapi()` once at startup. It answers `GET` and `HEAD` as `text/markdown; charset=utf-8` (the media type of Markdown, RFC 7763) with `Cache-Control: no-cache`, and it is not listed in the OpenAPI document. `llms_url` cannot equal `openapi_url`, `docs_url` or `redoc_url`, and a route on the same path stops startup. `hinoki new` does not enable it.

The page is public, like the OpenAPI document when that is served. It is built only from the document, so it leaves out what the document leaves out: `include_in_schema=False` actions and the admin's pages. Leaving an action out neither hides it nor authorizes anything. The text names security schemes, never credentials.

The renderer, [`hinoki.ai.llms.render_llms`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/reference/tools.md), is Python: it reads the dictionary that the Python OpenAPI builder produces and does no I/O. The finished page is handed to Kiso as a prebuilt static answer, like the document and the viewers. [Hinoki's own documentation for agents](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ai-workflow.md#docs-for-agents) is a separate set of files.

## The document version

The `openapi` field is `3.2.0` by default. `Hinoki(openapi_version="3.1")` or the `docs.openapi_version` setting (`"3.1"` or `"3.2"`) writes a `3.1.0` document instead; any other value raises `ValueError`. `hinoki openapi` and the served document follow the application's choice. The version changes one thing: where a `QUERY` action is written. Every other operation, schema and component is the same in both.

```python
from hinoki import Hinoki

app = Hinoki(openapi_version="3.1")  # keep a 3.1 document for a 3.1-only consumer
```

OpenAPI 3.2.0 was checked against the bundled and current readers; use `"3.1"` for a consumer that only reads 3.1. `@apidevtools/swagger-parser` 13.1.0, for one, rejects every 3.2.0 document, and `openapi-typescript` 7.13.0 reads a 3.2 document but leaves its `query` operations out.

## QUERY operations

An action declared with `@http.query` is written under the path item's `query` field in a 3.2 document (Path Item Object, [OpenAPI 3.2.0 section 4.9](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.2.0.html#path-item-object)), with the same operation object as any other method: operation ID, parameters, request body, responses and security.

```json
{"paths": {"/search": {"get": {"operationId": "search_page"}, "query": {"operationId": "search"}}}}
```

With `openapi_version="3.1"` there is no such field, so the same operation object is written under the `x-query` extension instead and the document stays valid 3.1. A 3.1 document with a `query` field would be invalid, and a 3.2 document never carries both, because the two entries would repeat the `operationId`.

Readers of a 3.1 document that look only at the standard method fields do not see `x-query` operations. The application MCP, `explain_action` and `hinoki openapi --breaking-against` read both fields, so a baseline written as 3.1 compares correctly with a 3.2 document.

## What is generated

* A unique `operationId` is derived from the handler's qualified name. If names collide, Hinoki appends a numeric suffix.
* A paginated response's envelope component is named after its items (`Page_Book`, `Page_integer`, `Page_string`). Two different security schemes, page envelopes or a page envelope and a `Schema` (a class named `Page_Book` beside `Page[Book]`) that would share a name get a numeric suffix (`KeyAuth_2`, `Page_array_2`, `Page_Book_2`) instead of overwriting each other; two different `Schema` classes with the same name are still a registration error.
* The first line of the handler docstring becomes `summary`; the remaining lines become `description`.
* Path, query and pagination parameters come from the bound handler signature. A list with [`filters=`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#filter-order-and-search-the-list) documents one typed query parameter per filter: `boolean`, `integer`, `number` or `string` schemas (with `format` for dates, instants, UUIDs and decimals, and an `enum` for a `Literal`), `name.from` and `name.to` for a `Range`, `name.null` for a nullable field, a comma-separated array (`style: form`, `explode: false`, `maxItems`) for `In`, `search` with its length limit, and `ordering` as an array whose `enum` is each declared key and its `-` form. The same parameters appear in 3.1 and 3.2 documents. Body fields and successful response fields come from `Schema` annotations. Parser and renderer media types supply the content types.
* Typed `UploadedFile` parameters generate a `multipart/form-data` request body with binary file properties. Repeated files use an array of binary items; optional single-file bindings are not required in the body or property list. A `Form[Schema]` body next to files is documented as one object holding the schema's fields and the file properties, with the schema's `additionalProperties` and both lists of required names. Text keys read dynamically through `request.POST` are not inferred or listed.
* A declared `errors=(...)` adds response entries for those `APIError` classes. Request binding and schema validation errors are documented as `422` where the action has request inputs.
* `access=...` adds a security requirement when its authentication provider supplies an OpenAPI scheme. Authentication responses are included in the operation.
* Admin HTML routes marked `hide_from_docs` are omitted.

A `dict[str, X]` field becomes `type: object` with `additionalProperties` (the value schema), `propertyNames` (the key schema) and `minProperties`/`maxProperties` from its declared entry limits. The framework bounds on client input (1000 entries, 256-character keys) are not part of the document because components describe responses too; see [dictionary fields](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-collections.md#dictionary-fields).

`date`, `time` and `timedelta` fields become `type: string` with `format: date`, `time` and `duration`. A `Decimal` field becomes `type: string`, `format: decimal` and a `pattern` for its text form, with `ge`/`le`/`gt`/`lt` as the string extensions `x-minimum`/`x-maximum`/`x-exclusiveMinimum`/`x-exclusiveMaximum` (JSON Schema's numeric keywords do not apply to a string, and a string keeps the exact value); examples and defaults are written as decimal text; `max_digits` and `decimal_places` are not written, nor is a `Decimal` field's `multiple_of`. An `int` field's `multiple_of` becomes `multipleOf`. IP address and network fields become `type: string` with `format: ipv4`, `ipv6`, `ipv4network` or `ipv6network`. A `Path` field becomes `type: string` with `format: path`, and a `Secret` field `type: string` with `format: password` and `writeOnly: true`. A `bytes` field becomes `type: string`, `format: byte` and `contentEncoding: base64`, and its decoded-size limits are not written either, since they count bytes rather than characters. See [dates, durations, decimals and bytes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-types.md#dates-durations-decimals-and-bytes).

An `Enum` or `Literal` field becomes `type: string` or `type: integer` with an `enum` list of the values (the member values, never the names), inline in the property; a nullable one is wrapped in `anyOf` with `null`. See [enums and literals](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-types.md#enums-and-literals).

A `set[X]` or `frozenset[X]` field becomes an array with `uniqueItems: true`, `tuple[X, ...]` an array of `X`, and a fixed `tuple[X, Y]` an array with `prefixItems`, `items: false` and equal `minItems`/`maxItems`. See [sets and tuples](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-collections.md#sets-and-tuples).

A [many-to-many ids field](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schemas.md#many-to-many-ids-fields) such as `tag_ids` (declared with `ids_name="tag_ids"`) is an array of `string` items with `format: uuid` (or the target key's type), `uniqueItems: true` and `maxItems` from its declared limit, in request and response schemas alike.

A plain union such as `int | str` becomes `anyOf` of its variants, and `Any` or `object` an unconstrained schema (`{}`). See [plain unions and `Any`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-collections.md#plain-unions-and-any).

Discriminated unions declared as `Schema` fields become OpenAPI `oneOf` schemas with a `discriminator` and explicit tag-to-component mapping. Variant tag fields appear as required string enums; the runtime uses the same tags to select exactly one branch. List items, nested fields and nullable unions retain that structure. For route input and response documentation, put the union inside a wrapper `Schema`; bare union return annotations are rejected instead of producing an incomplete schema. The return value is also checked against the annotation at runtime ([details](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#the-response-is-checked-against-the-annotation)).

```yaml
oneOf:
  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/Cat"
  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/Dog"
discriminator:
  propertyName: type
  mapping:
    cat: "#/components/schemas/Cat"
    dog: "#/components/schemas/Dog"
```

See [Collections and unions: discriminated unions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-collections.md#discriminated-unions) for the Python declarations and validation behavior.

For file binding syntax, limits and the in-memory boundary, see [upload files](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#upload-files).

An action annotated `-> Stream` or `-> File` documents its `200` response as `application/octet-stream` with `{"type": "string", "format": "binary"}`, and `-> EventStream` as `text/event-stream` with `{"type": "string"}`. The media type a `Stream` sends is chosen by the handler at run time, so the document does not list it. An annotation such as `-> Stream | NoteOut` also documents the plain arm, under the media types of the route's renderers, next to the streamed one. See [stream a response](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md).

Add a useful docstring to each handler because it is the source for operation text:

```python
@http.get("/tasks/{task_id}")
async def get_task(task_id: UUID) -> TaskOutput:
    """Read one task.

    Returns the task visible to the authenticated caller.
    """
    ...
```

## Per-action controls

`include_in_schema`, `tags`, `deprecated` and `operation_id` are options of `@http.get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete` and `query`:

```python
from hinoki import Access, Hinoki, Schema, http

from notes.security import staff_auth  # any authentication provider

admin_only = Access(auth=staff_auth, permissions=["ops:run"])


class Started(Schema):
    status: str


class Totals(Schema):
    tasks: int


@http.get("/ops/reindex", access=admin_only, include_in_schema=False)
async def reindex() -> Started:
    return Started(status="started")


@http.get("/v1/totals", tags=["tasks"], deprecated=True, operation_id="totalsV1")
async def totals() -> Totals:
    return Totals(tasks=0)


app = Hinoki(include=[reindex, totals])
```

* `include_in_schema=False` leaves the action out of `Hinoki.openapi()`, `hinoki openapi` and `/openapi.json`. The action is still registered, served and protected by its `Access` exactly as before: leaving it out neither hides it from a caller who knows the path nor authorizes anything. A path whose actions are all left out is not listed, and a `Schema` or security scheme used only by left-out actions does not appear under `components`.
* `tags` lists non-empty names, in order and without repeats, written to the operation's `tags`.
* `deprecated=True` writes `deprecated: true`. A deprecated action also tells its callers at run time: each response carries a `Deprecation` header and the call is logged as a warning, see [deprecate an action](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md#deprecate-an-action).
* `operation_id` replaces the generated operation ID. It must be a non-empty string, and two documented actions with the same value stop `include` with a `RegistrationError`; a generated ID never takes a value that an action declared. A left-out action does not take part in that check.
* `RouteGroup(prefix, include_in_schema=..., tags=...)` sets defaults for its actions: an action's own `include_in_schema` wins, and its `tags` follow the group's.
* `crud(...)` takes `include_in_schema` as one flag for the whole resource or a mapping by action (`{"delete": False}`; unknown names are refused), plus `tags` and `deprecated` for every generated action. It has no `operation_id`, because one value cannot name several actions.
* An MCP tool is built from the OpenAPI document, so `expose_as_mcp` refuses an action left out with `include_in_schema=False` instead of exposing it. The admin's HTML pages are always left out of the document and are not affected by these options.

## Deprecate an action

```python
from datetime import date

from hinoki import Schema, http


class Totals(Schema):
    tasks: int


@http.get("/v1/totals", deprecated=date(2026, 11, 22))
async def totals_v1() -> Totals:
    return Totals(tasks=0)
```

`deprecated` takes `True`, `False` or the `datetime.date` the action was deprecated on (a `datetime` is refused). It does three things:

* The document marks the operation `deprecated: true`.
* Every response, success or error, carries a `Deprecation` header: `@<unix seconds>` for a date (the form of RFC 9745, midnight UTC), `true` when no date is given.
* The `hinoki.deprecated` logger warns `deprecated action called: GET /v1/totals (N call(s) since the last report)`. An action is reported at most once per minute, with the calls it stayed quiet about, so a busy action does not flood the log; the state is one entry per deprecated action. Nothing is logged at startup.

The header and the warning are produced by the Python pipeline, so a deprecated action leaves [the native lane](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#what-is-native-and-what-still-runs-in-python) (`hinoki routes --lanes` shows `lane_reason` `deprecated`) and, for generated CRUD, the native CRUD plan. The response and the access check do not change. There is no `Sunset` header.

## Current limits

`operation_id` is per action only, and `deprecated` is per action or set for every action generated by one `crud(...)`; a `RouteGroup` sets `tags` and `include_in_schema` but has no group-wide `deprecated` or `operation_id`. There is no tag metadata (descriptions) in the document's top-level `tags`. Response bodies are generated from annotations; every action's return value is checked against its annotation at runtime, and an annotation that cannot be checked stops the app at startup ([details](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#the-response-is-checked-against-the-annotation)). See [project status](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/status.md) for other API boundaries.

# Authentication and access

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md

Every endpoint is public until you attach an `Access` policy. A policy pairs an
authentication provider (how a request proves who it is) with the permissions an
action needs. Write both once and name the policy on each private action.

```python
# blog/apps/blog/security.py
import hashlib

from hinoki import Access, BearerAuth, Caller, Permission

from .models import User


def hash_token(token: str) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest()


class BlogPermission(Permission):
    WRITE = "posts:write"


class TokenAuth(BearerAuth[User]):
    """Looks the token's digest up in ``blog_users``; editors get the write scope."""

    async def resolve_token(self, token: str) -> Caller[User] | None:
        user = await User.aget_or_none(token_hash=hash_token(token))
        if user is None:
            return None
        scopes = frozenset({BlogPermission.WRITE}) if user.is_editor else frozenset()
        return Caller(id=str(user.id), user=user, permissions=scopes)


auth = TokenAuth()
editor = Access(auth=auth, permissions=[BlogPermission.WRITE])
reader = Access(auth=auth)
```

This is the [Blog example's security module](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/apps/blog/security.py).

## Name your permissions

Subclass `Permission`, an empty string enum, and use its members in policies and
callers. `Access` and `Caller` store each permission as its string value, so
`BlogPermission.WRITE` and `"posts:write"` match each other in checks, reprs and
logs; plain strings are still accepted. Passing one string instead of a
collection (`permissions="posts:write"`) is a `TypeError`.

## Define a provider

Pick the base class for where the credential travels and implement one hook:

| Base class | Credential | Implement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BearerAuth[User]` | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | `resolve_token(token)` |
| `APIKeyAuth[User]` | the `x-api-key` header | `resolve(value)` |
| `HeaderAuth[User]` | the header named by `header` | `resolve(value)` |

The hook returns a `Caller` with a stable `id`, your user object and its
permissions, or `None` when the credential is unknown. It may be `async def` or
`def`; a synchronous hook runs on the bounded sync executor, so it may use
blocking libraries.

## Attach a policy

Name the policy with `access=` on the HTTP decorator and annotate a
`Caller[User]` parameter to receive the authenticated caller:

```python
# blog/apps/blog/drafts.py
from hinoki import Caller, http

from .models import Post, User
from .schemas import PostCreate, PostOut
from .security import editor


@http.post("/drafts", status=201, access=editor, atomic=True)
async def create_draft(data: PostCreate, caller: Caller[User]) -> PostOut:
    post = await Post.acreate(
        data,
        author_id=caller.user.id,
        publication_id=caller.user.publication_id,
    )
    return PostOut.from_model(post, author_name=caller.user.name)
```

Take the owner from `caller.user`, never from the request body. Permissions say
*what* a caller may do; whether a given row is theirs is still your query (the
Blog's `owned_post` helper in
[`api.py`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/apps/blog/api.py)
shows one way).

To protect a whole group, set the policy once on a `RouteGroup`
(`RouteGroup("/invoices", access=billing_staff)`); an action may override it, and
`access=None` makes one action public on purpose.

## What clients receive

| Request | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| No credential | `401` with a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge |
| A credential the hook rejects (returns `None`), or a value that is not `Bearer <token>` | `401` with the challenge |
| A valid caller without a required permission | `403` |
| A policy without permissions (`reader` above) | any authenticated caller passes |

A policy without permissions is legitimate ("any signed-in user"), and it is easy
to write by accident; the [rule](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md) `HNK-ACC-002` asks you to list such
actions explicitly.

## Hash passwords

`hinoki.crypto.PasswordHasher` hashes and verifies with Argon2id in Rust, off the
event loop. Create it where you own its lifetime (a factory or a module) and call
`close()` at shutdown, or use it as a context manager (`with` or `async with`).
Its worker threads start on first use; a closed hasher starts them again if it
is used, and a hasher that is garbage-collected shuts them down.

```python
# blog/apps/blog/passwords.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from dataclasses import dataclass

from hinoki import Module, Resource
from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher
from hinoki.modules import ModuleContext


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class PasswordService(Resource):
    hasher: PasswordHasher


class Passwords(Module):
    name = "passwords"

    @asynccontextmanager
    async def lifespan(self, ctx: ModuleContext) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
        hasher = PasswordHasher()
        ctx.provide(PasswordService, PasswordService(hasher))
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            hasher.close()
```

Inject `PasswordService` into handlers (see [Application modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md)):

```python
async def change_password(new_password: str, passwords: PasswordService) -> str:
    return await passwords.hasher.hash(new_password)


async def password_matches(
    password: str, stored: str, passwords: PasswordService
) -> bool:
    return await passwords.hasher.verify(password, stored)
```

`hash_sync` and `verify_sync` exist for scripts and seeds; `needs_rehash(stored)`
tells you when to rehash after a parameter change, and `random_token()` returns a
URL-safe random token for opaque credentials. When the hashing queue is full, the
hasher raises `HashingBusy`, a `503`. The Blog's
[accounts module](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/apps/blog/accounts.py)
shows a complete login with constant-time behaviour for unknown users.

## Verify JSON Web Tokens

Subclass `JWTAuth[User]`, list the keys and implement `resolve_claims`, which
turns verified claims into a `Caller` (or `None`). Read secrets from a
`settings.Secret` field and pass it as the key: `JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", app_settings.jwt_key)` accepts `bytes`, text or a `Secret`, and the key never appears in its `repr`.

For `JWTAuth`, Rust verifies the signature and registered claims using the current key snapshot. `now()` and the configured issuer, audience, leeway (0 to 120 seconds; a provider with another value fails when it is built) and expiry policy are read for each verification. A request already verifying with a captured key snapshot finishes with that snapshot; a later verification observes key rotation. Rust does not turn token claims into a `Caller`: the application's `resolve_claims` hook still runs for every valid token, and remains responsible for loading or rejecting the identity and deciding its permissions. Sync, async and sync functions returning awaitables follow the normal hook execution path.

## Claims-only tokens on the native lane

`ClaimsJWTAuth` is a `JWTAuth` whose caller comes from the token alone: `sub` (a
non-empty string) becomes `Caller.id`, the claim named by `scope_claim` (default
`scopes`, a list of strings) becomes the permissions, and `Caller.user` is `None`.
No database lookup happens, so a token cannot be revoked before it expires: keep
lifetimes short.

```python
# notes/tokens.py
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import ClassVar

from hinoki import Access, Caller, Permission, Schema, http
from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth, JWTKey


class NotesPermission(Permission):
    WRITE = "notes:write"


class Tokens(ClaimsJWTAuth):
    keys: ClassVar[Sequence[JWTKey]] = (
        JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", b"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"),
    )  # read the key from a Secret in a real application
    issuer = "https://api.example.com"
    audience = "notes"


class WhoAmI(Schema):
    id: str
    permissions: list[str]


tokens = Tokens()
writer = Access(auth=tokens, permissions=[NotesPermission.WRITE])


@http.get("/me", access=writer)
async def me(caller: Caller[None]) -> WhoAmI:
    return WhoAmI(id=caller.id, permissions=sorted(caller.permissions))
```

`tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["notes:write"]}, ttl=900)` signs with the
first key that can sign and sets `iat`, `exp`, and `iss`/`aud` when configured.

### The policies of the billing examples {#billing-policies}

The endpoint, CRUD and transaction guides import `billing_staff` and
`billing_admin` from one module. Declare the policies once and import them
wherever an action or `RouteGroup` names them:

```python
# notes/security.py
from collections.abc import Sequence
from typing import ClassVar

from hinoki import Access, Permission
from hinoki.crypto import ClaimsJWTAuth, JWTKey


class BillingPermission(Permission):
    MANAGE = "billing:manage"
    ADMIN = "billing:admin"


class StaffTokens(ClaimsJWTAuth):
    keys: ClassVar[Sequence[JWTKey]] = (
        JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", b"0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef"),
    )  # read the key from a Secret in a real application


tokens = StaffTokens()
billing_staff = Access(auth=tokens, permissions=[BillingPermission.MANAGE])
billing_admin = Access(auth=tokens, permissions=[BillingPermission.ADMIN])
```

A token from `tokens.issue({"sub": "u1", "scopes": ["billing:manage"]}, ttl=900)`
passes `billing_staff`; without a token the answer is `401`, and with a token
that lacks the permission it is `403`.

Generated CRUD routes protected by an unmodified `ClaimsJWTAuth` can run on the native lane. Rust only admits requests: a single `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header whose token verifies (signature, expiry, issuer, audience, `sub`) and carries every required permission goes straight to the native action. Every other request, including a missing, malformed, expired, forged or under-privileged one, is handed to the Python pipeline, which answers exactly as it does without the native lane (`401` with the challenge, or `403`). With `owner` and `identity_key = caller_id`, create, update and delete are native too: Rust sets the owner column from `sub`, and update/delete are constrained to rows that `sub` owns. Foreign or missing rows, and MySQL/MariaDB, are answered by the Python pipeline. A subclass that overrides a method, a modified instance, or any other auth class keeps the route on Python. The route's key, issuer, audience, leeway and permission snapshot is rechecked about once per second; reassigning them disarms the native plan until the worker restarts, so a rotation reaches native routes after that interval, not per verification. `hinoki routes --lanes` shows which lane each route uses.

Rust verifies the token on these routes too: a handler route protected by an unmodified `ClaimsJWTAuth` (not generated CRUD) is authenticated by Rust, which admits the caller or answers `401` or `403` itself with the same body and `WWW-Authenticate` challenge as Python, in the same order relative to path/query errors, the rate limit and body validation. Rust defers to Python for anything it cannot decide identically: several `Authorization` headers, a value that is not a plain `Bearer <token>`, or a request Rust already found malformed. A rate limit still runs afterwards in Python, with the admitted caller. Error handlers registered with `app.errors` do not apply to these answers, on either path, because they translate other exceptions. The provider and policy are checked about once per second as for CRUD routes.

## Errors and edge cases

- Return `None` for an unknown credential; let unexpected exceptions propagate, they are server errors, not `401`.
- `JWTAuth` leeway must be 0–120 seconds; another value fails when the provider is built.
- Providers hold no per-request state: one instance serves every request and worker thread.
- Hinoki does not create users, sessions or permission rules: those remain your application's data and policy.
- A refusal by an access policy emits an `AuthRejected` [event](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md#authentication-and-rate-limit-events) (`missing`, `invalid` or `forbidden`, the route template and the method; never credentials or the requested path) when the application has a handler for it. The handler cannot change the answer. On Kiso, a route that Rust would authenticate is authenticated by Python while such a handler is registered, so the event can fire.

## See also

- [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md): make "every private action has a policy" a checked promise.
- [Hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md): the browser-facing side of security.
- [Authentication reference](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/reference/auth.md)

# Application sessions

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sessions.md

Application sessions keep small JSON state on the server and identify it with a
random cookie token. The raw token is sent to the client; the store keeps only
its SHA-256 digest. This is separate from the optional admin's session table
and cookie.

Configure a store explicitly. The CSRF key must be at least 32 bytes; keep it in
a secret setting or environment variable, and configure the same value on every
worker:

```python
from collections.abc import Mapping

from hinoki import Access, Caller, Hinoki, http
from hinoki.sessions import (
    DatabaseSessionStore,
    Session,
    SessionAuth,
    SessionModule,
    SessionSettings,
)

session_settings = SessionSettings(csrf_secret=secret_from_environment)


@http.post("/login")
async def login(session: Session) -> dict[str, str]:
    user = await verify_credentials()
    await session.rotate()  # issue a fresh token after authentication
    session["user_id"] = str(user.id)
    session.subject = str(user.id)
    return {"status": "signed_in"}


def resolve_user(data: Mapping[str, object]) -> Caller[User] | None:
    user_id = data.get("user_id")
    return load_caller(user_id) if isinstance(user_id, str) else None


session_auth = SessionAuth(resolve_user)


@http.get("/me", access=Access(auth=session_auth))
async def me(caller: Caller[User]) -> UserSchema:
    return UserSchema.from_user(caller.user)


app = Hinoki(
    include=[login, me],
    modules=[SessionModule(DatabaseSessionStore(), session_settings)],
)
```

`csrf_secret` takes `bytes`, text or a `settings.Secret` (encoded as UTF-8) of at least 32 bytes; it is left out of the settings' `repr` and comparisons, and `settings.csrf_key()` returns the bytes.

`SessionAuth` resolves a `Caller` from the read-only session data and works with
`Access` and `Caller[T]`. It documents the configured cookie name as an OpenAPI
cookie security scheme. If `SessionSettings.cookie_name` is customized, pass the
same name to `SessionAuth(cookie_name=...)`. `SessionModule(store, settings)`
requires its `SessionSettings`.

A custom `Auth` that composes `SessionAuth` (for example, one that tries a bearer
token and then the session) is detected automatically: Hinoki loads the session
and applies the CSRF rules below. Set `uses_session = True` on an `Auth` class
that reads the session in another way.

`SessionAuth` also works on `@http.websocket` routes. The session is loaded
read-only during the handshake, and an unknown or expired cookie refuses the
connection. The handshake `Origin` is checked by the websocket origin rules.

## State and response lifecycle

`Session` is request-scoped. It provides `get`, item lookup and assignment,
`del session[key]`, `clear`, `rotate`, `invalidate`, `csrf_token`, `is_new`,
`modified` and `subject`. Values must be JSON serializable; the default encoded
payload limit is 16 KiB. `None` is a normal value inside the mapping. Nested
values returned by reads are copies; assign the updated value back through
`session[key]` to persist a nested change.

Hinoki loads a session when a route declares `session: Session` or uses
`SessionAuth`. Mutations are saved and `Set-Cookie` is added only after the
handler returns successfully (that is, without raising an exception) and after
any `atomic=True` SQL transaction has committed, so a session store failure
does not roll back an already-committed SQL transaction. A returned `Response`
with an error status is still a successful handler return. If the handler
raises, pending changes and cookie changes are discarded.

`rotate()` issues a fresh token and revokes the old one on successful response;
use it on login and privilege changes to prevent fixation. `invalidate()`
revokes the current token and sends a clearing cookie. Revocations are retained
until the session's absolute expiry, so an already-running request cannot
restore a revoked token with a stale write. `MemorySessionStore` drops a revoked
session's data immediately and keeps only a bounded record of revoked tokens.

The cookie defaults to `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure`, and `Path=/`.
`cookie_secure=False` is available for local HTTP development. The absolute
timeout defaults to 14 days and the idle timeout to one day. A successful
request refreshes the idle expiry after the 60-second touch interval. Missing,
malformed and expired cookies start as an anonymous session; they do not emit a
cookie unless the handler changes the session.

## CSRF

Unsafe methods (`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `QUERY`) on a route that uses a
session or `SessionAuth` require a valid `X-CSRF-Token` when the request carries
an existing session cookie. The token is an HMAC-SHA256 value bound to that
session; `session.csrf_token()` returns it for a frontend to place in the
header. When `Origin` is present it must match the request origin, and an
explicit `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` or `none` is rejected. `GET`, `HEAD` and
`OPTIONS` are safe methods.

For example, a page or JSON bootstrap action can return `session.csrf_token()`;
the browser then sends that value in `X-CSRF-Token` for writes. A missing or
invalid token receives 403 `csrf_rejected`. Store failures fail closed with 503
`session_unavailable`; a session is never silently treated as anonymous when
the store is down.

The bootstrap action must establish a token before asking for the CSRF value:

```python
@http.get("/csrf")
async def csrf_bootstrap(session: Session) -> dict[str, str]:
    if session.is_new:
        await session.rotate()
    return {"csrf_token": session.csrf_token()}
```

The successful response persists the session and sends its cookie; subsequent
unsafe requests can send the returned CSRF token with that cookie.

## Stores, migrations and limits

| Store | Visibility and ownership | Capacity and cleanup |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MemorySessionStore(max_sessions=10_000)` | Per worker process; workers do not share sessions | Bounded by session count; it removes expired sessions and returns 503 when full of live or revoked sessions |
| `DatabaseSessionStore()` | Shared by workers through the application's `Database` | No configured row cap; call `purge_expired()` from a scheduled maintenance task |

`DatabaseSessionStore` depends on `DatabaseModule` when it is not given a
database directly. It expects the `hinoki_sessions` table. Apply the SQL at
`migrations_path() / "0001-initial.sql"` through an explicit project migration
and review/apply that migration before starting the application. Importing the
module and starting the worker do not create or alter tables.
`purge_expired()` deletes rows past their absolute expiry, including revoked
token tombstones; revoked rows remain until that expiry.

The database store keeps JSON session data as plain text, so do not put secrets
in session values unless the application encrypts them before storage or the
database's at-rest protections meet its policy. Sessions identify a subject for
revocation with `delete_by_subject`; they do not implement user ownership or
authorization by themselves. The application still owns account checks and
permission policy. Database cleanup is explicit; Hinoki does not start a
background purge task.

`SessionTooLarge` is a 413 response. A malformed store row or database failure
is reported as `SessionUnavailable` (503) without exposing the token, SQL or
stored data. Session migrations and revocation are distinct from file storage
and cache migrations.

# Hosts, CORS and HTTPS

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md

A new application answers any `Host`, sends no CORS headers, never redirects to
HTTPS and trusts no proxy. That keeps development friction-free; before a
deployment, name what it serves. The built-in groups (`cors`, `security`,
`server`) are set from the environment, `.env` or a TOML file the class names;
a value assigned to such a group in the class body is not read.

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(
    settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env", toml="settings.toml"
):
    pass
```

```toml
# settings.toml
allowed_hosts = ["api.example.com"]

[cors]
origins = ["https://app.example.com"]

[security]
redirect_https = true
hsts_seconds = 31_536_000

[server]
trusted_proxies = ["10.20.0.0/16"]
```

Every field can also come from the environment, which is usually where a
deployment sets them and which wins over the TOML file:

```sh
NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=api.example.com,.example.org
NOTES_CORS__ORIGINS=https://app.example.com,http://localhost:5173
NOTES_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS=true
```

## Debug, allowed hosts and CORS {#debug-allowed-hosts-and-cors}

These three are off or permissive by default, so an application behaves the same
until you set them.

### `debug` {#debug}

With `debug` on, the `500 internal_error` answer for an unhandled exception also carries a `debug` object:

```json
{
  "error": "internal_error",
  "request_id": "5f0c…",
  "debug": {
    "exception": "builtins.RuntimeError",
    "message": "the cache is cold",
    "traceback": ["Traceback (most recent call last):\n", "…"]
  }
}
```

Declared errors, validation errors and the other framework answers are unchanged, and the exception is logged either way. Exception messages can contain data you would not publish, so keep `debug` off in a deployment; each worker logs a warning at startup while it is on. `debug` changes nothing else: it does not enable documentation pages, relax authentication or skip the host check (with an admin or a WebSocket route and `allowed_hosts` at `*` it narrows the hosts to loopback, see below), and `hinoki dev` does not set it.

### `allowed_hosts` {#allowed_hosts}

The `Host` header of every request must match one entry:

| Entry | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `*` (the default) | Any host; nothing is checked |
| `api.example.com` | That host, on any port |
| `.example.org` | `example.org` and every subdomain |
| `127.0.0.1`, `::1` | That address (`[::1]:8000` in the header) |

Matching ignores case, the port and a trailing dot. The header must be exactly one host with an optional port; a request for another host, with two `Host` headers or without a usable one, receives `400 disallowed_host` before routing, authentication and body reading; documentation routes are covered too. Entries are names: a scheme, port, path, non-ASCII text (write an international name in its ASCII IDNA form, `xn--...`) or a partial wildcard such as `*.example.com` fails at load, and `*` cannot be mixed with other entries. A dot entry is as wide as it reads: `.com` allows every `.com` host.

Set the list in a deployment that is reachable under more names than it should answer to. While `allowed_hosts` is `*` (the default, and the case for an app built without settings) and `debug` is off, each worker logs a warning at startup (logger `hinoki.runtime`, shown with the default logging settings): every `Host` header is accepted, so links, redirects and cache keys built from it, such as a password-reset link, can name a host the client chose (Host header injection). Name the hosts the deployment serves to silence it, for example `allowed_hosts=("app.example.com",)`, or `(".example.com",)` for a domain and its subdomains (`NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=app.example.com`). It is only a warning for a plain API, so the default keeps working in development. An app that includes the [admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md) or registers a [WebSocket route](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/websockets.md) is refused at startup instead (the lifespan fails with a message naming `allowed_hosts`, and `hinoki serve` logs the error and exits with status 1; the server may already have logged that it is listening, but it answers no request): the admin's CSRF check and the WebSocket same-origin check compare the `Origin` header with the `Host` header, so with `*` a DNS-rebinding page (`Host: evil.example`, `Origin: https://evil.example`) would pass both. Name the served hosts. `debug` lifts the refusal for local development only, and then the app accepts loopback hosts only: with `debug` on and `allowed_hosts` at `*`, an app that serves an admin or a WebSocket route accepts only the Host names `localhost`, `*.localhost`, any `127.0.0.0/8` address and `[::1]` (with or without a port, in any case, with or without a trailing dot) for the whole app, and any other `Host` receives `400`, so a DNS-rebinding page cannot reach a development server; set `allowed_hosts` to serve other names (an explicit list is always used as given). An app without an admin or a WebSocket route still accepts any `Host` under `debug`. Each worker logs a startup warning while the loopback-only rule applies. With `debug` on the any-host warning is not logged, and the in-process test clients (`ASGIClient`, `SyncClient`) and the MCP `run_scenario` tool, which receive no network `Host` header, do not log it either.

The in-process test clients send no `Host` header, so a test of an application with a restrictive list passes one: `await client.get("/x", headers={"host": "api.example.com"})`.

### `cors` {#cors}

CORS is off while `cors.origins` is empty: no header is added and `OPTIONS` requests receive `405`. With origins configured:

- A request whose `Origin` is listed receives `access-control-allow-origin` with that origin and `vary: origin`, on every answer including errors, so a browser client can read a `401` or `422` body. `credentials = true` adds `access-control-allow-credentials: true`; `expose_headers` is sent as `access-control-expose-headers`.
- A request from any other origin, or without an `Origin`, is served normally without the permission headers and still carries `vary: origin`, so a shared cache never hands one origin's answer to another; the browser refuses to hand the response to the page. CORS tells browsers what to allow. It is not authentication and does not stop a non-browser client.
- A preflight (`OPTIONS` with `Origin` and `Access-Control-Request-Method`) is answered with `204`, the configured `methods`, `headers` and `max_age`, without reaching a route or its access policy. A preflight from an origin that is not listed receives `403 cors_origin_denied`.

Origins are compared exactly, in lower case as browsers send them: `https://app.example.com` and `https://app.example.com:8443` are different origins, and a trailing slash or path is refused at load. Browsers leave a default port out of `Origin`, so list `https://app.example.com`, not `https://app.example.com:443`. The single entry `*` answers every origin with `access-control-allow-origin: *`; it cannot be combined with `credentials`, and browsers will not send cookies or HTTP authentication to it.

The application policy applies to every route that does not declare its own, including the ASGI and WSGI adapters (see [per-route CORS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md#cors-per-route) below). An answer that already sets `access-control-allow-origin` itself (a `Response` with that header) is sent as it is, without the policy's headers.

### Per-route CORS {#cors-per-route}

An action can carry its own policy with `cors=http.Cors(...)`, for a public feed, a partner endpoint or a route that must not be readable from the origins the rest of the application allows. `http.Cors` takes the fields of `settings.CorsSettings` (`origins`, `methods`, `headers`, `expose_headers`, `credentials`, `max_age`) and requires at least one origin:

```python
# notes/apps/feed/api.py
from hinoki import Schema, http

from notes.security import reader  # an `Access` policy

partner = http.Cors(origins=("https://partner.example",), credentials=True)


class Feed(Schema):
    feed: str


@http.get("/feed/partner", access=reader, cors=partner)
async def partner_feed() -> Feed:
    return Feed(feed="partner")
```

- **Precedence.** The route's policy replaces the application's for that route; nothing is merged, so the application's origins do not apply to it. An action without `cors=` keeps the application policy, and a route with `cors=` works even while the application's `cors.origins` is empty.
- **Preflight.** A preflight is answered for the route the browser asks about: `Access-Control-Request-Method` names the method, the request path names the route. A route with its own policy answers with its own `methods`, `headers`, `max_age` and origin check (`403 cors_origin_denied` for an origin it does not list). A method that no route has on that path is answered by the application policy. A preflight never runs the route's `access` policy, a transaction or the handler.
- **Answers.** Every answer from a matched route, errors from `access` or validation included, carries that route's headers and `vary: origin`. Answers before a route is known (`404`, `405`) carry the application's.
- **Groups and generated CRUD.** `RouteGroup("/feed", cors=http.Cors(...))` is the default of its actions (`cors=None` on an action returns it to the application policy), and `crud(..., cors=http.Cors(...))` gives all generated actions the policy.

Kiso decides these natively; the ASGI and WSGI adapters apply the same rules in Python.

## Security headers and HTTPS {#browser-security-headers-and-https}

Every HTTP response gets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, the configured `X-Frame-Options` and `Referrer-Policy`, including errors, OpenAPI/docs and admin responses. Defaults are `SAMEORIGIN` and `same-origin`, preserving the admin's existing referrer privacy default. These fields are owned by the app security policy: configured values replace same-named headers returned by a route.

The choices are enums rather than arbitrary strings, and environment/TOML values must match the listed wire values exactly. `FrameOptions` provides `deny` and `sameorigin`. `ReferrerPolicy` provides `no-referrer`, `no-referrer-when-downgrade`, `same-origin`, `origin`, `strict-origin`, `origin-when-cross-origin`, `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` and `unsafe-url`. `unsafe-url` can disclose the full referring URL to another origin; use it only when that is intended.

```toml
# settings.toml
[security]
redirect_https = true
hsts_seconds = 31_536_000
hsts_include_subdomains = true
frame_options = "deny"
referrer_policy = "strict-origin"
```

For configuration loaded from the environment, set `NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=api.example.com` and `NOTES_SECURITY__REDIRECT_HTTPS=true`. A wildcard host policy cannot be combined with the redirect: Hinoki requires an explicit host allowlist before constructing an absolute `Location`, which avoids redirecting an attacker supplied `Host` value. The redirect is `308`, preserves the method and raw path/query, and runs before route lookup, authentication and body reading. A configured CORS preflight is answered before redirecting so browser preflight requests remain usable.

HSTS defaults off. Hinoki emits it only when the request's effective scheme is HTTPS. Behind TLS termination, configure the exact proxy addresses in `server.trusted_proxies`; an untrusted `X-Forwarded-Proto` does not enable HSTS or suppress the redirect. `hsts_preload` also requires `hsts_include_subdomains` and a `max-age` of at least one year. Use HSTS only after confirming that HTTPS is available for every covered host: browsers retain the policy after the response.

## Reverse proxies and request IDs {#reverse-proxies-and-request-ids}

Forwarded metadata is ignored unless the immediate socket peer matches `server.trusted_proxies`. Configure only the addresses or CIDRs of proxies that remove client-supplied forwarding headers and write their own values. For example:

```toml
# settings.toml
# The private address used by this deployment's ingress, not every private network.
[server]
trusted_proxies = ["10.20.0.0/16"]
request_id_header = "x-correlation-id"
trust_request_id = true
```

From a trusted peer, Hinoki accepts a single `X-Forwarded-Proto` value of `http` or `https` and walks a bounded `X-Forwarded-For` chain from the peer side to the first untrusted address. `Request.scheme` and `Request.client` use those validated values. Invalid, repeated or ambiguous values fall back to the socket scope. `X-Forwarded-Host` is never used: `Host`, `allowed_hosts` and generated URLs continue to use the original Host header.

On a listener bound to `::`, an IPv4 peer can appear as `::ffff:a.b.c.d`, which a plain IPv4 entry does not match (the proxy is then untrusted); see [behind a reverse proxy](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#behind-a-reverse-proxy).

Request IDs are generated by default. With `trust_request_id=True`, one inbound configured header is accepted only from a trusted immediate peer and only when it is 1–128 visible ASCII characters without commas or controls. Otherwise Hinoki generates a new ID. The selected value appears in `Request.request_id`, built-in error JSON and the configured response header. The proxy must sanitize the incoming header before forwarding it; do not trust a broad network range merely because it is private.

Set `logging.include_request_id=true` to add the resolved ID to Hinoki's own log records while a request is being handled. Text logs append `request_id=<id>` and JSON logs include a `request_id` field. The ID matches the response's configured request ID header. Startup and other records outside a request omit the field. This setting is off by default, and it does not change application or third-party logger handlers.

## Errors and edge cases

- An invalid `allowed_hosts` entry, a `*` mixed with names, or a CORS origin with a path fails when settings load, before any worker starts.
- A served app with the admin or a WebSocket route, `allowed_hosts` at `*` and `debug` off does not start; with `debug` on it answers `400` to every `Host` that is not loopback (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `[::1]`). The in-process test clients are exempt.
- `redirect_https=True` with `allowed_hosts` left at `*` is refused at load: the redirect needs a host it can trust.
- A request for an unlisted host receives `400 disallowed_host`; a preflight from an unlisted origin receives `403 cors_origin_denied`.
- Tests with a restrictive host list pass the header: `await client.get("/health", headers={"host": "api.example.com"})`.

## See also

- [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md): how values are loaded, named and inspected.
- [Kiso server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#behind-a-reverse-proxy): addresses behind a proxy on Kiso.
- [Errors](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/errors.md): the JSON bodies of these answers.

# Rules

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md

Rules are typed promises about your application: "every private action names a
policy", "writes are atomic", "no response leaks `password_hash`". Each one is a
Python object with a stable ID, deterministic behaviour and an exact fix line.
They are optional, and a project created with `hinoki new` starts with them on:

```python
# notes/rules.py
"""The project's rules. Weaken them only with the owner's decision (see hinoki-rules.toml)."""

from hinoki import Actions, Schemas, Transactions  # add Models with your first model
from hinoki.rules import RuleSet

project_rules = RuleSet(
    # Anything not public on purpose names an access policy, and the policy names permissions.
    Actions.require_access(match="notes.*", except_=["notes.api.health"]),
    Actions.require_permissions(match="notes.*", except_=["notes.api.health"]),
    # Responses are concrete Schema types and lists are paginated.
    Actions.forbid_model_responses(match="notes.*"),
    Actions.require_return_type(match="notes.*"),
    Actions.require_pagination(match="notes.*"),
    # Writes run in a transaction that rolls back before errors become HTTP.
    Transactions.require_atomic(),
    # Secrets never reach a client, and request text is bounded.
    Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", "password", "token"),
    Schemas.require_string_limits(),
    # Turn these on with your first model (a model rule that matches no model
    # fails the check): tables are pinned and foreign keys are indexed.
    # Models.require_explicit_table(match="notes.*"),
    # Models.require_foreign_key_index(match="notes.*"),
)
```

`hinoki.toml` lists the set under `[project]`, and `Hinoki()` loads it (see
[which rules run](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-rules-run)):

```toml
[project]
application = "notes.main:app"
rules = ["notes.rules:project_rules"]
```

Check it at any time:

```sh
hinoki check
```

## The twelve rules

| ID | Rule | Phase | Checks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `HNK-ACC-001` | `Actions.require_access(match="*", except_=())` | startup | every matching action names an `Access` policy (public by default is the common hole) |
| `HNK-ACC-002` | `Actions.require_permissions(match="*", except_=())` | startup | an action with an `Access` policy names at least one permission, so "any authenticated caller" is never implicit |
| `HNK-API-001` | `Actions.forbid_model_responses(match="*", except_=())` | startup | no action returns a `Model` (or a list or page of them): responses are `Schema` classes |
| `HNK-API-002` | `Actions.require_return_type(match="*", except_=())` | startup | every action annotates a concrete return type (not missing, `Any` or `object`; `None` is fine for a `204`) |
| `HNK-API-003` | `Actions.require_pagination(match="*", except_=())` | startup | a `GET` action never returns a plain `list[...]` (alone or in a union): it returns a `Page` |
| `HNK-TXN-001` | `Transactions.require_atomic(methods=("POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"), match="*", except_=())` | startup | state-changing actions declare `atomic=True`, on the action or its `RouteGroup` |
| `HNK-SCH-001` | `Schemas.forbid_exposure(*fields)` | startup | the named fields never appear in a response `Schema`: nested, in a subclass, in a union variant, as a field, an alias or a computed field; an action returning a `dict` is reported as unverifiable |
| `HNK-SCH-002` | `Schemas.require_string_limits()` | startup | every text field a client sends (nested, in containers, `dict` values and union variants included) has `max_length` or `one_of`; `Enum` and `Literal` fields pass |
| `HNK-DB-001` | `Models.require_explicit_table(match="*")` | startup | matching models pin their table with `@db.table(...)` or `table=`, so renaming the class cannot rename the table |
| `HNK-DB-002` | `Models.require_foreign_key_index(match="*")` | startup | every foreign-key column leads an index, a primary key or a unique constraint |
| `HNK-MAIL-001` | `EmailTemplatesMatch()` | static | every registered [email template](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md) loads and matches its context `Schema` (opt-in, see [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#an-opt-in-rule-email-templates)) |
| `HNK-IMP-001` | `Imports.forbid(source, target)` | static | modules under `source` never import `target`, read from the source files; dynamic imports are reported, not ignored |

Every built-in rule has severity `error`. `HNK-API-002` matters most for actions
with `validate_response=False`: any other action with an unusable return
annotation already stops the app. `HNK-TXN-001` does not check the admin's own
routes, which open their own short transactions.

## An opt-in rule: email templates

`EmailTemplatesMatch()` (`HNK-MAIL-001`, phase `static`) is listed in the table but runs only when you put it in your `RuleSet`. It reads every registered [email template](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md) (the files included) and checks it against its context `Schema`, reporting one diagnostic per template that is refused. Because it reads files it declares the effect `files`, so `hinoki check` reports it as unverifiable unless you pass `--allow-effects`:

```python
from hinoki.rules import EmailTemplatesMatch, RuleSet

rules = RuleSet(EmailTemplatesMatch())
```

```sh
hinoki check --rules myproject.rules:rules --allow-effects
```

## Choose what a rule covers

Action rules match `fnmatch` patterns against an action's qualified name:
`module.function` for a function, `module.Class.method` for an API class (named
after the class it is mounted on), and `module.<Model>Crud.<action>` for a
`crud(...)` value, where `module` is the one that calls `crud(...)`. A bare `health` matches nothing; write
`notes.api.health` or `*.health`. `except_` takes the same patterns and is how
you say "public on purpose". The Blog example names its exceptions once:

```python
# examples/blog/blog/rules.py
PUBLIC = [
    "blog.apps.blog.api.health",
    "blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.listing",
    "blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.one",
    "blog.apps.blog.accounts.*.login",  # public on purpose: it is how you sign in
]
SIGNED_IN = ["blog.apps.blog.accounts.*.me"]  # any signed-in user, no permission

blog_rules = RuleSet(
    Actions.require_access(match="blog.*", except_=PUBLIC),
    Actions.require_permissions(match="blog.*", except_=[*PUBLIC, *SIGNED_IN]),
    Transactions.require_atomic(except_=["hinoki.ai.mcpapp.*"]),
    Schemas.forbid_exposure("token_hash", "password_hash"),
    Imports.forbid(source="blog.apps.blog.models", target="blog.apps.blog.api"),
    # ... and the other six rules, see the file
)
```

Blog passes `blog_rules` and its waiver file to `Hinoki(...)` by hand. Tracker
lists two sets in its manifest instead,
`rules = ["tracker.rules:policy", "tracker.rules:layers"]`, and its
`Hinoki(...)` call names no rules.

The model rules match the model's *module* (`blog.*`) and report unverifiable
when no model matches, even with `*`. In a project with `hinoki.toml`,
`hinoki check` first imports the models of every `[[apps]]` entry, so they are
found without importing them from the application module. `require_access` and
`require_atomic`
report unverifiable when a pattern other than `*` matches no action. Neither
passes silently.

## Which rules run

The application's rules are, in this order of precedence:

1. `Hinoki(rules=...)`, when you pass it. An explicit argument wins, even an
   empty `RuleSet()`, and the manifest is not read for rules.
2. The `[project] rules` list of `hinoki.toml`, when `rules=` is omitted and the
   manifest's `project.application` names the module that builds the app.
3. Otherwise none.

`rules` is a list of `module:attribute` entries, each a `RuleSet`. The sets are
merged in the order listed into one `RuleSet`, so the report keeps that order.
The same rule (same id and summary) listed by two entries is a `ProjectError`
naming both entries, never a silent override; rules that share an id but differ
in their arguments, such as two `Imports.forbid(...)`, are different rules. An entry that does not import, is not a `RuleSet`, or
a list of anything else is rejected the same way. You edit the list by hand;
no command writes it. `manifest_rules()` (from `hinoki.project`) is the explicit
form, for `Hinoki(rules=manifest_rules())` or a test.

`hinoki check` and `hinoki mcp` run `--rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE` when you give it
and otherwise the app's own rules, which are the two sources above.

## When rules run

| Where | Rules | Waivers | On failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Application startup (`hinoki dev`, `hinoki serve`, any ASGI server, the test clients) | startup rules of the [application's rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-rules-run) | the [waiver file](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-waiver-file) | startup fails with `RegistrationError` listing every failing diagnostic |
| `hinoki check` | both phases (or `--phase`) | the waiver file, or `--waivers` | exit code `1` |
| `hinoki mcp` | both phases | the waiver file, or `--waivers` | reported to the agent |

Startup enforcement means a broken promise never serves traffic. During a
migration you can pass `enforce_rules=False` to `Hinoki(...)`: violations are
then logged as a warning instead.

## Read the results

`hinoki check` prints one line per finding, with its location and a `fix:` hint.
This output comes from a deliberately broken project in Hinoki's own tests,
checked from a clone of the repository:

```sh
hinoki check tests.projects.rulesapp:create_app --rules tests.projects.rulesapp:rules
```

```text
tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] GET /health (health) declares no access policy
  fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose)
tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-ACC-001 [violated] POST /items (create) declares no access policy
  fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose)
tests/projects/rulesapp.py:12: HNK-TXN-001 [violated] POST /items (create) does not declare atomic=True
  fix: add atomic=True to the action (or declare it on a RouteGroup(..., atomic=True) group)
2 rule(s): 3 violated, 0 unverifiable, 0 waived
```

Each status means one thing: **violated** (demonstrated), **unverifiable** (the
check could not decide: a dynamic import, a pattern that matched nothing, a
return type that does not name its schema, or a rule that crashed), **waived**
and **warning** (a notice about the waiver file itself). Unverifiable fails like
a violation; it is never a pass. A warning never fails.

The fix line each rule prints:

| ID | `fix:` |
| --- | --- |
| `HNK-ACC-002` | name at least one permission in the Access policy of the action |
| `HNK-API-001` | return a Schema (for example PostOut.from_model(row)) instead of the Model |
| `HNK-API-002` | annotate the action's return type (a Schema, or None for status 204) |
| `HNK-API-003` | return Page[Item] or CursorPage[Item] and paginate the action |
| `HNK-SCH-001` | remove the field from the response Schema, or return a Schema that does not carry it |
| `HNK-SCH-002` | bound the field: Annotated[str, Field(max_length=...)] or one_of=... |
| `HNK-DB-001` | name the table with @db.table(...) or table=... on the model |
| `HNK-DB-002` | index the column: @db.indexed("<column>") on the model, or an index or unique group that starts with it |
| `HNK-IMP-001` | move the code to an allowed layer, or depend on it through the layer in between |

`hinoki check --format json` prints the same diagnostics as versioned data
(`schema_version`, `rules`, `summary`, and per diagnostic `rule`, `severity`,
`phase`, `status`, `message`, `location`, `explanation`, `subject`, `waiver`,
`fix`) for CI, editors and agents. `summary` counts each status (`violated`,
`unverifiable`, `waived`, `warning`) and adds `failing`, the number that sets
the exit code. `schema_version` is `2`: version 1 reported waiver notices as
`violated` and had no `warning` count. Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` failing, `2`
the check could not run. The other options are on
[Inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#check).

## Accept an exception with a waiver

Prefer `except_` for things that are public or special *by design*. A waiver is
for a known violation the owner accepts for a while. It lives in
`hinoki-rules.toml` at the project root, which `hinoki new` creates:

```toml
# hinoki-rules.toml
[[waiver]]
rule = "HNK-ACC-001"
target = "tests.projects.rulesapp.health"
reason = "liveness probe is public by design"
owner = "platform-team"
expires = 2027-01-31
```

`rule`, `target`, `reason` and `owner` are required. `target` is an `fnmatch`
pattern on the diagnostic's subject and must be bounded: a literal prefix of at
least five characters containing a dot (`shop.api.*`, never `*`). `expires` is
optional and must be a TOML date, written without quotes; the waiver applies
through that day and expires once the current UTC date is later. The waived diagnostic
keeps its line and gains the decision:

```text
tests/projects/rulesapp.py:7: HNK-ACC-001 [waived] GET /health (health) declares no access policy
  fix: add access=<policy> to the action (or list it in except_ when it is public on purpose)
    waived: liveness probe is public by design (platform-team, until 2027-01-31)
```

An expired waiver stops applying and reports `HNK-WVR-002`; one that matches
nothing reports `HNK-WVR-001`. Both have status `warning`: they print as
`[warning]`, count under `warning(s)` in the summary (`summary.warning` in JSON)
and never change the exit code. A diagnostic that means "the rule
could not do its job" cannot be waived. An invalid or unreadable file makes
`hinoki check` exit with `2`.

### Which waiver file

`hinoki check`, `hinoki mcp` and application startup read the same file:

1. The file named by `Hinoki(waivers=...)`, or by `--waivers` on `check` and
   `mcp`. A named file must exist.
2. Otherwise `hinoki-rules.toml` at the project root: the directory of the
   nearest `hinoki.toml`, searched from the working directory upwards. Running
   from a subdirectory of the project finds the same file.
3. Without a `hinoki.toml`, `hinoki-rules.toml` in the working directory.

```python
app = Hinoki(rules=rules, waivers="config/hinoki-rules.toml")
```

A missing default file means no waivers. A directory or a broken symbolic link
with that name is an error, not an absent file. `hinoki mcp --waivers PATH` also
applies `PATH` to the app that `run_scenario` starts.

### Waivers at startup

Application startup applies the waiver file the same way as `hinoki check`.
This app requires access on every
action, yet it starts and serves `/health` because the owner waived it. It
passes `rules=` by hand, the explicit form, to keep the example in one file:

```python
# shop/main.py
from hinoki import Actions, Hinoki, Schema, http
from hinoki.rules import RuleSet


class Health(Schema):
    status: str


@http.get("/health")
def health() -> Health:
    return Health(status="ok")


app = Hinoki(rules=RuleSet(Actions.require_access()), include=[health])
```

```toml
# hinoki-rules.toml
[[waiver]]
rule = "HNK-ACC-001"
target = "shop.main.health"
reason = "liveness probe is public by design"
owner = "platform-team"
```

Without the waiver, `hinoki serve` fails at startup with
`RegistrationError: 1 rule violation(s)`.

At startup:

- An absent default file means no waivers.
- An invalid or unreadable file, or a missing file named with `waivers=`, fails
  startup with `RegistrationError` ("invalid waivers:
  .../hinoki-rules.toml: waiver #1: missing target"), even with
  `enforce_rules=False`.
- An expired waiver does not apply: the violation fails startup and the
  `RegistrationError` also lists the `HNK-WVR-002` notice. Without a remaining
  violation the notice is logged as a warning.
- `HNK-WVR-001` (unused waiver) is reported only by `hinoki check` and
  `hinoki mcp`: startup runs only the startup rules, so a waiver for a static
  rule such as `HNK-IMP-001` is expected to match nothing there.

Waivers are the owner's decision: tools read the file and never write it. Put it
under CODEOWNERS; the generated `AGENTS.md` tells agents the same.

## Your own rules

Subclass `hinoki.rules.Rule` with a stable `id`, an `explanation`, an optional
`fix` and a `check` that yields diagnostics. `phase` defaults to
`Phase.STARTUP` and `severity` to `Severity.ERROR`.

```python
# notes/rules.py
from collections.abc import Iterator

from hinoki.rules import Diagnostic, Project, Rule, qualified, where


class NoDelete(Rule):
    id = "NOTES-API-001"
    explanation = "This project archives rows instead of deleting them."
    fix = "use PATCH to set archived=true"

    def check(self, project: Project) -> Iterator[Diagnostic]:
        for route in project.app.routes:
            if route.method == "DELETE":
                yield self.diagnostic(
                    f"DELETE {route.path} removes a row",
                    where(route.handler),
                    subject=qualified(route),
                )
```

Add `NoDelete()` to the `RuleSet`. `where(obj)` gives a `file:line` location;
`qualified(route)` gives the subject that waivers match (without a subject the
location is used; an empty subject cannot be waived). A rule that needs side
effects (running code, files, network, a database) lists them in `effects` and
