only runs under `hinoki check --allow-effects`; at startup it is refused and
reported as unverifiable. `RuleSet` raises `ValueError` for an empty ID or the
same ID twice.

## Errors and edge cases

- A rule that raises is reported as `unverifiable` with "the rule failed to run", never skipped.
- `HNK-IMP-001` runs only in `hinoki check` and `hinoki mcp`; it needs the source files of the checked packages (`--package`, default: the target's top-level package).
- The model rules in a project without models are unverifiable, which is why the scaffold keeps them commented out.

## See also

- [Inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#check): every `hinoki check` option.
- [Authentication and access](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md): what `HNK-ACC-001/002` ask for.
- [Build with a coding agent](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ai-workflow.md): the same diagnostics for agents through `hinoki mcp`.

# Application modules

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md

A module owns something that lives as long as a worker or a command run: a
connection pool, a client, a thread pool. It opens the resource at startup,
provides it to the rest of the application and closes it when the run ends.
Nothing is opened at import time.

```python
# notes/passwords.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from hinoki import Module, ModuleContext
from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher


class Passwords(Module):
    name = "passwords"

    @asynccontextmanager
    async def lifespan(self, ctx: ModuleContext) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
        hasher = PasswordHasher()
        ctx.provide(PasswordHasher, hasher)
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            hasher.close()
```

Install it on the application. The rules come from `hinoki.toml`, so the call
names only what is specific to this app:

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki

from notes.passwords import Passwords
from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

app = Hinoki(
    settings=ProjectSettings,
    title="Notes",
    modules=[Passwords()],
)
```

Each worker runs `lifespan` up to `yield` before it answers requests, and the
`finally` block when it stops, even if a later module fails to start.

## Use what a module provides

`ctx.provide(Type, value)` registers a value under its type; `ctx.get(Type)`
returns it (or raises `LookupError`) and `ctx.find(Type)` returns `None` instead.
The value is reachable from:

| Where | How |
| --- | --- |
| Another module's `lifespan` | `ctx.get(PasswordHasher)`, with `requires = (Passwords,)` |
| A startup or shutdown hook | `ctx.get(PasswordHasher)` |
| A management command | `context.get(PasswordHasher)`, with `requires = (Passwords,)` |
| A rate-limit policy | `context.resource(PasswordHasher)` |

```python
# notes/commands.py
from argparse import ArgumentParser, Namespace

from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher
from hinoki.management import Command, CommandContext

from notes.passwords import Passwords


class HashPassword(Command):
    name = "hash-password"
    help = "print the Argon2id hash of a password"
    requires = (Passwords,)

    def add_arguments(self, parser: ArgumentParser) -> None:
        parser.add_argument("password")

    async def handle(self, context: CommandContext, args: Namespace) -> None:
        print(await context.get(PasswordHasher).hash(args.password))
```

With `commands=[HashPassword]` on the application, `hinoki manage hash-password s3cret`
starts only `Passwords` (and what it requires), runs the command and closes it.
Request handlers can receive a module-provided value as a parameter when its
type inherits `Resource`. Model methods also find the worker's `Database`
through the ORM context. Ordinary module values remain available through
`ModuleContext` in lifespans, hooks and commands, and through the policy context
where supported.

## Inject a worker resource into a handler

Declare a concrete `Resource` type, provide its instance from a module, then use
that type as a handler parameter. Hinoki resolves the annotation when routes are
registered and injects the worker's instance for each request:

```python
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from hinoki import Hinoki, Module, ModuleContext, Resource, http


class Mailer(Resource):
    async def send(self, address: str, subject: str) -> None: ...


class MailerModule(Module):
    name = "mailer"

    @asynccontextmanager
    async def lifespan(self, ctx: ModuleContext) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
        mailer = Mailer()
        ctx.provide(Mailer, mailer)
        yield


@http.post("/welcome")
async def welcome(email: str, mailer: Mailer) -> dict[str, str]:
    await mailer.send(email, "Welcome")
    return {"status": "sent"}


app = Hinoki(include=[welcome], modules=[MailerModule()])
```

The same annotation works on function handlers, synchronous `def` handlers and
methods on an `API` class. A resource parameter does not cause Hinoki to build a
`Request`; declare `request: Request` only when the handler needs request data.
Resource parameters are not client inputs, so they do not appear in the OpenAPI
document or MCP tool schema. Kiso also leaves them out of the Rust route input
list; a route can keep its native route specification when its other inputs and
handler behavior meet the native-path requirements.

Resources are mandatory worker contracts. A default value, a name that collides
with a `{path}` parameter, or two parameters requesting the same resource type
raises `RegistrationError` during registration. After all modules start and
before startup hooks run, Hinoki checks every required type with
`ModuleContext.get`. A missing provider fails startup with the route and type in
the error; the worker does not become ready.

## The database module

A `database: settings.DatabaseSettings` field on your settings class is enough:
Hinoki installs `DatabaseModule` (from `hinoki.db`) before any declared module, so
a module with `requires = (DatabaseModule,)` can call `ctx.get(Database)` in its
lifespan. Declaring `DatabaseModule`, or a subclass of it, in `modules=` replaces
the automatic one; modules that require `DatabaseModule` still start after it.
See [database connection ownership](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#8-database-connection-ownership).

## The email module

An `email: settings.EmailSettings` field installs `EmailModule` (from `hinoki.mail`) the same way: one `Mailer` per worker, opened in the lifespan and closed at shutdown, available as `ctx.get(Mailer)`, to `mail.send(...)` in handlers and hooks, and to commands that declare `requires = (EmailModule,)`. Declaring `EmailModule` in `modules=` replaces the automatic one. See [send email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md).

## Declare modules

`modules=` accepts instances and classes. An instance is the plain choice; a class
is built with its `from_settings(settings)` classmethod, which you override to
read your settings (the default raises `TypeError` and says so).

`requires` decides the order: dependencies start first and stop last. An empty or
duplicate `name`, a missing requirement, a cycle, or a type provided twice fails
startup with `ModuleGraphError`. A module whose class extends a required class
satisfies that requirement.

Keep `lifespan` bounded (it shares `lifecycle.startup_timeout`), fail fast when a
required service is unavailable, and close what you own in `finally`.

## Startup and shutdown hooks

For an action at the edge of a worker's life that owns no resource, such as
warming a cache, logging the build or flushing a counter, list functions on the
application instead of writing a module (`ProjectSettings` here declares a
`database` field, so the database module is installed):

```python
# notes/main.py
import logging

from hinoki import Hinoki, ModuleContext
from hinoki.db import Database

from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

log = logging.getLogger("notes")


async def warm_cache(ctx: ModuleContext) -> None:
    await ctx.get(Database).fetch("SELECT 1")


def say_goodbye(ctx: ModuleContext) -> None:
    log.info("worker stopping")


app = Hinoki(
    settings=ProjectSettings, on_startup=[warm_cache], on_shutdown=[say_goodbye]
)
```

A hook takes the worker's `ModuleContext` (`ctx.settings`, `ctx.get(Type)`, `ctx.tasks`). It is `async def`, or a plain `def` that runs on the bounded sync executor like a sync handler. Model methods reach the worker's database inside a hook as they do inside a request.

Pass hooks as a `list` or `tuple` when constructing `Hinoki`; the app's `on_startup` and `on_shutdown` tuples are read-only. Hooks must be callables, not async generators, and must return `None`. A plain `def` may instead return an awaitable, which Hinoki awaits; use `async def` when the hook needs to await work directly.

| | Startup hooks | Shutdown hooks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run | Once per worker, after every module has started, in the listed order | Once per worker, before background tasks, the sync executor and the modules are closed, in the listed order |
| Time limit | Share `lifecycle.startup_timeout` with the modules | Each has its own `lifecycle.shutdown_timeout` |
| Requests | Answered `503 not_ready` until the last hook returns | Answered `503 not_ready` from the moment shutdown begins |
| A hook fails or times out | Startup fails: later hooks do not run, no shutdown hook runs, the modules already started are closed, and the server is told that startup failed. The log has the traceback; the message names the hook (`startup hook 'warm_cache' failed to start: TimeoutError`) | It is logged and reported as a shutdown error; the remaining hooks and the module cleanup still run |

Shutdown hooks run only after a startup that completed, and a shutdown hook is not the `finally` of a startup hook. Use this rule to choose: **a resource you own is a module** (its lifespan closes it even when a later step of startup fails); **an action is a hook**. A plain `def` hook that is still running when its time limit passes cannot be interrupted; it keeps its executor thread until it returns.

Hooks run where the application serves requests: under `hinoki dev`/`serve` and any ASGI server, on the first request of each WSGI worker, and in the [test clients](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md). `hinoki manage` commands, `check`, `routes` and `migrations` do not run them.

## Scripts outside the server

For app maintenance tasks, declare a [management command](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#manage) and list its required module classes in `Command.requires`. Hinoki starts only those modules and their dependencies for one command run, so a database module is opened and closed without starting the HTTP server or unrelated modules.

Standalone scripts outside Hinoki's server or management-command runner have no module lifespan. Open their own `Database` and close it explicitly; do not import a module-global pool. The blog seed script demonstrates this pattern.

## Errors and edge cases

- `ctx.get` for a type nobody provided raises `LookupError: <Type> was not provided`; declare the providing module in `requires`.
- A module class without `from_settings` in `modules=` fails at construction: pass an instance instead.
- `hinoki check`, `routes` and `migrations` do not start modules or run hooks.

## See also

- [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md): where a module reads its configuration.
- [Command line](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#manage): running management commands.
- [Sync and async](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md): where sync hooks run.

# Cache values

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cache.md

`Cache` stores bounded byte values or JSON-compatible values with an explicit
finite TTL. Install a backend module and request `Cache` in the handler:

```python
from datetime import timedelta

from hinoki import Hinoki, Schema, http
from hinoki.cache import Cache, CacheModule, MemoryCache


class Summary(Schema):
    total: int


@http.get("/summary")
async def summary(cache: Cache) -> Summary:
    cached = await cache.get_schema("summary", Summary)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached
    fresh = Summary(total=await calculate_total())
    await cache.set_schema("summary", fresh, ttl=timedelta(seconds=60))
    return fresh


app = Hinoki(
    include=[summary],
    modules=[CacheModule(MemoryCache(max_entries=5_000, max_bytes=32 * 1024 * 1024))],
)
```

The API includes async `get`, `set`, `delete`, `get_bytes`, `set_bytes`,
`get_schema`, `set_schema` and `get_or_set`, plus `get_sync`, `set_sync`,
`delete_sync`, `get_bytes_sync` and `set_bytes_sync`. A sync handler can use the
sync methods. The memory backend calls its Rust cache directly; the database
backend bridges its sync methods to the worker event loop, so use those only in
a Hinoki sync handler or another Hinoki sync execution context.

`get` returns `None` for a miss or expired value. `None` cannot be stored as a
JSON value because that would make a stored null indistinguishable from a miss;
use a tagged object if the application needs that distinction. `set` always
requires a TTL between a positive value and 366 days. Keys are UTF-8 strings of
1–256 bytes without NUL. `cache.namespace("users")` returns a view that prefixes
keys and enforces the same full-key limit. The view delegates to its cache, so a
namespace taken from a `DatabaseCache` follows that cache's worker binding and
cleanup.

`set_schema` stores the schema's declared fields only: `@computed_field` values
are omitted and recomputed when `get_schema` validates the value again, so
schemas with the default `extra="forbid"` round-trip. A schema containing a
`Secret` field, including in a nested schema, is rejected with `ValueError`
instead of caching a masked or plain secret.

`get_or_set` reads, calls its factory on a miss and writes the result. It does
not coalesce concurrent misses, so applications with expensive factories may
need their own single-flight or locking policy. Schema validation mismatches in
`get_schema` delete the stale value and return a miss; malformed JSON raises
`CacheDecodeError`.

## Backends and ownership

| Backend | State and visibility | Limits and expiration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MemoryCache(max_entries=10_000, max_bytes=64 MiB)` | Rust `hinoki.core.MemoryCache`, owned by one worker process; not shared by other workers | Both entry count and encoded bytes are bounded; each value defaults to at most 1 MiB; monotonic TTL and clock-style eviction |
| `DatabaseCache()` | Uses the worker's `Database`; visible across processes sharing that database | Default value limit 1 MiB; TTL is checked on read; call `purge_expired()` from scheduled maintenance |

The native memory cache is guarded by a Rust mutex, copies bytes at the Python
binding, and uses a second-chance clock for eviction. Its state is process-local;
multiple workers do not share or invalidate each other's entries. The database
backend is shared through the selected database, but has higher I/O cost and no
configured global table-size quota. Values are stored as hex text, so database
storage uses more bytes than the original payload. No periodic cleanup job is
started by Hinoki.

`CacheModule(MemoryCache(...))` needs no database. `CacheModule(DatabaseCache())`
requires the application's `DatabaseModule` and uses that worker's connection
pool. The database backend needs the `hinoki_cache` table. Apply the SQL at
`migrations_path() / "0001-initial.sql"` through an explicit reviewed project
migration; neither import nor lifespan creates a table.

## Failures

Cache failures are visible by default. `CacheUnavailable` is 503,
`InvalidCacheKey` is 400, `CacheValueTooLarge` is 413 and `CacheDecodeError` is
500. Invalid TTLs and non-JSON values raise `ValueError` or `TypeError` before
the backend is called. Backend database errors become `CacheUnavailable`; a
route that wants a best-effort fallback should catch `CacheError` explicitly.

Cache injection does not add a `Request` parameter and is excluded from the
OpenAPI document and MCP input schema. A route that uses a cache still follows
the normal Python handler boundary when its cache calls are ordinary Python
awaitables; the Rust memory backend only moves byte storage, expiry and
eviction into Rust. The cache does not implement HTTP response caching, ORM
query caching, distributed invalidation, or security-sensitive rate limiting.

# Transactions

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md

An action opts into a database transaction with `atomic=True`. The transaction
opens for the request and commits only after the handler returns and the
response body is encoded and rendered. Set it once on a `RouteGroup` and every
write method of the group is atomic:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/api.py
from uuid import UUID

from hinoki import RouteGroup

from notes.security import billing_staff

from .models import AuditEvent, Invoice  # AuditEvent: any model of yours
from .schemas import InvoiceIn, InvoiceOut

invoices = RouteGroup("/invoices", access=billing_staff, atomic=True)


@invoices.post("/", status=201)  # atomic: a write method in an atomic group
async def create_invoice(data: InvoiceIn) -> InvoiceOut:
    invoice = await Invoice.acreate(data)
    await AuditEvent.acreate(subject=invoice.reference, action="created")
    return InvoiceOut.from_model(invoice)


@invoices.post("/{invoice_id}/remind", status=204, atomic=False)  # writes nothing
async def remind(invoice_id: UUID) -> None: ...
```

On a single action, write `@http.post("/invoices", atomic=True)`. Hinoki checks
the returned value against the response annotation before encoding it (see
[the response check](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#the-response-is-checked-against-the-annotation)).

## What rolls back

If the handler raises, response encoding/rendering fails, the request times out, or the task is cancelled, the transaction rolls back before the error response is translated. A value that does not match the response annotation is rejected as a `500`, and the transaction rolled back, unless the action opts out with `validate_response=False`. Returning a streamed response (`Stream`, `EventStream`, or `File`) from an `atomic=True` action annotated `-> http.Response` is rejected as a `500` inside the transaction and rolls back as well, whereas returning a plain non-stream `http.Response` with a `4xx` status (such as `409`) is a normal return and commits; raise an `APIError` when a rejected operation should roll back.

Session persistence (`Session.commit()`) runs after the handler and its `atomic=True` SQL transaction have committed, so a session store write failure happens in a separate boundary after the SQL commit. Do not send email, write local files, or perform another irreversible side effect inside the transaction; arrange it after the transaction commits, or use an outbox owned by the application.

`RouteGroup(..., atomic=True)` makes `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` atomic
by default; `GET` actions are not. An action opts out with `atomic=False`.

A project created with `hinoki new` enforces `Transactions.require_atomic()`
(`HNK-TXN-001`), so a write that opts out stops `hinoki check` and startup until
you record the decision. List the action in `except_` in `notes/rules.py`:

```python
# notes/rules.py, listed in `rules` of hinoki.toml
from hinoki import Transactions
from hinoki.rules import RuleSet

project_rules = RuleSet(
    # ... the other rules
    Transactions.require_atomic(except_=["notes.apps.billing.api.remind"]),
)
```

A temporary exception goes in `hinoki-rules.toml` instead ([waivers](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#accept-an-exception-with-a-waiver)).

## Atomic blocks and functions in application code

`db.atomic` (`from hinoki import db`) opens the same kind of scope in your own code, on the database that is current for the task: the one a request makes active, or the one set with `hinoki.orm.use_database(...)`. Use it as a block:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/operations.py
from hinoki import db

from .models import AuditEvent, Invoice


async def mark_paid(invoice: Invoice) -> None:
    async with db.atomic():
        invoice.paid = True
        await invoice.asave()
        await AuditEvent.acreate(subject=invoice.reference, action="paid")
```

or as a decorator on an `async def`, with or without parentheses:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/operations.py
@db.atomic
async def settle_all() -> int:
    return await Invoice.filter(paid=False).aupdate({"paid": True}, returning=False)


@db.atomic()
async def reopen(invoice_id: UUID) -> None:
    await Invoice.aupdate(id=invoice_id, paid=False)
```

Each call of a decorated function opens its own scope: returning commits, an exception rolls back and propagates. The wrapper keeps the function's name, docstring, signature and annotations (`functools.wraps`).

In a sync handler, hook or helper, use the same API without `await`: `with db.atomic():` as a block, or `@db.atomic` on a plain `def`. The sync model methods (`create`, `update`, `bulk_create`, ...) inside it run in the same transaction:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/operations.py
@db.atomic
def settle_all_sync() -> int:
    return Invoice.update_where({"paid": False}, {"paid": True}, returning=False)


def mark_paid_sync(invoice: Invoice) -> None:
    with db.atomic():
        invoice.paid = True
        invoice.save()
```

The sync forms only work on a worker thread served by Hinoki, as the sync model methods do; on the event loop they raise `RuntimeError` (use `async with` there). A nested sync scope is a savepoint, like the async one. Raw `Database.execute` and `fetch` remain async-only (see [sync and async](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md)).

`db.atomic()` is `current_database().atomic()` resolved when the block is entered or the function is called. When you hold a `Database` yourself (a script, a module lifespan, `ctx.get(Database)`), call `database.atomic()` directly; it behaves the same. `Database.migration()` is the separate, exclusive scope used for migrations.

### Nesting and savepoints

A scope opened while another scope of the same task is already open becomes a savepoint, whether it comes from `atomic=True`, `async with`, or a decorated function. An exception inside the inner scope rolls back only that savepoint; the outer transaction continues and commits when it ends. A decorated function called from an `atomic=True` action therefore joins the request's transaction as a savepoint rather than committing on its own.

```python
# notes/apps/billing/operations.py
async def create_with_discount(data: InvoiceIn, coupon_id: UUID) -> Invoice:
    async with db.atomic():
        invoice = await Invoice.acreate(data)
        try:
            async with db.atomic():  # SAVEPOINT
                await Coupon.aupdate(id=coupon_id, used=True)
                raise CouponExpired()
        except CouponExpired:
            pass  # only the coupon update is undone
    return invoice  # the invoice committed when the outer block ended
```

A child task cannot share its parent's active transaction: opening a nested scope from another task raises `DatabaseError`.

### Decorated functions and routes

A function decorated with `@db.atomic` can also be a route handler (put the HTTP decorator outermost). Binding, OpenAPI and the native server see the original signature, and the handler runs inside its own atomic scope. That scope covers the handler call only: it commits when the handler returns, before the response is encoded. `atomic=True` on the action is the declaration that also covers response encoding, and it is what `HNK-TXN-001` (`Transactions.require_atomic`) reads: the rule does not inspect decorators, so an action that is only decorated with `@db.atomic` is still reported. Prefer `atomic=True` on actions and keep `db.atomic` for application code that the action calls.

On the native server lane, a handler is still Python code: Rust calls the Python function, so a `@db.atomic` function behaves exactly as on the Python pipeline, including the rollback when it raises.

## After-commit callbacks

`Database.after_commit(callback)` (for example `current_database().after_commit(...)`) registers a sync or async callable without arguments to run after the outermost transaction commits, which is where email, queue publishing and cache invalidation belong. Callbacks run in registration order; a rollback of the transaction, or of the savepoint scope that registered them, drops them, and an exception in one is logged without undoing the commit. Calling it outside a transaction raises `DatabaseError`. Model hooks register through `self.after_commit(callback)`; see [lifecycle hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-hooks.md).

```python
# notes/apps/billing/operations.py
from hinoki.orm import current_database


async def issue(data: InvoiceIn) -> Invoice:
    async with db.atomic():
        invoice = await Invoice.acreate(data)
        current_database().after_commit(lambda: publish("invoice.issued", invoice.id))
    return invoice
```

A send that fails after the commit is logged and does not undo the commit; the callback is not retried. For an email, `current_database().after_commit(lambda: mail.send(message))` sends only once the data is durable and never on rollback; see [send email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md#send-after-a-commit).

## Errors and edge cases

- `after_commit` outside a transaction, or a nested scope opened from a child task, raises `DatabaseError`.
- The sync forms raise `RuntimeError` on the event loop.
- An action that is only decorated with `@db.atomic` is still reported by `HNK-TXN-001`; declare `atomic=True`.

## See also

- [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md): `Transactions.require_atomic` makes atomic writes a checked promise.
- [Lifecycle hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-hooks.md): `self.after_commit` in model hooks.
- [Sync and async](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md)

# Settings

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md

Settings are typed, immutable classes. You declare the fields your application
needs; Hinoki adds the groups every application has, reads values from the
environment, `.env` and TOML once, and refuses to start when something is wrong.

```python
# notes/settings.py
from typing import Literal

from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env"):
    database: settings.DatabaseSettings
    support_email: str = "support@example.com"
    stripe_key: settings.Secret | None = None
    theme: Literal["light", "dark"] = "light"
```

`notes/main.py` passes the class with `Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings)`, which
loads it while building the application. Your fields are then on `app.settings`,
and modules read them as `ctx.settings`.

## Declare fields

A field without a default is required. Use plain types (`str`, `int`, `bool`,
`tuple[str, ...]`, `Literal[...]`, `X | None`), `settings.Secret` for anything
confidential, and a `settings.Settings` subclass for a group of your own. Settings
types live in the `hinoki.settings` namespace (`settings.AppSettings`,
`settings.DatabaseSettings`, `settings.Secret`, `settings.Settings`,
`settings.SettingsError`); name your loaded value `app_settings` so the namespace
is not shadowed.

`settings.AppSettings` brings the built-in groups: `execution`, `lifecycle`,
`logging`, `docs`, `server`, `pagination`, `cors`, `compression`, `metrics`, `security`, `events` and `admin`, plus
`timezone`, `debug` and `allowed_hosts` (see [Hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md)).
`docs.openapi_url`, `docs.docs_url`, `docs.redoc_url` and `docs.llms_url` default to `None`; the
generated `main.py` passes `openapi_url` and `docs_url` as `Hinoki(...)` arguments, which win over settings; the other two stay off. `llms_url` must start with `/`.

## Built-in fields and defaults

| Group | Field | Default | Constraint or effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `execution` | `sync_workers` | `8` | `1` to `1024` worker threads |
| `execution` | `sync_queue` | `64` | `0` or greater queued calls |
| `execution` | `request_timeout` | `30.0` seconds | Must be positive; request expiry returns `504` |
| `execution` | `max_body_bytes` | `1048576` (1 MiB) | `1` to `1073741824` bytes; larger request bodies return `413` |
| `execution` | `max_query_bytes` | `8192` (8 KiB) | `1` to `1048576` raw query-string bytes; larger queries return `414` |
| `execution` | `max_header_bytes` | `32768` (32 KiB) | `1` to `1048576` combined header bytes; larger headers return `431` |
| `execution` | `max_streams` | `64` | `1` or greater; streams open at once per worker, more answer `503` with `Retry-After: 1` before the handler runs |
| `execution` | `stream_idle_timeout` | `None` (uses `request_timeout`) | Must be positive; seconds a `Stream` may stay silent before it is cut |
| `execution` | `sse_keepalive` | `15.0` seconds | Must be positive; quiet seconds before an `EventStream` sends a comment (`keepalive=None` on the stream turns it off) |
| `execution` | `max_websockets` | `1000` | `1` or greater; open [WebSocket](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/websockets.md) connections per worker (Kiso), more are refused with `503` before the upgrade |
| `execution` | `ws_max_message_bytes` | `1048576` (1 MiB) | `1` to `1073741824`; a larger WebSocket message closes the connection with `1009` |
| `execution` | `ws_queue` | `64` | `1` or greater; messages queued in each direction of a WebSocket (Kiso) |
| `execution` | `ws_ping_interval` | `20.0` seconds | Must be positive, or `None` to send no pings (Kiso) |
| `execution` | `ws_pong_timeout` | `20.0` seconds | Must be positive; a peer that does not answer a ping in time is dropped (Kiso) |
| `execution` | `ws_close_timeout` | `5.0` seconds | Must be positive; how long a WebSocket close handshake may take (Kiso) |
| `lifecycle` | `startup_timeout` | `30.0` seconds | Must be positive |
| `lifecycle` | `shutdown_timeout` | `10.0` seconds | Must be positive |
| `logging` | `level` | `info` | `debug`, `info`, `warning`, `error` or `critical` |
| `logging` | `format` | `text` | `text` or `json` |
| `logging` | `config` | unset | `module:attribute` of a `logging.config.dictConfig` mapping (or a function returning one) for your own loggers, handlers and formatters |
| `logging` | `include_request_id` | `false` | Add the active request ID to Hinoki log records for request correlation |
| `docs` | `title` | `Hinoki API` | OpenAPI info title |
| `docs` | `version` | `0.1.0` | OpenAPI info version |
| `docs` | `openapi_url` | `None` | JSON document route; disabled when `None` |
| `docs` | `docs_url` | `None` | Swagger UI route; requires `openapi_url` |
| `docs` | `redoc_url` | `None` | ReDoc route; requires `openapi_url` |
| `docs` | `llms_url` | `None` | llms.txt route; does not need `openapi_url` |
| `docs` | `openapi_version` | `3.2` | `3.2` or `3.1`: the document's `openapi` version; `Hinoki(openapi_version=...)` overrides it. See [the document version](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md#the-document-version) |
| `server` | `server` | `kiso` | `granian` or `kiso`; `--server` overrides it. See [Kiso server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md) |
| `server` | `interface` | `asgi` | `asgi` or `wsgi`: what `hinoki serve` calls (a Hinoki application or a WSGI callable); `--interface` overrides it. See [WSGI](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#wsgi) |
| `pagination` | `page_size` | `20` | Page size an action's `PageNumberPagination()` leaves out; `1` to `max_page_size`. See [Pagination](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md) |
| `pagination` | `max_page_size` | `100` | Largest `page_size` a client may ask for |
| `pagination` | `cursor_secret`, `cursor_ttl_seconds` | unset | `settings.Secret` of at least 32 bytes that signs cursors, and an optional lifetime in seconds; see [Pagination](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md) |
| `events` | `handler_timeout` | `5.0` seconds | Must be positive; seconds each handler may run. See [Events](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md) |
| `events` | `max_handlers` | `16` | `1` or greater; handlers per event and phase |
| `events` | `max_depth` | `4` | `1` or greater; how deep handlers may emit events |
| `server` | `host` | `127.0.0.1` | Bind address used by `hinoki dev/serve` |
| `server` | `port` | `8000` | `1` to `65535` |
| `server` | `workers` | `1` | `1` to `256`; `dev` uses one worker for reload |
| `server` | `runtime_threads` | `1` | Must be positive |
| `server` | `backlog` | `1024` | Must be positive |
| `server` | `access_log` | unset | One line per request on either server. Unset logs in `hinoki dev` only (or whenever `access_log_format` is set); `true` or `false` decides for `dev` and `serve` |
| `server` | `access_log_skip` | unset | Kiso only: paths the log leaves out, exact or a `*` prefix; failures are still logged |
| `server` | `server_timing` | unset | Kiso only: add a `Server-Timing` header with the time taken and the serving lane; unset means `hinoki dev` only, so browser developer tools show it |
| `server` | `sighup` | unset | Kiso only, `hinoki serve`: `"reload"` (also what unset means) replaces the workers one at a time on `SIGHUP`, `"stop"` stops the server instead; see [reload on `SIGHUP`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#reload-on-sighup) |
| `server` | `reuse_port` | unset | Kiso only: on Linux, multi-worker `hinoki serve` on a non-zero port gives each worker its own `SO_REUSEPORT` socket; `false` forces one shared listening descriptor everywhere; refused under Granian |
| `server` | `recent_requests` | unset | Kiso only: file that also receives each request as a JSON line for `hinoki mcp`'s `recent_requests` tool; works with the access log off |
| `server` | `access_log_slow_ms` | unset | Kiso only: keep only answers at least this slow (ms); failures are still logged |
| `server` | `access_log_format` | unset | Kiso only (Granian refuses it): `pretty`, `plain`, `json` or `logger` (route to the `hinoki.access` Python logger). Unset is `pretty` on a colour terminal and `plain` otherwise |
| `server` | `max_connections` | unset (10000) | Kiso only: open-connection limit, `1` to `1000000`; refused under Granian |
| `server` | `header_read_timeout` | unset (10 seconds) | Kiso only: time to receive request headers, and the keep-alive idle limit; refused under Granian |
| `server` | `body_read_timeout` | unset (10 seconds) | Kiso only: silence allowed while a body is read (at most half of `execution.request_timeout`); refused under Granian |
| `server` | `write_timeout` | unset (30 seconds) | Kiso only: how long a response write may make no progress before the connection is closed; above 0 and at most 3600; refused under Granian |
| `server` | `native_dispatch` | unset (on) | Kiso only: run the `async def` handlers it can prove safe without an asyncio task (see [the native handler lane](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#the-native-handler-lane)); `false` keeps every handler in an asyncio task; refused under Granian |
| `server` | `tls_cert_file`, `tls_key_file` | unset | PEM certificate chain and private key; both or neither, and both must exist. Serves HTTPS on either server; Kiso reads them once at start |
| `server` | `http2` | `false` | Serve HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN `h2`, with `http/1.1` as fallback); needs `tls_cert_file` and `tls_key_file`, otherwise refused when settings load. No cleartext HTTP/2; on either server |
| `server` | `trusted_proxies` | empty | IP addresses or CIDRs allowed to supply forwarded client/protocol metadata; an IPv6 zone id (`fe80::1%lo0`) is refused when settings load, whichever server runs |
| `server` | `request_id_header` | `x-request-id` | HTTP header used for generated request IDs; other framework-owned names are refused |
| `server` | `trust_request_id` | `false` | Accept a validated inbound ID only from a peer in `trusted_proxies` |
| `cors` | `origins` | empty | Allowed browser origins (`scheme://host[:port]`), or the single entry `*`; empty disables CORS |
| `cors` | `methods` | `GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, QUERY` | Methods a preflight allows |
| `cors` | `headers` | `authorization, content-type` | Request headers a preflight allows |
| `cors` | `expose_headers` | empty | Response headers a browser script may read |
| `cors` | `credentials` | `false` | Allow cookies and HTTP authentication; refused together with `*` |
| `cors` | `max_age` | `600` seconds | `0` to `86400`; how long a browser may cache a preflight |
| `compression` | `enabled` | `false` | Compress responses with brotli or gzip; Kiso only (`serve --server granian` refuses it). The other `compression` fields are in [compress responses](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/compression.md#settings) |
| `metrics` | `listen` | unset | `host:port` of the Prometheus metrics listener; Kiso only (`serve --server granian` refuses it). The other `metrics` fields are in [export Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md#settings) |
| `admin` | `secret` | unset | The server secret (32+ bytes, from the environment or `*_FILE`) that keys the admin's CSRF tokens; an admin without its own `secret=` needs it |
| `admin` | `session_hours` | `12` | `1` to `720`; a signed-in admin session ends this long after sign-in, whatever else happens |
| `admin` | `idle_minutes` | `120` | `1` to `session_hours * 60`; ... or this long after its last request |
| `admin` | `min_password_length` | `12` | `8` to `128`; the shortest password the admin's own users may have |
| `admin` | `theme` | unset | A built-in admin theme name (`studio`, `console`, `paper`, `bento`) used by an `Admin` without its own `theme=`; an unknown name is refused when the settings load |
| `security` | `redirect_https` | `false` | Send known HTTP requests to HTTPS with `308`; requires explicit `allowed_hosts` |
| `security` | `hsts_seconds` | `0` | `0` to `63072000`; emit HSTS only when the effective scheme is HTTPS |
| `security` | `hsts_include_subdomains` | `false` | Add `includeSubDomains`; requires nonzero `hsts_seconds` |
| `security` | `hsts_preload` | `false` | Add `preload`; requires subdomains and at least one year of HSTS |
| `security` | `frame_options` | `sameorigin` | `settings.FrameOptions.DENY` or `.SAMEORIGIN` |
| `security` | `referrer_policy` | `same-origin` | A supported `settings.ReferrerPolicy` enum value |
| (top level) | `timezone` | `UTC` | IANA timezone name used by `app.now()` |
| (top level) | `debug` | `false` | Adds exception details to `500` answers; development only |
| (top level) | `allowed_hosts` | `*` | Host names, `.domain` or `*`; other `Host` values receive `400`; `*` with `debug` off refuses to start an app that includes the admin or a WebSocket route; with `debug` on, such an app accepts loopback hosts only (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `[::1]`) |

`settings.DatabaseSettings` is an optional field you declare in your own settings class, not a `settings.AppSettings` group. Its `url` defaults to `sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3`; `max_size` defaults to `10` connections per worker and must be at least `1`.

`settings.EmailSettings` is optional in the same way: an `email: settings.EmailSettings` field installs the [email module](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md). Its `backend` (`smtp`, `console` or `memory`) is required and has no default; `password` is a `Secret` (`NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD` or `NOTES_EMAIL__PASSWORD_FILE`). Every field, its default and its range are in [send email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md#settings).

## Where values come from

`load` is the only place configuration is read; `Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings)`
calls it for you. Highest first:

| Source | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `overrides=` in code (tests) | `ProjectSettings.load(overrides={"theme": "dark"})` |
| the process environment | `NOTES_THEME=dark` |
| a `*_FILE` variable (container secrets) | `NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe` |
| the `.env` file the class names | `NOTES_THEME=dark` in `.env` |
| the TOML file the class names | `theme = "dark"` in `settings.toml` |
| the default in the class | `theme: ... = "light"` |

Name a TOML file on the class with `toml="settings.toml"` (a project created with
`--server granian` already does). Tables map to groups: `[database]` with
`max_size = 12` sets `database.max_size`. TOML cannot hold `settings.Secret`
values or the database URL; keep those in the environment or `*_FILE` files.
`load(prefix=..., dotenv=..., toml=...)` overrides what the class declared. A
TOML file named on the class or passed to `load` must exist and parse (an empty
file is fine); a missing `.env` is skipped. Relative `.env` and TOML paths
resolve from the current directory, so start the server from the project root.

Load the class yourself when module code needs a typed value before the
application exists:

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki

from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

settings = ProjectSettings.load()
app = Hinoki(settings=settings, title=f"Notes ({settings.theme})")
```

Routes, events, middleware and rules come from `hinoki.toml`, so `Hinoki(...)`
needs no `include=`, `events=` or `rules=` here.

## Variable names

The variable is the prefix plus the field name in capitals; a group nests with a
double underscore.

| Field | Variable |
| --- | --- |
| `support_email` | `NOTES_SUPPORT_EMAIL` |
| `stripe_key` | `NOTES_STRIPE_KEY` |
| `database.url` | `NOTES_DATABASE__URL` |
| `execution.sync_workers` | `NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS` |
| `logging.format` | `NOTES_LOGGING__FORMAT` |

Values are converted strictly: integers are ASCII digits (no `1_000`, no `0x10`), booleans are `true/false/yes/no/on/off/1/0`, lists are comma separated (use `tuple[str, ...]` to keep them immutable), `Literal[...]` takes one of its choices, and an empty value for `X | None` means `None`.

## Mistakes fail at startup, all at once

A variable that starts with your prefix and looks like one of your settings but names no field is an error (a typo guard; `strict=False` turns it off). It looks like a setting when its first word starts a field's variable (`NOTES_DATABASE_URL`, `NOTES_SERVER__PROT`) or when it is spelt close to one (`NOTES_THEMES`). Other variables that only share the prefix belong to another program and are ignored: systemd's `JOURNAL_STREAM` does not break a project whose prefix is `JOURNAL_`. A missing required value, a bad number or a value that is not one of the choices is an error too, and **every problem is listed together**, with variable names and reasons but never values:

```text
invalid settings:
  NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS: must be an integer
  NOTES_DATABASE__MAX_SIZE: must be an integer
  NOTES_THEMES: unknown setting
```

## Keep secrets secret

* Declare them as `settings.Secret` (or `settings.Secret | None`). A `settings.Secret` (the same type as `hinoki.Secret`) prints as `**********` in `repr`, `str`, logs and error messages, and as `***` in `describe()` and the settings command; you get the real text only with `secret.reveal()`, at the one place that needs it (where the payment client is built: `app_settings.stripe_key.reveal()`).
* Put secrets in the environment, a secret manager that exports variables, or **files**: with Docker or Kubernetes secrets set `NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/stripe`; the file's content (without the trailing newline) is the value. Only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read; setting both `NOTES_STRIPE_KEY` and `NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE` is an error.
* A `.env` file is for development; never commit it. Pickling or serialising a settings object stores its secrets in plain text, so don't.
* A `validate()` method you add to a group shows its message in errors, so never put a field's value in it.

## See what is in effect

```sh
hinoki settings
```

```text
NOTES_DATABASE__URL            environment  ***
NOTES_EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS  default      8
NOTES_STRIPE_KEY               file         ***
NOTES_THEME                    .env         dark
```

The second column is where each value came from: `override`, `environment`,
`.env`, `toml`, `file` or `default`. The command reads the prefix, `.env` and
TOML file the class declares; `--prefix`, `--dotenv` and `--toml` override them.
`--format json` prints the same for tools, and `--example` writes a ready
`.env.example`: every variable with its default and type, required values blank
to fill in, and the optional ones with no printable default (secrets such as the
database URL, values that default to unset) commented out, so a copied file
keeps their defaults:

```sh
hinoki settings --example > .env.example
```

## Logging and your own loggers {#your-own-loggers}

Declare loggers, handlers and formatters with a standard [`logging.config.dictConfig`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.config.html#logging-config-dictschema) mapping, and point `logging.config` at it:

```python
# notes/logs.py
LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "formatters": {"short": {"format": "%(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s"}},
    "handlers": {"console": {"class": "logging.StreamHandler", "formatter": "short"}},
    "loggers": {"orders": {"handlers": ["console"], "level": "INFO"}},
}
```

```sh
NOTES_LOGGING__CONFIG=notes.logs:LOGGING
```

The value may also name a function that returns the mapping. It is applied when each worker starts, right after Hinoki's own `hinoki` logger setup, with `disable_existing_loggers` off unless your mapping sets it. A mapping that configures the `hinoki` logger replaces Hinoki's handler on it. A target that cannot be imported or is not a mapping raises during startup. Kiso's access log is written by Kiso; set `server.access_log_format = "logger"` to route it through the `hinoki.access` logger.

## Database connection ownership {#8-database-connection-ownership}

A `database: settings.DatabaseSettings` field is all it takes: Hinoki installs
`DatabaseModule` for it (a module declared in `modules=` replaces it). With
nothing configured, the URL is the local SQLite file
`sqlite://./.hinoki/local.sqlite3`, and the module creates its hidden directory
and file when it starts. [Configure a database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md) covers the URL,
the connection fields, TLS and each backend.

The module opens a pool in each worker's startup lifespan, fails startup if the
database is unreachable, and closes that worker's pool on shutdown. Nothing
connects when modules or models are imported. Each worker owns its own pool,
so budget `replicas × workers × max_size` against the server database's
connection limit.

One-off scripts have a different lifecycle: they open a short-lived `Database`
themselves ([use the database from a script](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md#use-the-database-from-a-script)).
`examples/blog/blog/apps/blog/seed.py` does so, applies migrations, inserts synthetic rows and
closes the pool in `finally`. It is a one-time seed for a fresh disposable
database, not a repeatable reset:

```sh
cd examples/blog
export BLOG_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://app:password@localhost/blog
uv run python -m blog.apps.blog.seed
```

Use a disposable database for the example. The seed command is not a production migration mechanism and is not run at app startup.

## Errors and edge cases

- Setting both `NOTES_STRIPE_KEY` and `NOTES_STRIPE_KEY_FILE` is an error; only a regular file up to 64 KiB is read.
- A variable with your prefix that looks like a setting (same first word, or a close spelling) but names no field is an error; other variables that only share the prefix, such as `JOURNAL_STREAM`, are ignored. Pass `strict=False` to `load` to turn the check off.
- The `server` group is applied by `hinoki dev` and `hinoki serve`, not by other ASGI servers ([Serving](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#settings-that-apply-to-one-server-only)).

## See also

- [Hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md)
- [Own resources with modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md)
- [Configure a database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md#configure-the-application)

# Serve an application

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md

From the project directory:

```sh
hinoki dev
hinoki serve
```

`hinoki dev` reloads on every change while you work; `hinoki serve` runs without
reload, with the workers your settings ask for. Both read the application from
`project.application` in `hinoki.toml`. To run another application, pass its
target: `module:app`, such as `hinoki dev notes.main:app`. A function callable
without arguments that returns an application (a factory) is also accepted.

On Kiso, when the application sets `docs_url`, `hinoki dev` prints the address of
the documentation page under the `listening on` line, for example
`docs: http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`, with the address in the brand colour on a
terminal that takes colour (plain text in a pipe, in CI or with `NO_COLOR` set);
nothing is printed when `docs_url` is unset.
`hinoki serve` prints it too when it runs a supervisor (more than one worker),
but not with a single worker, which runs in the command's own process.

Each worker imports the target, then opens what the application owns (database
pool, modules) in its lifespan and closes it on shutdown. Importing your code
never opens a connection. See [database connection ownership](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#8-database-connection-ownership).

## Choose a server

Both commands run on **Kiso**, Hinoki's own Rust server, unless you choose
**Granian**:

| | Kiso (default) | Granian |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Hinoki's HTTP server in the native extension (Rust: hyper, tokio, rustls) | A general-purpose ASGI server, installed with the `server` extra |
| Runs on the native lane | Eligible routes skip Python routing and binding ([details](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#what-is-native-and-what-still-runs-in-python)) | Every request goes through the ASGI pipeline |
| Access log | Kiso's own, with `access_log_format`, `access_log_skip`, `server_timing` | Granian's |
| Hinoki [middleware](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md) | Yes; the route runs in Python instead of the native lane | Yes, identical |
| ASGI wrapper around the app | Not possible: there is no ASGI boundary | Yes, run the wrapper with `granian` ([metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#metrics-and-tracing)) |
| WSGI | `--interface wsgi`: Python threads behind Kiso's listener, not native ([WSGI](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#wsgi)) | `--interface wsgi` |

Choose per run with a flag, or per project in settings:

```sh
hinoki serve --server granian
```

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(
    settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env", toml="settings.toml"
):
    pass
```

```toml
# settings.toml
[server]
server = "granian"
```

`hinoki new --server granian` (or the server question of `hinoki new`) writes the
same choice to `settings.toml`; `NOTES_SERVER__SERVER=kiso` overrides it for one
environment. What Kiso runs natively, its limits, signals and proxy handling are
on [Kiso server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md).

## Set host, port and workers

They come from the application's `server` settings group; flags override them:

| Setting | Variable | Default | Flag |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `server.host` | `NOTES_SERVER__HOST` | `127.0.0.1` | `--host` |
| `server.port` | `NOTES_SERVER__PORT` | `8000` | `--port` |
| `server.workers` | `NOTES_SERVER__WORKERS` | `1` | `--workers` (serve) |
| `server.runtime_threads` | `NOTES_SERVER__RUNTIME_THREADS` | `1` | |
| `server.backlog` | `NOTES_SERVER__BACKLOG` | `1024` | |
| `server.access_log` | `NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG` | unset | Unset logs in `hinoki dev` only (or whenever `access_log_format` is set); `true` or `false` decides for both |
| `server.access_log_skip` | `NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_SKIP` | unset | Kiso only: comma-separated paths the log leaves out (health checks); exact, or a prefix when the entry ends with `*` |
| `server.server_timing` | `NOTES_SERVER__SERVER_TIMING` | unset | Kiso only: add a `Server-Timing` header (`kiso;dur=3.2;desc="native"`: milliseconds the server took and the serving lane, with the same values as the access log's [`lane`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#limits)); unset means `hinoki dev` only |
| `server.recent_requests` | `NOTES_SERVER__RECENT_REQUESTS` | unset | Kiso only: file that also receives each request as a JSON line, read by the `recent_requests` tool of [`hinoki mcp`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md); rotated near 1 MiB |
| `server.access_log_slow_ms` | `NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_SLOW_MS` | unset | Kiso only: keep only answers at least this slow, in milliseconds |
| `server.access_log_format` | `NOTES_SERVER__ACCESS_LOG_FORMAT` | unset | Kiso only: `pretty`, `plain`, `json` or `logger`. Unset is `pretty` on a colour terminal and `plain` otherwise |
| `server.reuse_port` | `NOTES_SERVER__REUSE_PORT` | unset | Kiso only: on Linux, multi-worker `hinoki serve` on a non-zero port gives each worker its own `SO_REUSEPORT` socket by default; set `false` to share one descriptor everywhere |
| `server.server` | `NOTES_SERVER__SERVER` | `kiso` | `--server` |

The connection limits and timeouts (`max_connections`, `header_read_timeout`, `body_read_timeout`, `write_timeout`), `native_dispatch`, the TLS files and `http2`, and `trusted_proxies` are described under [Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md) and in the [settings table](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#built-in-fields-and-defaults). Left unset, they are `None` in `hinoki settings` and Kiso applies its own defaults (for example 10000 connections and a 10-second header timeout), so that Granian can refuse the Kiso-only ones only when you set them.

`dev` always runs one worker with reload. `hinoki settings` shows what is in
effect ([Inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#settings)).

Before serving a deployment, narrow [`allowed_hosts`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md#allowed_hosts)
to the names it answers to (`NOTES_ALLOWED_HOSTS=app.example.com`). While it is
the default `*` and `debug` is off, each worker logs `allowed_hosts is '*' and
debug is off: ...` at startup, on every server.

## Settings that apply to one server only

`hinoki serve` refuses a setting the chosen server cannot honour, by name, and exits with status 2; it never ignores it or falls back to the other server.

| Setting | Kiso | Granian |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `host`, `port`, `workers`, `runtime_threads`, `backlog`, `access_log`, `trusted_proxies`, `request_id_header`, `trust_request_id`, `tls_cert_file`, `tls_key_file`, `http2` | applied | applied |
| `max_connections`, `header_read_timeout`, `body_read_timeout`, `write_timeout`, `native_dispatch`, `reuse_port`, `access_log_format`, `access_log_skip`, `access_log_slow_ms`, `recent_requests`, `server_timing` | applied when set | refused when set |

If the native extension of a build has no Kiso, `--server kiso` fails with an error that says so.

## Optional startup probe

`Hinoki(startup_url="/health")` reserves one public, fixed `GET`/`HEAD` endpoint and returns `{"status":"ok"}` after that worker's lifespan startup has completed. The setting is off by default. Its path must be a literal ASCII path; query strings, fragments, parameters, percent escapes and dot segments are rejected. It must not match an application route or an enabled OpenAPI/docs path. The endpoint is not an application route and does not appear in OpenAPI or generated CRUD/MCP tools.

This is a **startup probe**, not a general readiness or liveness check. A `200` says that startup completed (and, on Kiso, its request wake reader was installed); it does not check database availability, downstream services, request capacity, or whether the Python event loop continues to make progress. It answers independently of the Python request queue when Kiso can apply the response directly. Before readiness it returns `503 not_ready`; during shutdown readiness is cleared before graceful draining begins.

ASGI/Granian and WSGI answer it in the Python pipeline after host, CORS and HTTPS-redirect checks. Kiso checks host restrictions, answers CORS preflights and redirects plain HTTP requests on its Tokio thread before it considers the probe. `GET` and `HEAD` negotiate `application/json` and validate query syntax; other methods return `405` with `Allow: GET, HEAD`, unless CORS answers a preflight first. WSGI reads request bodies before the pipeline, so its body-size behavior differs from Kiso for a body sent to this `GET`/`HEAD` endpoint. WSGI also starts lazily on the first request and uses its adapter-level `503` if startup fails. Since WSGI exposes a decoded `PATH_INFO` rather than the raw request path, percent-encoded aliases may be indistinguishable from the literal probe path there.

## Other runners

`dev` and `serve` are conveniences. The application is a plain ASGI app, so any
ASGI server can run it directly; the `server` settings group is then ignored,
because only `hinoki serve` applies it:

```sh
granian --interface asgi notes.main:app
```

## Metrics and tracing

Kiso exports Prometheus metrics (off by default; see [export Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md)). Hinoki ships no tracing integration and no health route besides the optional [startup probe](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#optional-startup-probe). On an ASGI server such as Granian there is no built-in exporter, and the application is a plain ASGI callable, so wrap it with the instrumentation you already use, or with a few lines of your own:

```python
# notes/metrics.py
import time


class Timing:
    """Report each request's method, status and duration to ``record``."""

    def __init__(self, app, record):
        self.app, self.record = app, record

    async def __call__(self, scope, receive, send):
        if scope["type"] != "http":
            await self.app(scope, receive, send)
            return
        started, status = time.monotonic(), None

        async def watch(message):
            nonlocal status
            if message["type"] == "http.response.start":
                status = message["status"]
            await send(message)

        try:
            await self.app(scope, receive, watch)
        finally:  # status stays None when the request was aborted before a response began
            self.record(scope["method"], status, time.monotonic() - started)


from notes.main import app as notes_app

app = Timing(notes_app, record=my_metrics.observe)  # serve with any ASGI server
```

What this measures is the time from the ASGI call to the last byte handed to the server, not what a client perceives. Keep method and status as labels; do **not** label by `scope["path"]` (it holds ids and has unbounded cardinality), the request ID (it is for correlating logs: `logging.include_request_id` adds it to each Hinoki log line) or the caller. Hinoki does not currently expose the matched route template to a wrapper, so per-route metrics need an application-level counter inside the handler or a gap report so a hook can be designed.

Kiso has no ASGI boundary, so this wrapper does not apply to it. Use its
built-in [Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md) instead.

## Streamed responses

Actions that return `Stream`, `EventStream` or `File` work on both servers. Kiso sends them from its own queue, with its idle timeout, keep-alive comments and disconnect check, and sends a `File` without the bytes entering Python. Granian receives each piece as an ASGI message, and a `File` through `http.response.pathsend` when the server offers it; there Hinoki's own pump handles the idle timeout, the keep-alive and the disconnect. `execution.max_streams`, `execution.stream_idle_timeout` and `execution.sse_keepalive` apply to both ([settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md)). Details and measured behavior: [stream a response](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md). Response compression exists on Kiso only; `compression.enabled` with `--server granian` is refused ([compress responses](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/compression.md)).

## WSGI

ASGI is the intended way to serve Hinoki. When a deployment can only run WSGI,
wrap the application:

```python
# wsgi.py
from hinoki.wsgi import WSGIAdapter

from notes.main import app

wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter(app)
```

```sh
hinoki serve wsgi:wsgi_app --interface wsgi                    # Kiso
hinoki serve wsgi:wsgi_app --interface wsgi --server granian   # Granian
```

`--interface wsgi` (or `server.interface = "wsgi"` on the application the
`WSGIAdapter` wraps) tells `hinoki serve` that the target is a WSGI callable
rather than a Hinoki application; the default is `asgi`. The target may be a
`WSGIAdapter` or any `(environ, start_response)` callable, but not a factory
and not a `Hinoki` application (the error names `WSGIAdapter`). A project
whose `server.interface` is `wsgi` refuses an ASGI target unless you pass
`--interface asgi`. `granian --interface wsgi wsgi:wsgi_app` still works for a
deployment that runs Granian directly.

### WSGI on Kiso

Kiso owns the listener and calls the callable from a fixed pool of Python
threads (`execution.sync_workers`) with a queue of `execution.sync_queue`
waiting requests; beyond both the answer is `503` with `Retry-After: 1`. **This
path is not native**: the application, the environment and every response chunk
are Python objects, and the request crosses the interpreter lock. Rust owns the
sockets, TLS, the access log, the limits and the end of the response.

* **Request body.** Read in full before the call, up to `execution.max_body_bytes`: `413` above it, `408` if it stalls, `400` if malformed. Kiso therefore answers `413` for a body Granian's WSGI interface would pass on (Granian has no limit).
* **Request path.** A path whose decoded form holds a NUL byte or a `.` or `..` segment (`%00`, `%2e%2e`, `%2f` included) answers `400` before the application is called.
* **Request headers.** Each becomes `HTTP_*` in the environment, and repeats are joined by a comma; repeated `Cookie` headers (one per cookie, as HTTP/2 clients send them) are joined by `; `. A header whose name contains an underscore is dropped, because `X_Foo` and `X-Foo` would both become `HTTP_X_FOO`; a client could otherwise pose as a header your proxy sets, such as `Remote-User`. Use dashes in custom header names.
* **Response.** Streamed: the head goes out with the first piece, a slow client slows the application down (a bounded buffer), and a client that leaves makes the next write fail and closes the iterable. An exception before the head answers `500` with an empty body and the traceback in the log; after it, the stream is reset instead of ending as complete. A header value with a line break or another control character is an error in `start_response`, so it answers `500` with the traceback too. A body shorter or longer than the `Content-Length` the application set closes the connection with an error line from Kiso. A `close()` of the iterable that raises after the whole body was sent is logged by the `hinoki.runtime` logger, and the response still ends normally.
* **Timeout.** `execution.request_timeout` bounds the time until the response starts (`504`) and, once it has started, the silence between two pieces of the body: an application that stays quiet longer has its stream reset and its iterable closed. A slow client does not count, only a slow application. A running sync call cannot be stopped; it keeps its thread until it returns.
* **Applies:** TLS and HTTP/2, `access_log` and `access_log_format`, `server_timing`, `max_connections`, header and body timeouts, `--workers` and graceful shutdown (`lifecycle.shutdown_timeout`).
* **Does not apply:** the native lane (`native_dispatch` is refused), host, CORS and redirect policies of the server (a wrapped Hinoki application still applies its own), and `trusted_proxies` (refused: the client address is the TCP peer).
* **Settings.** A plain callable has no settings of its own, so `server`, `execution` and `lifecycle` come from the environment (`EXECUTION__SYNC_WORKERS`, `SERVER__WORKERS`, ...); a bad value stops the command with status `2`. A `WSGIAdapter` uses its application's settings.
* **Lifespan.** A plain callable has none. A `WSGIAdapter` starts its application's modules when the worker starts, not on the first request, and stops them on a graceful stop.

The adapter itself buffers its responses, so streaming reaches the client only from a plain callable. Its other specifics below apply on both servers.

The adapter drives the same ASGI callable on a background event loop that it owns, so routing, binding, access, errors, limits and the OpenAPI document behave as under ASGI. Specifics:

* **Startup is lazy** under Granian (Kiso starts them with the worker). Modules (including the database pool) start on the first request of each worker process, so a pre-forking server can import the file in its master process. If startup fails, every request answers `503` with `not_ready` and the error is logged.
* **Shutdown** runs on `WSGIAdapter.close()` or, otherwise, at interpreter exit. A server that kills workers without exiting normally skips it, as it would any `atexit` hook.
* **Async handlers** run on the adapter's loop and **sync handlers** on the bounded executor, as under ASGI. Each WSGI server thread blocks for the duration of its request, so concurrency is the server's thread count rather than the event loop.
* **Bodies are buffered.** Request bodies are read up to `max_body_bytes` plus one byte, so an oversized upload still answers `413`. On Kiso the bytes of the bodies being read are bounded by what the threads and the queue could hold (`(threads + queue) * max_body_bytes`); a request that would pass it answers `503` before its body is read. Responses are complete before they are sent: an application with an action that returns `Stream`, `EventStream` or `File` is refused when the adapter starts (`WSGIStartupError` naming the actions; serve it with ASGI or Kiso, see [streaming](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md)), and a client disconnect is not reported to the handler.
* **Paths.** The server decodes the path once and the adapter passes it on without decoding again, so a client's `%2520` reaches the handler as `%20`, as under ASGI. A percent-encoded slash (`%2F`) cannot be told apart from a real one in WSGI and is not available inside a path parameter. A bad `Content-Length` answers `400`.
* **One protocol per process.** Do not serve the same application object over ASGI and WSGI in one process; the adapter owns its own loop and module lifespan. Run two processes if you need both.

The path is checked against Kiso and Granian (`--interface wsgi`, with one and two workers) by a parity test, not against every WSGI server.

## Going to production

Before the first deployment:

- Run `uv run hinoki check` and `uv run pytest`; both must pass.
- Set `debug` off and narrow [`allowed_hosts`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md#allowed_hosts) to your host names.
- Serve over HTTPS, with the TLS files or a proxy listed in `trusted_proxies`.
- Give secrets (`Secret` settings, `cursor_secret`) through the environment, never the repository.
- Apply migrations once per deployment, from one process, not from every worker's startup.
- Set `workers` and the connection limits for the machine, and check `GET /health` after the rollout.

## Errors and edge cases

- `error: X is neither an application nor a factory`: the target names something else, for example an ASGI wrapper; run wrappers with `granian`.
- `error: Granian is not installed; install the server extra`: run `uv sync` in a generated project (it depends on `hinoki-api[server]`), or use Kiso.
- `hinoki dev` reloads with `watchfiles`, also part of the `server` extra, on either server; without it `dev` exits with that message and `serve` still works.
- `--workers` outside the supported range is refused on Kiso; `0` means "use `server.workers`".
- `--interface wsgi` with `server.native_dispatch` or `server.trusted_proxies` set on Kiso exits with status `2` and names the setting.
- `--interface wsgi` with a `Hinoki` application or a non-callable exits with an error that points to `WSGIAdapter`. A factory exits with status `2`: `error: wsgi:create_app is a factory; for --interface wsgi name a WSGI callable, such as WSGIAdapter(app) from hinoki.wsgi`. Build the application at import time instead, as in `wsgi_app = WSGIAdapter(create_app())`.
- A Kiso-only setting under `--server granian` exits with status `2` and names the setting.

## See also

- [Kiso server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md)
- [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#built-in-fields-and-defaults)
- [Command line](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md)

# Kiso server

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md

Kiso is the HTTP server inside Hinoki's native extension, written in Rust on
hyper, tokio and rustls. It is what `hinoki dev` and `hinoki serve` run unless
you choose Granian, and it can answer many requests without entering Python.

```sh
hinoki serve --workers 4
```

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(
    settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env", toml="settings.toml"
):
    pass
```

```toml
# settings.toml
[server]
server = "kiso"
workers = 4
```

`--server kiso` selects it explicitly when a project defaults to Granian. Choose
Granian instead when you need an ASGI wrapper around the application
([Serve an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#choose-a-server)).

## Request-head fuzzing

The fuzz workflow checks Kiso's HTTP/1 request-line and header
handling with two focused targets. `head_framing` checks chunk-boundary
invariance, the hard head-size bound, parser safety and that declared-length
bodies stay opaque. `request_head_limits` checks the `httparse` header-slot
bound, header-byte accounting, query-limit precedence and exact limit
boundaries. These targets run alongside the host, redirect, declared-length
and WebSocket fuzzers in CI; locally they can be run with
`cargo +nightly fuzz run head_framing` and
`cargo +nightly fuzz run request_head_limits`.

## What is native and what still runs in Python

The listener, HTTP/1.1 parsing, connection and header limits, body framing and its limits and timeouts, route matching, the request ID, and the answers that need no application code run on the native runtime without taking the Python interpreter lock. Without host, CORS or HTTPS-redirect policies, a request the native layer can answer by itself is answered there: unknown paths and methods (`404`, `405` with `Allow`), oversized request lines or headers, `503` while the worker is not ready or the in-flight limit is reached, and malformed requests. When one of those policies is active, the Rust classifier checks it first and then answers unmatched requests itself, with the same CORS headers as the Python pipeline. The response carries the same security headers, request ID, CORS and HSTS policy as one produced by the application.

The lifespan, handwritten handlers and their database calls still use Python. The OpenAPI document and the documentation pages and assets are built once at startup by the same Python code and answered by the Rust classifier for `GET` and `HEAD` (other methods continue to route lookup), with the same status, headers, request ID, CORS and security headers; they cross into Python only when a request target is not plain ASCII. Host allow-list checks, CORS preflight answers and HTTPS redirects run in the Rust classifier before docs and route lookup, with the same response order and headers as the Python pipeline. For matched routes that continue through the Python pipeline, Kiso also percent-decodes the captured path values and passes them to Python; an invalid UTF-8 escape is carried as an error marker and reported at the same point where the pipeline previously decoded it. Python still applies `str`, `int`, UUID, bool and custom converters, and owns authentication, hooks, body/query binding, handlers, error translation and response assembly.

For an eligible public `GET`, `DELETE`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `QUERY` function, Kiso skips Python route matching and request binding. It accepts parameters from the path and query string annotated `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool` or `UUID` with the built-in converter, and query parameters whose default has exactly that type. Rust decodes provided values, converts them with the same rules as the Python converters (an invalid value gives the same `422`), validates the full query, negotiates `Accept`, and prepares the handler arguments. An absent optional query uses its declared default, including when a wrapper observes the keyword arguments; an empty value is still an explicitly supplied empty string. Missing required or repeated query parameters use the same validation response as the Python pipeline. Error translation and `Response` creation remain in Python; JSON encoding uses Hinoki's Rust encoder, and Rust finalizes the response headers and suppresses the body for `HEAD`. Those final headers include the CORS headers for the request's `Origin`, on successful and error answers alike, exactly as the Python pipeline adds them; an answer that sets its own `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` keeps its CORS headers. An async handler runs in its ordinary asyncio task, unless it qualifies for [the native handler lane](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#the-native-handler-lane); a sync handler uses the bounded executor. If a sync handler returns an awaitable, Hinoki awaits it on the same request task after the executor call completes. An integer longer than 18 digits is left to the Python pipeline, which applies Python's own integer limits. A body method is eligible with exactly one `Schema` body parameter and only built-in parsers (`JSONParser`, `FormParser`, `TextParser`, `BytesParser`, exact types without overrides; a custom parser or a `JSONParser.prepare` override uses the Python pipeline). The route's parser is chosen from the `Content-Type` after the body is read, so an unlisted type is the same `415`. Its body is read from the native connection only when the handler's turn comes, after content negotiation, with the same limits, and is then decoded and validated by the Rust decoder and validator. The failures keep the order and the answers of the Python pipeline: a declared length above the limit or a body read failure first, then a malformed query string, then the content type (`415`) and malformed JSON (`400`), then one `422` listing every path, query and body problem in declaration order. A refusal before the body is read closes the connection, as on the Python pipeline. The automatic path does not accept several body parameters, file or `Request` parameters, custom parsers, multipart uploads, defaults on path parameters, custom response headers or custom renderers. The built-in `JSONRenderer`, `HTMLRenderer`, `TextRenderer` and `XMLRenderer`, alone or several on one route, are eligible: Rust negotiates `Accept` (including `406`) and Python renders with the chosen one, exactly as on the Python pipeline. A subclass of a built-in renderer or one with extra attributes is custom. A route with an `access` policy stays eligible, with at most one `Caller` principal parameter: Python authenticates the request before anything else, so the order of the answers (`400`, `invalid_query`, `401`/`403`) matches the Python pipeline, and the body is still read only after authentication succeeds. When that access policy uses an unmodified [`ClaimsJWTAuth`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md#claims-only-tokens-on-the-native-lane), Rust also answers the refusals itself (`401` with the challenge, or `403`) without crossing into Python, and hands the admitted caller to the handler. A route with a `rate_limit` policy is eligible too: Python asks the policy, with the same client address as the Python pipeline (the forwarded client when the TCP peer is a trusted proxy, otherwise the peer) and the authenticated caller, right after authentication and before negotiation, the body and validation, so a refused client gets the same `429` or `503` without the server reading its body. A route with `atomic=True` stays eligible: the handler runs inside the same transaction as on the Python pipeline, the commit follows the encoding of the answer, and any error or timeout rolls back before it is translated. Host restrictions, CORS and HTTPS redirects are checked natively and do not make an otherwise eligible route fall back. Every other route uses the full Python request pipeline for binding, validation, error translation and response assembly. The request body is read natively only when that pipeline asks for it, after authentication, so an unauthenticated client cannot make the server buffer a body. Handlers themselves remain Python code; this is not an application written in Rust, and no performance figure is claimed here. A `Query[Schema]` parameter of a `GET` or `DELETE` is eligible too (Python converts and validates the query string, reporting errors in the pipeline order; it does not combine with a body). A `Form[Schema]` or `XML[Schema]` body is eligible too: the text is converted and validated as described in [Form bodies](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#form-bodies) and [XML bodies](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#xml-bodies).

## The native handler lane

An `async def` handler that only talks to the database through the ORM can run without an asyncio task: Kiso drives its coroutine itself, runs each database wait on the native runtime and sends the answer from there. Hinoki decides this once per route at worker startup, by reading the handler's own source. A route takes the lane when:

* it is a `GET`, `DELETE`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `QUERY` that is eligible for the native path above (a body method takes one `Schema` body and built-in parsers);
* the function is a plain `async def`, not wrapped by a decorator;
* every `await` in it is an ORM call on a `Model` class:
    * a read: `Model.aget(...)`, `Model.aget_or_none(...)`, `Model.aget_as(...)`, `Model.aget_or_none_as(...)`, or `Model.filter(...)` / `Model.all()` with `filter`, `select_related`, `prefetch_related`, `order_by`, `limit` and `offset`, ending in `aget`, `aget_as`, `aget_or_none_as`, `afirst`, `acount`, `aexists`, `aproject`, or `apaginate_as`, or awaited directly;
    * a write: `acreate`, `aupdate`, `aupdate_where`, `adelete`, `abulk_create`, `abulk_update`, `abulk_delete`, or `aupdate` / `adelete` ending a `filter(...)` chain. A write counts only on a model that overrides none of the write hooks (`before_save`, `before_create`, `after_create`, `after_save`) or the methods the write calls (`insert`, `asave`, `from_schema` and the like); `asave`, `aupdate_from` and `aupdate_within` on an instance stay on asyncio.

These keep a route in an asyncio task: `async with`, `async for`, `yield`, async comprehensions, local names that shadow a model, and any other `await` (`asyncio.sleep`, an HTTP client, another coroutine).

* **Guards and bodies.** A guarded route (`access`, `rate_limit`, `Query[Schema]` or several renderers) is served the same way, and so is a body method.
