The built-in `RateLimit` counts in one SQL statement on the native runtime without an asyncio task, so a route that uses it keeps its lane. Guards run first inside the driven coroutine, in the order of the asyncio path (credentials, then the rate limit, then the body and the request values), and the body is read on the native runtime.
* **Class APIs.** A handler of a class API takes the lane when the class keeps the stock constructor (no `__init__` or `__new__` of its own in the class or its bases) and adds no `response_headers`. The instance is built per request, as on the asyncio path; a class that builds itself with application code stays on asyncio. The constructor is read once at startup.
* **Transactions.** An `atomic=True` route runs its handler inside a transaction opened, committed or rolled back on the native runtime, and an error is translated only after the rollback, as on the asyncio path.
* **Invalid requests.** A request Rust already finds invalid (a bad path encoding, an invalid path or query parameter, an unacceptable `Accept`) stays on the asyncio path.
* **Moving to asyncio.** A provider or policy that awaits something only asyncio can run (a custom provider calling an HTTP service, a custom rate limit policy whose store awaits on asyncio) moves the request to an asyncio task at that point, once, with what is left of the timeout. A transaction already open goes with it, so later savepoints still nest and the rollback is unchanged. The same happens if a write hook is added to a model after startup and awaits asyncio.

`hinoki routes --lanes` shows the choice, and `hinoki.runtime` logs the reason for every route at debug level.

The behaviour is the same on both paths: status, headers, body, error translation, the request ID and the `request_timeout` (a `504`). An error from a driven handler, and a failure of a generated CRUD action, is translated in place when no error handler you registered can match it; an exception one of your handlers matches is translated in an asyncio task, because the handler may await. Each request has its own context, so `request_id` and the database are the ones of that request. The handler's steps after its first run on the event-loop thread, so a task it starts still finds the loop. If a driven handler awaits something only asyncio can run (a database backend without native waits), it is moved to an asyncio task at that point and continues with what is left of the request timeout. At shutdown, running handlers are cancelled like request tasks.

What it assumes: model classes and their ORM methods are not replaced after startup. Set `server.native_dispatch = false` to keep every handler in an asyncio task. No performance figure is claimed here.

`hinoki routes --lanes` shows, per route, whether Kiso runs it natively and, if
not, why ([Inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#routes)).

## Generated CRUD

Generated CRUD plans can also execute public `create` (`POST`), `update` (`PATCH`) and `delete` actions in Rust. These routes use the native path only when their model and schemas are supported and they have no assignment rule or custom CRUD hook (an `owner` is allowed only with `identity_key = caller_id`, and a `scope` with `RowScope.by_caller` or `RowScope.by_claim` on a text non-key column outside the update schema, on any supported database), and their access policy, if any, uses an unmodified [`ClaimsJWTAuth`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md#claims-only-tokens-on-the-native-lane). A missing, empty or non-string required claim on a scoped route answers `403 Forbidden` before opening a transaction or querying. Rust reads and validates the bounded request body, runs the database transaction, fetches the written row where the response requires it, and encodes the response before commit. Writes continue to completion if the client disconnects. A unique-constraint violation returns `409 Conflict` by default; a registered application error handler takes precedence. Routes that are ineligible or become stale use the ordinary Python CRUD pipeline. A model with a handler for `Created`, `Updated` or `Deleted` ([model events](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md#model-events)) is ineligible for the matching action only, reason `model_event_handlers`. Plans are selected automatically at worker startup and checked once per second; a changed plan is disarmed until the worker restarts. This path adds no public setting.

These model features are supported on the native CRUD lane:

* `SoftDeleteModel` (or `@db.soft_delete()`): a `delete` stamps the soft-delete column (and `updated_at`) with an `UPDATE`, and every native read sees live rows only, with the same SQL as the Python lane.
* UUIDv4 or UUIDv7 keys from `uuid_pk()`, and `urlsafe_token()` columns that no schema writes, all generated in Rust.
* `Decimal` and `date` columns. A stored `Decimal` that Rust cannot render exactly as Python would, such as one Python writes in exponent form, is handed back to Python for that request.

`Enum` columns, `RowScope.by(...)` and `CursorPagination` lists stay on the Python lane. Run with the `hinoki.server` logger at debug level to see, at startup, why each generated CRUD route stays on the Python lane.

The measured phase 1 path is documented in the [native CRUD orientation run](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rust-crud-orientation.md). It is a single-host, workload-specific measurement and does not establish general or production performance.

Routes with a [many-to-many ids field](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md#many-to-many-fields) take the same path when each relation is scoped with `all_rows(Target)`, `own_rows(Target, column)`, `RowScope.by_caller(Target, column)` or `RowScope.by_claim(Target, column, claim)` and no `Linked`/`Unlinked` handler is registered. Rust reads the ids of a page with one extra `SELECT` on the bridge table, and on create and update it parses the set, locks the owner row (with its row scope and owner policy), checks the targets against the scope and writes the bridge in the row's transaction; the response is encoded before commit, with the ids read inside it. Python is entered only for a key Rust cannot read, which the Python lane then answers. `RowScope.by(...)`, a scope callable, a `link_queryset` override or a hook keeps the route on the Python lane.

## Limits

* HTTP/1.1, plus HTTP/2 over TLS when `server.http2` is on (see below). WebSocket upgrades are accepted for the actions declared with `@http.websocket` (see [WebSockets](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/websockets.md)); any other `Upgrade` header is ignored and the request is answered as plain HTTP, and no other protocol is ever switched to. There is no cleartext HTTP/2 (neither prior knowledge nor `Upgrade: h2c`).
* A request line plus headers larger than `execution.max_header_bytes`, or a query longer than `execution.max_query_bytes`, is refused (`431`, `414`). A body larger than `execution.max_body_bytes` is refused with `413`, by `Content-Length` before any byte is read or, for chunked bodies, as soon as the total passes the limit. A client that sends nothing for `body_read_timeout` seconds (10 by default, never more than half of `execution.request_timeout`) gets `408`, and so does one that trickles data: the whole body must arrive within six times `body_read_timeout`. After a `413` Kiso closes the connection once it has read and discarded at most 1 MiB of what the client is still sending, or after 2 seconds, whichever comes first. A client that streams much more than the limit before it reads can therefore see a connection reset instead of the `413`, depending on the socket buffers of the two hosts; a body slightly above the limit gets the `413`.
* A client that does not finish its request headers within `header_read_timeout` seconds (10 by default) is disconnected; the same timer closes idle keep-alive connections.
* TLS is optional: set `server.tls_cert_file` and `server.tls_key_file` (PEM; the key may be PKCS#8, PKCS#1 or SEC1) and Kiso speaks HTTPS with rustls (TLS 1.2 and 1.3, the library's default cipher suites, no client certificates, ALPN `http/1.1`, or `h2` then `http/1.1` with `server.http2`). The files are read once at start, so a renewed certificate needs a restart (a rolling restart of the workers is enough). A plaintext client on a TLS port gets a TLS alert, never an answer, and the handshake must finish within `header_read_timeout`. Requests over TLS have the scheme `https`, so the HSTS policy applies. `hinoki serve` warns when the key is readable by every local user. Granian takes the same two settings (the framework asks it for TLS 1.2 and up and HTTP/1.1 only, as Kiso does, unless `server.http2` is on). A trusted proxy's `X-Forwarded-Proto` overrides the scheme, `http` included, on both servers. The handshake and the request head each have their own `header_read_timeout`, so a slow client can hold a connection slot for up to twice that time. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, leave them unset and list the proxy in `trusted_proxies` instead.
* HTTP/2 is opt-in: set `server.http2 = true` together with the TLS files (it is a settings error without them, on both servers). The server then offers ALPN `h2` and `http/1.1` and serves each connection with the protocol it negotiated; a client that offers only `http/1.1`, or no ALPN, still gets HTTP/1.1. Requests reach the application unchanged, with `http_version` `2` in the ASGI scope; the `:authority` pseudo-header becomes the `Host` and wins over a `host` header that differs. Limits are fixed, not settings: 32 concurrent streams per connection (the 33rd is refused), a 64 KiB stream window, header lists bounded by `execution.max_header_bytes` and at most 100 header lines per request (`cookie` fields count once; more is answered `431`), and the h2 library's rapid-reset protections. A connection counts as one slot of `max_connections`, but every stream in flight uses backend capacity (the in-flight limit and the queue) like a request of its own, so size those limits for connections times 32. The server also drops a connection on which more than 100 streams end before their response completed (client resets) within a fixed 10-second window; it is closed without a `GOAWAY`. The count is per connection, not per client: a client can pass about twice the bound across a window boundary, and a new connection starts from zero. A connection with no open stream for `header_read_timeout` is closed gracefully (`GOAWAY`; a stream opened in the race with the `GOAWAY` is accepted and then cut when the shutdown timeout ends). A response that sends no data for `write_timeout` seconds (a client that keeps its flow-control window at zero, or stopped reading) also gets the connection a `GOAWAY`: hyper cannot reset one stream from outside, so the other streams have the shutdown timeout to finish and the stalled one is cut with the connection. Progress is tracked per response, so opening new streams does not hide a stalled one. Keep-alive pings every 30 seconds drop a peer that stopped answering. Set `write_timeout` above 32 x 16 KiB divided by the slowest client bandwidth you expect to serve: HTTP/2 shares the window between streams unevenly, so on a slow link each of 32 concurrent downloads can wait that long between two chunks and be taken for stalled while bytes still flow. A request with several `host` headers and no `:authority` is refused with `400`. A client that trickles the head of one stream while others are open is not bounded by `header_read_timeout`. On stop the server sends `GOAWAY`, lets streams in flight finish, and aborts what is left after the shutdown timeout. Not provided: cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c), server push, and WebSocket or `CONNECT` over HTTP/2. Granian with `server.http2` negotiates HTTP/2 itself (`http` mode `auto`), under its own limits.
* A client that stops reading a response for `write_timeout` seconds (30 by default) is disconnected; any progress restarts the timer.
* `max_connections` (10000 by default) bounds open connections. Requests waiting for the application are bounded by an in-flight limit and a queue; beyond them the answer is `503`.
* Requests with ambiguous framing (for example `Content-Length` together with `Transfer-Encoding`, repeated lengths, or a bare line feed in the head) are refused with `400` and the connection is closed.
* On start, Kiso names itself on stderr before the `listening on ...` line (which stays on stdout, where tools wait for it): its version, the mode (`serve` or `dev`, which reloads on file changes), the worker count, the scheme, whether the access log is on and whether the native handler lane is on. In a terminal (and with `NO_COLOR` unset) it is the same banner `hinoki new` draws: a branch (`╭─`, `│`, `╰─`) titled **Kiso** (no image, on any terminal) with the tagline and the version, then the facts as aligned `mode`, `workers`, `scheme`, `access log` and `native lane` rows, wrapped to fit the terminal; otherwise it is one plain line, for example `Kiso 0.0.1 (Hinoki's Rust server): serve, 4 workers, http, access log off, native lane on`.
* The access log is one line per answered request, written to stderr by Kiso: `127.0.0.1:52341 - "GET /items?limit=5 HTTP/1.1" 200 OK 3.2ms`. The time is how long the server took to decide the answer, not including writing it to the client, and the line is printed for every answer, including the ones the server gives itself (`404`, `429`, `503`). When stderr is a terminal (and `NO_COLOR` is unset) the line is coloured in the style of a development console: `INFO:` in green, the request in bold, the status by class (2xx green, 3xx cyan, 4xx yellow, 5xx red) and the time dimmed. Control characters in the target are shown as `\xNN`. Other formats and filters:
    * `server.access_log_format = "json"` writes one JSON object per line instead, for a log pipeline: `{"time":"2026-11-19T19:56:25.881Z","peer":"127.0.0.1:52341","method":"GET","path":"/items","query":"limit=5","http_version":"1.1","status":200,"duration_ms":3.2,"lane":"python"}`. `time` is RFC 3339 UTC. `lane` says where the request was first routed: `early` for an answer from the transport or the classifier, `native` for a [generated CRUD plan](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#generated-crud) that Rust executes, and `python` for every request handed to the Python side, including handlers on the [native handler lane](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#the-native-handler-lane), so it can differ from what `hinoki routes --lanes` shows. `route` is the pattern that matched, e.g. `/items/{id}`, so requests can be grouped without parsing paths (absent when no route matched). Quotes and control characters are escaped.
    * `server.access_log_format = "logger"` hands each request to the Python `hinoki.access` logger instead of writing to stderr, so your own handlers, formatters and filters (see [your own loggers](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#your-own-loggers)) decide where it goes; each record carries the JSON fields as `record.access`. Kiso queues up to 4096 records and a logging thread passes them to Python in batches, taking the GIL once per batch; when the logger falls behind, new records are dropped rather than slowing requests.
    * Setting a format turns the log on, in `serve` too, unless `access_log` is `false`.
    * `access_log_skip = ["/health", "/static/*"]` leaves noisy paths out and `access_log_slow_ms = 100` keeps only slow answers; failures (status 400 and up) are always logged.
* A client that disconnects does not cancel its running handler; the handler finishes and its answer is discarded.
* A WSGI callable (`--interface wsgi`) runs in Python threads behind this listener, not on the native lane: see [WSGI on Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#wsgi-on-kiso) for what applies to it.
* An answer Kiso cannot send as given (an informational status, a header name or value HTTP does not allow, an unreadable `content-length`) becomes a bare `500`, and the reason is written to stderr, for example `kiso: error: the response cannot be sent (invalid header "x-evil"); answering 500 instead`. The access log records the `500`. A streamed body that is shorter or longer than its `content-length` is cut off with an error line on stderr and the connection is closed (HTTP/1.1) or the stream reset (HTTP/2), so the client never mistakes it for a complete answer. The access log keeps the status of the head here, because it is written when the head is decided.

## Streamed responses

An action that returns `Stream`, `EventStream` or `File` is never served by the native handler lane (`lane_reason` `streamed response`): its handler and its iterator run in Python, and each piece crosses to Rust as a Python `bytes`. After that the server frames the body (`transfer-encoding: chunked` on HTTP/1.1), keeps a bounded queue of 8 pieces so a slow client slows the iterator down, checks a declared `content-length`, applies `execution.stream_idle_timeout` to a `Stream`, sends a keep-alive comment to an event stream every `execution.sse_keepalive` seconds, and ends an event stream normally on shutdown. A `File` is opened and sent by the server, and its bytes never enter Python.

A client that leaves is noticed when the server next writes to it, so a stream that keeps producing is closed at once, while a silent one is closed at its next keep-alive or idle timeout. A body that fails after the head is cut instead of ending as complete, and the access log keeps the status of the head. See [stream a response](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md).

## Response compression

With `compression.enabled` Kiso compresses eligible bodies with brotli or gzip after the application has answered, on HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, for whole answers, streams, event streams and files. It negotiates `accept-encoding`, adds `Vary`, skips small or non-text bodies and answers with `cache-control: no-transform`, flushes a stream whenever its producer pauses, and sends an answer uncompressed when `compression.max_concurrent` compressions are already running. It is a Kiso feature: Granian does not compress. See [compress responses](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/compression.md).

## Workers, signals and restarts

With one worker and `server.sighup = "stop"` (or where the system has no `SIGHUP`, as on Windows) `hinoki serve` runs the server in its own process. With several workers, with the default `sighup` (one extra supervisor process even for one worker) and always under `hinoki dev` it starts a supervisor that starts each worker as a fresh process that imports the target and builds the application. Databases and pools open inside each worker's lifespan, never in the supervisor.

* **Listening sockets and `SO_REUSEPORT`.** On Linux, when `hinoki serve` runs more than one worker on a non-zero port (and `server.reuse_port` is not `false`), the supervisor probes `host:port` to validate it and then closes its probe socket before spawning workers; each worker opens its own `SO_REUSEPORT` listening socket (honouring `backlog`) after its lifespan startup succeeds, so the Linux kernel distributes incoming connections across per-worker accept queues. On macOS and other non-Linux platforms (where `SO_REUSEPORT` does not load-balance across sockets), with one worker, with `port = 0` (ephemeral port), under `hinoki dev`, or when `server.reuse_port = false`, the supervisor opens one listening socket (honouring `backlog`) and passes the descriptor down to every worker; connections are then spread by the operating system's accept on that shared socket.

* `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` (Ctrl-C) stops accepting, lets running requests finish for up to `lifecycle.shutdown_timeout`, runs the lifespan shutdown and exits. `SIGHUP` does the same when `server.sighup` is `"stop"` and [reloads](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#reload-on-sighup) otherwise. A worker still running five seconds after that is killed. A second signal kills the workers immediately. Once the stop begins the supervisor closes its own copy of the socket, so a client that connects while the workers drain is refused. `--workers` must be 1 to 256 (`0` uses `server.workers`).
* A worker that exits on its own, whether it failed to start or crashed, is not restarted: the supervisor stops the other workers and exits with a non-zero status. Restart policy belongs to the process manager (systemd, a container runtime) that runs `hinoki serve`.
* The listening socket is opened before the lifespan startup of a supervised worker finishes, so connections wait in the backlog until a worker accepts them. With one worker the socket is opened after a successful startup.
* If the supervisor is killed without a chance to clean up, its workers notice within a second of finishing their startup and stop. The workers' copy of the listening socket is not inherited by processes a handler starts.
* A socket that cannot be opened (address in use, a bad port or host) is reported as `error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ...` with exit status 2, with one worker or several.

## Reload on `SIGHUP`

`kill -HUP <supervisor pid>` (or `ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID` in a systemd unit) replaces the workers of a running `hinoki serve` with new ones, without closing the listening socket. The supervisor does this one worker at a time:

1. It starts a new worker on the same socket (or, with per-worker `SO_REUSEPORT` on Linux, with the same `host:port`, so the new worker binds its own `SO_REUSEPORT` socket only after its lifespan startup succeeds). The new process imports the target and reads the settings, so changed code, `.env` and TOML files, TLS certificates, and CORS, host and security policies take effect.
2. It waits until the new worker has run its lifespan startup and serves. The wait is `lifecycle.startup_timeout` plus five seconds.
3. It sends `SIGTERM` to the old worker, which stops accepting (closing its `SO_REUSEPORT` socket immediately on Linux so new connections go only to the active workers), lets the requests it has finish (up to `lifecycle.shutdown_timeout`), runs its lifespan shutdown and exits. It is killed if it is still running five seconds after that.
4. It moves to the next worker. At most one extra worker runs at a time, so the database connections of an application are at most `(workers + 1) × pool_max` while a reload runs.

```text
reloading: SIGHUP (generation 2)
reloaded 4 workers (generation 2)
```

The supervisor's own settings are not reloaded: `host`, `port`, `backlog`, `workers`, `server`, `interface` and `metrics.listen` need a restart, as do the environment variables of the supervisor process. Migrations are never run by a reload: run `hinoki migrations apply` before sending the signal.

* A new worker that exits, fails its lifespan startup or is not ready in time is killed, and the reload stops with `error: reload stopped at worker K of N; the other workers keep running`. The workers not yet replaced keep serving the old code (workers already replaced stay new); another `SIGHUP` retries them all. The supervisor does not exit.
* A `SIGHUP` that arrives during a reload is remembered once and handled when it ends. `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` during a reload stops everything, the new and the old workers, as usual.
* A worker that crashes outside a reload still stops the supervisor, as above.
* `server.sighup = "stop"` keeps the earlier behavior (`SIGHUP` stops the server). `hinoki dev` always reloads on file changes and `SIGHUP` stops it. Windows has no `SIGHUP`, so there the setting has no effect and the server runs as for `"stop"`. Granian refuses `server.sighup`.
* A request that a client has already sent to the old worker when it is told to stop is answered, not refused with a `503`: the worker reports not ready only after its connections have drained.
* The reload is orchestrated by the supervisor, which is Python; the drain of the old worker and the TLS loading of the new one are Rust. With metrics, see [several workers](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md#several-workers).

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(
    settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env", toml="settings.toml"
):
    pass
```

```toml
# settings.toml: reload is on by default; "stop" turns it off
[server]
workers = 4
sighup = "reload"
```

```sh
hinoki serve notes.main:app &
kill -HUP "$(pgrep -f 'hinoki serve')"
```

## Reload with `hinoki dev`

The supervisor watches the project directory (`*.py`, `*.toml` and `.env` files; `.venv`, `.git` and caches are ignored) and, on a change, stops the worker gracefully and starts a new one on the same socket, so a client connecting during the restart waits instead of being refused. If the new code fails to import or start, the error is printed (a short `error: cannot load ...` line for a missing module or name, a traceback for other failures), `waiting for changes` follows, and the next edit starts the worker again; connections wait in the meantime. The host, port, `backlog` and the choice of server are read once when `hinoki dev` starts: change them and restart the command. The other `server` settings (limits, `trusted_proxies`, `runtime_threads`) are read again by every restarted worker. The watcher ignores `.venv` but not a virtual environment with another name, such as `venv/`: keep it outside the project directory or it triggers reloads. The first import of the target happens in the command itself, so an error there stops it with a message instead of waiting. `dev` needs `watchfiles` (the `hinoki-api[server]` extra) and uses one worker.

## Behind a reverse proxy

`server.trusted_proxies` works as described in [Hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md#reverse-proxies-and-request-ids): the native layer matches the TCP peer against it for the request ID and the HSTS and scheme policy of its own answers, and the request pipeline resolves the forwarded scheme and client address of the requests it handles from the same peer. The rate limit of a natively served route resolves its client the same way, so `RateLimitContext.client` is the same on both lanes. Points to know:

* Entries are IP addresses or CIDRs. An IPv6 address with a zone id such as `fe80::1%lo0` is refused when settings load, for either server (earlier versions loaded it and the ASGI path matched it; Kiso cannot take it).
* On a listener bound to `::` that also accepts IPv4 (the default on many systems, for example Linux with `bindv6only=0` and macOS), an IPv4 peer appears as `::ffff:a.b.c.d`. A plain IPv4 entry such as `10.0.0.5` or `10.0.0.0/8` then never matches, and the proxy is treated as untrusted. That fails closed, and the ASGI path behaves the same. Either bind an IPv4 host (`--host 0.0.0.0`) or list the mapped form, for example `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104`.
* A request ID that a trusted proxy sent and Hinoki refused is logged as `ignored invalid request ID from trusted proxy`; for requests answered natively the warning is aggregated once a second with a count.

## Errors and edge cases

- A build whose native extension has no Kiso fails `--server kiso` with an error that says so.
- A socket that cannot be opened is reported as `error: cannot listen on HOST:PORT: ...` with exit status `2`.
- A worker that exits on its own is not restarted: restart policy belongs to your process manager.

## See also

- [Serve an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md)
- [Request lifecycle](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/request-lifecycle.md)
- [Native CRUD orientation run](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rust-crud-orientation.md)

# Test an application

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md

A project created with `hinoki new` already has a test that runs a request
through the whole stack, without a network socket:

```python
# tests/healthtest.py
from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient

from notes.main import app


async def test_health_answers_through_the_whole_stack() -> None:
    async with ASGIClient(app) as client:
        reply = await client.get("/health")
    assert (reply.status, reply.body) == (200, {"status": "ok"})
```

Run it with `uv run pytest`. The generated `pyproject.toml` sets
`asyncio_mode = "auto"` and collects files named `*test.py`.

`ASGIClient` runs the application's startup (modules, database pool, startup
hooks and [rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md)) when the block opens and its shutdown when it
closes. A reply has `status`, `headers`, `body` (decoded JSON, or text) and `raw`
bytes.

## Test protected actions

`token=` sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, so a test exercises the real
provider and policy:

```python
# tests/billingtest.py
from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient

from notes.main import app


async def test_invoices_need_a_staff_token() -> None:
    async with ASGIClient(app) as client:
        anonymous = await client.get("/billing/invoices")
        unknown = await client.get("/billing/invoices", token="not-a-token")
    assert anonymous.status == 401
    assert unknown.status == 401
```

## Use a disposable database

The application reads its settings when its module is imported, so point the
prefix variable at a throwaway database first. A `conftest.py` at the project
root is imported before any test module:

```python
# conftest.py
import os

os.environ["NOTES_DATABASE__URL"] = "sqlite://./.hinoki/test.sqlite3"
```

This applies when the settings declare `database: settings.DatabaseSettings`.
Create the tables once, with the same variable:

```sh
NOTES_DATABASE__URL=sqlite://./.hinoki/test.sqlite3 uv run hinoki migrations apply
```

When `settings.toml` sets `engine` and its connection fields, a URL conflicts
with them (`set either url or engine with its fields, not both`). Override the
fields instead, and clear the server-only ones SQLite refuses:

```python
# conftest.py
import os

os.environ.update(
    NOTES_DATABASE__ENGINE="sqlite",
    NOTES_DATABASE__NAME=".hinoki/test.sqlite3",
    NOTES_DATABASE__HOST="",
    NOTES_DATABASE__USER="",
)
```

Apply the migrations with the same variables, and pass the same keys under
`"database"` to `overrides=` in the example below.

When one test needs other settings, build a second application from the same
code instead of changing the shared one. Give `main.py` a `create_app(settings)`
factory, as [`examples/notes/notes/main.py`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/notes/notes/main.py)
does (`create_app`, line 12). The factory lives in the module `hinoki.toml`
names as `project.application`, so `Hinoki(...)` fills routes, events,
middleware and rules from the manifest. This example only calls `/health`, so
its new database needs no tables; to give a test migrated tables, copy them as
[below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md#give-each-test-its-own-database):

```python
# tests/settingstest.py
from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient

from notes.main import create_app
from notes.settings import ProjectSettings


async def test_health_with_its_own_database() -> None:
    settings = ProjectSettings.load(
        overrides={"database": {"url": "sqlite://./.hinoki/other.sqlite3"}}
    )
    async with ASGIClient(create_app(settings)) as client:
        assert (await client.get("/health")).status == 200
```

A `Hinoki(...)` built in any other module (a test, a script) does not read the
manifest; pass what you want explicitly (or use `manifest_routes()`,
`manifest_events()`, `manifest_middleware()` and `manifest_rules()` from
`hinoki.project`).

Use synthetic rows and credentials, and never point test settings at production
data.

### Give each test its own database

The tests above share one file, so rows one test writes are still there in the
next. To start every test from empty, migrated tables, migrate a database in the
test's temporary directory with the app's own migrations and build the
application on it, as
[`examples/notes/notes_tests/conftest.py`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/notes/notes_tests/conftest.py) does:

```python
# tests/conftest.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from pathlib import Path

import pytest
from hinoki.db import Database
from hinoki.orm import migrator
from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient

from notes.main import create_app
from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

MIGRATIONS = Path(__file__).parents[1] / "notes" / "apps" / "notes" / "migrations"


@pytest.fixture
async def client(tmp_path: Path) -> AsyncIterator[ASGIClient]:
    url = f"sqlite://{tmp_path / 'test.sqlite3'}"
    database = await Database.connect(url, max_size=1)
    await migrator.apply(database, MIGRATIONS)
    database.close()
    settings = ProjectSettings.load(overrides={"database": {"url": url}})
    async with ASGIClient(create_app(settings)) as client:
        yield client
```

A test takes `client` as an argument; whatever it writes is gone in the next
test. The migrations come from the app's own directory, so a new migration is
picked up without extra steps. In a project with several apps, apply each app's
migration directory in dependency order. The fixture builds SQLite files only.

## Test email

With `email: settings.EmailSettings` set to `backend=EmailBackend.MEMORY`, every sent message is kept in the worker's `mailer.outbox` and nothing leaves the process; `outbox` entries carry the `Message` and the rendered bytes. A sample test is in [send email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md#test-with-the-memory-backend). For SMTP behaviour use a fake server on `127.0.0.1` and synthetic `example.com` addresses. To test a template without sending, call `template.render(context)` (it returns the three parts) or run `hinoki mail preview`; see [email templates](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md).

## Catch undeclared errors

`ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True)` fails the test when an action answers an
HTTP error that is missing from its `errors=` declaration, so the OpenAPI
document cannot drift from what the action really does.

`ASGIClient` and `SyncClient` (for synchronous tests, [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md#synchronous-tests-and-time)) both have `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch`, `delete`, `head`, `options` and
`query` (the HTTP `QUERY` method; its body goes in `json=` or `body=`, while the
`query=` option of every call is the query string), plus
`request(method, path, ...)` for any other method.

The path is only the path: a `?` or `#` in it raises `ValueError` instead of being routed as part of the path (which would answer a 404 for the wrong reason). Send the query string with `query=`:

```python
reply = await client.get("/items", query="limit=10&offset=20")
```

## Test file uploads

`ASGIClient` and `SyncClient` accept `data=` and `files=` and build the multipart boundary and `Content-Type` header for you. Use a sequence of file tuples to send repeated field names in order:

```python
# tests/uploadtest.py
async with ASGIClient(app) as client:
    response = await client.post(
        "/documents",
        data={"title": "Report"},
        files=[("document", "report.txt", b"contents", "text/plain")],
    )
    assert response.status == 201
```

Each file tuple is `(field_name, filename, content_bytes, content_type)`. Form data may be a mapping or an ordered sequence of `(name, text)` pairs; sequences retain repeated names. Do not pass `json=` or raw `body=` together with `data=`/`files=`; the helper owns the multipart content type and boundary. The application enforces its configured complete-body and per-part limits. This helper sends complete in-memory bodies and does not model streaming uploads. For streamed responses see [test streams](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md#test-streams).

## Headers and hosts

`headers=` accepts a mapping or a sequence of `(name, value)` pairs. Use pairs to send a repeated header; Hinoki's request header mapping joins repeated values with `", "`. A client can add a default `Host` header to each request:

```python
# tests/headerstest.py
async with ASGIClient(app, host="api.example.com") as client:
    response = await client.get(
        "/health", headers=[("X-Trace", "first"), ("X-Trace", "second")]
    )
```

The default remains no `Host` header. Set `headers={"host": "other.example.com"}` on a call to override the client's host. Because the clients run in-process, they do not log the startup warning about the default `allowed_hosts = *` that a served worker logs ([Hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md#allowed_hosts)).

## Test streams

`client.get()` waits for the end of a streamed response and returns the whole body. To see the head and the pieces as they are sent, use `client.stream()`; leaving the block tells the application that the client disconnected, so the source of the stream is closed:

```python
# tests/eventstest.py
from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient

from notes.main import app


async def test_events_arrive_one_by_one() -> None:
    async with ASGIClient(app) as client:
        async with client.stream("GET", "/notes/events", token="t") as reply:
            assert reply.status == 200
            assert reply.headers["content-type"].startswith("text/event-stream")
            first = await anext(reply.chunks())
```

`reply.chunks()` yields each piece as the application sent it, and raises the error that cut the response, if one did. `reply.read()` collects the rest. `SyncClient.stream()` is the same with `with` and a plain iterator. A stream that never ends makes `client.get()` fail with `BodyTooLarge` once the body passes `max_bytes` (10 MiB; pass `max_bytes=` to change it), so a test cannot hang on it. The in-process client runs the ASGI pump, not Kiso's: it shows what the client receives and when the source is closed, not the server's queue, timeouts or keep-alive.

## Synchronous tests and time

`SyncClient` is available for synchronous test functions. It runs the app's lifespan and refuses unsafe nested use from a running event loop.

For deterministic time, `ManualClock` is a thread-safe callable clock. It accepts and returns timezone-aware instants normalized to UTC; `advance(seconds=...)` and `set(datetime)` control its value. A naive datetime raises `ValueError`. Pass it to `app.now(clock)` or other code that accepts a `Clock`.

## Test the layers separately

Keep business operations independent of `Request` and HTTP response types when practical. Test ownership and state transitions against a disposable database, then test route binding, access, status codes and error declarations through `ASGIClient`.

## Repository checks

From the checkout, the documented gates are:

```sh
uv run --locked ruff check .
uv run --locked ruff format --check .
uv run --locked mypy
uv run --locked complexipy . --failed
uv run --locked pytest --cov
cargo fmt --all --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace
uv run --locked --group docs mkdocs build --strict
```

PostgreSQL-dependent Python and Rust tests require `HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL`; without it those tests are skipped. Migration conformance tests for MySQL and MariaDB also require `HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL` and `HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL`, respectively. CI provides disposable real-server services. See [toolchain and CI](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/toolchain.md) for the Rust complexity check, the pre-commit hooks and the packaging checks.

# Command line

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md

Every task in a Hinoki project has a `hinoki` command. Inside a project created
by `hinoki new`, run them through `uv run`, which uses the project's locked
environment:

```sh
uv run hinoki dev
uv run hinoki check
uv run hinoki migrations apply
```

## Commands

| Group | Command | What it does | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Start | `hinoki new [NAME]` | Create a project; asks for what the flags leave out, ending with "Create an app now?" (`--app NAME`, `--no-app`). | [Create a project](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md) |
| | `hinoki app create\|add\|list` | Add an app, register an existing package, list the apps. | [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#app) |
| | `hinoki dev` / `serve` | Run with reload / run for production, on Kiso or Granian; `--interface wsgi` serves a WSGI callable. | [Serve](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md) |
| | `hinoki shell` | Python shell with the app, its settings and models, top-level `await`. | [Shell](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/shell.md) |
| Inspect | `hinoki check` | Run the architecture rules. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#check) |
| | `hinoki doctor` | Environment, manifest and app diagnostics. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#doctor) |
| | `hinoki routes` | Every route with its access policy and server lane. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#routes) |
| | `hinoki events` | Every event handler in execution order, the event limits and the apps' `events` targets. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#events) |
| | `hinoki mail check` | Read and check every registered email template against its context. | [Email templates](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md#checked-at-startup) |
| | `hinoki mail preview NAME` | Render one registered email template from a sample or a JSON context, without sending. | [Email templates](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email-templates.md#preview) |
| | `hinoki settings` | Effective settings and their sources, secrets redacted. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#settings) |
| | `hinoki openapi` | Print, write or diff the OpenAPI document. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#openapi) |
| | `hinoki llms` | Print, write or check the API as llms.txt Markdown for agents. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#llms) |
| | `hinoki version` | The Hinoki version; `--verbose` adds Python, platform, native core and Granian. | [Inspect](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#version) |
| Data | `hinoki migrations plan\|status\|apply\|sql` | Plan and apply migrations for every registered app. | [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#migrations) |
| | `hinoki admin create-superuser\|set-password` | Manage admin users from the terminal. | [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#admin) |
| Integrate | `hinoki mcp` | Serve project context to an AI agent over MCP. | [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#mcp) |
| | `hinoki skills list\|install` | Write the optional agent skills. | [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#skills) |
| | `hinoki manage [COMMAND]` | Run a command your application defines. | [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#manage) |
| | `hinoki completion SHELL` | Print a completion script. | [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#help-and-completion) |

## Targets and short commands

In a project, `hinoki.toml` names the application (`[project] application`), so
commands take no target: `hinoki dev`, `hinoki check`, `hinoki routes`.

To use another application, pass a target, `module:attribute`, imported from
the current directory: `hinoki dev notes.main:app`. A function that returns an
application (`module:create_app`) is also accepted, and `hinoki settings` also
accepts a settings class.

When a target does not import, run the command from the project root (where
`hinoki.toml` is), check that the packages have `__init__.py` files and that the
attribute name is right. The commands report
`error: cannot load notes.main:ap: ...` and exit with a non-zero status.

### Help and completion {#help-and-completion}

`hinoki --help` lists the commands in groups (Start, Inspect, Data, Integrate); `hinoki COMMAND --help` shows one command's options. A mistyped command or migrations action gets a suggestion:

```text
hinoki: error: argument <command>: invalid choice: 'chek' (choose from 'check', ...)
  did you mean 'check'?
```

The completion script is generated from the real parser, so it follows the commands and options of the installed version:

```sh
eval "$(hinoki completion bash)"     # in ~/.bashrc
eval "$(hinoki completion zsh)"      # in ~/.zshrc, after compinit
hinoki completion fish | source      # in ~/.config/fish/config.fish
```

It completes command, subcommand and option names; it does not complete option values or project-specific names such as apps.

### Terminal output

On a colour terminal, `doctor`, `check` and `routes` print a coloured report: a status glyph per check (`✔` ok, `▲` warning, `✘` failed or violated, `?` unverifiable, `–` skipped or waived) with the fix on its own line, and routes with coloured methods. The `check` summary is green only when the exit code is `0`. When output is piped or redirected, or with `NO_COLOR` or `TERM=dumb`, the text is plain and unchanged, and `--format json` is never styled.

## `app` {#app}

The generated `hinoki.toml` registers no app unless `hinoki new` created one (the last question in a terminal, or `--app NAME`): the project package keeps `main.py`, settings, rules and the health route, and models live in apps. It lists the generated rules in `[project] rules = ["NAME.rules:project_rules"]`, so `main.py` passes no `rules=`. Create each one with:

```sh
uv run hinoki app create billing
uv run hinoki app create gateway --no-models
```

This creates `NAME/apps/billing/{models.py,api.py,routes.py,migrations/}` (or omits `models.py` and `migrations/` with `--no-models`) and registers the app in `hinoki.toml`, printing the `Mount("/billing", billing_routes)` snippet to add to `NAME/routes.py` if the app should be served over HTTP. Cross-app foreign keys require the referencing app to list the referenced app in `requires` in `hinoki.toml`; migrations are then planned/applied in dependency order across the full app graph. The project registry is explicit: Hinoki does not scan arbitrary installed packages or run imports at install time.

Both commands report `hinoki.toml`: `hinoki new` lists it among the generated files and `app create` says it registered the app there.

`--no-models` creates an API-only app without persistence, and `--requires` (comma-separated) sets dependencies directly. `app create` writes no events module: to add one, create the module yourself and use `app add --events` or the app's `events` key (see [Events](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md#declaring-handlers-in-hinokitoml)). Middleware and rules are project-wide lists in the `[project]` table that you edit by hand (see [Middleware](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md#declaring-middleware-in-hinokitoml) and [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-rules-run)). In a terminal, `app create` asks for whatever is not given — the name and, when other apps exist, `requires` — with the same prompts, Esc-to-cancel (exit 130, nothing created) and `NO_COLOR` handling as `hinoki new`. Without a terminal or with `--no-input` it never asks: the name is required (exit 2) and the default is no `requires`.

To register a package that already exists, name its modules. Nothing is created or imported; only `hinoki.toml` changes:

```sh
uv run hinoki app add billing --models legacy.billing.models
uv run hinoki app add invoices --models legacy.invoices.models --migrations legacy.db.invoices --requires billing
uv run hinoki app add gateway --requires billing
```

`--models` is optional: omit both `--models` and `--migrations` to register an API-only app without persistence. When `--models` is given, `--migrations` defaults to the `migrations` package next to the models module (`legacy.billing.migrations`); passing `--migrations` without `--models` is rejected. `--events module:attribute` registers the app's event `Handlers`. The whole manifest is validated before it is replaced, so a duplicate name, an unknown or cyclic `--requires`, or a malformed module name leaves `hinoki.toml` untouched and exits 2. Whether the modules import is checked later, when a command such as `hinoki migrations plan` loads the app.

List the registered apps from the project root or any subdirectory:

```sh
uv run hinoki app list
uv run hinoki app list --format json
```

The text output shows each app in dependency order with its model module and migration package (or `models: none` for API-only apps), the `events` target when set, and prerequisites. JSON contains the same fields (`name`, `models`, `migrations`, `requires`, `events`) under an `apps` key. The command only reads and validates `hinoki.toml`: it does not import app modules, connect to a database or start the app. Without a manifest, it prints an error and exits 2.

## `admin` {#admin}

The admin's own users are managed from the admin itself, except the first one:

```sh
uv run hinoki admin create-superuser ada            # asks for the password twice, no echo
printf '%s\n' "$ADA_PASSWORD" | uv run hinoki admin set-password ada --password-stdin
```

A password is read from a terminal prompt or, with `--password-stdin`, from one line of standard input; it is never taken from the command line, where other users of the machine could read it, and it is never printed. Without a terminal and without the flag the command stops; with the flag on a terminal it still prompts without echo, and a line longer than a password can be is refused unread. Ctrl-C or Ctrl-D at the prompt exits with status `2`, and a refused connection is reported as such, naming the masked database and its source (status `1`), not as missing tables. The database is chosen as for `hinoki migrations`: `--database`, `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL`, the project application's installed `DatabaseModule` or `database` setting, then the project's local SQLite; the command prints it on standard error as `database: … (from …)`, and stops with status `2` when the project's application or database cannot be resolved. The user tables must exist: register and apply them first (`hinoki app add admin ...`, `hinoki migrations apply admin`, see [create the admin's tables](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md#create-the-admins-tables) and [who may sign in](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md#who-may-sign-in)); otherwise the command exits 1 and says so. Usernames are lower-cased; the shortest password is `admin.min_password_length` of the project application's `admin` settings (the default without a project). Exit status is `0` on success, `2` for a refused input (a taken name, a weak or mistyped password, an unknown user).

## `migrations` {#migrations}

In a project, migration modules come from `hinoki.toml`; you never pass model or
migration paths:

```sh
uv run hinoki migrations plan --check
uv run hinoki migrations plan billing --name add-invoice-index
uv run hinoki migrations status
uv run hinoki migrations apply
uv run hinoki migrations sql 0001-initial
```

`status` and `apply` cover all registered apps in dependency order. Writing a
`plan` in a multi-app project needs the app name (`plan billing`, or
`--app billing`); read-only `plan --check` and `plan --dry-run` without an app
cover every app in dependency order. `sql` searches every app; `--app` narrows
it when two apps share a migration name. `--name` is optional for a
focused plan: Hinoki derives a stable slug from the first planned table change
(for example, `create-table-notes`); pass `--name initial-notes` to override
it. All-app previews cannot use `--name`. Numbering is automatic. `apply`
initializes the configured local SQLite database when no database is configured.
In a manifest project the implicit `.hinoki/local.sqlite3` file, and a relative
SQLite path from the application's settings, are rooted beside `hinoki.toml`,
even if you run the command from a subdirectory; relative SQLite URLs given
with `--database` or `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL` remain relative to the current
working directory. Added
apps have separate migration ledger namespaces, so identical numbered
filenames do not collide; a project whose root package was
registered as an app (older scaffolds) retains its unprefixed migration keys. `apply billing` includes its declared prerequisite
apps for migration application.

`plan --check` fails CI (exit 1) when the models have changes that no migration
file records, and exits 2 when the database it plans for cannot be resolved; it
never connects to a database. In a project it imports the application to read
its database unless `--database` or `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL` is set. Migration
safety across apps, destructive changes and the ledger are explained in
[Migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md).

Without a `hinoki.toml`, name the modules explicitly:

```sh
hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations plan --models myapp.models --name add-index --dry-run
hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations apply
hinoki migrations --dir myapp/migrations sql 0001-initial
```

`plan` requires `--models MODULE`; `--name` is an optional slug override and is derived from the first planned table change when omitted. `--dry-run` prints operations without writing files. Destructive operations require `--allow-destructive`. plan/status/apply target `--database`, then `HINOKI_DATABASE_URL`, then the `DatabaseModule` or `database` setting of the project's application, then the local SQLite file at `.hinoki/local.sqlite3` ([which database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md#which-database)); `plan`, `status` and `apply` print the chosen database and its source on standard error with the credentials masked, and stop with exit 2 when the project's application or database cannot be resolved. A URL given as an argument is visible in the process list and shell history, so keep a URL containing a password in the environment. When the connection fails, the command prints `error: database: …` with a `fix:` line and exits 1; the error itself does not repeat the URL. `sql NAME` prints a migration's SQL. Use a disposable database while reviewing migrations.

On an animated terminal, `plan` and `apply` show a spinner while they work and finish with a timing line (`✔ applied   1.2s`); the commands' own output is printed unchanged before it. Piped output, `NO_COLOR`, `TERM=dumb`, `CI` and `HINOKI_ANIMATE=0` print only the commands' own output.

## `mcp` {#mcp}

```sh
uv run hinoki mcp
```

The development server uses MCP over stdio. It accepts `--rules`, repeatable `--package`, repeatable `--models`, and `--waivers` with the same target meanings as `check`. `--rules` defaults to the application's rules and `--package` to the package that contains it, as for [`hinoki check`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#check). `--requests PATH` names the file the `recent_requests` tool reads (default `.hinoki/requests.jsonl`; see `server.recent_requests`). `--scenarios off|read|write` controls whether `run_scenario` is registered: `read` allows GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and QUERY; `write` allows every supported method. Scenarios start the real app, run handlers and lifespan hooks, and may write data even for a GET. Keep the tool server owner-controlled and point the app at a disposable database.

The development MCP is separate from application MCP, which is mounted with `expose_as_mcp` and an explicit action allowlist. See the [development MCP guide](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md) for tool inputs and results.

## `skills` {#skills}

```sh
hinoki skills list
hinoki skills install            # from a project directory
hinoki skills install --force    # replace skills that already exist
```

Agent skills are short Markdown playbooks that point an assistant at the real Hinoki tools (the development MCP and the CLI). `list` prints each skill name and description. `install` reads `hinoki.toml`, then writes `.claude/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md` for each one, with the project package name filled in; an existing file is kept and reported unless `--force` replaces it. Without a manifest it prints an error and exits `2`. `hinoki new --skills` writes the same files at creation. They are optional and never written otherwise.

| Skill | Playbook |
| --- | --- |
| `hinoki-add-endpoint` | add an action with its `Schema` types, access policy and test |
| `hinoki-fix-rule` | fix a rule diagnostic without editing the rules or waivers |
| `hinoki-review-api` | run `hinoki openapi --breaking-against` before and after a change |
| `hinoki-test-api` | exercise operations with the generated valid and invalid bodies of `hinoki.ai.samples.request_cases` |

## `manage` {#manage}

```sh
uv run hinoki manage --help
uv run hinoki manage greet Peppe
```

Commands are declared on the app with `Hinoki(commands=[...])`. Each command subclasses `hinoki.management.Command`, gives itself a lower-case name, and adds arguments through `add_arguments(parser)`. In a scaffolded project, `hinoki manage` lists commands and `hinoki manage greet Peppe` runs one; the manifest's `project.application` supplies the app target. Outside a registered project, use `hinoki manage TARGET COMMAND`. `--help` after a command shows its arguments.

```python
# app.py, with `application = "app:app"` in hinoki.toml
from argparse import ArgumentParser, Namespace

from hinoki import Hinoki
from hinoki.management import Command, CommandContext


class Greet(Command):
    name = "greet"
    help = "print a greeting"

    def add_arguments(self, parser: ArgumentParser) -> None:
        parser.add_argument("name", nargs="?", default="world")

    def handle(self, _context: CommandContext, args: Namespace) -> None:
        print(f"Hello, {args.name}!")


app = Hinoki(commands=[Greet])
```

The Tracker example declares a real command, `Seed`, in
[`examples/tracker/tracker/commands.py`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/tracker/tracker/commands.py);
`uv run hinoki manage seed` creates a demo member from its directory, after
`uv run hinoki migrations apply`.

`handle(context, args)` may be synchronous or asynchronous. A sync handler runs on Hinoki's bounded executor. It can read `context.settings` and retrieve resources with `context.get(Type)` or `context.find(Type)`. Declare module classes in the command's `requires` tuple; Hinoki starts those modules and their dependencies for the command, then closes them before it exits. Other app modules are not started. A command with no requirements starts no app modules.

Commands run inside the project process and can modify data. Use disposable databases when developing or testing a command that writes. A handler returns `None` for success or an exit code from 0 through 255. Unknown commands and invalid arguments exit 2; a command failure exits nonzero. App settings load when Hinoki constructs the app, but module resources open only for the selected command.

## Errors and edge cases

- A mistyped command gets a suggestion (`did you mean 'check'?`) and exits 2.
- A target that does not import, or is neither an application nor a factory,
  stops the command with an `error:` line before anything runs.
- Commands that need `hinoki.toml` (`app`, `skills install`) exit 2 without one.
- Interactive prompts (`new`, `app create`) never appear without a terminal or
  with `--no-input`; Ctrl-C or Esc cancels with status 130 and writes nothing.

## See also

- [Create a project](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md)
- [Inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md)
- [Serve an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md)
- [Development MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md)

# Create a project

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md

`hinoki new` creates a working project: an application with a health route,
typed settings, architecture rules, a test and instructions for AI agents.
From the Hinoki checkout:

```sh
uv run hinoki new
```

## Answer the questions

In a terminal, `hinoki new` asks for everything the command line leaves out:

| Question | Answers | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project name | lower-case letters and digits, single underscores between words, starting with a letter | none |
| Parent directory | any path | `.` (here) |
| Database | `none`; `sqlite` (local file in `.hinoki/`); `postgresql` (also writes `.env.example`) | `none` |
| Server | `kiso` (Hinoki's own Rust server: native handler lane, access log); `granian` (general-purpose ASGI server: runs any ASGI app) | `kiso` |
| Agent instructions and MCP config? | yes / no | yes |
| Agent skills? | yes / no | no |
| Initialize a git repository? | yes / no | yes |
| Install dependencies (uv sync)? | yes / no | yes |
| Create an app now? | yes / no | yes |
| App name (only after yes) | the same rule as the project name; an invalid name is asked again | `core` |

Each answer collapses into a summary line. When the files are written, the
command lists the key ones, creates the app you named with the same code as
[`hinoki app create`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#app) (and registers it in `hinoki.toml`), runs
`git init` and `uv sync` with a timer, and ends with the next commands to type.
When no app was created, the summary says how to add one. Nothing is written
until the last answer, so Ctrl-C, Esc or end of input cancels cleanly (exit 130).

## Create a project without questions

Every question has a flag. `--no-input` never asks and uses the defaults for
what is missing, which suits scripts and CI (without a terminal no question is
asked either):

```sh
uv run hinoki new notes --no-input --database sqlite --git --install
```

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `NAME` | the package name; required with `--no-input` |
| `--dir PATH` | parent directory; the project is `PATH/NAME` |
| `--database none\|sqlite\|postgresql` | see [Choose a database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md#choose-a-database) |
| `--server kiso\|granian` | see [Choose a server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md#choose-a-server) |
| `--agent-files` / `--no-agent-files` | write `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.mcp.json` |
| `--skills` / `--no-skills` | also write the [agent skills](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#skills) under `.claude/skills` |
| `--git` / `--no-git` | run `git init`; no commit is made. Without a prompt: off |
| `--install` / `--no-install` | run `uv sync`. Without a prompt: off |
| `--app NAME` | also create this app and register it, without asking. The name is checked before anything is written |
| `--no-app` | create no app and do not ask about one; the two flags exclude each other |
| `--hinoki SOURCE` | where the project installs Hinoki from; see [below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md#where-hinoki-comes-from) |

## What you get

```text
notes/
├── hinoki.toml          project registry: application, routes, apps
├── hinoki-rules.toml    rule waivers (an example, commented out)
├── pyproject.toml       dependencies, pytest, Ruff
├── README.md
├── AGENTS.md            agent instructions (with CLAUDE.md and .mcp.json)
├── notes/
│   ├── main.py          the application
│   ├── api.py           the health endpoint
│   ├── routes.py        the routes hinoki.toml points to
│   ├── settings.py      typed settings (NOTES_ variables and .env)
│   └── rules.py         architecture rules
└── tests/
    └── healthtest.py    one test, no database needed
```

`hinoki.toml` names the application, so project commands find it on their own.
`notes/main.py` creates `Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, ...)` and automatically
loads `[project] routes` (`notes/routes.py`), where you mount exposed apps with
`Mount("/<name>", ...)`. The `rules` list in the same table is how the
application gets `notes/rules.py` (see [which rules run](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-rules-run)).

```toml
# hinoki.toml
[project]
application = "notes.main:app"
routes = "notes.routes:routes"
rules = ["notes.rules:project_rules"]
```

The project package holds no models and registers no app. Models live in apps:
The last question of `hinoki new` (or `--app billing`) creates the first one;
`uv run hinoki app create billing` adds more later. Either way it writes
`notes/apps/billing/` and adds the `[[apps]]` entry for it
([`hinoki app create`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#app)).

## Run it

```sh
cd notes
uv run pytest
uv run hinoki dev
```

Run `uv sync` first if you answered no to installing. The application answers
on <http://127.0.0.1:8000/health>, with its documentation at `/docs`.

## Choose a database

`sqlite` and `postgresql` add one field to `notes/settings.py`:

```python
class ProjectSettings(settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env"):
    database: settings.DatabaseSettings
```

Its value comes from `NOTES_DATABASE__<FIELD>` variables (two underscores
between the group and the field) in the environment or in `.env`; keep `.env`
out of git. With no value set it is the SQLite file
`.hinoki/local.sqlite3`. `postgresql` also writes `.env.example` with a
placeholder URL; copy it to `.env` and fill it in:

```sh
# .env.example
NOTES_DATABASE__URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/notes
```

`none` declares no field, and a request that queries a model fails with
`no database is active`. Add the field above when you add models. [Configure a
database](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/databases.md) lists the URL forms and the connection fields.

No database is created or contacted. Create the tables with
[`hinoki migrations apply`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md) once you have models.

## Choose a server

`kiso` needs no configuration. `granian` writes `settings.toml` with
`[server] server = "granian"`, which the settings class reads. Either way,
`NOTES_SERVER__SERVER` and `--server` on `dev` and `serve` override the choice.
[Serve an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md) compares the two.

## Where Hinoki comes from {#where-hinoki-comes-from}

This repository's pre-alpha Hinoki framework (package `hinoki-api`) is not published on PyPI yet; the [`hinoki` name](https://pypi.org/project/hinoki/) belongs to an unrelated legacy package. The generated `pyproject.toml` therefore names this repository as the source under `[tool.uv.sources]`:

| Given | Source written |
| --- | --- |
| `--hinoki /path/to/checkout` | that checkout, editable |
| `--hinoki https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki@REV` (or `git+https://...`) | that repository, pinned to `REV` when given |
| nothing, running from a source checkout | the checkout you ran it from |
| nothing, any other installation | the public repository, default branch |

Checkout paths and Git source values are escaped as TOML strings.

## How it looks in a terminal

On a colour, UTF-8 terminal (macOS and Linux) the prompts sit on a guide rail and answer to keys: type a name (backspace edits, Ctrl-U clears), move through the database and server lists with ↑/↓ or pick one by number, and switch yes/no with ←/→ or `y`/`n`; Enter confirms. Each answered prompt collapses into one summary line. The run then lists the key files it created, times `git init` and `uv sync` (with a spinner while they run) and ends with the next commands. Every colour terminal shows the same banner: a branch (`╭─`, `│`, `╰─`) titled `Hinoki` with the tagline and the version, then the Python version and the documentation and source addresses; `hinoki app create` shows the same banner. Elsewhere the prompts are numbered lists and `[Y/n]` questions answered with Enter.

Output that is piped, `NO_COLOR` and `TERM=dumb` give plain ASCII with no escape sequences. `HINOKI_ANIMATE=0` (or `CI`) turns off the tagline animation and the spinner. When the terminal reports a light background through `COLORFGBG`, darker shades of the same colours are used. Ctrl-C or Esc cancels before anything is written (exit status 130); so does the end of input.

## Errors and edge cases

- The name must be lower-case letters and digits, with single underscores between
  words (`my_shop`, `api_v1`), starting with a letter, and not
  `hinoki`, a Python keyword or a standard-library module such as `json`, which
  would shadow
  imports in the project. A refused name is asked again; with `--no-input` the
  command exits 2.
- An app name follows the same rule. A refused name is asked again; `--app` with a bad
  name exits 2 before anything is written. If the project is written but the
  app cannot be created, the error is printed, the project stays and the exit
  status is 2.
- `PATH/NAME` must not exist or must be empty; nothing is overwritten.
- `git` or `uv` missing or failing prints a warning and keeps the project.
- Nothing else is installed or run.

## See also

- [Installation](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/getting-started.md)
- [Quick start](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/quick-start.md)
- [Command line](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md)
- [Test an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md)

# Inspect an application

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md

These commands load the application, report and exit. None of them serves
requests, opens a database or writes files (except `openapi --output`):

```sh
uv run hinoki doctor
uv run hinoki routes
```

Each accepts `--format json` for scripts. On a colour terminal the reports use
`✔` ok, `▲` warning, `✘` failed and `–` skipped; piped output, `NO_COLOR` and
`TERM=dumb` give plain text.

## Diagnose a project with `doctor` {#doctor}

```sh
uv run hinoki doctor
uv run hinoki doctor --format json
```

With no target, `doctor` uses `project.application` from `hinoki.toml`. If there
is no manifest or default target, it reports environment checks and marks app
checks as skipped. An explicit `TARGET` names another app (`module:app`).
Loading it imports your Python code, so module-level code may have its
own side effects. Hinoki does not start app or module lifespans, run hooks,
start a server, run architecture rules, connect to a database, or write files.

The report covers manifest validity, Python/native extension and optional
Granian availability, route registration, configured typed settings, and
in-memory OpenAPI generation. An app with no settings object reports that
check as skipped; a custom non-`Settings` object is a warning. JSON output has
`schema_version: 1` and stable check IDs. Settings values are not included.
When the application cannot be loaded, the finding names the exception class;
for a Hinoki declaration error with no chained cause (for example a missing
admin secret) it also shows the message, on one line and truncated. Other
exception messages are not included. Exit status is `0` when no
diagnostic failed, `1` for invalid manifest or app diagnostics, and `2` when a
requested target cannot be loaded. Warnings and skipped checks remain visible.

Database connectivity and applied migration state are intentionally separate:
use [`hinoki migrations status`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md) for the live ledger and
[`hinoki migrations plan --check`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md#check-migration-drift) for
model-to-file drift.

## Check the rules with `check` {#check}

```sh
uv run hinoki check
uv run hinoki check --phase static
```

| Option | Effect | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--rules MODULE:ATTRIBUTE` | the `RuleSet` to run | the application's own rules: `Hinoki(rules=...)`, else the `[project] rules` of `hinoki.toml` ([which rules run](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-rules-run)) |
| `--package PACKAGE` | package for the static import checks; repeat for several | the package that contains the target |
| `--phase startup\|static` | run one phase | both |
| `--waivers PATH` | waiver file; must exist | the app's `waivers=`, else `hinoki-rules.toml` at the project root ([which file](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-waiver-file)) |
| `--format text\|json` | human or versioned JSON output | `text` |
| `--allow-effects` | also run checks declared effectful (files, network, database) | off |

Exit status is `0` when no rule fails, `1` for violations and `2` when the target
or the checks cannot run. An application with no rules passes with `0 rule(s)` and
a warning on standard error, since nothing was checked. What each rule checks, and
how to read and waive a result, is in [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md).

## List routes with `routes` {#routes}

```sh
uv run hinoki routes
```

From `examples/tracker`:

```text
GET     /activity                  MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.activity.api.Feed.list
GET     /activity/{item_id}        MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.activity.api.Feed.retrieve
GET     /health                    public                    tracker.routes.health
GET     /members/me                MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.members.api.me
GET     /tasks                     MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.list
POST    /tasks                     MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.create
DELETE  /tasks/{item_id}           MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.delete
GET     /tasks/{item_id}           MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.retrieve
POST    /tasks/{item_id}/complete  MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.complete
```

Each row is method, path, access (the provider and its permissions, or `public`)
and handler, sorted by path. The handler is the action's rule subject, the name
that `except_` and waivers match: an action of an `API` class is named after the
class it is mounted on, even when it inherits the method. `--path` keeps paths
that start with the prefix, `--method` one method; no match prints
`no routes match` and exits 1:

```sh
uv run hinoki routes --path /tasks --method GET
```

```text
GET     /tasks            MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.list
GET     /tasks/{item_id}  MemberTokens[tracker:use] tracker.apps.tasks.api.Tasks.retrieve
```

`--lanes` adds, per route, whether [Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#the-native-handler-lane) runs
the handler natively (`native`) or through the Python pipeline (`python`), with
the reason. The access log's `lane` field means something narrower: a request
for a `native` route here still logs `python` unless Rust runs a generated CRUD
plan for it. JSON always has `method`, `path`, `handler`, `access`, `status`,
`lane` and `lane_reason`.

## List event handlers with `events` {#events}

```sh
uv run hinoki events
uv run hinoki events notes.main:app --format json
```

Prints each registered [event handler](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/events.md#seeing-what-is-registered) in
execution order (event, phase, collection, `async` or `sync`, handler), the
`events` limits, and the `events` target each app declares in `hinoki.toml`.
`--format json` has `handlers`, `limits` and `apps`. It reads the application
and the manifest only; an unloadable target exits 2.

## Export the OpenAPI document with `openapi` {#openapi}

```sh
uv run hinoki openapi --output openapi.json
uv run hinoki openapi --check openapi.json
uv run hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json
```

The command builds the app without serving it or opening a database; it works even when `openapi_url` is disabled. With no file option it prints deterministic JSON (sorted keys, two-space indentation and a trailing newline). `--output FILE` writes those bytes. `--check FILE` compares parsed JSON, so formatting differences do not count as drift. Exit status is `0` when the file matches or is written, `1` when its JSON differs, and `2` when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or invalid JSON. `--output` and `--check` cannot be used together.

`--breaking-against BASELINE` compares the generated document with an earlier OpenAPI JSON file (the released version) and prints one `breaking: …` line per change that would break an existing client.

Reported: a removed operation or success response, new or newly required request input (a parameter that becomes required, a required request body where there was none), a removed response property or JSON body, a changed type (parameters included), a changed type, and a request enum that narrows or a response enum that widens. Additions are compatible and are not reported. Exit status is `0` when nothing breaks, `1` when something does, and `2` when the target cannot load or the baseline is missing or not a JSON object. It cannot be combined with `--output` or `--check`. The comparison reads the documents only; it does not check behavior that an OpenAPI document does not describe.

Run `--check` in CI to catch an OpenAPI document that drifted from the code, and
`--breaking-against` with the last released document before a release. See
[OpenAPI](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md) for what the document contains.

## Render llms.txt with `llms` {#llms}

```sh
uv run hinoki llms
uv run hinoki llms --output llms.txt
uv run hinoki llms --check llms.txt
```

Renders the application's OpenAPI document as an [llms.txt](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md#llms) Markdown text: a title, the version, then the operations grouped by first tag with their summary, deprecation, security scheme names and request and response components. Like `openapi`, it builds the app without serving it or opening a database and works when `openapi_url` is disabled; an action with `include_in_schema=False` is not listed. With no file option it prints the text; `--output FILE` writes the same text as UTF-8 with LF line endings on every platform, and `--check FILE` compares it exactly, except that a CRLF line ending in the file (a Windows checkout with `autocrlf`) counts as LF. Exit status is `0` when the file matches or is written, `1` when it differs, and `2` when the target cannot load or the check file is missing or unreadable, or the output cannot be written. `--output` and `--check` cannot be used together.

## Show settings with `settings` {#settings}

```sh
uv run hinoki settings
uv run hinoki settings --format json
uv run hinoki settings --example
```

The target is an application with typed settings or a settings class
(`notes.settings:ProjectSettings`). Each value is shown with where it came from;
`settings.Secret` values are redacted. `--prefix`, `--dotenv` and `--toml`
replace the sources the class declares. `--example` prints a `.env.example` with
defaults and types, leaving required fields blank and commenting out optional
values with no printable default (secrets, unset values). See
[Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#see-what-is-in-effect).

## Report versions with `version` {#version}

```sh
uv run hinoki version --verbose
```

The default prints `hinoki X.Y.Z`. `--verbose` adds the Python version, platform, native extension path and Granian version; Granian is reported as `not installed` when its optional package is absent. Use `--format json` for machine-readable output. Details the binding does not expose, including its bundled SQLite library version, are omitted rather than inferred.

## Errors and edge cases

- A target that does not import prints an `error:` line with the import failure
  (`error: cannot load TARGET: …` for `routes` and `openapi`) and exits
  non-zero (2 for `check`, `routes` and `openapi`).
- Importing the target runs your module-level code; keep import-time
  side effects out of it.
- `openapi` options `--output`, `--check` and `--breaking-against` exclude each
  other.
- `doctor` without `hinoki.toml` still checks the environment and marks the
  application checks skipped.

## See also

- [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md)
- [OpenAPI](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md)
- [Troubleshooting](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/troubleshooting.md)
- [Command line](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md)

# Interactive shell

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/shell.md
