`hinoki shell` opens Python with your application loaded and its database
connected, so you can try queries against real data:

```sh
uv run hinoki shell
```

```pycon
>>> await Note.filter(body="").acount()
3
>>> [note.title for note in await Note.all()]
['Ship it', 'Ship the docs', 'Ship the tests']
>>> settings.database.url
Secret('***')
```

## What is in the namespace

| Name | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `app` | the application from `hinoki.toml` (`[project] application`) |
| `settings` | its validated settings |
| model classes | every concrete model of every registered app, by class name (`Note`, …) |

Two models with the same class name in different apps stop the shell before the
prompt; select the modules you need with `--models`. A model may not be called
`app` or `settings`.

## Await at the prompt

The shell keeps one event loop for the session, so top-level `await` and
multiline statements work. Use the async ORM methods (`acount()`, `aget()`,
awaiting a query): the synchronous ones are meant for `def` handlers and cannot
block the shell's loop.

## Choose the application and models

```sh
uv run hinoki shell --models notes.apps.notes.models
uv run hinoki shell notes.main:app
```

In a project the target defaults to `project.application`, and every registered
app's models are loaded; repeat `--models` to load only some. Outside a project,
pass a target (`module:app`); `--models` is then optional.

## What starts and what does not

Each module the application installs, the database first, starts in dependency
order and closes when the session ends. The application's `on_startup` and
`on_shutdown` hooks do not run, so nothing sends mail or seeds data behind your
back, and migrations are never applied: run
[`hinoki migrations apply`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md) yourself.

Unmanaged asyncio tasks are cancelled on exit. Each task gets up to two waits of
`lifecycle.shutdown_timeout` (10 seconds by default); a task still running after
the second cancellation is abandoned. Startup is bounded too: if a module
suppresses cancellation while opening, the shell stops the loop and cannot
guarantee that the module released what it had opened.

!!! warning "Real data, your privileges"
    Code at the prompt runs with your user's privileges against the configured
    database and can change it. Point the settings at a development database.

## How it looks

On a colour terminal the shell opens with the Hinoki banner, which lists the
application title, the settings class, the loaded models and the Python version,
and a `hinoki ❯` prompt. `NO_COLOR`, `TERM=dumb` and `HINOKI_ANIMATE=0`
behave as for [`hinoki new`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/new-project.md#how-it-looks-in-a-terminal); without
colour the shell prints `Hinoki interactive shell; use Ctrl-D or Ctrl-C to exit.`
and Python's `>>>` / `...` prompts.

## Errors and edge cases

- Without a terminal the shell exits 2: "`hinoki shell` requires an interactive
  terminal".
- Ctrl-D exits, Ctrl-C at the prompt exits, Ctrl-C during a cell interrupts that
  cell. `exit()`, `quit()` or `raise SystemExit` in a cell also end the session
  and close the app modules; the shell exits 0 whatever code is passed.
- A model module that does not import stops the shell with
  `cannot load model module '…'`; a duplicate class name with
  `model name 'Note' occurs in both '…' and '…'`. Both exit 2.
- Outside a project without a target: `pass TARGET outside a project with
  hinoki.toml`.

## See also

- [Models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md)
- [Own resources with modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md)
- [Command line](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md)

# Typing

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/typing.md

Hinoki's public APIs use Python annotations so a type checker can catch mistakes in handlers, decorators and schema construction. The repository is checked with mypy in strict mode; other checkers and IDEs have not been evaluated systematically.

Run the project's check from its checkout:

```sh
uv run --locked mypy
```

In a project created by `hinoki new`, mypy is part of the `dev` dependency
group:

```sh
uv run mypy notes
```

## Typed surfaces

| Contract | Result |
| --- | --- |
| HTTP decorators | Preserve a handler's parameter and return types. `http.*` and `RouteGroup` methods share the same typed keyword options, so `atomic="yes"` or a misspelled keyword such as `stauts=201` is a type error. |
| `Schema` classes | Generated constructors check required, unknown and mistyped fields; `Field(default_factory=...)` preserves the value type. `@derive(...)` synthesizes fields at runtime, so declare explicit fields when you need static attribute checking on a public schema. |
| Application and route groups | `Hinoki.include`, `API` classes and `RouteGroup` provide typed declarations. Unknown include items fail at app construction. |
| Authentication context | Annotate a parameter as `Caller[User]` to receive the typed caller and application user. |
| Decorator composition | User decorators should preserve signatures with `functools.wraps`, `ParamSpec` and `TypeVar`. For standalone handlers the final decorated function is dispatched. With `RouteGroup`, put the HTTP decorator outermost so it captures the final sync or async wrapped handler. |

Hinoki separates three checks: a preserved handler signature for the type checker, statically known fields on explicitly annotated `Schema` classes, and registration-time validation of the route contract when `Hinoki` builds its routes.

## ORM method signatures

Model construction and common instance operations are typed. Some ORM methods that accept arbitrary model field names still have broad keyword signatures, so a checker may not catch a misspelled field passed to these methods:

```python
task = Task(title="Write docs")  # constructor fields and values are checked
await task.asave()
```

Fields inherited from an abstract model are part of the checked constructor. Fields that come from a plain (non-model) mixin exist at run time but are not constructor arguments for a type checker; use an abstract model when you need them checked.

`Model.acreate(**values)` and some filter/update keyword calls cannot currently verify each field name against the model class. Use the constructor plus `asave()` when you want field-level checking on insertion. This limitation does not affect runtime validation of model fields or database constraints.

The return types of the write methods are checked: `aupdate` returns the model, `aupdate_where` and `QuerySet.aupdate` a list of it, and with a literal `returning=False` each returns `int` ([writes that do not read the row back](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md#writes-that-do-not-read-the-row-back)). A `returning` value that is a plain `bool` gives the union of both. `acreate` and `insert` return the model either way. Unpacking a dictionary into `aupdate(**values)` or `update(**values)` gives `Any`, because the dictionary could hold `returning`; pass `returning=True` explicitly to keep the model type.

The Python package includes typing metadata, and the compiled `hinoki.core` module has a matching stub. See the [API reference](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/reference/index.md) for the public signatures.

# Add an admin

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md

`hinoki.admin` gives staff a list, search, create, edit, bulk actions and a dashboard for your models, behind its own sign-in page, users and per-model permissions. It ships in `hinoki-api` (no extra to install); nothing is served until you mount it with `Mount("/admin", site)`, its migrations are applied explicitly, and importing it never touches a database.

```python
# blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py
from hinoki.admin import Admin, ModelAdmin, Tone

from .models import Post, User

site = Admin(site="Blog Studio")


@site.admin(Post)
class PostAdmin(ModelAdmin[Post]):
    columns = ("title", "published", "author_id", "created_at")
    readonly = ("created_at",)
    badges = {"published": {True: ("Published", Tone.OK), False: ("Draft", Tone.WARN)}}


site.register(User)  # a model with the default admin
```

```python
# blog/routes.py
from hinoki import Includable, Mount

from .apps.blog.adminsite import site

routes: list[Includable] = [Mount("/admin", site)]
```

The [Blog example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py) builds a fuller site the same way, with a theme, links, a dashboard and activity; its [`routes.py`](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/routes.py) mounts it beside the API and its `hinoki.toml` registers the admin's tables as the `admin` app.

## Create the admin's tables

The admin keeps its users in five tables of your database (four active plus the legacy login-window table). Register them as an app, apply the migrations, then create the first user:

```sh
hinoki app add admin --models hinoki.admin.users.models --migrations hinoki.admin.users.migrations
hinoki migrations apply admin
hinoki admin create-superuser alice    # asks for the password twice
```

| Table | Migration | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hinoki_admin_users` | `0001-initial` | Username, Argon2id password hash, active and superuser flags, last sign-in |
| `hinoki_admin_sessions` | `0001-initial` | The SHA-256 of each session token, its user, expiry and last request |
| `hinoki_admin_grants` | `0001-initial` | One row per user, model and action |
| `hinoki_admin_login_windows` | `0002-login-windows` | Fixed-window counters of earlier versions; no policy reads it any more and it can stay empty |
| `hinoki_admin_rate_limits` | `0003-rate-limits` | Buckets of `DatabaseLoginWindow`: a digest of the client and the route, and a counter state |

Every other user is created from the admin's Users section. `hinoki admin set-password alice` resets a password from a shell; both commands are described in [`hinoki admin`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#admin).

## Set the signing secret

The admin signs its forms and cookies with `admin.secret` from the app's settings. Give it at least 32 random bytes through the environment:

```sh
export BLOG_ADMIN__SECRET="$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(48))')"
```

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `admin.secret` | none | Signing key, at least 32 bytes |
| `admin.session_hours` | `12` | A session ends this long after sign-in |
| `admin.idle_minutes` | `120` | A session ends after this long without a request |
| `admin.min_password_length` | `12` | Shortest password accepted |
| `admin.theme` | none | Built-in theme (`studio`, `console`, `paper`, `bento`) for an `Admin` that sets no `theme=`; `studio` when neither is set |

`Admin(secret=...)` overrides the secret and `Admin(theme=...)` the theme for one site. An admin with neither stops the app at startup. So does an admin served with `allowed_hosts` at its default `*` and `debug` off: the CSRF check trusts the `Host` header it compares the `Origin` with, so name the served hosts; `debug` only lifts the refusal for local development, and then the whole app accepts loopback `Host` names only (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `[::1]`; any other `Host` receives `400`) unless `allowed_hosts` names the hosts (see [Hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md#allowed_hosts)). The in-process test clients are not affected.

## Who may sign in

`Admin()` without `access=` uses its own users:

* A **superuser** holds every permission.
* Other users hold **grants** per model and action: `view`, `add`, `change`, `delete`. A bulk action needs `change`.
* A model without a grant is missing from the sidebar, and its pages answer `404`.
* Grants wrap each model admin's `can`: an override can narrow what a grant allows, never widen it.
* An inactive user cannot sign in.

To use your own identity instead (single sign-on, an existing user table), pass an access policy: `Admin(access=Access(auth=..., permissions=[...]))`. The admin then has no sign-in pages and no tables, and your callers' permissions decide what `ModelAdmin.can` allows. See [authentication and access](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md).

## The sign-in page

`login` shows a centred card with the site name, the title **Sign in**, a username field, a password field and a full-width button, in the active theme's colours and in its light or dark mode. Every page of the admin redirects there (`303`) when the browser has no valid session.

| Request | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `POST login`, correct credentials | `303` to the admin root with a new session cookie; any previous session token is closed, never reused |
| `POST login`, wrong username or password | `401` "Wrong username or password." |
| `POST login`, expired or forged form | `403` "The form expired or is invalid. Reload and try again." |
| `POST login`, too many attempts | `429` (see [limit sign-in attempts](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md#limit-sign-in-attempts)) |
| `GET login` while signed in | `303` to the admin root |
| `POST logout` | `303` to `login`; the session ends and its cookie is cleared |

Usernames are stored in lower case: 1 to 150 letters, digits and `. _ @ + -`, starting with a letter or digit. An unknown username costs the same hashing work as a wrong password and gets the same answer.

`password` changes the signed-in user's password. The form asks for the current password, a new one (at least `admin.min_password_length` characters) and the new one again. A wrong current password, two different new ones or a password that breaks the length rule answer `422` with the reason on the form; an expired form answers `403`. Success ends every other session of the user and redirects (`303`) to the admin root (`?done=password`) with a new session.

### The logo

The sidebar and the sign-in card show a bookmark icon by default. `logo=` replaces it with another built-in icon or with an image you serve yourself:

```python
Admin(site="Blog Studio", logo="layers")  # a built-in icon
Admin(site="Blog Studio", logo="/static/logo.svg")  # an image from your app
```

An image path must start with a single `/`: the admin's content security policy only allows same-origin images, so an `https://` URL or `//host/...` is refused with a `ValueError` when the `Admin` is built, as is an unknown icon name. The built-in icons are the `i-*` symbols of the admin sprite (`bookmark`, `layers`, `folder`, `users`, `tag`, `image`, ...).

### Sessions and cookies

* The session is a random token in the `hinoki_admin_session` cookie: `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, scoped to the admin's path. The database stores only its SHA-256, so a copy of the table cannot be replayed.
* Every form carries a signed CSRF token that must equal the `SameSite=Strict` `hinoki_csrf` cookie. On the sign-in form the token is signed for signing in; on every other form it is bound to the signed-in user. A form is also refused when the browser marks it as sent from another site (`Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` or `same-site`) or its `Origin` header names another host; a request without these headers relies on the token alone.
* Cookies are `Secure` on HTTPS. Behind a TLS-terminating proxy, set `server.trusted_proxies` so the forwarded scheme is believed, or pass `Admin(secure_cookies=True)`: cookies are then always `Secure` and named `__Secure-hinoki_admin_session` and `__Secure-hinoki_csrf`, so a sibling site cannot plant them. Changing the option signs everyone out once.
* A session ends after `admin.session_hours`, after `admin.idle_minutes` without a request, on sign-out, on a password change and when its user is deactivated. Reactivating a user never revives an old session.

## Manage users

A superuser sees a **Users** section in the sidebar: create a user, choose the models and actions it may use, rename, deactivate, change a password or delete.

* Only a superuser opens it. No grant does, because a user who could edit users could grant itself everything.
* The permission checkboxes list `view`, `add`, `change` and `delete` for each registered model.
* An empty password on edit keeps the current one. A new one signs the user out everywhere. Passwords are never written back into the page.
* You cannot deactivate yourself, remove your own superuser status or delete yourself. Every write checks that an active superuser remains; `hinoki admin create-superuser` recovers if two superusers demote each other at the same instant.
* Deleting a user removes its sessions and grants.

`Admin(users=AdminAccounts(), manage_users=False)` leaves the section out, for a site whose users are created another way. `AdminAccounts.set_active(user, False)` deactivates a user from code and ends its sessions.

## Limit sign-in attempts

The sign-in and password forms pass through a rate limit policy before any password is hashed, and hold no database connection while hashing.

| Policy | Counts in | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LoginWindow(limit=10, window=60)` (default) | One worker's memory | Each worker counts on its own and forgets on restart: a brake, not a shared limit. Holds at most 10,000 clients and drops the oldest. |
| `DatabaseLoginWindow(limit=10, window=60)` | `hinoki_admin_rate_limits` | One limit for every worker and host, the [`RateLimit`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#rate-limit-an-action) algorithm: a burst of `limit`, then one attempt every `window / limit` seconds, and a refused attempt costs nothing. Clients are stored as digests. |

```python
# blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py
from hinoki.admin import Admin
from hinoki.admin.users import AdminAccounts
from hinoki.admin.users.limits import DatabaseLoginWindow

site = Admin(users=AdminAccounts(login_limit=DatabaseLoginWindow()))
```

Both count per client address and route (a flood on the sign-in never spends the password change's attempts). `DatabaseLoginWindow` is a `RateLimit` subclass, so it keeps its table within a bound, deletes expired rows while counting, and, while the table is full of live ones, counts every new address in one shared window per route, ten times as large. Separately, each user name is delayed after repeated wrong passwords, from any address: past five failures the delay doubles up to five minutes, before any hashing, in the memory of one worker. Unknown names are counted the same.

An IPv6 address counts by its /64. Requests without a known address share one window ten times as large, so set `server.trusted_proxies` behind a proxy. With `DatabaseLoginWindow`, keep host clocks in sync: each host stamps the windows it opens. Any other policy works too; see [rate limit an action](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#rate-limit-an-action).

## Serve it under another path

The `Mount` prefix decides where the admin lives; links, assets and the cookie path follow it. `Mount("/ops", site)` serves it at `/ops`. `Admin(prefix="/staff")` adds a path of its own after the mount (`/ops/staff`). An admin included without a `Mount` is served at `/admin`; `Admin(prefix="")` serves it at the root of its mount.

## Errors and edge cases

| When | What fails |
| --- | --- |
| Startup, no `admin.secret` and no `secret=` | `RegistrationError`: "admin: no secret to sign its forms with; set `admin.secret` …" |
| `Admin(access=..., users=...)` | `ValueError`: pass one or the other |
| `register` of `AdminUser`, `AdminSession` or `AdminGrant` | `RegistrationError`: a plain model admin would show password hashes and let a grant holder promote itself |
| `register` with a slug that is taken or reserved (`static`, `search`, `login`, `logout`, `password`) | `RegistrationError` |
| `DatabaseLoginWindow` before `0003-rate-limits` is applied | Sign-in fails with `503 rate_limit_unavailable` on the missing table; apply the migration first |
| One address racing many sign-ins at the same instant | `429` rather than an uncounted attempt |
| A form posting a many-to-many key that is unknown, outside the user's view or too long | The form is shown again with one generic message and nothing is saved ([details](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin-customize.md#many-to-many-fields)) |

## See also

* [Customize the admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin-customize.md)
* [`hinoki admin` commands](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#admin)
* [Authentication and access](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md)
* [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md)

# Customize the admin

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin-customize.md

A `ModelAdmin` states only what the model does not already say. Class attributes shape the list and the form; methods change behaviour; templates and themes change the look.

```python
# blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py
from typing import Any

from hinoki import Caller
from hinoki.admin import Admin, ModelAdmin, Tone, action

from .models import Post

site = Admin(site="Blog Studio", per_page=8)


@site.admin(Post)
class PostAdmin(ModelAdmin[Post]):
    columns = ("title", "published", "author_id", "created_at")
    search = ("title", "slug")
    readonly = ("created_at",)
    badges = {"published": {True: ("Published", Tone.OK), False: ("Draft", Tone.WARN)}}
    tabs = ("published",)  # one tab per badge: Published | Draft
    fieldsets = {"Organization": ("author_id", "published")}

    @action(confirm="Publish the selected posts?")
    async def publish(self, posts: tuple[Post, ...], principal: Caller[Any]) -> None:
        await Post.filter(id__in=[p.id for p in posts]).aupdate({"published": True})
```

## Register a model

`@site.admin(Post)` registers a `ModelAdmin` class for a model. `site.register(...)` takes a model class, which gets the default admin, or a `ModelAdmin` class that names its model with `model=`. The slug in the URL is the table name with dashes (`blog-posts`), or the class attribute `slug = "posts"`.

## Shape the list and the form

| Attribute | Effect | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `columns` | Columns of the list | The model's fields |
| `search` | Columns the search box looks in | The first three text columns the list shows |
| `readonly`, `exclude` | Shown but not editable; never shown | `()` |
| `badges` | Value → `Badge(label, tone, icon)` or `(label, tone[, icon])` | Plain text |
| `tabs` | One tab per badge of the named column | None |
| `fieldsets` | `Fieldset`s, or a dict of title → field names | One group |
| `per_page`, `show_count` | Page size; row count in the sidebar | The site's `Admin(per_page=20, show_count=False)` |
| `bulk_delete` | Offer bulk delete where `can(principal, "delete")` allows | `True` |
| `allow_hard_delete` | Offer physical deletion in the Deleted view | `False` |

`Tone` (`NEUTRAL`, `ACCENT`, `OK`, `WARN`, `DANGER`, `INFO`) is the color role of badges, stats and events. Without configuration the label and plural come from the model, the order from `@db.ordered_by` and the "last modified" line from its `@db.timestamps()` column.

Search matches a row when any `search` column contains the typed text, compared case-insensitively as text (a number or date matches its printed form). Naming an `exclude`d column in `search` is refused at registration, because which rows match would reveal its value.

Form inputs follow the column type: text, number, checkbox, UUID, datetime, `date`, `time` (without a UTC offset), `Decimal` (finite values only) and `Enum` (a select of member names). Another type is shown read-only. A time or decimal that is retyped but means the stored value (`09:30` for `09:30:00`, `12.5` for `12.50`) is not saved again.

Datetime fields use the app's `settings.timezone` (UTC without built-in settings): stored instants are shown there and edited `datetime-local` values are read there, then saved as UTC-aware datetimes. A time that does not exist or occurs twice during a daylight-saving change is refused for correction.

### Soft-deleted models

For a model using `@db.soft_delete()` or `SoftDeleteModel`, the admin's Active
list and default `queryset(principal)` contain live rows. When `tabs` is unset,
the list shows Active and Deleted views; `?deleted=1` selects the latter. With custom `tabs` the Deleted view is a last tab after them. The
default `deleted_queryset(principal)` is `self.model.only_deleted()`. Override
it to add tenant or ownership filters; the admin always narrows it to rows with
a delete timestamp, and uses that same scope for restore and hard-delete.

The `deleted_at` and every tracked `changed_at` column are automatically
readonly unless excluded. Deleting a row uses soft deletion. Deleted rows
cannot be edited or deleted through the regular row form before restoration.
The Deleted view offers restore to users allowed to `change` each row. Physical
purging is hidden and refused unless the model admin opts in with
`allow_hard_delete = True`; each selected row must also pass `can(principal,
"delete", row)`.

## Override behaviour

Each method below is called by the framework; override what you need and call `super()` for the rest.

```python
# blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py
from typing import Any

from hinoki import Caller
from hinoki.admin import Avatar, ModelAdmin, Refusal
from hinoki.orm import QuerySet

from .models import Post


@site.admin(Post)  # the site created above
class PostAdmin(ModelAdmin[Post]):
    def queryset(
        self, principal: Caller[Any]
    ) -> QuerySet[Post]:  # rows this caller sees, in every statement
        return Post.filter(author_id=principal.user.id).select_related("author")

    def can(
        self, principal: Caller[Any], action: str, row: Post | None = None
    ) -> bool:  # narrows a grant, never widens it
        if action == "delete" and row is not None and row.published:
            return False
        return super().can(principal, action, row)

    def display(
        self, row: Post, column: str
    ) -> Any:  # a list cell: text, a Badge or an Avatar
        if column == "author_id":
            return Avatar(row.author.name)
        return super().display(row, column)

    async def check(
        self, values: dict[str, Any], principal: Caller[Any], row: Post | None
    ) -> dict[str, str]:  # {field: message} refuses
        if values.get("published") and not (values.get("title") or (row and row.title)):
            return {"title": "A published post needs a title."}
        return {}

    async def remove(self, row: Post, principal: Caller[Any]) -> None:
        if row.published:
            raise Refusal("Unpublish the post first.")  # shown on the page
        await super().remove(row, principal)
```

* `queryset(principal)` decides which rows a caller sees; counts and pages come from it. `can(principal, "view", row)` then trims the fetched page, so a page may hold fewer rows than `per_page`.
* `save(values, principal, row=None)` and `remove(row, principal)` are the only places that write; run a domain operation there instead of a raw write. `Refusal` raised in either rolls the write back and shows its message.
* `stats(principal)` returns the dashboard `Stat`s for the model.
* Mass assignment, excluded columns and out-of-scope rows are refused by the framework.

## Add fields that are not columns

`extra_fields` (or an `extras()` method, when the choices depend on what is registered) adds form fields that are not columns:

* `Extra("password", "Password", "password")`: a masked input, never filled in again.
* `Extra("tags", "Tags", "choices", choices=(("a", "A"), ("b", "B")))`: checkboxes; the value is a `frozenset` of the checked ones.

They reach `check` and `save` next to the columns, so `save` takes them out before writing the row; `extra_initial(row)` returns what the edit form shows. The Users section is built this way (`hinoki.admin.users.useradmin`).

### Many-to-many fields

A model's [`many_to_many`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md#many-to-many) field appears in its add and edit forms as a multi-select named after its ids field (`<field>_ids`, or its `ids_name`) when the target model is registered with the same admin and the signed-in user may view it. The options are what that target's admin lists for the user (its `queryset`), at most 200, with the linked rows first. Saving replaces only the links to rows the user can see; links to rows outside that scope are kept. A key that is unknown, hidden from the user or longer than 200 characters is refused with one message (`Some choices are not available.`) and nothing is saved, so a hidden row cannot be told from a missing one. More than the field's `max_items` selections is refused the same way.

When the options are truncated the form says so; narrow them with `?link_q_<ids_name>=text` on the form URL (the text is cut at 100 characters and matched against the target admin's `search` columns, or its primary key). A target that is not registered or not viewable leaves the field read-only: the form shows no count and ignores any posted value. A name in `readonly` shows the links without changing them. The row and its links are written in the request's transaction, so a refused link rolls the row back too.

## Add a bulk action

Mark an async method with `@action`. The list shows the button once rows are selected:

```python
# blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py
from typing import Any

from hinoki import Caller
from hinoki.admin import ModelAdmin, action

from .models import Post


@site.admin(Post)
class PostAdmin(ModelAdmin[Post]):
    @action(confirm="Publish the selected posts?")
    async def publish(self, posts: tuple[Post, ...], principal: Caller[Any]) -> None:
        ids = [post.id for post in posts]
        await Post.filter(id__in=ids).aupdate({"published": True})
```

* The action name is the method name with `_` written as `-`; the label defaults to "Publish selected". `view`, `add`, `change` and `delete` are reserved.
* The name is also the permission checked by `can(principal, name, row)`. Every selected row is checked against the queryset and `can` before confirmation and again before execution; one denied row refuses the whole action.
* The action runs in the admin's write transaction with the selected rows locked, on at most 200 distinct rows (more answer `400`). A failure rolls everything back; success redirects to the list with a notice.
* Handlers still apply their own domain conditions to writes that involve related records or external state.

## Replace the HTML or the stylesheet

`Admin(templates="admin_ui")` reads `admin_ui/components/NAME.html` before the built-in component of the same name (`shell`, `sidebar`, `table`, `form`, `field`, `auth` for the sign-in page, ...) and appends `admin_ui/admin.css` after the theme. Copy the built-in component from the package as a starting point; keep its `{{ value }}` (escaped) and `{{{ raw }}}` placeholders.

```css
/* admin_ui/admin.css */
.hn-auth-card { border-radius: 0; }
.hn-nav-item[aria-current="page"] { font-weight: 800; }
```

## Choose or build a theme

Four built-in styles, each with light and dark modes; the system preference picks the initial mode and the toggle overrides it. Pick one with `Admin(theme="bento")`.

| Style | Navigation | List | Edit | Look |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Studio** (default) | Sidebar | Cards with a table | Drawer beside the list | Soft violet, rounded |
| **Console** | Top bar | Dense monospaced grid | Drawer | Neon cyan and teal, square |
| **Paper** | Quiet text index, centred column | Document rows | Own page | Serif type, terracotta |
| **Bento** | Icon rail (bottom tab bar on phones) | Grid of cards | Own page | Ink outlines, offset shadows, yellow accent |

=== "Studio"

    ![Studio, light](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-studio-list-light.png)
    ![Studio, dark](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-studio-list-dark.png)

=== "Console"

    ![Console, light](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-console-list-light.png)
    ![Console, dark](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-console-list-dark.png)

=== "Paper"

    ![Paper, light](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-paper-list-light.png)
    ![Paper, dark](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-paper-list-dark.png)

=== "Bento"

    ![Bento, light](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-bento-list-light.png)
    ![Bento, dark](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-bento-list-dark.png)
    ![Bento edit form in dark mode](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-bento-edit-dark.png)
    ![Bento on a phone: the rail becomes a bottom tab bar](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/screenshots/admin-bento-phone-light.png)

A `Theme` is a set of `--hn-*` design tokens for both schemes, plus `edit` (`"drawer"`, `"page"`), `layout` (`"sidebar"`, `"topbar"`, `"index"`, `"rail"`) and `list_style` (`"table"`, `"rows"`, `"cards"`). Start from a built-in one:

```python
# blog/apps/blog/adminsite.py
import dataclasses

from hinoki.admin import THEMES, Admin

studio = THEMES["studio"]
forest = dataclasses.replace(
    studio,
    name="forest",
    label="Forest",
    light={**studio.light, "accent": "#1f6f50", "accent-hover": "#17543c"},
    dark={**studio.dark, "accent": "#5cc79b", "accent-hover": "#7ad6b0"},
    layout="topbar",
    extra_css=".hn-brand-text strong { letter-spacing: .04em; }",
)
site = Admin(theme=forest)
```

`extra_css` is appended after the tokens; `default_mode="dark"` starts dark until the user switches. The text and surface colour pairs of the built-in themes are tested against WCAG AA contrast. Bento was checked in Chromium and Firefox at 1440, 390, 360 and 320 px; WebKit was not run.

## Errors and edge cases

All of these fail when the `Admin` is created or the model registered, not on a request:

| Mistake | Error |
| --- | --- |
| A `ModelAdmin` naming a different model than the one registered | `RegistrationError` |
| `search` naming an `exclude`d column | `RegistrationError` |
| A bulk action named `view`, `add`, `change` or `delete` | `RegistrationError` |
| A template file that is not a component, an unknown placeholder, `{{ }}` changed to `{{{ }}}`, or a `form`, `table`, `confirm` or `auth` override without `{{ csrf }}` | `TemplateError` |
| A theme with a missing token, unknown layout or bad name | `ValueError` from the `Theme`, before any page is served |

## See also

* [Add an admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md)
* [Define models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/models.md)
* [Admin API reference](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/reference/admin.md)

# Expose actions over MCP

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/app-mcp.md

`expose_as_mcp` publishes selected HTTP actions as tools for a remote MCP client. Each tool call is dispatched through the app like an HTTP request, so the action's authentication, access policy, validation and transaction still apply.

```python
# notes/main.py
from hinoki import Hinoki
from hinoki.ai.mcpapp import expose_as_mcp

from notes.security import billing_staff
from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

app = Hinoki(
    settings=ProjectSettings,
    title="Notes",
    openapi_url="/openapi.json",
    docs_url="/docs",
)  # routes and rules come from hinoki.toml
mcp = expose_as_mcp(
    app,
    tools=["notes.apps.billing.api.list_invoices"],
    access=billing_staff,
)
app.include(*mcp)  # POST /mcp
```

`Hinoki(...)` has already included the routes listed in `hinoki.toml`; `expose_as_mcp` selects among those, so call it after the app exists. It raises `ExposureError` right away when the patterns select no allowed action (for example only writes with `allow_writes=False`), a streaming action or one left out of the OpenAPI document. The [Blog example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/main.py) does the same for one read-only action of an `API` class (`blog.apps.blog.api.Posts.drafts`, with the `editor` policy).

## Choose the tools

`tools` are `fnmatch` patterns over qualified action names, the same names rules match: `module.function`, or `module.Class.method` for an action of an `API` class. `"notes.apps.billing.api.*"` selects every action of that module. Generated CRUD actions are named after the module that declares the `crud(...)` value (`notes.apps.billing.routes.InvoiceCrud.list`, see [Generated CRUD](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md)), so a module pattern selects them too.

* Only `GET`, `HEAD` and `QUERY` actions are exposed by default. A `QUERY` tool takes the request body as its input.
* `allow_writes=True` also exposes `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` actions. Use it only when write tools are intended and `access` permits them.
* The tool name, description, path and query parameters and JSON body shape come from the action's OpenAPI operation. Unknown arguments are rejected and path values are encoded as path segments.
* The MCP route never exposes itself.

## Protect the endpoint

`access` is required. An intentionally public endpoint says so twice: `access=None, public=True`.

* Prefer bearer credentials for a remote client; cookie authentication with write tools needs particular care.
* The endpoint accepts JSON `POST` requests. Set `allowed_origins` to the exact browser origins when browser clients are expected; other cross-site browser requests are refused.
* Tool output is capped at 100,000 bytes (longer text is cut and marked `truncated`); a request message over 1,000,000 bytes answers `413`.

## Errors and edge cases

| When | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| `tools=[]` | `ExposureError` at the call |
| `access=None` without `public=True` | `ExposureError` |
| A pattern matches no included action, or the action is not in the OpenAPI document | `ExposureError` naming it |
| An action that returns `Stream`, `EventStream` or `File` matches `tools` | `ExposureError` naming it: a tool returns one complete result, so a [streamed response](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md) cannot be exposed |
| `Transactions.require_atomic()` is enabled | The MCP endpoint is a `POST` without a transaction of its own; exclude it with `except_=["hinoki.ai.mcpapp.*"]`. Each tool call still runs the action's own transaction. |

The endpoint does not provide MCP resources, prompts, sessions or OAuth discovery.

## See also

* [Development MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md): a local server that describes the project to coding agents
* [Authentication and access](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md)
* [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md)

# Development MCP

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md

`hinoki mcp` starts an MCP server on stdio that describes your app, its rules and its models to a coding agent. It never writes source code, rules or waivers. The one exception to reading only is `run_scenario`, which you enable with `--scenarios`: it runs real handlers and can change data ([below](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md#run-requests-against-the-app)).

```sh
hinoki mcp
```

The application defaults to `project.application` in `hinoki.toml`, the rules to the app's own rules (`Hinoki(rules=...)`, else the `[project] rules` of `hinoki.toml`) and the package to the application's package; pass `--models` to describe models. Projects made by `hinoki new` contain a `.mcp.json` that starts this server for the agent. Protocol messages go to stdout as newline-delimited JSON-RPC; diagnostics go to stderr.

## Options

| Option | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TARGET` | the project application | Another app, as `module:app` |
| `--models MODULE` | none | Model modules to describe; repeatable |
| `--rules MODULE:NAME` | the app's rules | Another `RuleSet` |
| `--package NAME` | the target's package | Packages the rules inspect; repeatable |
| `--waivers PATH` | as for `hinoki check` ([which file](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#which-waiver-file)) | The owner's waiver file, read only; must exist. `run_scenario` starts the app with it too |
| `--requests PATH` | `.hinoki/requests.jsonl` | Where `recent_requests` reads |
| `--scenarios off\|read\|write` | `off` | Registers `run_scenario` (see below) |

## Tools

Each result is JSON in `structuredContent` and in a text block, with a `tool_version`. A failed call sets `isError` and carries an `error` message.

| Tool | Input | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `inspect_project` | `{}` | App title and version; each action's `id`, `method`, `path`, `status`, `access`, `atomic`, `pagination`, `parsers`, `renderers` and `location`; model metadata (with `--models`, including a `many_to_many` entry per relation: `to`, `bridge`, `ids_name`, `max_items`); the enabled rule count |
| `list_rules` | `{}` | Enabled rules and the waivers with their file, target, reason, owner and expiry |
| `explain_action` | `{"action": "module.function"}` | Signature, docstring, access and `atomic`, the OpenAPI operation and the action's diagnostics. A class method or a unique bare handler name also works |
| `explain_error` | `{"code": "validation_error"}` | Meaning and fix of a framework error code, HTTP error code or rule ID |
| `check_project` | `{}` or `{"phase": "static"}` | Rule diagnostics with waivers applied, plus `ok` and `failing`; `phase` is `startup` or `static`. Effectful checks are not run |
| `propose_model` | `{"name": "Article", "fields": [...]}`; optional `table`, `owner`, `path`, `unique_together` | Source text for a model, its input, patch and output `Schema` classes and CRUD actions. Returned, never written. Field types: `str`, `int`, `float`, `bool`, `uuid`, `datetime`, with `nullable`, `unique`, `max_length` |
| `recent_requests` | `{}` or `{"limit": 20, "status_min": 400, "path_contains": "/invoices"}` | The newest requests the development server answered (`method`, `path`, `query`, `status`, `duration_ms`, `lane`), oldest first; `limit` is 1 to 200 |

`recent_requests` reads the file Kiso writes when `server.recent_requests` is set; it keeps about the last 1 to 2 MiB, and without it the result is empty with a note. The `query` field is the raw query string and is not redacted: keep tokens out of query strings and treat the file as sensitive.

## Run requests against the app

`--scenarios read` or `--scenarios write` adds `run_scenario`. Its input needs `path` (a plain URL path starting with `/`); `method` (default `GET`), `query` (without `?`), string `headers` and `json` are optional. The result holds the HTTP `status`, response `headers`, the body text (at most 20,000 bytes, with `truncated`) and the parsed JSON when there is some.

| Mode | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `QUERY` |
| `write` | Also `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` |

!!! warning "Scenarios run your real handlers"
    The app's lifespan and handlers run in-process, so even `read` can change data (a `GET` handler may write). Each request has a 15-second limit. Enable scenarios only yourself, never on an agent's request, and only against a disposable database.

## Errors and edge cases

* A failed app startup is reported to the client without its message, which may contain a connection string; the details go to stderr.
* Rule checks with side effects are never run by this server; use `hinoki check --allow-effects`.
* The server was exercised with the official `mcp` Python client (initialize, `tools/list`, `tools/call`); other clients are untested.

## See also

* [Build with a coding agent](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ai-workflow.md)
