# Build with a coding agent

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ai-workflow.md

A project made by `hinoki new` is ready for a coding agent: rules already on, an `AGENTS.md` with the conventions, and an MCP server that describes the app. This page shows the loop and where the agent's authority ends.

```sh
hinoki new shop    # asks for the directory, database, server, agent files, skills, git and uv sync
cd shop
uv sync            # unless you answered yes to uv sync
uv run pytest
uv run hinoki check
```

The generated tests pass and `hinoki check` exits 0; this repository's own test suite generates a project and runs both on every change.

## Hinoki at a glance

A model that has seen other Python web frameworks tends to write their code. This summary is the part of these docs that corrects that; it is also the first block of [`llms.txt`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ai-workflow.md#docs-for-agents).

* Import from `hinoki`: `Hinoki`, `Schema`, `Access`, `RouteGroup`, `http`, `db` and `crud`. A model class comes from `hinoki.orm` (`from hinoki.orm import Model, field, pk`).
* Declare actions with `@http.get`, `@http.post`, `@http.put`, `@http.patch`, `@http.delete` or `@http.query`, then pass them to `Hinoki(include=[...])`. Parameters and the return type are annotations.
* Name an `Access` policy with `access=`; leave it out only for an action that is public on purpose. Writes use `atomic=True`, alone or on a `RouteGroup`.
* Request bodies and responses are `Schema` classes. Never return a `Model`: convert it with `XOut.from_model(row)`.
* Load relations explicitly with `select_related(...)` or `prefetch_related(...)`; nothing loads lazily.
* `crud(Model, ...)` generates list, retrieve and write actions for a model.
* Run `hinoki check` after each change; `hinoki mcp` serves the real registry, rules and models to the agent.
* Does not exist here: `BaseModel`, `Depends`, `APIRouter`, `@app.get(...)` and `with get/post` blocks.

```python
from hinoki import Hinoki, Schema, http


class Greeting(Schema):
    message: str


class GreetingIn(Schema):
    name: str


@http.get("/greeting")
async def read_greeting() -> Greeting:
    return Greeting(message="hello")


@http.post("/greeting", atomic=True)
async def create_greeting(body: GreetingIn) -> Greeting:
    return Greeting(message=f"hello {body.name}")


app = Hinoki(include=[read_greeting, create_greeting])
assert "/greeting" in app.openapi()["paths"]
```

A test runs this block against the installed package, so the names and syntax above stay true. See [function-based APIs](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/function-endpoints.md) for `RouteGroup` and [structure an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md) for the conventions.

## What the project contains

| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `AGENTS.md` | Commands, conventions, a pointer to [Hinoki's docs for agents](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ai-workflow.md#docs-for-agents) and where the agent's authority ends; `CLAUDE.md` points to it |
| `rules.py` | Eight rules on from the start (below), listed in `hinoki.toml` as `[project] rules = ["<package>.rules:project_rules"]` so the application loads them without a `rules=` argument; the model rules `HNK-DB-001` and `HNK-DB-002` commented out until the first model exists, because a model rule that matches no model fails |
| `.mcp.json` | Starts the [development MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md) |
| `hinoki-rules.toml` | The owner's waivers |

| Rule | Promise |
| --- | --- |
| `HNK-ACC-001`, `HNK-ACC-002` | Every action names an access policy and a permission |
| `HNK-API-001`, `HNK-API-002` | Responses are concrete `Schema` types |
| `HNK-API-003` | Lists are paginated |
| `HNK-TXN-001` | Writes run in a transaction |
| `HNK-SCH-001` | Fields such as `password_hash` never appear in a response `Schema` |
| `HNK-SCH-002` | Request text has a length limit |

`AGENTS.md` states the same conventions as [structure an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md): public only on purpose, `atomic=True` for writes, `Schema` classes in responses, explicit relation loading, server values win on create, migrations as reviewed SQL.

## Give the agent tools

* **The development MCP** lets the agent read the real registry, rules and models, explain one action or error code, check the project and draft a model. It never writes source code, rules or waivers; only `run_scenario`, when you enable it, runs real handlers. See [development MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md).
* **Skills** (optional): `hinoki skills install` writes four playbooks under `.claude/skills/`: `hinoki-add-endpoint`, `hinoki-fix-rule`, `hinoki-review-api` and `hinoki-test-api`. Each names the MCP tool or command to run and what belongs to the owner. See [`hinoki skills`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/cli.md#skills).
* **Errors that say what to do**: validation errors list every problem with a path and a stable code, and a registration error names the action and parameter.

## The loop

1. The agent reads the project with `inspect_project`.
2. It makes one small change: a model, a `Schema`, an action.
3. It runs `pytest`, `ruff`, `mypy` and `hinoki check`.
4. A violation is a stable rule ID, a location and an explanation; the fix is a code change.

**Waivers are the owner's decision.** `hinoki-rules.toml` is read by the tools, never written, and a waiver needs a reason, an owner and a bounded target. An agent that edits it to pass a check breaks `AGENTS.md`; the framework cannot stop someone with write access, but the change is visible in review. Put the file under `CODEOWNERS`.

## Check a change against clients

```sh
hinoki openapi --output openapi-baseline.json
hinoki openapi --breaking-against openapi-baseline.json
```

Take the baseline from the released version. The second command exits `1` and lists each change that breaks an existing client: removed operations or response fields, new required input, narrowed enums, changed types. See [`hinoki openapi`](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#openapi).

`hinoki llms` renders the same document as an [llms.txt](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/openapi.md#llms) text of your application's own operations, for an agent that works on a client of it; `Hinoki(llms_url="/llms.txt")` serves it. Neither is on by default.

## Generate request bodies

`request_cases` reads an OpenAPI document and returns one `RequestCase` per operation with a JSON body: `method`, `path`, a valid `body`, and `invalid`, a list of `(description, body)` pairs that each break one constraint.

```python
# tests/bodiestest.py
from hinoki.ai.samples import request_cases

from shop.main import app

CASES = request_cases(app.openapi())  # one per operation with a JSON body
```

Parametrize a test over `CASES`: send `case.body` and expect a `2xx`, then send each body in `case.invalid` and expect `422`.

It raises `CannotSample` for a schema it cannot build a value for, such as a regular-expression pattern. Fill path parameters with real values before sending, and use a disposable database.

## Docs for agents

Every build of this site also publishes the documentation as plain Markdown, in the layout of [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/):

| File | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `llms.txt` | An index: the block above, then one link and description per page, grouped like the guides. Reference, project pages, the changelog and benchmarks are under `Optional` |
| `llms-full.txt` | Every page except the `Optional` ones, concatenated in navigation order |
| `<page>.md` | One page as Markdown, for example `crud.md` or `tutorial/1-models.md`; links inside it are absolute, and a `reference/` page lists each documented name with its signature and a link to the rendered page |

The generated `AGENTS.md` points an agent at `llms.txt` and tells it to prefer these files and the development MCP over guessing from other frameworks.

Each documentation version has its own copy, for example `https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/llms.txt` and `https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md`; the root `https://hinoki.caspel.dev/llms.txt` follows the default version (see [documentation versions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/documentation-versions.md)). The files come from the same pages as the site, and the build fails when a link or a description is missing.

## Limits

* The development MCP describes and checks a project. To let an agent use a running app, [expose selected actions over MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/app-mcp.md).
* Rules check declarations, not what a function body does. Import rules read the project's own files and report dynamic imports as unverifiable.
* `propose_model` is a starting point: owner scoping, pagination and `unique_together`, but no business rules, state transitions or other relations.
* This workflow was verified by generating a project and running its tests and `check`, and by one fresh agent adding an owner-scoped resource from `AGENTS.md` alone. One run by one agent is evidence, not a benchmark.

## See also

* [Development MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/dev-mcp.md)
* [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md)
* [Structure an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md)

# Best practices

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/best-practices.md

Practical defaults for building, securing, optimizing, testing and operating a Hinoki application in production. Each recommendation below matches behavior the framework implements and checks; see [Structure an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md) for the three-layer architecture and architectural rules behind them.

## 1. Project structure and modules

### Separate HTTP, operations and persistence

Keep route handlers thin and push business rules into plain async operations that take typed values (`Caller`, `Schema`, IDs) rather than `Request` objects. That lets HTTP actions, management commands, admin hooks, MCP tools and tests share the same logic without duplicating checks.

* Use [function-based APIs](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/function-endpoints.md) grouped with `RouteGroup` by default so shared `access=`, `atomic=` and `errors=` declarations live in one place.
* Use [`API` classes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/class-endpoints.md) when you need `@crud(...)` resources, lifecycle hooks or shared inheritance.
* Declare routes in each app's `routes.py` and keep URL prefixes in `hinoki.toml` ([register routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/routes.md)).
* Enforce layer direction with `Imports.forbid` in your project rules ([rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md)).

### Own worker resources with `Module`, never at import time

Importing a Python module must not open sockets, pools or files, and must not hold global mutable per-request state. Wrap every long-lived client or pool in a `Module` whose `lifespan` opens the resource per worker, exposes it via `ctx.provide(...)`, and closes it in `finally`:

```python
# notes/passwords.py
from collections.abc import AsyncIterator
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from hinoki import Module, ModuleContext, Resource
from hinoki.crypto import PasswordHasher


class Passwords(Module):
    name = "passwords"

    @asynccontextmanager
    async def lifespan(self, ctx: ModuleContext) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
        hasher = PasswordHasher()
        ctx.provide(PasswordHasher, hasher)
        try:
            yield
        finally:
            hasher.close()
```

Declare `requires = (...)` when one module depends on another so startup and shutdown order stay explicit. If handlers need a worker-owned dependency directly, subclass `Resource`, provide it from a `Module`, and annotate it on the handler signature ([application modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md#inject-a-worker-resource-into-a-handler)). For the database, declaring `database: settings.DatabaseSettings` on your settings class automatically installs `DatabaseModule` per worker.

### Type configuration with `AppSettings` and `Secret`

Subclass `settings.AppSettings` once for the project, give it a prefix, and type every credential as `settings.Secret`:

```python
# notes/settings.py
from hinoki import settings


class ProjectSettings(
    settings.AppSettings, prefix="NOTES_", dotenv=".env", toml="settings.toml"
):
    database: settings.DatabaseSettings
    jwt_key: settings.Secret
```

* Never hardcode secret defaults or commit secrets in `settings.toml` (TOML rejects `Secret` fields at load).
* Supply secrets through environment variables (`NOTES_JWT_KEY`) or container secret files (`NOTES_JWT_KEY_FILE=/run/secrets/jwt_key`).
* Call `.reveal()` only at the boundary that constructs the client or key (`JWTKey("2026-11", "HS256", app_settings.jwt_key)` accepts `Secret` directly without revealing it). `Secret` redacts itself in `str`, `repr`, logs and `hinoki settings`.
* Keep `strict=True` (the default) so typos in prefixed environment variables fail at startup instead of silently falling back to defaults. See [settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md).

## 2. API contracts and `Schema`

### Separate input, patch and output `Schema` classes

Models describe tables; `Schema` classes describe the public wire contract. Never return a `Model` instance directly from an action. Define separate `Schema` classes by role:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/schemas.py
from datetime import datetime
from decimal import Decimal
from typing import Annotated
from uuid import UUID

from hinoki import UNSET, Field, Schema, Unset, derive

from .models import Invoice


class InvoiceIn(Schema):
    reference: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)]
    amount: Annotated[Decimal, Field(gt=0, max_digits=10, decimal_places=2)]
    due_at: datetime


class InvoicePatch(Schema):
    reference: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)] | Unset = UNSET
    paid: bool | Unset = UNSET


@derive(Invoice, exclude=("internal_notes",))
class InvoiceOut(Schema):
    pass
```

* Omit server-assigned fields (`id`, `author_id`, `tenant_id`, `created_at`) from input `Schema` classes, and pass them explicitly as keyword arguments to `Model.acreate(data, author_id=caller.user.id)` so server values always win.
* Use `UNSET` defaults on patch `Schema` classes and apply them with `await row.aupdate_from(patch)` so only sent fields are written.
* Turn on `Actions.forbid_model_responses()` and `Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", ...)` in your [rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md) to prevent accidental leaks. See [schemas](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schemas.md) and [schemas from models](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/model-schemas.md).

### Keep `validate_response=True` enabled

`@http.*` and `RouteGroup` enable `validate_response=True` by default. Leave it enabled: Hinoki checks the handler's return value against its return annotation before encoding the response, catching contract drift early and rolling back an `atomic=True` transaction instead of committing after a broken answer. Reach for `validate_response=False` only for intentional escape hatches where the return type cannot be checked ([requests and responses](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#the-response-is-checked-against-the-annotation)).

### Use strict, explicit scalar types and avoid lazy I/O

* Use timezone-aware `datetime` (and `time` with an offset on the wire), `UUID` for opaque identifiers, `Decimal` with `max_digits`/`decimal_places` for money (never `float`), and `Enum` or `Literal` for closed sets ([scalar field types](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/schema-types.md)).
* Never trigger I/O during `Schema` serialization. Relations in Hinoki are never lazy, so load every related row before calling `from_model(...)` or projecting.

## 3. Security, authentication and `Access`

### Centralize authorization in reusable `Access` policies

Endpoints are public by default. Define authentication providers (`BearerAuth`, `JWTAuth`, `ClaimsJWTAuth`, `APIKeyAuth`, `HeaderAuth`) and `Permission` enums once, compose them into named `Access` policies, and attach them on the `RouteGroup` or action:

```python
# notes/security.py
from hinoki import Access, BearerAuth, Caller, Permission


class BillingPermission(Permission):
    READ = "billing:read"
    WRITE = "billing:write"


class TokenAuth(BearerAuth[User]):
    async def resolve_token(self, token: str) -> Caller[User] | None: ...


auth = TokenAuth()
billing_reader = Access(auth=auth, permissions=[BillingPermission.READ])
billing_writer = Access(auth=auth, permissions=[BillingPermission.WRITE])
```

Keep `Actions.require_access` (`HNK-ACC-001`) and `HNK-ACC-002` enabled so every public or permissionless action is an explicit decision ([authentication and access](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md), [rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md)).

### Enforce ownership and tenant scoping everywhere

Permissions control *what* a caller may do; your queries control *which rows* they may touch. Enforce the same scope across manual actions, generated CRUD, MCP tools and admin:

* **Manual writes:** fold ownership or tenant checks into the write statement itself (`await Invoice.aupdate_where({"id": invoice_id, "tenant_id": caller.user.tenant_id}, {"paid": True})`) to avoid check-then-write races.
* **Generated CRUD:** configure `owner=` / `own_rows(...)` or override `get_queryset(self, principal)` on the `API` class ([generated CRUD](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/crud.md)).
* **Admin and MCP:** override `ModelAdmin.queryset(self, principal)` and `ModelAdmin.can(...)` in the [admin](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/admin.md); [MCP tools](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/app-mcp.md) reuse the action's `Access` policy and handler directly.

### Apply rate limits, CORS, host checks and safe errors

* **Rate limiting:** attach `RateLimit(limit, window, ...)` to sensitive actions such as login or token issuance (`@http.post("/auth/login", rate_limit=RateLimit(5, 60, headers=True), atomic=True)`). The default `DatabaseLimits()` storage shares counters across every worker and host via the `hinoki_rate_limits` table (apply its migration at deploy time); use `MemoryLimits()` only in development or tests. Keep `on_error="closed"` (the default) on security-critical endpoints so a storage outage fails closed with `503` ([rate limiting](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/endpoints.md#rate-limit-an-action)).
* **Hosts, CORS and HTTPS:** before deploying, narrow `allowed_hosts` from `*` to the exact host names you serve, list explicit browser origins in `cors.origins` (or per-route `http.Cors(...)`, never `*` with `credentials=True`), and enable `security.redirect_https` and `security.hsts_seconds` alongside exact `server.trusted_proxies` CIDRs when behind a reverse proxy ([hosts, CORS and HTTPS](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/web-security.md)).
* **Safe errors:** keep `debug = false` in production so unhandled exceptions return `500 internal_error` with a `request_id` and no traceback or exception message. Raise declared `APIError` subclasses (`errors=(InvoiceAlreadyPaid,)`) and do not catch broad `Exception` inside handlers — let the framework roll back and translate the error ([errors](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/errors.md)).

## 4. ORM, queries and transactions

### Eliminate N+1 queries and use bulk writes

Hinoki never lazy-loads relations; accessing an unloaded relation raises `RelationNotLoaded`. Load exactly what the response needs in the query that fetches the rows:

* Use `select_related("customer")` for forward foreign keys (one `LEFT JOIN`).
* Use `prefetch_related("invoices")` (or scoped `prefetch_related(tags=...)`) for reverse foreign keys and many-to-many relations (bounded chunked queries). See [relations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/relations.md).

For multi-row writes, prefer bulk methods over loops:

```python
# Batch writes instead of awaiting inside a loop
created = await Invoice.abulk_create(items, returning=False)
updated = await Invoice.abulk_update(modified_rows)
deleted = await Invoice.abulk_delete(obsolete_ids)
count = await Invoice.filter(paid=False, overdue=True).aupdate(
    {"reminded": True}, returning=False
)
```

Pass `returning=False` on `abulk_create` and `QuerySet.aupdate` when you do not need the written rows back ([query and write rows](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md)).

### Scope transactions tightly and respect service boundaries

* Put `atomic=True` on multi-step write actions (or on the `RouteGroup`, setting `atomic=False` on pure reads and no-write `POST` actions). `atomic=True` commits only after the response is validated and encoded, and rolls back before error translation.
* Never return `Response(status=4xx)` to signal an error from an `atomic=True` action: a returned `Response` commits the transaction. Raise an `APIError` instead.
* Use `async with db.atomic():` or `@db.atomic` inside reusable operations; nested scopes automatically become savepoints.
* Never perform irreversible external side effects (sending email, publishing messages) inside an open transaction. Register them with `current_database().after_commit(...)` so they run only after the outermost commit ([transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md), [send email](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/email.md)).
* Never join across service databases or pretend a local transaction spans a remote HTTP call. Store foreign service IDs as plain values, wrap remote calls in operations with explicit timeouts, and design multi-service writes to be idempotent ([more than one service](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md#12-more-than-one-service)).

### Paginate every list and choose the right strategy

Never return an unbounded table scan; enforce `Actions.require_pagination` in your project rules.

* **`PageNumberPagination()`** when clients need page numbers and a `total` count. On read-only endpoints (`atomic=False`) backed by PostgreSQL or MySQL with `database.max_size >= 2`, pass `concurrent=True` to run the `COUNT(*)` and page-row queries in parallel (inside a transaction or on SQLite, Hinoki automatically runs them sequentially).
* **`CursorPagination()`** for deep or rapidly growing feeds where constant-time pages matter and `total` is unnecessary. Set a 32+ byte `pagination.cursor_secret` via the environment or `*_FILE`, index the sort columns in sort order, and never order by a sensitive column (cursors are HMAC-signed, not encrypted). See [pagination](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md).

## 5. Performance and Rust fast paths

### Project read-only lists and pages directly in Rust

When a read-only endpoint returns a list or page of a `Schema` without mutating the items in Python, use `aproject(Schema)` or `apaginate_as(Schema, page, concurrent=True)`:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/api.py
from hinoki import RouteGroup
from hinoki.pagination import Page, PageNumberPagination, PageParams

from .models import Invoice
from .schemas import InvoiceOut

invoices = RouteGroup("/invoices", access=billing_reader)


@invoices.get("/", pagination=PageNumberPagination())
async def list_invoices(page: PageParams) -> Page[InvoiceOut]:
    return (
        await Invoice.all()
        .select_related("customer")
        .apaginate_as(InvoiceOut, page, concurrent=True)
    )
```

`aproject` and `apaginate_as` (and their sync twins `project` and `paginate_as`) encode eligible scalar and `select_related` schemas directly from Rust rows into JSON bytes without constructing intermediate Python `Model` or `Schema` objects. Accessing `.items` or iterating materializes Python `Schema` instances lazily from the owned rows without a second query, and schemas with computed fields, hooks, validators or `prefetch_related` fall back to normal hydration transparently ([pagination](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/pagination.md#direct-schema-projection), [queries](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md)).

### Keep hot routes on Kiso's native lane

On [Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md), eligible routes skip Python routing and request binding, and plain `async def` handlers whose `await`s are stock ORM calls can run on the native handler lane without an asyncio task.

* Use built-in parsers and renderers (`JSONParser`, `JSONRenderer`, etc.) and plain `async def` handlers without wrapper decorators when you want native dispatch.
* For stateless bearer tokens, `ClaimsJWTAuth` verifies tokens and answers `401`/`403` refusals in Rust without entering Python ([claims-only tokens](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md#claims-only-tokens-on-the-native-lane)).
* Inspect every route's lane and why any route falls back to Python with:

```sh
uv run hinoki routes --lanes
```

See [inspect an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/inspect.md#routes) and [Kiso server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#the-native-handler-lane).

### Never block the event loop; size workers and pools together

* Write `async def` handlers with `a...` ORM methods by default. Never call blocking network, file or database libraries inside an `async def` handler.
* If you must call a blocking library, make the handler a plain `def` and use the sync ORM twins (`get`, `create`, `paginate`, `with db.atomic():`) so Hinoki runs it on the bounded sync executor (`execution.sync_workers`, default `8`; `execution.sync_queue`, default `64`). Beyond both, requests answer `503 overloaded` ([sync and async code](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md)).
* Size `server.workers`, `server.runtime_threads` and `database.max_size` together. Each worker owns its own database pool, and a rolling `SIGHUP` reload on Kiso runs at most one extra worker at a time, so budget:

```text
replicas × (server.workers + 1) × database.max_size <= database max connections
```

Keep `server.runtime_threads` (default `1`) small unless profiling shows the Rust runtime threads are saturated, and measure changes against a baseline instead of guessing ([settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md#8-database-connection-ownership)).

## 6. Testing

### Use disposable databases, synthetic fixtures and `ASGIClient`

Tests must never touch production data, real accounts or external mail servers. Point test settings at a throwaway database (an isolated per-test SQLite file migrated with `migrator.apply`, or disposable PostgreSQL/MySQL/MariaDB servers via `HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, `HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL` and `HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL`) and drive requests in-process through `ASGIClient` (or `SyncClient` for synchronous tests) from `hinoki.testing`:

```python
# tests/billingtest.py
from hinoki.testing import ASGIClient

from notes.main import create_app


async def test_invoice_access_and_validation(test_settings) -> None:
    app = create_app(test_settings)
    async with ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True) as client:
        # Anonymous and unauthorized callers are refused
        assert (await client.get("/billing/invoices")).status == 401
        assert (await client.get("/billing/invoices", token=viewer_token)).status == 403

        # Invalid payloads fail with 422 before hitting the handler
        bad = await client.post(
            "/billing/invoices",
            token=staff_token,
            json={"reference": "", "amount": "-5.00"},
        )
        assert bad.status == 422
```

* Pass `strict_errors=True` to `ASGIClient` so any error response missing from an action's `errors=` declaration fails the test before OpenAPI can drift.
* Test every `Access` policy with denial cases (`401` missing/invalid credential, `403` missing permission, and cross-tenant or non-owner access) as well as happy paths.
* Inject `ManualClock` from `hinoki.testing` for deterministic timestamps, token expiry and rate-limit windows, and use `EmailBackend.MEMORY` to assert on `mailer.outbox` without network I/O ([test an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/testing.md)).

## 7. Production and operations

### Run migrations as a dedicated deploy step

Never run migrations from a worker lifespan or startup hook. Plan and review SQL migrations during development, then apply them once per deployment from a single release job before rolling the new application workers:

```sh
uv run hinoki migrations plan billing
uv run hinoki migrations apply
```

Check for pending or destructive changes in CI before deploying ([migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md)).

### Serve on Kiso with graceful shutdown and startup probes

Run `hinoki serve` (which uses Kiso by default) behind your process manager or container orchestrator with `debug = false`, explicit `allowed_hosts`, and either TLS (`server.tls_cert_file`, `server.tls_key_file`, optional `server.http2`) or an ingress listed in `server.trusted_proxies`:

```toml
# settings.toml
allowed_hosts = ["api.example.com"]

[server]
workers = 4
sighup = "reload"
access_log_format = "json"
access_log_skip = ["/health"]
access_log_slow_ms = 200

[lifecycle]
startup_timeout = 30.0
shutdown_timeout = 15.0

[logging]
level = "info"
format = "json"
include_request_id = true

[metrics]
listen = "127.0.0.1:9100"
```

* **Graceful shutdown and reloads:** `SIGTERM` stops accepting new connections, drains in-flight requests for up to `lifecycle.shutdown_timeout`, and runs module shutdown cleanly. Sending `SIGHUP` to the Kiso supervisor (when `server.sighup = "reload"`, the default) replaces workers one by one without closing the listening socket ([Kiso server](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md#reload-on-sighup)).
* **Startup probe:** opt in with `Hinoki(startup_url="/health")` to expose a fixed `GET`/`HEAD` endpoint returning `200 {"status":"ok"}` once worker startup completes (`503 not_ready` before startup or during shutdown). Treat it as a startup probe — it does not query the database or downstream services ([optional startup probe](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#optional-startup-probe)).
* **Metrics and structured logs:** enable Kiso's dedicated Prometheus listener via `metrics.listen` (protected by `metrics.allow` or `metrics.token` whenever bound off loopback; never exposed on the application port), emit JSON application logs with `logging.format = "json"` and `logging.include_request_id = true`, and emit JSON access logs with `server.access_log_format = "json"` ([export Prometheus metrics](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/metrics.md), [serve an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md)).

### Pre-deploy checklist

Before shipping a release:

1. Run `uv run hinoki check` and `uv run pytest` with zero failures.
2. Run `uv run hinoki routes --lanes` to confirm critical routes take the expected serving lane.
3. Confirm `debug` is off, `allowed_hosts` is narrowed, and all `Secret` values come from the environment or `*_FILE`.
4. Apply migrations once (`uv run hinoki migrations apply`) before starting or reloading workers.
5. Verify `GET /health` (if enabled) and the Prometheus `/metrics` scrape after rollout.

# Sync and async code

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md

Each worker runs one event loop. `async def` is the native style; a plain `def` handler or hook is fully supported and runs on a bounded thread pool, with the request's context and blocking ORM twins that never block the loop.

Two actions added to the `invoices` group of [function endpoints](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/function-endpoints.md), answering with a one-field `Schema`:

```python
# notes/apps/billing/api.py  (in the invoices group's module)
from hinoki import Schema


class UnpaidCount(Schema):
    count: int


@invoices.get("/unpaid/count")
async def count_unpaid() -> UnpaidCount:  # async: await the a... method
    return UnpaidCount(count=await Invoice.filter(paid=False).acount())


@invoices.get("/unpaid/count-sync")
def count_unpaid_sync() -> UnpaidCount:  # sync: the twin without the "a"
    return UnpaidCount(count=Invoice.filter(paid=False).count())
```

The group carries the access policy and `atomic=True` for both.

A name with the `a` prefix awaits the database (`aget`, `acreate`, `acount`); the same name without it is the blocking twin. A queryset is lazy until evaluated: `await queryset` is the async form of `queryset.list()`.

## Choose a style

* Prefer `async def`. Use `def` for code that is naturally blocking: a library without async support, or CPU work measured to be short.
* Never call blocking code from an `async def`. From a `def`, use the sync twin instead of calling an `a...` coroutine.
* CPU-heavy work belongs in a separate process, not in either pool.
* A sync ORM call made on the event loop raises, naming the `a...` method to use.

## What runs where

| Surface | Async | Sync | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Action handlers | `async def` | `def` | Sync runs on the executor |
| CRUD hooks (`get_queryset`, `written_queryset`, `to_schema`, `store`, `change`, `remove`) | `async def` | `def` | Same executor as handlers |
| Auth providers (`authenticate`, `resolve`, `resolve_token`, JWT `resolve_claims`) | `async def` | `def` | Sync hooks run on the executor |
| Model writes and lookups | `acreate`, `aget`, `aget_or_none`, `aget_as`, `aget_or_none_as`, `aupdate`, `aupdate_where`, `adelete`, `asave`, `aupdate_from`, `abulk_create`, `abulk_update`, `abulk_delete` | The same names without `a` | Sync calls work only inside a sync handler or hook served by Hinoki; both take `returning=False` ([queries](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/queries.md#writes-that-do-not-read-the-row-back)) |
| QuerySet reads | `await qs`, `afirst`, `aget`, `aget_as`, `aget_or_none_as`, `acount`, `aexists`, `aproject`, `apaginate`, `apaginate_as` | `list`, `first`, `get`, `get_as`, `get_or_none_as`, `count`, `exists`, `project`, `paginate`, `paginate_as` | |
| QuerySet writes | `aupdate`, `adelete` | `update`, `delete` | |
| Relations | `select_related`, `prefetch_related` | same | Never lazy in either style |
| Raw SQL (`Database.fetch`, `fetch_one`, `execute`) | async | none | Async-only escape hatch |
| Transactions | `atomic=True` | same | The runtime owns it |
| Atomic blocks | `async with db.atomic():`, `@db.atomic` on `async def` | `with db.atomic():`, `@db.atomic` on `def` | Sync forms raise `RuntimeError` on the loop ([transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md#atomic-blocks-and-functions-in-application-code)) |
| `Schema`, `Request`, `Response`, parsers, renderers | plain code | same | No I/O |
| Password hashing | `await hasher.hash/verify` | `hash_sync`, `verify_sync` | Async calls use their own bounded pool |
| Error handlers (`app.error_handler`) | `async def` | `def` | Run on the loop: no blocking calls |
| Module lifespans | async context manager | none | Resources belong to the worker's loop |
| Startup and shutdown hooks | `async def hook(ctx)` | `def hook(ctx)` | `Hinoki(on_startup=..., on_shutdown=...)`; sync runs on the executor |
| Admin hooks (`stats`, `check`, `save`, `remove`) | `async def` | none | The admin runs on the loop |
| Tests | `ASGIClient` | `SyncClient` | Same behaviour |

## Size the pool

`execution.sync_workers` (default `8`) threads serve sync handlers and hooks; `execution.sync_queue` (default `64`) requests may wait for one. A full queue answers `503 overloaded` with `Retry-After`. See [settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md).

## Errors and edge cases

* **Sync hooks share the pool with sync handlers.** A flood of bad credentials or slow hooks can fill the queue and turn legitimate sync work into `503`. Keep sync hooks short, reject malformed credentials before touching the database, and prefer async hooks.
* **A sync auth hook runs before the action's transaction opens**, so it is never part of it.
* **Sync model calls work only inside the app's sync handlers and hooks.** In a test body, use the async API (an async fixture) or your own connection, also with `SyncClient`.
* **Async only:** module lifespans, admin hooks, background tasks (`ctx.tasks.start_soon` takes coroutines) and raw `Database` SQL. A sync error handler runs on the loop and must not call the ORM; its failure is treated as unhandled.
* **`SyncClient`** works only inside its `with` block and raises a timeout error after `timeout` seconds (default 60).

The test suite exercises sync and async handlers, sync authentication hooks, ORM calls through both clients, mixed traffic and cancellation against a disposable database.

## See also

* [Request lifecycle](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/request-lifecycle.md)
* [Transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md)
* [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md)

# Concepts

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/concepts.md

How the parts of Hinoki fit together. Each guide explains one part in detail.

## A model is stored data; a `Schema` is API data

A `Model` describes a table and its queries (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB). A `Schema` validates what an endpoint accepts or returns. A response `Schema` exposes only the fields clients should see: `@derive(Invoice)` copies fields from a model, but you still decide the boundary, and a handler returns `InvoiceOut.from_model(row)`, never the row.

## A declaration is reused

An action's signature and decorator options state its route, inputs, access policy, transaction (`atomic=`), declared errors and response. Routing, binding, the OpenAPI document, the rules, the admin and MCP all read that one declaration. Actions are [plain functions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/function-endpoints.md), optionally grouped in a `RouteGroup` with shared options, or [methods of an `API` class](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/class-endpoints.md). Each app lists them in its `routes.py`, and the project's `routes.py` mounts exposed apps with `Mount(...)` ([register routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/routes.md)).

## One application object

A server process serves one `Hinoki` object: the one `project.application` in `hinoki.toml` names, or the target given to `hinoki serve`. Declare it at module level:

```python
# notes/main.py
import stripe
from hinoki import Hinoki, errors

from notes.settings import ProjectSettings

app = Hinoki(settings=ProjectSettings, title="Notes")


@app.error_handler(stripe.CardError)
def card_error(error: stripe.CardError) -> errors.APIError:
    return errors.APIError(error.user_message, status=402, code="card_declined")
```

`Hinoki(...)` loads `[project] routes`, app `events`, `[project] middleware` and `[project] rules` that `hinoki.toml` declares (each of `include=`, `events=`, `middleware=` and `rules=` you pass replaces its manifest value; for example, the [Blog example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/blog/blog/main.py) passes `include=` for conditional routes) and opens nothing, so importing the module is safe: commands, servers and tests use the same `app`. The `[[apps]]` of `hinoki.toml` register app packages (optional `models`/`migrations`, `events`, `requires`), not further `Hinoki` objects.

## One request

The server hands each request to the compiled router and binding layer: Kiso, the default server, does so from Rust and queues matched requests for the Python pipeline; with Granian the request crosses the ASGI adapter first. Hinoki authenticates the caller, checks access, validates inputs, runs the handler, checks the return value against its annotation and renders the response. A transactional action commits after the response is prepared; a failure rolls back before it becomes an HTTP error. Handwritten handlers and hooks run in Python on both servers: the runtime is not an all-Rust server. Details: [request lifecycle](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/request-lifecycle.md).

## Worker resources

Each server worker owns its module lifespan and database pool: startup creates them, shutdown closes them. Nothing is opened at import or shared across workers. Scripts outside the server manage their own short-lived connections. See [modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md).

## Optional rules

Rules check declared routes, schemas, models and imports. Hinoki ships twelve; each reports a violation, a pass, or that it could not verify its promise. They do not prove what a function body does. Turn on the ones that suit the application and run them at startup and in development. See [rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md).

## See also

* [Request lifecycle](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/request-lifecycle.md)
* [Structure an application](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md)
* [Sync and async code](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md)
* [Glossary](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/glossary.md)

# Request lifecycle

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/request-lifecycle.md

The order matters: validation, access and transactions fail in different ways and at different moments.

1. **Accept.** Kiso accepts the connection, answers what needs no application code and hands the rest to the request pipeline ([Kiso](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/kiso.md)). With `--server granian`, Granian calls the ASGI application, which reaches the same pipeline.
2. **Route.** Hinoki matches the method and path.
3. **Authenticate and authorize.** For an action with an access policy, the provider resolves a `Caller` and the policy checks permissions. A `rate_limit=` policy runs next. The body has not been read yet, so an unauthenticated or rate-limited client cannot make the server buffer it.
4. **Bind.** Hinoki negotiates the response type from `Accept` (`406` when nothing fits), reads the body of `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `QUERY` requests, then binds and validates path, query, header and body values.
5. **Open the transaction** for an `atomic=True` action.
6. **Run the handler**, then check its value against the return annotation (a mismatch is `500 internal_error`, inside the transaction, unless the action sets `validate_response=False`) and render it. A returned `Response` is neither checked nor rendered.
7. **Commit** after the response is prepared. An exception or cancellation rolls back before the HTTP error is produced.

An unhandled exception never becomes a successful response, and a failed commit is an error. A renderer must not perform hidden database I/O.

## Limits

| Setting | Default | When exceeded |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `execution.request_timeout` | 30 s, through response preparation | `504 timeout`; an open transaction rolls back |
| `execution.max_body_bytes` | 1 MiB (also each multipart part) | `413 payload_too_large` |
| `execution.max_query_bytes` | 8 KiB | `414 uri_too_long` |
| `execution.max_header_bytes` | 32 KiB, names and values combined | `431 headers_too_large` |
| `execution.max_streams` | 64 open streams per worker | `503` with `Retry-After: 1`, before the handler runs |

The size checks run before routing. A sync handler already running when the timeout expires cannot be stopped: it keeps its executor slot until it returns, and its result is discarded. Let the proxy or ASGI server enforce its own request-line and header limits too.

## Streamed responses

For an action that returns `Stream`, `EventStream` or `File`, everything up to the moment the handler returns the object (access, rate limit, binding, validation, the handler, middleware and `request_timeout`) works as for any action, and an error there is the usual JSON answer. Before the handler runs, the worker takes one of its `execution.max_streams` places, or answers `503` with `Retry-After: 1`. The head is then sent, and the body is produced and sent piece by piece: the pieces are not checked against an annotation, a failure can only cut the connection, and the place is given back when the body ends. See [stream a response](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/streaming.md).

## Request IDs

Each response carries a request ID in `server.request_id_header` (`x-request-id`), and built-in error JSON repeats it as `request_id`. Hinoki generates it; with `server.trust_request_id=True` it accepts a validated inbound ID, only from a trusted proxy.

## Startup and shutdown

`lifecycle.startup_timeout` (30 s) and `lifecycle.shutdown_timeout` (10 s) bound the worker lifespan. A startup failure is reported through the ASGI lifespan protocol; shutdown cleans up resources within its deadline. [Startup and shutdown hooks](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md#startup-and-shutdown-hooks) run inside those limits.

## Where Rust runs

Routing, parsing, validation and selected serialization run in Rust; the server hand-off (Granian and the ASGI adapter, or Kiso's queue) crosses Python objects. See [sync and async code](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md) for which executor runs what.

## See also

* [Transactions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/transactions.md)
* [Errors](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/errors.md)
* [Serving](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md)

# Structure an application

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md

Opinionated, with reasons. Each practice below is **enforced** by the framework, checkable with an optional **rule**, or a **convention** left to review. The [Tracker example](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/tree/main/examples/tracker) shows them together: `api` → `operations` → `models`, row permission in the statements, the direction enforced by `Imports.forbid`, operations tested without HTTP.

## 1. Three layers, one direction

```text
HTTP layer      actions (functions or API classes)   shapes, status codes, access, atomic=True
   │
   ▼
Operations      plain async functions                one business operation each; no HTTP types
   │
   ▼
Persistence     Model / QuerySet                     tables, relations, explicit loading
```

* **HTTP layer** turns a request into typed values (`Schema`, path and query parameters, `Caller`) and an operation's result into a response `Schema`. No business rules, no SQL.
* **Operations** hold the rules ("an editor may publish only their own draft"). They take plain arguments (`principal`, a `Schema`, IDs), so an action, a CLI command, a test, an admin hook or an MCP tool can call them. An action that reads cookies or headers cannot be reused; an operation can.
* **Persistence** never imports the HTTP layer. **Rule:** `Imports.forbid(source="notes.apps.billing.models", target="notes.apps.billing.api")`, and the same for operations → api.
* Small apps may skip the middle layer. Add it when an action holds a rule another entry point needs.

## 2. Where each concern lives

Actions are [functions](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/function-endpoints.md) by default, grouped in a `RouteGroup` that states shared options once; an [`API` class](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/class-endpoints.md) earns its place for `crud(...)` resources with hooks or inherited actions.

| Concern | Put it | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routes | Each app's `routes.py`; prefixes only in `hinoki.toml` ([register routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/routes.md)). **Convention** | One place to read the map; one source per path segment |
| Authentication | A provider (`BearerAuth`, `JWTAuth`, …) returning a `Caller` | One path for HTTP, admin and MCP |
| Coarse permission | `access=` on the action, or once on its `RouteGroup`. **Public is the default**: protect on purpose. **Rule:** `Actions.require_access` | A forgotten policy is the most common hole |
| Row permission (owner, tenant) | The **statement**: scope `aupdate`/`adelete` by owner so check and write are one operation | No check-then-write race; hidden rows look missing (`404`). If the API promises a distinct `403`, make the conditional write and its fallback explicit, and document what it reveals |
| Input validation | The `Schema` (types, constraints, patterns) | Strict, no coercion, validated in Rust before your code runs |
| Business rules | Operations | Testable without HTTP |
| Transactions | `atomic=True` on every write. **Rule:** `Transactions.require_atomic` | Commit after the response is encoded; rollback before the error becomes HTTP |
| Errors | Raise `APIError` subclasses and declare them: `errors=(InvoiceAlreadyPaid,)`. Translate exceptions you cannot change once with `@app.error_handler(...)` | The declaration feeds OpenAPI, MCP and `ASGIClient(app, strict_errors=True)`. A database `UniqueViolation` is already `409 unique_conflict`. **A returned `Response` commits the transaction** |
| Secrets | Settings and the environment, never defaults | Nothing to leak from the repository |

## 3. `Schema` classes and models

* Models describe tables; `Schema` classes describe the API. **Never return a model**: respond with `InvoiceOut.from_model(row)`. Name classes by role: `InvoiceIn` (what a client may set), `InvoicePatch` (every field `UNSET` by default), `InvoiceOut` (what a client may see, often `@derive(Invoice)`). **Rules:** `Actions.forbid_model_responses()` refuses a `Model` return type, also inside `list`, `Page` and unions; `Schemas.forbid_exposure("password_hash", …)` keeps columns out of responses through nesting and subclasses.
* Create from a `Schema` and add what only the server knows: `await Post.acreate(data, author_id=principal.user.id)`; server values win. Update with `await row.aupdate_from(patch)`, which writes only what was sent.
* A server-assigned field does not exist in the input `Schema` at all; the keyword override is a second line of defence.
* Constraints and patterns belong on the `Schema`, in the Rust pattern syntax (whole value, no look-around).

## 4. Relations and queries

* Relations are never lazy. Load what the response shows (`select_related` for single values, `prefetch_related` for collections) in the function that builds the response, so the cost is visible in one place.
* Paginate every list (`pagination=` + `PageParams` + `Page[...]`). Never return an unbounded list; never load a whole table to count or aggregate (use `acount()`, filters or SQL). **Rule:** `Actions.require_pagination`.
* Filter and order only by names you choose; never pass client-supplied column names to `filter` or `order_by`. For a generated list, declare them once in a `hinoki.filters.FilterSet` (`done: Eq[bool]`, `search = Search("title")`, `ordering = (...)`) and pass `filters=TaskFilters` to `crud(...)`, as [Tracker](https://github.com/caspel26/hinoki/blob/main/examples/tracker/tracker/apps/tasks/filters.py) does.

## 5. Sync and async

Prefer `async` handlers. A sync handler runs on a bounded pool and uses the sync model methods; it must not block for long, and a full queue answers `503 overloaded`. Password hashing has its own bounded pool. Never call blocking code from an `async` handler. See [sync and async code](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/sync-async.md).

## 6. Modules

An application is a set of modules with explicit dependencies and a lifespan (`DatabaseModule`, your own `Module`). Importing a module registers and opens nothing. Resources are created once per worker, in its lifespan. Migrations are a deploy step, never run at startup or from every worker. A standalone script owns and closes its own short-lived connection.

## 7. Migrations

```sh
hinoki migrations plan billing
hinoki migrations apply
```

`plan` writes reviewable SQL and a state file; destructive operations are flagged and need `--allow-destructive`, and a new `NOT NULL` column without a default is flagged. Review the SQL like code and apply it to a disposable database first. See [migrations](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/migrations.md).

## 8. Testing

* Run database tests against disposable servers for each backend you support: `HINOKI_TEST_DATABASE_URL` (PostgreSQL), `HINOKI_TEST_MYSQL_URL`, `HINOKI_TEST_MARIADB_URL`. Without a URL those tests are skipped: read the skip summary; one backend's green run is not conformance for another.
* Drive HTTP behaviour through the ASGI client (no sockets); test operations directly.
* For security code, use independent test vectors and inject the clock (`JWTAuth.now`).

## 9. Security defaults to keep

HTTPS terminates somewhere you control (`Admin(secure_cookies=True)` behind a proxy); `access=` on everything that is not public on purpose; CSRF on every cookie-authenticated form (the admin does it); a strict CSP; Argon2id passwords; JWT keys with a fixed algorithm and a `kid`; no token, password or hash in logs or error bodies; uploads within the 1 MiB body limit; no real personal data in tests or fixtures.

## 10. Rules to turn on from day one

`hinoki new` enables eight rules (`HNK-ACC-001`, `HNK-ACC-002`, `HNK-API-001`, `HNK-API-002`, `HNK-API-003`, `HNK-TXN-001`, `HNK-SCH-001`, `HNK-SCH-002`) and leaves the model rules `HNK-DB-001` and `HNK-DB-002` commented out until the first model exists. Turn those on then, and add `Imports.forbid` (`HNK-IMP-001`) for the direction in [section 1](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md#1-three-layers-one-direction). List the rule modules in the manifest, `[project] rules = ["tracker.rules:policy", "tracker.rules:layers"]`, and `Hinoki()` loads them; project-wide `middleware` is listed the same way (see [rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md) and [middleware](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md#declaring-middleware-in-hinokitoml)). Waivers live in `hinoki-rules.toml`, are the owner's decision, carry a reason and a bounded target, and are never edited by tools or agents to pass a check.

## 11. Anti-patterns

* Returning a `Model`, or a dict built from one.
* A business rule inside an action that another entry point also needs.
* `Response(4xx)` from an `atomic=True` action: it commits.
* Client-supplied column names reaching `filter` or `order_by`.
* Applying migrations at startup; creating a pool at import.
* A broad waiver (`*`), or editing waivers to silence a rule.
* Catching `Exception` in an action to "keep going": let the framework translate it and roll back.
* `app.include(...)` in a project with `hinoki.toml`: list the routes in `routes.py`.

## 12. More than one service

Split a system only for a reason you can name (independent deploys, different scaling, a team boundary); every split costs something the framework cannot hide.

* **No joins, no shared transaction.** A foreign key never crosses a service. Store the other service's ID as a plain value and treat its answers as snapshots. A write across two services is a sequence of calls that can half-fail: make each step idempotent and decide what a retry does before writing the code.
* **Each service owns its tables.** Others call its API, never its database. Its migrations belong to it and are applied by its deploy step ([section 7](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md#7-migrations)).
* **The caller is a `Caller` too.** Service-to-service calls authenticate like any client (a JWT with a service identity and narrow permissions); do not forward the end user's token unless the callee must act as that user.
* **Wrap every remote call in an operation** ([section 1](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/patterns.md#1-three-layers-one-direction)) with a timeout and a failure you chose (`502` or `503`), never a client library's exception.
* **Share contracts, not models.** Publish the response `Schema` classes or the OpenAPI document; keep models private.

A runnable two-service example and a client helper do not exist yet.

# Glossary

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/glossary.md

One word, one meaning. "Schema" has four meanings in this field, so the docs keep the word for one of them.

## The four schemas

| Write | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Schema` (code font) | The Hinoki class for typed, validated request and response data: `class InvoiceIn(Schema)`. Always capitalised and in code font; say "a response `Schema`". |
| table state, migration state | What the migration planner records about the tables (`migrations/NNNN-name.state.json`). Never "the database schema". |
| OpenAPI document | The generated `/openapi.json`. Its `components.schemas` entries are "OpenAPI schema objects". |
| JSON Schema | The standard the OpenAPI document uses to describe bodies, always by its name. |

## Names

| Name | Origin |
| --- | --- |
| Hinoki | 檜, the Japanese cypress of temples: fragrant, durable wood. |
| Kiso | Hinoki's Rust server, named after the Kiso Valley (Nagano, Japan), known for its hinoki forests such as Akasawa. |
| mailer | The per-worker email resource (`hinoki.mail.Mailer`): it owns the SMTP connection pool, is opened in the worker's lifespan and closed at shutdown. |
| email template | A `hinoki.mail.Template`: a subject, HTML and optional text in a small fixed language, checked against a context `Schema` and rendered in Rust. Not an admin template or an HTML page. |

## Projects and apps

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| manifest | `hinoki.toml`: the project's application, its `[project] routes` map, middleware and rules, and its registered `[[apps]]` with their optional persistence, events and dependencies. |
| project application | The `Hinoki` object named by `project.application` (`notes.main:app`); the one a server process serves. |
| app | A package listed under `[[apps]]` (with optional `models`/`migrations`, `events`, `requires`, and reusable `routes.py`). Not a second `Hinoki` object. |
| app mount | `Mount("/billing", billing_routes)` in the project's `routes.py`, deciding whether and at which prefix an app is exposed over HTTP. |
| target | `module:attribute` naming an app, such as `notes.main:app`. Commands use `project.application` from `hinoki.toml` when it is omitted. |

## Code

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Model` | A class mapped to a table. Without `@db.table`, the name is `<app>_<plural>`: `notes.apps.billing.models.Invoice` → `billing_invoices`. A column reaches a client only through a `Schema`. |
| action | One declared endpoint (`@http.get`, `@invoices.post`, ...): a function or an `API` class method. |
| route group | A `RouteGroup`: functions under one path prefix with shared `access=`, `atomic=` and `errors=`. |
| `Access` | The access policy of an action: an authentication provider and required permissions. |
| `Caller` | Who is making the request, as resolved by the provider. |

# Use other libraries

Source: https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/ecosystem.md

Hinoki has its own `Schema` and `Model` classes. It does not accept Pydantic, SQLAlchemy or Django models as request bodies, responses or tables. This page says why, what that costs, and which extension points exist today.

## Why the framework owns them

- **One declaration feeds every output.** Request binding, the response check, OpenAPI, application MCP, the admin and [rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md) read the same `Schema` and `Model` classes, so they can promise the same contract.
- **The hot paths are native.** Routing, selected request parsing and ORM execution run in Rust against Hinoki's own declarations, without calling back into a validation library or a foreign ORM per request.
- **Rules need known structure.** "A response `Schema` never exposes `password_hash`" is checkable because the `Schema` is an inspectable Hinoki class.

## What this costs

- A library that expects its own model type does not plug in: a Pydantic-based SDK, a SQLAlchemy extension or a Django app cannot be given a Hinoki `Model` or `Schema`.
- There is no adapter from SQLAlchemy, Django or Pydantic models, and no plugin system.
- Databases are SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB through Hinoki's own drivers; another ORM's connections are not shared with its pool.

## Bring a library anyway

Anything that works on plain Python data works with Hinoki. `Schema.to_dict()` and `Schema.dump()` return plain data, and a `Schema` is built from plain values:

```python
# notes/apps/quotes/api.py
from hinoki import Schema, http

from notes.apps.quotes.client import fetch_quote  # any library returning plain data


class Quote(Schema):
    symbol: str
    price: float


@http.get("/{symbol}", access=None)
async def quote(symbol: str) -> Quote:
    raw = await fetch_quote(symbol)
    return Quote(symbol=raw["symbol"], price=raw["price"])
```

Keep the translation at the edge of the handler, and keep a second store's connections in a [module](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md) so their lifetime follows the worker. Hinoki does not time-box what that code does.

## Extension points

| You want to | Use | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add an authentication scheme | Subclass `BearerAuth`, `APIKeyAuth` or `HeaderAuth` | [Authentication](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md#define-a-provider) |
| Reuse a permission rule | A typed `Access` policy | [Authentication](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/authentication.md) |
| Accept or answer another body format | A parser or renderer | [Parsers and renderers](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/codecs.md) |
| Translate a library's exception | `app.error_handler(Kind)` | [Errors](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/errors.md) |
| Own a resource per worker | A module with `ctx.provide` and `ctx.get`, or a `DatabaseModule` subclass | [Modules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/modules.md) |
| Enforce a team convention | Subclass `hinoki.rules.Rule` | [Rules](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/rules.md#your-own-rules) |
| Add typed configuration | `settings.AppSettings` | [Settings](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/settings.md) |
| Ship routes in a package | Anything a `routes` list accepts: a function, a `RouteGroup`, an `API` class, a `Mount`, or an object with an `api()` method | [Register routes](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/routes.md) |
| Expose actions to an agent | `expose_as_mcp` with an allowlist | [Expose actions over MCP](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/app-mcp.md) |
| Add metrics, tracing or other cross-cutting behaviour | Wrap the ASGI application | [Serving](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#metrics-and-tracing) |
| Run where only WSGI is available | `WSGIAdapter` | [Serving](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/serving.md#wsgi) |

Cross-cutting behaviour around an action belongs in a [middleware](https://hinoki.caspel.dev/dev/middleware.md), which behaves the same on Kiso and Granian. An ASGI wrapper still works on Granian and sees the request before and after Hinoki. To run another web application next to Hinoki, put it behind the same reverse proxy or dispatch by path in your own ASGI code.
